#3221. When Electric Cars Were for Women

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Early carmakers decided women wanted cars that were quiet, clean, and easy to start

Allison Marsh is a professor at the University of South Carolina and the codirector of the Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society.

When automobiles were still a novelty, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion.

At the turn of the last century, the automobile industry was still new and evolving rapidly. In 1898, there were about 50 carmakers in the United States. A decade later, that number had increased fivefold. In 1901, the companies produced 7,000 vehicles. By 1910, production had reached 181,000.

For several decades, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion, and nobody was sure which technology would come out on top. Steam had the legacy of locomotive technology behind it but came with a risk of fire. Steam-powered vehicles could also become exceedingly hot, depending on the placement of the boiler and the steam piping. Both gasoline and electric cars faced logistical challenges: How far could you travel without refueling or charging? You could always throw an extra can of gasoline in the back of the car, but charging a battery involved more planning. The infrastructure for long-distance travel was not yet in place.

Before the invention of the electric starter in 1911, gasoline-powered engines had to be started with a hand crank; once running, they were loud and emitted noxious fumes. Fully electric vehicles, by contrast, were easy to start; you just turned on the main battery switch, often with a key, and there was no foul exhaust to deal with.

Electric carmakers looking for a way to differentiate their products decided that these attributes made their vehicles perfect for women. (Electric cars were also marketed to doctors so that they could make house calls in the middle of the night without waking the neighbors.) General Electric, which made car chargers based on mercury-arc rectifiers, was so captivated by the idea of women driving electric cars that the company created a series of advertisements featuring stylishly dressed women plugging in their cars and posing with their charging stations.

In ads for its electric car chargers, General Electric featured women using the equipment.miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

A young woman named Fannie Goodnow was an early EV adopter. She owned a 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton, an open two-seater that really did look like a horseless carriage, and she used a GE mercury-arc rectifier to charge it.

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt invented the mercury vapor lamp, which became the basis for the mercury-arc rectifier used in car-charging systems. Bettmann/Getty Images

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt is generally credited with the invention of the mercury-arc rectifier. During the first decade of the 20th century, Hewitt received several U.S. patents for electric lamps and other apparatus for transmitting and using electric currents. U.S. patents 968,896 and 1,163,706, granted to Percy H. Thomas, advanced Hewitt’s designs. Thomas was chief electrician for the Cooper Hewitt Electric Co., which Hewitt had cofounded with George Westinghouse to manufacture and sell his lamps.

The mercury-arc rectifier functioned as a diode. In a car charger like the one Fannie Goodnow used, it converted alternating current from the power grid into direct current needed to charge the car’s battery. A small amount of liquid mercury contained in a glass tube would vaporize and glow as electricity passed through it. Coupled with the carbon anodes, the vapor allowed current to flow in only one direction. This unit took about 12 hours to charge a drained battery.

I couldn’t find any records as to why Fannie Goodnow opted for an electric car. But as a well-to-do woman living in the Boston area, she had more than a half dozen automobile producers to choose from. The one she chose was S.R. Bailey & Co. of Amesbury, Mass.

This early electric car charger used a mercury-arc rectifier to convert AC to DC.Heritage Museums & Gardens

According to Galen Handy, who maintains the Early Electric Vehicles website, Samuel Robinson Bailey started in the carriage and sleigh business as a teenager, winning a best-in-show prize at a carriage exhibition in Portland, Maine, in 1855. Bailey developed a reputation as an inventor and designed processes to streamline the manufacture of his vehicles. He went into business for himself in 1882. Just over a decade later, one of Bailey’s carriages won a gold medal at the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago.

Bailey’s son Edwin attended the exposition, where he likely would have seen a vision of the future: the Morrison electric wagon. This six-passenger, battery-powered vehicle ferried visitors and VIPs around the fairgrounds. It wasn’t long before automobiles began eating into the carriage business. In December 1906, with the carriage industry collapsing, S.R. Bailey & Co. announced it was getting into electric vehicles.

Bailey’s first model, the Victoria Phaeton, used an Edison alkaline battery. Thomas Edison had been working on a lighter, more reliable, and more powerful battery for the auto industry since the 1890s, and announced the achievement with great fanfare in 1903. Unfortunately for Bailey and other carmakers who deployed it, the battery leaked and wouldn’t hold a charge. Edison was forced to go back to the drawing board. By 1910, he had a better battery in production, but by then his friend Henry Ford had introduced the Model T, setting the stage for the internal combustion engine to take over the market.

While Edison toiled to improve his tech, Bailey pivoted to a battery from the Gould Storage Battery Co. of Depew, N.Y. Gould also supplied batteries for railroads, utilities, subways, elevators, and farms. Goodnow’s Victoria Phaeton used a 30-cell lead-acid battery housed in a wooden box that was suspended under the chassis. The standard battery had a range of 64 to 80 kilometers; a larger battery with 50 percent more capacity was available for an upcharge. With the standard battery, the Victoria Phaeton cost US $2,000 (about $73,000 today, or about the list price of an upscale EV like the Audi Q8 or BMW i5).

Fannie Goodnow’s electric car charger now resides at the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. But her 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton has been lost to history. Shown here is a 1911 version of that model.Sarah Thornington/Heritage Museums & Gardens

Goodnow installed a mercury-arc rectifier charging station in the barn adjacent to her parents’ summer home in Hull, Mass. Bill Lillie of Vintage Electric Cars notes that the charging plug was of an unusual design. This is, of course, one of the banes of any early adopter: nonstandardized plugs and cables. The Electric Vehicle Association of America, which formed in 1910, tried to put forward a standard so that electric vehicles could be charged at any charging station. (Modern EV owners can no doubt relate.) But savvy electric car owners knew to carry spare plug adapters and cables when traveling.

When Edison’s improved battery was finally available, Bailey began using it in the Victoria Phaeton and then went on a publicity blitz. In September 1910, the carmaker sponsored a round-trip tour from New York to Boston, with a side trip up New Hampshire’s Mount Washington, totaling about 1,600 km. Sadly, the “This Car Climbed Mt. Washington” bumper sticker hadn’t yet become popular.

Thomas Edison supplied the batteries for an electric car made by S.R. Bailey & Co., which then went on a publicity road trip from New York to Boston. miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

Although Thomas Edison posed for a photo with the new Bailey Victoria Phaeton that featured his new battery, he himself chose a Detroit Electric Victoria for his own use. (Edison was known to be a terrible driver, so someone else likely chauffeured him around.)

Unable to compete against the rising tide of Model Ts, S.R. Bailey sold its factory in 1915, having produced about 500 to 600 electric vehicles.

Although the vehicle Fannie Goodnow chose turned out to be just a blip in automotive history, I like to imagine her driving about town in a beautiful car that embodied all the quirks of early adoption. I hope her friends didn’t make fun of her for investing in electric just before internal combustion took off. I hope she didn’t get stranded without the proper charging cable. I do not know what happened to her or her Victoria Phaeton, but her charging station remained in situ until 2022, when it was donated to the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. Now it stands ready to tell stories of technological change and adoption that continue to resonate today.

Part of a continuing series looking at historical artifacts that embrace the boundless potential of technology.

An abridged version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue.

References For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.

Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

Allison Marsh is a professor in Women and Gender Studies at the University of South Carolina and codirector of the university’s Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society. She combines her interests in engineering, history, and museum objects to write the Past Forward column, which tells the story of technology through historical artifacts. Marsh is currently working on a book on the history of women in electrical engineering.

#3220. Omar Hamdi says AI will test whether PR firms can really scale

Pathos chief Omar Hamdi argues that AI should make PR more efficient, measurable and useful to growth companies, rather than replace human judgement.

Omar Hamdi, founder and CEO of Pathos Communications, right, on a panel at Press Gazette’s Media Strategy Network USA in New York in March 2026.

City A.M. reported on 6 October that the share of UK firms spending on public relations and management consultants fell to 4.2% in September, even as overall business spending rose 3.1% year on year and spending on AI services increased rapidly.

For Omar Hamdi, chief executive of London-listed Pathos Communications plc, those figures are less a death notice for PR than a sharper test of its economics.

The question suggested by those figures is not only whether companies will cut agency budgets as AI tools spread. It is whether agencies can use technology to deliver more useful work, more consistently, at a price and margin that make sense.

Hamdi’s answer, by his account, is to build a PR company where software takes on more of the preparation, targeting and business development, while people still handle the relationships and judgement that matter when a company is trying to be understood.

Pathos’s recent numbers give that argument a public company frame. Investegate published Pathos’s results for the six months ended 30 June 2026 on 9 September, reporting 14% revenue growth, 36% adjusted EBITDA growth, an 80% rise in customer cash receipts and reoccurring customers accounting for 36% of revenue, compared with 16% a year earlier.

The same announcement said Pressella, its AI virtual publicist, and PathosMind remained on track for general availability in the first half of 2027.

Proactive Investors reported on the same day that Pathos’s first-half adjusted EBITDA rose as higher revenue, improved operating leverage and lower bad debt charges fed through to profitability. That is the operational point Hamdi keeps returning to. He says the firm’s technology is helping with lead generation, lead nurturing and onboarding, while repeat and reoccurring customer relationships are becoming a larger part of the business.

The practical change, as Hamdi describes it, starts before a prospect has spoken to anyone at Pathos. The technology analyses news, shares potential hooks and article ideas, and prepares materials for the human conversation that follows. By the time a meeting takes place, he says the team can have article drafts, business cases and current news hooks ready.

In delivery, he says Pathos is using algorithmic matching between client stories and publishers to improve the chances that content succeeds.

That matters because the addressable market Hamdi is thinking about is not a small pool of blue-chip communications departments. He points to a global market of 400 million SMEs.

In his telling, the technology is intended to make a serious PR experience available to companies that may not have had the time, budget or confidence to hire a conventional agency.

Prospects sometimes respond to outreach, he says, as if Pathos is already doing part of the publicist’s job. One reaction he recalls is: “I feel like you’re already my PR firm.”

The aim is not simply more automated content. Hamdi’s emphasis is on preparation that changes the quality of the first human interaction. He says clients felt they were getting the same experience they would receive if a highly qualified PR person with decades of experience had spent a day working with them, and were getting that experience “before they’d even met with us for the first time.”

There is also an internal productivity argument. Hamdi says the technology affects how the team works, not only how prospects are contacted.

“It just makes their job much more efficient, much more lubricated, the velocity of the business has improved,” he says. The efficiency of Pathos’s business development, he adds, is higher than it has ever been.

For business readers, the more interesting claim is not that AI can write faster. It is that what was originally a services company may be able to grow by becoming a technology company with a service layer. Hamdi says Pathos is adding larger and stronger publishers to its platform, which can support better margins with those publishers. “We’re getting more efficient as we scale,” he says.

Yahoo Finance reported on 15 October that Hamdi discussed rising repeat and reoccurring revenue, Pathos’s aim of building a sustainable, profitable listed business, and the planned first half 2027 launch of its AI-powered virtual publicist.

The broader bet is still to be tested as Pressella and PathosMind move toward wider availability. But the direction is clear enough. In Hamdi’s view, PR’s future belongs less to firms selling hours and more to operators that can use technology to scale judgement, preparation and relevance, without stripping out the human work that gives PR its value.

#3219. iPhone Duo durability tested on unfolding livestream, now over 260,000 folds

CNET built a ‘Fold-a-Phone’ machine that’s been constantly folding and unfolding iPhone Duo for over a week to test durability, while livestreaming daily. Here’s how it’s going.

How durable is the iPhone Duo’s hinge and folding display? Several early reviews tried to answer that question, including in some cases by building machines that constantly folded and unfolded the device.

But perhaps the best test yet is still ongoing.

CNET built a custom ‘Fold-a-Phone’ machine that has been folding and unfolding the iPhone Duo 24 hours per day, 7 days a week for over a week now.

It’s livestreaming the process here on YouTube every weekday from 1-5 p.m. ET.

When the livestream wrapped up yesterday, iPhone Duo had hit just over 260,000 folds.

So far, the hinge and crease seem to be holding up extremely well. But CNET says it will continue testing daily until at least November 20 to see if anything might change over time.

What do you think of the iPhone Duo folding test results so far? Let us know in the comments.

#3217. Guarding the Gates of Knowledge

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

AI can fake a plausible paper at the push of a button. Can detection tools and peer review keep up?

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

A recent scroll through social media got me thinking about trust. About half my feed was filled with AI slop that astute users would call out as being machine-generated, often to the embarrassment of the rube who unknowingly spread it and sometimes to the delight of the poster who shared it deliberately because they found it amusing or useful for sowing confusion.

Remember the good old days of GPT-3 when we could ask the chatbot anything and it would almost instantly and very confidently spit back a plausible but false answer? That’s when the word “hallucination” as applied to AI answers entered the lexicon. Six years and several versions of a few different chatbots later, I still can’t trust the answers I get, even though Claude or Gemini often do useful work for me. That’s the thing about current AI: Trust but verify. And verify you must.

Apply that maxim at scale to maintain the integrity of the scientific record and you get an idea of the challenge facing publishers of peer-reviewed scholarship. In “I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper,” freelance writer and doctor of applied mathematics Benjamin Skuse tells the story of the human gatekeepers trying to beat back the rising tide of AI slop by attempting to get his own AI-generated papers past IEEE’s defenses.

“He basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper.’ And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it.” —Eliza Strickland

As features and AI beat editor Eliza Strickland told me, Skuse was surprised at just how effortless it was to generate a paper that was more or less plausible and more or less science. For one of his experiments, “he basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper,’” she said. “And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it. He just launched it into the maw of the publishing engine.”

Skuse discovered that the combination of IEEE’s human-review processes and research-integrity checker programs are currently keeping pace in what amounts to a cat-and-mouse game against people using free tools. But the more advanced LLMs are no longer making the same dumb mistakes the free versions do. That leaves publishers locked in an arms race between increasingly plausible slop and the systems aimed at detecting it.

Scholarly publishers aren’t the only ones trying to hold the line against slop. So is that global depository of human-generated knowledge, Wikipedia. For this month’s Five Questions, Strickland interviewed Ellia Lebleu, a founding member of WikiProject AI Cleanup, a volunteer effort to detect and delete AI-generated material from the platform. Lebleu’s team is confronting the same problem as commercial publishers, but with fewer people and fewer tools.

“Wikipedia is known as a repository of human-generated information, and they want to hold on to that,” says Strickland. “Who knows how long they’ll be able to do that.”

If we can’t collectively assume that the scientific record is trustworthy or that basic facts about the world are accurate, then our understanding of what is real unspools into uncertainty. Perhaps that delights quantum scientists and the grifters who thrive in an information environment where there is no shared reality. But that uncertainty ultimately undermines trust in the institutions that exist to curate the corpus of human knowledge and to promote the advancement of science and technology for the benefit of humanity.

Or maybe in a world where AI is doing the science and writing the papers, it won’t matter whether or not humans trust the outputs. As Strickland put it, “Doesn’t it just feel crazy that we’ll have AI writing for other AIs at some point? We’ll just get left out of the loop.”

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

#3216. iOS 27.3 gives Apple One’s high-end tier a compelling upgrade

iOS 27.3 is coming next month and is packed with new features, including some that make Apple One Premier more compelling than ever.

Apple One launched in 2019 with Individual, Family, and Premier plans. And in the seven years since, the service bundle has stayed remarkably consistent.

Every plan has always included Apple Music, Apple TV, Apple Arcade, and iCloud+. And the high-end Premier option adds Apple News+ and Fitness+ alongside more iCloud storage.

Apple News+ has gotten a lot better over the years. Following the New York Times playbook, Apple has added daily puzzle games, food-focused content like recipes, and audio stories, all while continuing to improve the basic news experience.

Apple Fitness+ keeps improving too, but there’s an upgrade in iOS 27.3 that makes it far more compelling in my view: Gym Strength.

Built-in video demonstrations accompany your personalized plan, making strength training accessible even for newcomers. And you can track your progress in the app, with key Apple Watch integration too.

I’ve used Fitness+ plenty and enjoyed it, but a comprehensive strength plan like this was a big gap in the service previously. With iOS 27.3 though, Fitness+ takes a big leap forward and makes Apple One Premier more compelling than ever.

Also relevant: with the new HomeView product and other Apple Home accessories almost here, Apple One Premier’s support for Apple Intelligence video summaries and clips with HomeKit Secure Video becomes more valuable. All of this together amounts to a stronger-than-ever Premier plan.

Apple One starts at $21.95/month and includes services like Apple TV, Apple Music, iCloud+, and more.

#3215. Meta adds real-time voice chat and animated avatars to its Muse app

Meta adds real-time voice chat and animated avatars to its Muse app

Meta has added live voice conversations to Muse, its personal AI agent, so users can talk to it instead of typing. The update also gives Muse an animated avatar that reacts as the conversation goes on.

The feature is available now in the Muse app on phones, the web and Mac, but only in the US for the moment. Users start a call by tapping the phone icon in the top-right corner of the app.

During a call, users can interrupt Muse at any point, and it answers straight away. Muse can also keep working on tasks in the background while the conversation continues, for example, while the user is out on a walk.

Alongside the voice, the avatar shows facial expressions and gestures that match the tone of the conversation. It also reacts while the user is still speaking.

Users can choose how much of it they see. They can talk with voice only, keep the avatar next to the conversation, or open it full screen. There are also hundreds of voices with different personalities, and users can switch between them at any time.

At Connect, Meta also said users would be able to shape a voice by describing it, for example by asking for a different speed or accent.

Meta suggests using the feature to brainstorm ideas, plan a trip or practise for a job interview or a presentation.

The avatars run on Muse Realtime Avatar, a model built by Meta Superintelligence Labs, the company’s main AI unit. Meta first showed the technology at its Connect conference in September.

In tests run by Meta’s own raters, people preferred its avatars to those of rivals Runway and HeyGen, the company said. However, Meta has also said that not all of its demonstrations reflect the avatars available in the app.

Muse itself launched in September as Meta’s answer to AI agents such as ChatGPT. It runs on the Muse Spark family of models, which Meta introduced in April, and it can already shop with retailers, send emails, and control apps on a Mac.

The launch is part of Meta’s heavy spending on AI, which includes its Hyperion data centre in Louisiana.

Voice conversations will come next to Meta’s AI glasses and to Muse Charm, a small clip-on device the company showed at Connect. Meta has not yet given a date for either.

#3214. IEEE Computer Society Chapter Offers Webinars With Industry Experts

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Attendees in Region 4 learn about AI, cybersecurity, and more

Siva Rama Krishna Varma Bayyavarapu is an IEEE senior member and secretary of the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter.

To help engineers keep up with emerging technologies such as AI, cloud computing, and sustainable infrastructure, and learn how they can be applied in practice, the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter recently launched its Tech Talk Series.

The live webinar series connects IEEE members, undergrad and graduate students, and engineering professionals from IEEE Region 4 with industry practitioners. The monthly sessions have covered AI governance and security, agentic systems, and related topics. The sessions featured speakers from Apple, software company Tavant, and cybersecurity concern Zscaler.

Upcoming sessions and registration details are available on the IEEE Region 4 virtual events calendar.

Rather than presenting on emerging technologies only at a conceptual level, speakers discussed the design decisions behind specific tools and systems, how the systems are structured, and implementation challenges. They also shared lessons learned from using the tools in their daily work.

Sessions also include technical walkthroughs and practical examples.

The live format allows attendees to discuss and compare their approaches when evaluating and implementing new technologies with those used by other organizations.

The organizers chose to make the series virtual so that chapter members and other attendees could participate in technical discussions with engineers from major technology companies and eliminate the need to travel.

For young professionals, the sessions connect what they’ve learned in a classroom with the realities of the workplace.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Attendees learn how practitioners approach projects such as system architecture, reliability, security, governance, and product delivery. For experienced professionals, the talks offer a forum to examine new ways of designing, securing, and operating software systems, and compare technical approaches. They can ask questions relevant to systems being evaluated or deployed within their organization.

The most recent webinar, Feeding and Fencing AI Agents: Engineering Governed Agentic Systems on Real-Time Data, featured Gajendra Babu Thokala, a senior engineering leader at Apple in Seattle.

The IEEE senior member explained how teams can move beyond adding isolated AI features to applications and instead build governed AI-agent systems that use real-time business data to complete multistep business workflows.

Another recent session, Building AI Native Products: A Playbook for Agentic Systems, explored how products built around AI agents differ from traditional software. It also covered how agentic systems can help users complete multistep tasks and workflows. IEEE Senior Member Sandeep Shivam, a product and technology leader at Tavant in Dallas, led the webinar.

Those two sessions illustrate the series’ purpose: helping participants understand what a technology can do and what is required to use it responsibly.

Future sessions are being planned on areas including enterprise AI, software reliability, and responsible AI usage. In addition to speakers from technology companies, the chapter also plans to invite speakers from startups, universities, and research organizations.

Upcoming sessions are expected to cover cloud platforms, enterprise integrations, and the responsible development of AI systems.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Undergraduate and graduate students are invited to participate to gain exposure to technical decision-making and challenges encountered in professional engineering environments.

Siva Rama Krishna Varma Bayyavarapu is an IEEE senior member and the secretary of the IEEE Computer Society Central Indiana Chapter. He is also the chair of the IEEE Central Indiana Student Activities Committee.

#3212. tvOS 27.2 adds new Apple TV 4K setting that’s an instant favorite

tvOS 27.2 launched last week as the latest software update for Apple TV 4K, and it includes a new setting I’m a big fan of: Shuffle for screen savers.

Screen savers have been one of the best Apple TV features since tvOS first launched in 2015. Largely that’s due to the gorgeous aerials captured around the world (and even from space).

Aerials are still my favorite type of Apple TV screen saver, but tvOS has steadily added other categories worth checking out too.

Currently inside Settings ⇾ Screen Saver you’ll find four categories:

The second and third options tap into your Apple Photos library and introduce the joy of seeing your favorite memories pop up on the big screen. Snoopy screen savers feature the beloved Peanuts character in a variety of entertaining scenes.

All of these screen saver options are great. But until tvOS 27.2, you had to select just one category and that’s all you’d ever see.

Now with tvOS 27.2, Apple has introduced a ‘Shuffle’ option that randomly cycles through screen savers from across all four categories.

It’s a welcome new setting, long overdue but I’ve been enjoying it a lot. The ability to be surprised by more different screen savers may sound like a small thing, but it’s a meaningful improvement to the Apple TV 4K experience.

Have you tried the new Shuffle setting for screen savers in tvOS 27.2? Let us know in the comments.

#3211. Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery

Advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated. The techniques reveal fine details in the sun’s corona, which is white in this image. The tiny pink shapes seen along portions of the edge of the blacked-out solar disk are prominences, which are extensions of relatively cool plasma that can jut out hundreds of thousands of kilometers into space.

The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza, it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing.

A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse.

In the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out.

“It will.” Miloslav Druckmüller glances calmly at his group of doctoral candidates, now making final checks of the equipment in preparation for totality. Here in Spain, on this 12th day of August, Druckmüller is getting ready for his 19th solar eclipse. He knows from long experience that weather can turn quickly when the moon’s shadow suddenly pushes the temperature down. Plus, there’s no sense in riling up the grad students any more than they already are.

Miloslav Druckmüller led the design and construction of a unique optical instrument that incorporates eight astrocameras. Each is equipped with a spectral filter for sensing and recording specific emission spectra from the solar corona. Each of those spectra, in turn, is associated with a particular ionic species of iron atoms. Because the temperature needed to ionize iron varies depending on the ionic species, analyzing the locations and relative abundance of these ionic species offers valuable insights into the distribution of heat in the corona.Václav Široký

During totality, the moon blocks the overwhelming glare of the solar disk, revealing delicate structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona. Using custom-built telescope systems and image-processing techniques that Druckmüller has spent decades developing, the researchers aim to gain insights into the processes in this enigmatic region that is otherwise hard to study. In addition to imaging the visible coronal light, the team will try to track the dispersal of superhot ions of iron into interplanetary space, which could give rare insights into the pattern of heat emanating from the corona.

And they’ll have 107 seconds to do all that.

Druckmüller is a professor of mathematics and image processing at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic and a leading figure in the Solar Wind Sherpas, an international team that studies the sun’s corona during total eclipses. In the solar eclipse world, he is nothing short of a legend, albeit a reluctant one.

An image from Miloslav Druckmüller’s first solar-eclipse expedition, to Hungary, vividly shows Baily’s Beads. These elongated white lights along a piece of the left edge of the blacked-out solar disk are caused by beams of sunlight shining through gaps in the irregular lunar surface during the eclipse. The pink shapes are solar prominences, which are jets of plasma extending out into space and held in place by the sun’s intense magnetic field.

He photographed his first solar eclipse in 1999, in what he thought would be a one-off lark. During that eclipse, the moon’s deep shadow missed Druckmüller’s native Czechia by just a few tens of kilometers, so he chased it to Hungary with a 30-year-old Soviet MTO 1,000-millimeter lens. All he remembers from that day is the rush of adrenaline he felt while trying to find the sun in the sky with the lens’s minuscule field of view and keep it in focus for the two minutes of the eclipse.

He insists that he has never enjoyed any of the eclipses he has photographed. “In fact, I have never properly seen any of those eclipses. You are just watching the screens, making sure that it’s all doing what it’s supposed to do. There are so many things that can go wrong and you can’t redo it.”

A composite sequence of photographs shows the 12 August 2026 solar eclipse as seen from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain.

Despite Druckmüller’s outward tranquility on this Spanish hillside, the stakes are high. Just 45 minutes ago, his group heard from their colleagues in Iceland, where viewing conditions had promised to be better than in Spain. But a vast low-pressure system had clouded the entire sky, leaving all three Iceland teams without a view.

On the Pico Trigaza mountain in Spain, two postgraduate researchers used a laser to get a rough, initial alignment for the tracking mount of an optical instrument. The alignment was necessary to precisely compensate for the Earth’s motion.

The corona has been a mystery for centuries. Though dimmer—by a factor of a million—than the sun’s visible surface, the corona is nevertheless extremely hot: about a million degrees Celsius compared to 5,500 degrees on the surface. Because the sun’s nuclear fusion engine churns at the star’s heart, it might seem that temperatures should fall farther from the core.

To observe the faint corona in visible light, researchers must block the sun’s ferocious glare. Specialized telescopes called coronagraphs do this with an opaque disk called an occulter. But because light bends around the occulter’s edges in an effect called diffraction, it must block an area much larger than that of the solar disk to prevent light from spilling over and ruining the images. But doing so means obstructing the inner part of the corona, which harbors the most important processes that underpin the puzzling phenomena of the sun’s upper atmosphere.

That’s why total eclipses matter so much to solar physicists. By sheer chance, the moon is exactly the right size and at just the right distance to completely cover the sun during a total solar eclipse. Because the moon is so far away from Earth, the view is not marred by diffraction, and the corona reveals itself nearly all the way down to the sun’s surface.

As astrocameras recorded spectral data about the sun’s corona, a laptop computer [on table, at left] displayed the phase of the eclipse.

Space probes can image the solar surface in other wavelengths, but those views have limitations, too. Spacecraft such as NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory do see the innermost parts of the corona in extreme ultraviolet light, explains Shadia Habbal, a solar physicist at the University of Hawaii and leader of the Solar Wind Sherpas project. “But it cuts off very quickly, so you don’t see its extension into space as well as we can see it in the visible emission lines” during an eclipse. “That’s the biggest advantage,” she says, of solar eclipse photography.

The European Proba-3 mission, launched in 2024, simulates total solar eclipses by flying two spacecraft in a formation 150 meters apart with one acting as an occulter and the other as the telescope. The instruments aboard that satellite, however, have limitations compared to the equipment used by the Solar Wind Sherpas team.

When Druckmüller developed the film from his 1999 eclipse expedition, the photographs didn’t do justice to the event’s eerie beauty. He spent countless evenings applying his expertise in numerical image processing in an attempt to re-create in his photographs the sights he witnessed in that Hungarian corn field.

It took two years, but eventually he succeeded. Where before there were dull views of the blackened lunar disk surrounded by the blunt wisps of the corona, Druckmüller revealed the subtlest details of the magnetic field lines stretching from the sun far into space. As his photographs circulated among solar physicists, invitations to eclipse expeditions began to arrive.

Solar researchers Miloslav Druckmüller and Shadia Habbal have been collaborating for two decades and 15 eclipses.

Habbal learned about the images from a Ph.D. student who had seen them at a conference presentation that didn’t credit Druckmüller. When Habbal’s team later published the images in a paper, they misattributed them to another researcher. Druckmüller found out through an astrophysicist friend. “I wrote her a rather disappointed email and she responded within 10 minutes,” Druckmüller recalls. “She really didn’t have a clue.”

The error was corrected, and within weeks, Habbal and Druckmüller began a collaboration that grew into a friendship. “Milos’s processing brings out details that nobody has seen before, and they tell you a lot about very tiny features in the corona that you don’t see otherwise,” says Habbal.

Capturing the corona’s delicate structures means finding a way to show its brightest and faintest features in the same image. “During the solar eclipse, the contrast between the darkest and brightest parts of the corona is enormous, possibly one to a million,” Druckmüller explains. “But a computer monitor only allows you to display a contrast ratio of one to about 800.” (Some modern monitors, particularly OLED ones, can deliver higher contrast ratios.)

The human eye can adjust to this enormous range of brightness, allowing an observer to see both the bright corona and the faint stars and planets that briefly emerge in the darkened sky. To bring those details together in a photograph, Druckmüller uses custom image-processing algorithms to combine exposures that capture different parts of that range.

Researchers Martin Šebek and Peter Urgoš make fine adjustments to the focus and alignment of the astrocameras on a key optical instrument before the 12 August solar eclipse.

To create a single image, Druckmüller’s teams need to take 200 individual frames during the eclipse at exposure times ranging from 0.001 second to two seconds. The data must then be calibrated against a vast number of reference images to filter out noise and imperfections. Flat fields, which depict a uniform light background, help correct for defects caused by telescope optics, dust spots, and variations in pixel sensitivity. Dark frames, taken with light blocked from the sensor, help correct for artifacts created by the camera’s image sensor itself. “It takes the computer more than two days to process one image,” Druckmüller says. Including the calibration data, a single finished image requires about 3,000 input frames.

Since 2008, teams directed by Habbal and Druckmüller have traveled to every total solar eclipse, spreading out across multiple locations to hedge against bad weather. About half of the teams return with usable data. For the others, it’s just a short and stressful voyage. For the 12 August eclipse, three groups deployed to Iceland and two to Spain.

The teams seek sites close to the center of the band of totality, where the moon blocks the sun for longest. In Spain, the 12 August band of totality cut across the north of the country; the center line of the shadow passed within 11 kilometers of Pico Trigaza, promising Druckmüller and his colleagues a precious 107 seconds of totality.

But duration is only part of the calculation. Totality on Pico Trigaza will commence 51 minutes before sunset, with the sun just 8 degrees above the horizon. That low, the rays must pass through a much thicker layer of the atmosphere than when the sun is higher in the sky, increasing the light distortion that complicates photography. At the researchers’ camp on Pico Trigaza, 1,600 meters above sea level, the thinner air should help a bit.

An abandoned hut on the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain was spruced up so that it could serve as a home base for the research team recording the 12 August solar eclipse.

“Iceland would have been a much better place for us than Spain because the sun was higher up, some 25 degrees above the horizon,” Druckmüller says wistfully. But Iceland’s notoriously unpredictable weather made Spain an essential backup.

If you pack a van with thousands of dollars’ worth of cameras and optical gear and then set out on a 2,351-kilometer journey, you shouldn’t be surprised if you finish the trip with a few striking photographs [top]. The sleeping arrangements for the grad students at the Pico Trigaza hut [bottom] were spartan, but the views were first-rate.Top: Martin Šebek; Bottom: Václav Široký

On the mountain, locals have spruced up a rustic, long-unused hut for the researchers, running power cables from a nearby telecommunication outpost and bringing in a water tank. Five Ph.D. students drove more than 2,000 kilometers from Brno and have spent nearly a week preparing the equipment. Druckmüller and his wife joined them two days before the eclipse. They cook on a small propane grill and sleep in sleeping bags on yoga mats. “We have plenty of space here to set up our telescopes, beautiful views, and a roof over our heads,” Druckmüller says with a grin. “It’s perfect.”

But even the best equipment and a carefully chosen site count for nothing if the clouds roll in. “So much work goes into the preparations and then, if you end up with nothing, you just feel terrible sadness,” says Jana Hoderová, an assistant professor of mathematics at Brno University of Technology and one of Druckmüller’s key collaborators.

As the moon continues to slide in front of the solar disk, the pesky cumulus cloud that kept everybody on edge begins to dissolve. It’s 10 minutes to totality. The relief is palpable.

The countdown on the computers that control the cameras has begun. The screens are now showing only a tiny orange sliver, and the evening is becoming perceptibly less bright.

Twenty astrophotography cameras, most of them drawing power from a car battery that was also buffering the cameras from any grid instabilities, are pointed at the sun. Alongside equipment capturing the corona’s visible light, the team has built an assembly of eight cameras to detect light emitted by various iron ions that arise in the corona.

Among the optical gear assembled at Pico Trigaza to capture the 12 August solar eclipse was a unique instrument designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona [at left]. Václav Široký

Those instruments looking for iron ions have been put together with resourcefulness and thrift. A colleague of Druckmüller’s laser-cut the aluminum plates holding the carefully aligned lenses in exchange “for two bottles of whisky.” The brackets and attachments were 3D-printed at Brno University of Technology. The lenses, produced for the defunct camera maker Contax, were bought at steep discounts on eBay. By far the most expensive elements are interference filters that isolate the wavelengths emitted by the iron ions.

Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still.

“That’s something nobody else in the world can do,” Druckmüller says with visible satisfaction. The unique technology, codeveloped with Habbal’s Hawaii team, has already enabled researchers to map the distribution of temperatures across the entire corona and to discover previously unseen structures, dubbed “smoke rings,” in the coronal plasma. The photographs also revealed the boundary region where the solar plasma becomes so thin that its ions stop colliding.

The optical assembly designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona is outfitted with astrocameras, each of which captures spectra from a different ionic species. To do that, each astrocamera is equipped with a spectral filter whose bandwidth is so narrow—one nanometer—that the filter appears as a mirror.Martin Fornůsek

“Iron is the most abundant of the heavy elements that we see in the solar corona,” says Habbal. “And because the corona is so hot, the iron atoms lose electrons and get ionized. The larger the loss, the higher the temperature.”

For example, a temperature of around 1.6 million °C is necessary to produce an iron ion that has lost 12 electrons. But only 1.4 million °C is needed to strip an iron atom of 11 electrons. Once it’s in a particular electrical state, the ion retains its specific ionization, even as it travels outward with the solar wind. Each of those ions, whether +11 or +12, emits a different wavelength of light, allowing the researchers to map not just temperatures within the corona, but also how those iron ions spread into interplanetary space and distribute heat. Habbal and her colleagues had long been trying to image those iron ions during solar eclipses. But it wasn’t until Druckmüller entered the picture that they were able to develop the gear and the mathematical techniques to do it.

With just a minute to go to totality, the researchers begin removing protective filters from the lenses. It’s 50 minutes to sunset, and the waning sun has just begun to light up the clouds above the horizon with the first tinge of orange. Then, suddenly, the evening begins a rapid and premature descent into darkness. Along the edge of the fantastically thin solar crescent, the brilliant orange points known as Baily’s Beads flash and disappear—the last fragments of photospheric light visible through deep lunar valleys. As totality begins, observers remove their glasses. The hot air cools. The graduate students remain quietly and intently focused on their gear.

Druckmüller looks up from his camera toward the darkened plains. Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still. The sky is ablaze with fiery colors all along the horizon where the deep lunar shadow drops off. Venus burns brilliantly in the southwest, a sharp white pinpoint in the darkened sky. The sound of camera shutters suddenly fills the air. Then, as quickly as it fell, the darkness begins to recede, bid farewell with another handful of golden Baily’s Beads.

The crowd erupts in cheers. The Ph.D. students throw themselves at each other and hug like they mean it.

“The students did most of the work this time, so I actually allowed myself to really look at it,” Druckmüller says. “It was beautiful. Pico Trigaza may not have been the best for science photography, but from the aesthetic point of view, it was extraordinary.”

The 2026 solar-eclipse team at Pico Trigaza in Spain included [from left] Magdalena Šrotířová, Peter Urgoš, Martin Fornůsek, Miloslav Druckmüller, Václav Široký, and Martin Šebek.Václav Široký

But for Druckmüller, this is just the beginning. While other eclipse chasers will race to release their images, he will take his time. He expects to publish the first visible-light images of the corona in about two weeks. Processing the iron-ion images, and uncovering whatever insights they may hold, will take months—maybe even a whole year.

“Probably until the next eclipse in 2027” in North Africa, Druckmüller says.

Who knows? Maybe he’ll even enjoy that one, too.

Tereza Pultarova is a London-based journalist specializing in aerospace and defense technologies. She is a native of the Czech Republic.

Those are some pretty impressive photos! It also seems like the iron ion filtering is pretty unique. I love seeing cases where people build something they want to see in the world with minimal outside support. Seems like it would be a solid return on more public money to seek out and support scrappy projects like this one.

#3210. Instagram launches free Edits video editor for Mac with 4K exports

Instagram announced on Thursday that it is bringing Edits, its short-form video editing app, to desktop on Mac.The app is free to download, but it works only on Macs with Apple Silicon chips, from the M1 onwards, and users need an Instagram account to sign in.

Instagram first launched Edits on phones in April 2025 as a rival to CapCut, the editing app owned by TikTok’s parent company, ByteDance. More than 50 million creators now use the mobile version, the company told Gulf News.

The Mac app looks similar to the mobile one, but it gives editors more room and more tools for complex projects.

These include a timeline with several tracks, keyframes for smooth transitions, audio waveforms, and colour wheels and curves for adjusting the look of a clip.

Users can also import their own fonts and colour presets, known as LUTs, and set their own keyboard shortcuts.

In addition, the app comes with Instagram’s library of licensed, royalty-free music, hundreds of effects and unlimited automatic captions.

Once a video is finished, creators can post it straight to Instagram from the Mac, with tags and location, instead of moving the file to their phone first. Alternatively, they can export it in vertical or horizontal formats, in up to 4K and without a watermark.

The desktop app also works with AI agents. By switching on the Model Context Protocol, a standard that lets AI assistants use other software, creators can ask an agent to handle parts of the editing for them.

Matthew Simari, who leads Edits, said users can connect the agent they prefer, including Meta’s own Muse assistant. For example, a creator could ask Muse for a rough cut and then finish the edit by hand.

Some features are still missing, however. Users cannot yet work on the same project on both their phone and their Mac, although saved audio and text styles from the mobile app already carry over.

There is also no version for Windows yet, and Instagram said it plans to update the Mac app every week.

#3208. Use Your Year-End Review to Reach for a Promotion

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Maintaining a document of your successes throughout the year gives you a starting point

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, a program that helps engineers through hands-on training.

This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!

When I landed my first job as a software engineer, I had a simple plan: Work hard and somebody would notice. Eventually a manager would tap me on the shoulder and hand me a promotion (probably with a nice little speech).

That plan stalled my career for about five years.

I switched jobs twice, kept my head down, read a stack of programming books, and sometimes pulled 12-hour days. I was never promoted. At my third job, out of frustration, I started interviewing at other companies and almost immediately got an offer for a senior engineer role.

So I went back to my job and quit. My team was blindsided. I liked my manager and the people I worked with, and they came back with a counteroffer. Then someone from HR asked me, “Why didn’t you just ask us?”

I took the counteroffer and stayed. Three jobs in, I finally got promoted, and all it took was asking (in the most dramatic way possible).

Today, I would take a different approach.

Year-end review discussions are a great time to push for a promotion. But at most companies, raises and promotions are largely settled before the formal review conversation happens. If the year-end review is the first time your manager hears you want a promotion, you’re usually too late.

Now is a great time to start the conversation.

Engineers tend to believe good work speaks for itself. It rarely does. Your manager is juggling a team, a roadmap, and their own boss. They see a fraction of what you do, and the work they don’t see might as well not exist when raises get decided.

Perception is reality, so you have to shape it. That means learning to brag a little.

A “brag document” is a running list of what you accomplished, when, and why it mattered. Add to it every two weeks or once a month, and write each entry so your manager’s manager would understand it.

Engineers tend to write things like “migrated the billing service.” A better entry reads “migrated the billing service, which cut failed payments by 30 percent and unblocked the Q3 pricing launch.” If there’s no number, name who benefited and how.

Include the work people forget to count, too: handling incidents, mentoring new hires, interviewing candidates, and writing the docs everyone else relies on. If you helped your team adopt AI tools this year, write that down. (It counts as leadership, whether or not anyone called it that.)

The document does two jobs. It gives you ammunition when you make your case, and it gives your manager something to ctrl + c then ctrl + v when they argue for you in meetings you’ll never attend.

Bragging builds the case. Asking forces action.

If your goal is a promotion or a raise, you might ask: “What would it take for me to get to [the next level] in the next year?”

A good manager will give you an outline that can turn into a plan. Push for specifics until you have deliverables you can work toward, then send a short recap email so the plan exists somewhere besides your manager’s memory. (Managers change jobs too.)

Sometimes the answer will still be “not this year,” and the reason may have nothing to do with you.

Budgets get frozen, promotion slots get capped, and decisions get made above your manager’s head where even a manager who wants to help can’t.

Don’t read too much into that. But be honest with yourself, too. Most of the time, a no means there’s something you aren’t doing yet. Find out what it is instead of guessing for five years like I did.

Asking costs you one slightly awkward conversation. Sitting back and waiting to be noticed can cost you years.

Don’t try this at home: To better understand the risk AI slop poses to scientific publishing today, IEEE Spectrum contributor Benjamin Skuse put IEEE’s research integrity checks to the test by submitting two entirely AI-generated papers. “Science has a spam problem. And the spam filter is getting clogged up…”

Policy change doesn’t just come down to paid lobbyists—lawmakers want to hear from working experts, too. One engineer shares what he learned from his first two visits to Capitol Hill.

Could community colleges help fill the coming talent shortage in the U.S. semiconductor industry? Alternatives to four-year university degrees are a promising option for the technicians who will be needed to run new fabs.

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, an online education platform that helps people break into AI and modern software roles through project-based learning and one-on-one mentorship with senior developers. Parsity helps career changers transition into software by focusing on practical skills, real-world systems, and the kind of experience companies actually look for.Outside Parsity, Brian works a senior software engineer in the SF Bay Area.Brian is also a father of three, and when he’s not working with students or building programs, you might catch him running around Lake Merritt in Oakland, California.

Park Hotels & Resorts Inc. (PK -8.31%) reported a net loss of $15 million for the third quarter, while comparable RevPAR increased 8.4% to $201.02. Management reported that broad-based strength in group and leisure demand drove performance, particularly in urban markets like Washington DC, Chicago, and Boston. The company raised its full-year 2026 guidance for RevPAR, Adjusted EBITDA, and Adjusted FFO per share following results that exceeded internal expectations. Strategic capital allocation efforts included the reopening of the Royal Palm South Beach following a $110 million renovation and the commencement of a $100 million project at the Hilton Hawaiian Village. Management also continued its noncore disposition strategy, completing the sale of the W Chicago – City Center for $19 million in October 2026.

Additionally, unless otherwise stated, all operating results will be presented on a comparable hotel basis.

This morning, Tom Baltimore, our Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, will provide an update on our strategic initiatives and review Park's third quarter performance and outlook for the year. While Sean Dell'Orto, our Chief Financial Officer, and Chief Operating Officer will provide updates on our capital investments and additional color on guidance. Following our prepared remarks, we will open the call for questions. With that, I would like to turn the call over to Tom.

Thomas Jeremiah Baltimore Jr.: Thank you, Ian and welcome, everyone. I am pleased to report that Park delivered another outstanding quarter with results meaningfully exceeding our expectations. RevPAR increased 8.4% year over year with growth accelerating from 9% in July to more than 13% in September. Despite weather related disruptions in Hawaii during August, and September. Results reflected broad based strength across the portfolio, supported by continued momentum in group, leisure, and higher rated business transient demand. RevPAR increased nearly 7% across both our resort and urban hotels. While our airport and suburban hotels grew approximately 20%, 14%, respectively. Turning to our major markets. Hawaii continues to be 1 of the most compelling growth opportunities in our portfolio.

RevPAR across our 2 resorts increased an impressive 7% despite the temporary disruption from 3 hurricanes which we estimate reduced combined RevPAR growth for the 2 resorts by nearly 280-basis-points during the quarter. Demand rebounded as conditions improved with September representing the strongest month of the quarter and RevPAR across our Hawaii resorts increased nearly 14%. Group was the primary driver of performance at both hotels in the third quarter with group rooms revenue more than doubling year over year. Which helped to drive a 110% increase in banquet and catering revenue. At Hilton Hawaiian Village, RevPAR increased 5% during the quarter. With occupancy reaching nearly 90% allowing for compression to drive stronger rates.

Particularly in September when average daily rate increased approximately 9% compared to last year. The resort also continued to gain market share achieving a RevPAR index of 105% for the quarter up 4 points from last year with gains across both occupancy and rate. Importantly, the index remains nearly 14 points below its 2021. The resort's renovated outlets and enhanced programming also helped drive record third quarter food and beverage performance with banquet and catering outlet revenue each growing 14% year-over-year. Orlando also delivered another strong quarter. With RevPAR increasing more than 5% led by continued outperformance at Bonnet Creek. The complex delivered another record breaking quarter generating its highest third quarter revenue ever.

Transient revenue increased nearly 19% year-over-year supported by premium rated luxury demand at the Waldorf. Further underscoring the exceptional quality of these properties Signia by Hilton, Orlando Bonnet Creek, and Waldorf Astoria Orlando, were recently ranked the number 2 and number 3 resorts in Orlando respectively, and Conde Nast Travelers 2026 Reader's Choice Awards. Bonnet Creek's continued strength following our significant investment demonstrates how targeted capital can elevate an asset strengthen its competitive positioning, and drive sustained earnings growth. EBITDA of the complex has grown from approximately $60 million to a level we expect to exceed $108 million this year. And we believe there is further upside as the complex continues to gain market share.

Our urban portfolio was another important source of strength. Led by Washington DC, Chicago, and Boston. Across our 2 DC Metro hotels, RevPAR increased by nearly 33% year-over-year. Supported by a 9-point increase in occupancy, and ADR growth of 16%. Group room nights increased 139% creating meaningful compression and supporting transient ADR growth of more than 17%. At our Hilton Chicago hotel, RevPAR increased more than 15% benefiting from a particularly strong citywide and event calendar and excellent transient pricing. Boston also delivered strong results. With portfolio RevPAR increasing approximately 13% supported by meaningful ADR growth, strong citywide demand, and high occupancy.

Finally, we are very excited about the early progress at Royal Palm South Beach following its approximately $110 million transformational renovation. The hotel welcomed its first guest in late July, making the third quarter very much a ramp up period. Even at this early stage, rate performance has been very encouraging with third quarter ADR of approximately $244, up nearly $60, and more than 30% above the comparable period in 2024, with September increasing to $264 or over 40% better than pre renovation results.

The team has also been focused on building awareness of the reimagined hotel posting leading travel media, Marriott sales leaders from around the world, and key industry groups, while benefiting from broad support from Marriott and our operating partners. Looking ahead, the demand backdrop is encouraging with 8 citywide events scheduled for Miami Beach in the fourth quarter. Expected to generate approximately 56 thousand room nights, up 70% compared to last year. We are also seeing strong early validation of the hotel's repositioning across both group and food and beverage. At the end of the third quarter, 2027 group revenue on the books totaled approximately $3.9 million already matching the comparable pace for 2024 the hotel's best year.

With an average daily rate, that is a $136 higher, or up nearly 40%. During the third quarter alone, the hotel booked more than 8 thousand future group room nights at $461 average daily rate, representing approximately $3.7 million of rooms revenue more than triple the amount booked during the same period in 2024. Banquet and catering has also been particularly strong. Booking nearly $1.7 million during the third quarter versus less than $200 thousand booked during the same period in 2024. Together, these early results demonstrate the opportunity to drive significantly higher rates and meaningfully higher total revenue across the property.

These results also reinforce our confidence that Royal Palm will become a meaningful contributor to Park's earnings growth over the next couple of years. On the capital allocation front, we continue to make meaningful progress executing on our noncore disposition strategy. In October, we completed the sale of the W Chicago – City Center, a 520-room hotel in Chicago for $19 million. The hotel was expected to generate an operating loss of approximately $1.3 million in 2026, with a forecasted loss of approximately $1.3 million in the fourth quarter. Making the sale immediately accretive to earnings while further enhancing the quality of our portfolio.

Our remaining noncore hotels now represent 3% to 4% of total portfolio value, and we remain committed to further reducing that exposure by year end. With active work streams on a number of assets underway. We are extremely pleased with our progress since launching the strategy late last year Of the 19 hotels originally identified as noncore, we have sold or otherwise disposed of 11 hotels, generating approximately $220 million in gross proceeds at an average multiple of more than 16x EBITDA. These transactions have reduced our exposure to lower growth assets and enabled us to focus our capital and resources on our highest quality hotels and markets.

The result is a higher quality portfolio with stronger margins, a better growth profile, and greater long term earnings potential. We believe this transformation has positioned Park to deliver sustained earnings growth and create long term shareholder value. As we look at the balance of the year, and into 2027, I remain encouraged by the strength across our portfolio. Despite continued geopolitical and macroeconomic uncertainty, The US economy and consumer remain resilient, healthy business activity and investment, including significant spending related to AI, should continue to support lodging demand, while historically low levels of new hotel supply provide a favorable backdrop for continued pricing power.

Against this backdrop, we expect to finish the year strong and enter 2027 with considerable momentum. Core group revenue pace is up nearly 6% and we have several distinct growth drivers. Including our recently completed capital investments, which are expected to provide meaningful embedded earnings growth. In Miami, 2027 will mark its first full year of operations at the Transformed Royal Palm South Beach. Early performance continues to reinforce our high confidence in the hotel's ramp toward approximately $28 million of stabilized hotel adjusted EBITDA by 2028 compared with approximately $3 million expected this year.

For 2027, we currently expect earnings to at least return to pre levels of approximately $14 million of EBITDA with Royal Palm alone expected to contribute approximately 200 basis points to total portfolio RevPAR growth. Hawaii represents another substantial opportunity. But the Ali'i Tower renovation expected to be completed in early 27, We will have invested approximately $350 million to strengthen the competitive positioning of our 2 resorts. With the major renovation activity behind us, solid group pace already on the books, and significant upside from recovering market share we believe our Hawaii portfolio is well positioned to continue closing the approximately $60 million EBITDA gap to its 2023 peak earnings over the next few years.

As a result, I believe Park is uniquely positioned to deliver outsized earnings growth over the next several years We have strengthened the portfolio through disciplined capital allocation, and active capital recycling, invested substantially in our highest return opportunities, and enhanced our financial flexibility through proactive balance sheet management. We are now positioned to realize the earnings benefits of that work creating a compelling path to higher EBITDA and meaningful long term value creation for our shareholders. And with that, I will turn the call over to Sean.

Sean Dell'Orto: Thanks, Tom. Overall, we were very pleased with our third quarter results. Which once again exceeded expectations with RevPAR increasing 8.4% to $201 and hotel adjusted EBITDA increasing 8% year-over-year, with hotel adjusted EBITDA margin expanding by 50 basis points to 25.7%. Adjusted EBITDA was $135 million for the quarter while adjusted FFO per share was $0.39, an increase of over 11%. We were also pleased to see broad based strength across the portfolio. Group rooms revenue increased more than 18%, while transient revenue grew over 5%, reflecting healthy demand across multiple customer segments. RevPAR growth was also well balanced, with occupancy increasing 2.4 percentage points and ADR up 5%.

Expenses increased 5% during the quarter compared with just under 4% in the first half of the year. With the reopening of the Royal Palm adding roughly 85 basis points of operating expense growth versus prior year. Excluding Royal Palm, cost per occupied room increased 3.7% in the quarter including an approximately 80-basis point impact from increased utility cost pressures. Which combined with higher occupancy and along with revenue based variable costs drove the expense growth for the quarter. But partially offset by a reduction in fixed costs mostly due to lower property insurance premiums from our annual policy renewal this past June.

Turning to capital investments, During the third quarter, we invested a total of $57 million in capital improvements, with full year CapEx expected to range between $270 million to $280 million In Hawaii, we commenced a comprehensive renovation of a 348-room Ali'i Tower Hilton Hawaiian Village in August. A $100 million project that includes a complete renovation of all guest rooms plus the addition of 3 guest rooms within the premium oceanfront tower. And enhancements to food and beverage outlets including the Tropics Bar and Grill, and 80% of the guest rooms across to nearly 3 thousand-room resort have been fully renovated.

And finally, in New Orleans, we commenced third and final phase of the main tower guest room renovation in May. Encompassing the remaining 489 guest rooms and expect the project to be completed by mid November. Upon completion, all 1.6 thousand-plus guest rooms then fully renovated, significantly enhancing the quality and competitiveness of 1 of our most important convention oriented assets. Turning to the balance sheet, we ended the third quarter with net debt of approximately $3.7 billion, translating to a trailing 12 month net debt to EBITDA ratio of just under 6x. A reduction of 0.2 of a turn since the beginning of the year.

Liquidity was $1.3 billion, including $295 million in cash and $1 billion of available capacity under our revolver. In September, we fully repaid the $1.275 billion CMBS loans secured by the Hilton Hawaiian Village Resort. Using the remaining $600 million of capacity under our delayed draw term loan together with proceeds from the $700 million delayed draw mortgage loan, secured by the Bonnet Creek complex. This transaction meaningfully extended our debt maturities by roughly 1.5 years. And we now have no significant maturities until Q4 of 28. We also finalized terms on a $205 million refinancing of Hilton Santa Barbara resort. Which will be used to repay the existing $150 million mortgage maturing in December.

And provide for future funding advances towards the property's comprehensive renovation currently planned for late 28. We expect to close this refinancing by the end of this month. With respect to our dividend, on October 15, we paid our third quarter cash dividend of $0.25 per share and on October 29, the Board approved a fourth quarter cash dividend of $0.25 per share to be paid on January 15, to stockholders of record as of December 31. The dividend currently translates to an annualized yield of approximately 6% based on recent trading levels.

Turning to guidance, following another stronger than expected quarter, we are increasing both our RevPAR and earnings guidance ranges to reflect our third quarter results and our updated expectations for the fourth quarter. Accordingly, we are raising our full year RevPAR outlook by 200 basis points at the midpoint to a new range of 5.5% to 6%. Which implies a fourth quarter growth rate between 5.5% to 7.5%. This updated outlook reflects the nearly 400 basis points of outperformance delivered during the third quarter as well as stronger than anticipated results at the start of the fourth quarter with preliminary October RevPAR increasing nearly 11%.

Driven by a 120-basis-point lift from Miami, coupled with double digit gains at Bonnet Creek, Key West, and Washington DC. From an earnings perspective, we are increasing adjusted EBITDA guidance by approximately $13 million at the midpoint to a new range of $635 million to $645 million while adjusted FFO guidance increases by approximately $0.08 per share at the midpoint to a new range of $2.00 to $2.05 per share. This increase to guidance also reflects an assumed annual increase in expenses of approximately 4.5% year-over-year, and 5.5% to 6.5% for the fourth quarter. With an approximate 150-basis-point impact from the reopening of Royal Palm.

Expenses are being driven by the stronger demand environment and higher occupancy expectations across the portfolio driving increases in variable costs such as labor and utilities. In addition, with respect to Royal Palm, expect fourth quarter hotel adjusted EBITDA at the property to be approximately $4 million, with full year EBITDA of approximately $3 million We very much look forward to welcoming many of you to the property next week when we host an investor tour and showcase the exceptional transformation firsthand.

#3206. Apple TV unveils return of hit comedy from Ted Lasso, Shrinking creator

Bad Monkey, an Apple TV comedy from the creator of Ted Lasso and Shrinking, returns soon for a new season. Here’s the just-released trailer for Bad Monkey season 2.

One of the biggest hitmakers at Apple TV is undoubtedly Bill Lawrence, co-creator of a trio of acclaimed comedies: Ted Lasso, Shrinking, and Bad Monkey.

Among the three, the Vince Vaughn-starring Bad Monkey is likely the one you’ve never heard of. But now is a perfect time to get caught up.

Bad Monkey season 2 debuts Wednesday, December 2 with one episode, followed by weekly releases through February 3.

Here’s Apple’s official plot summary, followed by the new trailer:

After Andrew Yancy (Vaughn) witnesses the murder of Florida’s finest fixer, an ambitious state attorney pairs him up with a strait-laced forensic accountant to solve the crime. Yancy finds himself embroiled in a turf war between rival criminal organizations as he navigates a variety of Florida oddballs, including an erudite mob boss, his unhinged son and a hard-edged young woman who needs Yancy’s protection. Meanwhile, Yancy contends with his aging father; unresolved romantic tension with Dr. Rosa Campesino (Natalie Martinez), who launches her own investigation into a mysterious rash; and a bombastic animal relocation specialist whose business threatens the local environment.

Joining several returning season 1 cast members is prominent addition John Malkovich. Malkovich plays a Miami mob boss that Vaughn’s Yancy finds himself up against.

You can watch Bad Monkey season 1 here on Apple TV.

Are you a fan of Bad Monkey? If you haven’t seen it yet, do you plan to watch? Let us know in the comments.

Apple TV is available for $14.99 per month, or you can get it discounted through the Apple One bundle.
