Even so, I assume that this impact will be relatively mechanical. Could you please help us quantify it more precisely? And I see the consensus on EBITDA [indiscernible] at $680 million next year. Does that seem reasonable to you considering the impact of the license exit?

Soraya Benchikh: I'll take the first part of the question. This is Soraya Benchikh. I'll take the first part of the question and then pass it over to Markus for the second part. Firstly, let me start with the gross margin and where we landed for the first quarter. Our gross margin declined, as you saw in our statement, by 120 basis points. About 50 basis points of this came from the headwinds from the Middle East freight and material costs, and the rest was basically down to unfavorable mix and excess and obsolescent stock. We're very focused on the controllable drivers that impacted excess and obsolescence stock.

And we're working through these through better planning basically to reduce this because we've had a scattered -- a more scattered approach to innovation with smaller innovations that weren't successful. So as we concentrate and you rightly highlighted in our statement that we've concentrated behind our 6 brands, we will shift to fewer and bigger launches, and that will also help us in terms of the planning and having less obsolescence stock. So this should reduce -- a better S&OP, better demand planning and forecasting and fewer bigger launches will reduce our E&O as we work the inventory down.

So these benefits will build over time, but we're very clear on what we can control in terms of the impact on the gross margin.

Markus Strobel: As for portfolio, first of all, we are very pleased with our top 6 brands growing 5% in the first quarter. Still more work to do because we need broader growth, we need faster growth, and we're working on that. But we are pleased with that. And we are also pleased with the progress we're making in our consumer business where decline was 8% in first half of fiscal '26 is now down to 3%, and we're catching up with market share. And on skin care, actually, we have very much improved profitability, and we are pretty happy with that, too.

Now what this means for your question, it is important for us that all of our business units do well, be it Prestige, be it consumer business, be it skin care, and we are on the way of doing that because it will also give us the strategic optionality of the future. So to answer your question directly, I would not draw conclusions from what happened in the first quarter to the future portfolio. That is far too early. We are in the middle of a strategic review. We will commit ourselves to complete it by the end of the calendar year, which is close, but we're still working on it. And that was Gucci, right? Back to you, Soraya.

Soraya Benchikh: Okay. This is the strategic review or the Gucci? No, Gucci.

Markus Strobel: I mean to say the impact of the Gucci exit.

Soraya Benchikh: Sorry, can you remind me what the impact of the exit? Okay. We're at the moment in the middle of transitioning the Gucci business. I think we've -- the exact timing of it is still to be determined. But in the impact of the Gucci exit, we have reached the deal on Gucci. We are protecting the fiscal '28 cash flow. And in terms of the value, have we communicated the value?

Soraya Benchikh: No, the value of the impact.

Markus Strobel: No, I can -- yes, we have -- I can step in here on the value of the impact. And we are addressing this at the moment as part of the overall savings package that we're also going to come out with before Christmas. But to give you an indication, and it's the same indication I gave last time, Gucci was a low double-digit part of our portfolio at a gross margin of about 70%, in line with the Prestige portfolio and an A&CP level of about 29% and a profitability in line with the Prestige portfolio. You can think about that Gucci impact is about [ 40% ] of the contribution of the net sales.

So it's a sizable impact that we will have to manage, but we have plans. We're finalizing the plans, and we will be back to you with those plans latest by January because we're going to complete this all by the end of this calendar year.

Soraya Benchikh: And just overall, the agreement basically that we reached with Gucci is to compensate 1 less year of profit and cash flow and inventory and also to fund the restructuring costs that will come out of it. So we've received $250 million upfront and the total value of the agreement is $400 million. I hope that answers the question.

Operator: We'll take our next question from Nik Modi with RBC Capital Markets.

Unknown Analyst: This is [ Clark Leon ] on for Nik Modi. In the prepared remarks, you called out a partnership with Brandlight that's designed to strengthen your visibility across AI-driven search. Can you give us a little bit more color on the measures of success of this partnership? And how you plan to optimize for different AI platforms given that each platform leverages unique combination of inputs to drive product recommendations?

Markus Strobel: Yes. Thanks, Clark. I mean, we are in the process of really modernizing our advertising quite drastically, both when it comes to advocacy, influencer, creator management, and when it comes to AI search. So the collaboration with Brandlight is a key pillar in the strategy. And I'm fully aware that the algorithms and the keywords and the content is different from platform to platform, but this is exactly why we are working with this company that gets us ahead of the game. And we are concentrating -- this is very important. We want to get this 100% right. We want to make a big impact. That's why we concentrated it on the top 6 brands in the top 5 markets.

This is something that we can -- so we'd rather go into depth market by market, brand by brand to get this right to have the right impact and to be in the top of AI searches versus going to broad in the beginning. So depth versus breadth. This is what we're doing with Brandlight.

Operator: We'll take our next question from Sydney Wagner with Jefferies.

Sydney Wagner: Congratulations on the Marc Jacobs license extension and just the success of that makeup launch. Curious to hear what differentiated the launch and which elements are maybe transferable across CoverGirl and the broader color portfolio? And then also just wondering with the contribution from the pipeline fill, would Prestige sell-in still have been aligned with sell-out if you excluded that benefit?

Markus Strobel: Thanks for the question, Sydney. So in terms of success factor, you mean for the makeup launch? Specifically that we can apply to CoverGirl?

Markus Strobel: I think there's a couple of principles that make this launch very successful initially, and we're going to keep it up. One principle is that we have co-developed the whole proposition together with Sephora. So being in a kitchen with the retailers is really some strategy that we're going to use in the future on all of our makeup brands going forward because it kind of enables us much more to win with the consumers that frequent that retailer, okay? So we're going to be much more focused on like which is Gen Z in the Sephora case. And you see the Marc Jacobs proposition really fits to it, thanks to that collaboration.

Number two, we have actually a fairly tight SKU portfolio on Marc Jacobs, which enables you to manage your SKU productivity and shelf space productivity much, much better. So this is something we will also apply to other brands. And number three, we will -- we have based this whole brand launch on advocacy, influencers, creators, not on broad-based mass marketing. And I think these are important learnings that we will transfer to other brands because they are very effective in terms of sellout, in terms of success. And you had a second question, right? Can you just remind me again? Oh, yes, the total Prestige sellout. I got it. Yes.

I -- if you take out -- on Prestige, you take out the Marc Jacobs Beauty pipeline because obviously, the shelves had to be filled in the first quarter. Our total Prestige business would still be up, like our top 6 would still be up, probably more in the neighborhood of 3% than 5%, but still growth.

Sydney Wagner: Okay. And if I can just squeeze one more in there. With the greater share of A&CP now concentrated behind the top 6 brands in Prestige and top 4 in Consumer, where the incremental investment be most visible? And which areas do you expect to have the biggest near-term impact there?

Markus Strobel: I think you will see the biggest impact in -- so we have allocated a lot of the incremental investment to improve our capabilities and our impact in advocacy. So this is all the working with influencers, creators that help us build our brands. And if you see, we have some good news to report. We have on Burberry, the share of influence we have in the category went up by 50 basis points. And in other brands, it also went up, up to 100 basis points. So we are getting much better in the influencer advocacy game, which drives the business today in fragrances and in makeup. So this is where the majority of the incremental investment will go.

Operator: We'll move next to Olivia Tong with Raymond James.

Olivia Tong Cheang: I wanted to ask you a couple of questions. First, if you wouldn't mind sort of expanding on what you see as the mile markers of success in this -- in what is clearly a transition year. I know the performance won't be linear. But Markus, can you help us understand how you gauge whether the plan is proceeding as expected? And Soraya, I'm interested in your thoughts on KPIs as well. And then specifically for Soraya, we talked a lot about what you can deploy within this organization when we met. And I wanted to focus on forecasting accuracy, specifically on inventory. And how far through the inventory cleanup are you?

Because excess and obsolescence is still a headwind even though sales drag was at the more favorable end of your guidance range. And just understanding what's going to change or has changed in forecasting and innovation planning to help that?

Markus Strobel: All right. So let me take the first part of the question. I think we are making good progress in our Coty.Curated strategy. You see this in the results of the first quarter. You see this in the concrete share of A&CP that we have increased behind the core brands. And I always talk about focus and sharper priorities, that's what we're doing. And an important element is also innovation. We have launched 4 bigger innovations in this quarter, BOSS Bottled Beyond for Her, the Mood Stones by Kylie, the Marc Jacobs Beauty and the Burberry Amber Vanilla.

And all of these launches are tracking ahead of their objectives, which tells us that disciplined initiative management and fewer, bigger, better is starting to work for us. So I've seen a lot of good green shoots here. We are not there, and we fully admit that because it takes time to make all these changes stick with the organization to embed them in the organization. But we're on our way. Would we like our progress to be faster? Yes, and we're fully working on it. And we will -- we can give you full guidance how this whole thing is going to look, come together once we complete our strategic review.

And once we also complete our savings and the restructuring program to make up for the contribution of the loss of Gucci, okay? So stay tuned. This will come very soon.

Soraya Benchikh: Yes. For -- so thank you for the question. So the forecasting reliability and our inventory -- working through our inventory. I think forecasting reliability, basically, we are working to improve our core tools and processes. We are enhancing our S&OP. We've developed and deployed some AI tools to actually help us with the backbone of our forecast. But I think the crux of the matter has been with the level of scattered innovations that we've had in the past, and we're working through the inventory remnants of this, and this takes time. We are getting more and more granularity and have a lot more visibility than we possibly have had in the past.

We had a little spike in inventory because of this, but I'm very confident as we work through it. And as Markus just said, by us focusing on fewer brands, and having bigger and fewer bets when I look at the cycle plan that we have planned over the next 18 months to 2 years, then we should be able to better forecast our innovations and be able to also course correct with the new tools to ensure that we're not holding on to too much stock. So in short, we're working on it. We're working through the inventory that we currently have, and we will get there, but it will just take a little bit of time.

Olivia Tong Cheang: Got it. Just following up a quick one. If you could give any early thoughts on holiday either in the Western markets or 11/11 in the East?

Markus Strobel: Holiday is just starting. What I can say about holidays, especially in the U.S., is that retailers are starting earlier with their holiday activities, and we're obviously actively participating in these activities because last year, the main activities happened very late in the quarter. And people don't like to wait for that. You want to have more security on your sales and your shipment, also from a retailer perspective. So holiday is starting earlier and earlier. That's the trend that I'm observing this year.

Operator: We'll take our next question from Jonna Kim with TD Cowen.

Jungwon Kim: First one on CoverGirl, you've seen nice improvement there. How sustainable do you think that growth improvement is just going forward? And what are key strategies that you have to improve the performance? And then just the second one, overall in the U.S. Prestige returned to growth in the quarter. How much of that is innovation versus the underlying trends in the core portfolio? And what gives you confidence that you can sustain or accelerate growth from here?

Markus Strobel: Okay. On CoverGirl. CoverGirl is under a program we are calling Color the Future, which is also like part of Coty.Curated. And we are very pleased with CoverGirl almost now catching up with the market in terms of consumption. Net sales are down just 2% this quarter versus almost like 8% in the first half of fiscal '26. And we've seen a gradual improvement quarter-by-quarter. And we hope this will expect -- this will go on like this.

What makes us very confident about this is that we have on CoverGirl, we have smaller innovation bundles, but more powerful innovation bundles, better innovation, more incremental innovation, innovation that needs to earn its place on the shelf and not just being thrown out there. And we already see early success in Q1 because the innovation we launched in spring, we're having actually lower returns than we had the year before. So that means things have been selling out better. Things have been more productive on the shelf, number one. Number two, we are very disciplined to supporting with media our 2 biggest properties like Simply Ageless and Lash Blast to not deviate into smaller things.

We're always on for our biggest properties that really drive the business and that are really liked by consumers. And number three, we have very exciting innovations going in the market right now and innovation coming up. You may have seen the new Showstopper Mascara of CoverGirl, which is a very exciting innovation with a proprietary mascara brush technology and a very luxurious packaging. So sharper bundles, more consistent advertising over time and better innovation makes us confident that we can sustain this trajectory.

On Prestige, I mentioned before that we are pleased with the 5% growth of the top 6 brands and even without the major launch of Marc Jacobs Beauty, which was the main launch, it would still be up 3%. And we have the innovations that we brought out now that looks strong. And these are innovations that I believe have staying power, and we can support as we go on. So we haven't seen the best of the innovation yet, especially if you consider that on BOSS Bottled Beyond for Her, we have not launched it yet in the U.S. and in the U.K. That's going to happen in spring. So still a lot of mileage in that innovation.

And ever since we've put out BOSS Bottled for Her, we have share growth on Hugo Boss in Germany, which is the biggest market for Hugo Boss after a long time. So we see not only shipment and sales growth, but we see sellout and share growth behind these innovations. So we are confident we can keep that up, and we have a fairly good pipeline on Burberry, on Boss, and on new brand Etro that we're going to bring out in the beginning of 2027. So we're fairly confident that our innovation will keep driving our business.

Operator: We'll take our next question from Javier Escalante with Evercore ISI.

Javier Escalante Manzo: Congratulations on the extension of Marc Jacobs. And this is basically my question, Markus. I believe that you managed this business with Procter a long time ago, and it was a very different view of the industry itself and the business model with licenses. I would like to hear your view, your strategic view about this license model, how it's evolving? 40 years to me qualify as a perpetuity. We see -- we saw something similar with Kering Beauté. Is this where the business is going? Like to unlock co-investment, you need these very long licenses to derisk situations like Gucci happening. Will you seek similar long-term partnerships with core brands like Burberry and BOSS? And I have a follow-up.

But this is -- if you can keep it very kind of like strategic, what's happening? This is 40 years is a long time. Tell us what's happening.

Markus Strobel: I think what's happening in the industry is the industry has become -- fragrances has been a growing category for the last couple of years, and it's still growing very nicely. It was just like 5% up globally in the first quarter. So there is a lot of activity. There's a lot of competition, and we launch things, we need investment and we need security that this investment is going to pay off and that we can continue to reinvest to drive these brands. So the longer the license contract, the better it is.

It's not only for us from an investment point of view, but often also better for the licensee because there's a royalty stream that they can bank on in the future. And interestingly enough, a lot of our contracts today are already brands that we either own or we are on almost perpetual licenses. So we feel good about the longevity of our fragrance, and we will be striving with all of our licenses and also new licenses to extend licenses as long as possible and as early as possible so that we all have security to invest.

Javier Escalante Manzo: So Markus, I take your response. I mean, you can agree or not, that, yes, you would be -- your inclination would be to go back to Burberry and to go back to BOSS and say, "We would love to continue the partnership. We are increasing our investment behind it, but we also need longer durations to derisk that investment and make this a true partnership for a long term." Is that a good characterization of what you just said?

Markus Strobel: That sums it up pretty well.

Javier Escalante Manzo: Okay. And then -- so basically, could you tell us what happened to -- because there were a lot of licenses prior. How many licenses are in Prestige? And in your curated approach, would you think that the idea would be to approach these licensees and unwind so that you have a more curated, but at the same time, a more sustainable, say, equity story proposition for minority shareholders?

Markus Strobel: I think when you look at the licensed fragrance portfolio, duration is one question. The other question is also like you want to have a portfolio that goes for the right target groups, if it's Gen Z, Gen X, probably a stronger region in North America. Some brands might be stronger in China, in Asia, in Europe. So you need to have a pretty good balance. What we're also striving for in the -- when we drive brands in the more uber-prestige market, uber-prestige, high prestige, super high prestige, no matter how you want to call it, is a growing part of the business.

We are just increasing our investment behind Atelier des Fleurs of Chloé, which is very successful in this investment -- in this area. We will be launching Etro in spring in the super premium segment. And we're just coming out with the Burberry Prorsum Collection also in the super premium segment. And the marketing in the super premium segment is slightly different than from the non-super premium segment because you've got to be strong in-store. So all of these brands have in terms of curation, have different KPIs that we need to respect. And we think we have a fairly balanced portfolio with world-class licensees and licensors.

Operator: We'll take our next question from Anna Lizzul from Bank of America.

Anna Lizzul: I was wondering if we could discuss more the outlook within the different geographies. There's certainly some encouraging results here from the Americas with improvements in innovation. But it looks like in Europe, a bit of a different dynamic given the softer market consumption there. I was wondering if you could touch on the broader political environment and the impact to sales? And also, how should we be thinking about the cost outlook, just given the pressures you're seeing from freight in the Middle East and what your level of confidence is on delivering on cost management to mitigate this in the near term?

Markus Strobel: Okay. Let me just go on what I see in terms of market development and our development in these markets, and then Soraya can add some color when it comes to costs out of the Middle East and how we're dealing with that. Again, yes, we are pleased with our progress in the U.S. It's the biggest fragrance market. So it's important for us to win. So not there where we need to be, but the progress and we will behind Coty.Curated make this stronger as we move along. We're also very pleased with our development in Asia. We have -- China had a particularly strong quarter in Q1. So our total Asia business is up 8% in net sales.

Europe is the area that we need to focus on fixing. We have good market growth in Spain, Italy. And we have a fairly soft market growth in Prestige in Germany and France. So the market growth in Europe is on average lower than in the other geographies, but it's a big part of our business. So we are very aware of that. We are making progress on Hugo Boss, which is our biggest brand in Europe. I just mentioned the BOSS Bottled for Her launch, which comes fully incremental because obviously, it's a female launch and BOSS is mostly a male brand. And this is our #1 target is to make Hugo Boss grow again in Europe.

And I think we're in a good way. We just signed a partnership. You may have seen that with HYROX in a lot of geographies. We're working together with HYROX in big events, which is going to increase our advocacy, our influencer and creator standing. So we are pleased with that. And then we also curate our portfolio in Europe. Hugo Boss important, Burberry important and the other brands, the regional brands that are important in countries like Germany, we're not neglecting. So we are not there where we need to be in Europe, but we're on the way.

Soraya Benchikh: Okay. When it comes to the outlook and looking at cost pressures, we really -- the Middle East headwinds that I outlined in describing the margin, we expect them to persist for the rest of the year. Currently, what we've built into our forecasting is particularly on oil that has impact our input costs, $30 million to $40 million impact. And we think that now if the barrel price stays above $100, we're going to be in the upper range of this. But generally, with the macro pressures, if they do continue at this level or intensify, we're looking to pull productivity and fixed cost levers first to preserve the room to invest behind the brand.

Productivity is happening on all lines of the P&L, not just on fixed costs. We're also looking at the ROI threshold on our marketing investments. We've rolled out tools to several markets to measure the effectiveness of our spend. So yes, this is a transition year. There's lots of moving parts, but we are going to work productivity really hard to preserve the investment behind our brands because our priority is still to achieve the quality growth that we're pursuing on the top line. I hope that answers it.

Operator: At this time, this concludes -- oh, I'm sorry, go ahead.

Markus Strobel: No, there's no more questions, let me just conclude the call, right?

Markus Strobel: Or do we have more questions?

Operator: We have no more questions at this time.

Markus Strobel: Okay. Okay. Let me just conclude it then. So to summarize it all, Q1 came ahead of our expectations, but it's obviously not where we want to be. We want to be better. Fiscal '27 is a transition year for us. And as we mentioned a couple of times, the recovery will not be linear. Still, we have very encouraging early signs. Our top 6 core Prestige brands grew 5% like-for-like, and we expect growth on our top 6 core Prestige brands in Q2 as well. We will keep investing behind our core brands, turning stronger performance into cash, and we also reduce debt. And we remain on track to complete the strategic review by the end of calendar 2026.

We know that your confidence is earned through consistent delivery, and we will be transparent and accountable along the way. So thanks for joining us today.

Operator: This concludes today's meeting. We appreciate your time and participation. You may now disconnect. Thank you.

#3173. Report: Apple captured half of global smartphone revenue in Q3

According to a new report from Counterpoint Research, Apple just recorded its highest-ever global smartphone revenue for a third calendar quarter. Here are the details.

In a report released earlier this week, Counterpoint Research mapped out the global smartphone market’s performance during the third quarter, which saw Apple capture its highest-ever share of industry revenue for the period.

Samsung, which came in second, accounted for 19% of global smartphone revenue, followed by Xiaomi at 6%, OPPO at 5%, and vivo at 4%.

In another record, Counterpoint says Apple saw the iPhone average selling price (ASP) hit an all-time-high of $1,031, up 19% year-over-year.

Counterpoint’s Research Director Tarun Pathak explained that the iPhone 18 Pro series contributed to Apple’s ASP growth, despite launching toward the end of the third calendar quarter:

“Apple remained the most resilient major brand in Q3 2026, with shipments nearly flat YoY. Apple has the pricing power to absorb rising memory costs and pass them on to consumers with minimal impact on demand. At the same time, ASP growth was supported by higher launch prices for the iPhone 18 Pro series, the absence of the base iPhone 18 from the launch and price increases across older models in September. Together, these factors helped Apple deliver strong revenue growth in an otherwise challenging market.”

Finally, the report noted that while Samsung still led the market in shipment share, its lead over Apple narrowed slightly, with the companies accounting for 22% and 21% of global smartphone shipments, respectively.

#3172. Windows 11 can run better on PCs with 8GB now, Microsoft says – here’s why

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Windows > Windows 11

The latest updates to Windows 11 offer improvements in speed, performance, and memory management.

The more memory your Windows PC has, the faster it should perform, especially when juggling multiple apps, files, and other data. My laptop has 32GB of RAM, while my desktop has a hefty 64GB, and both are absolutely zippy. Does that mean computers with only 8GB of memory, or even less, are also-rans? Nope, not according to Microsoft.

Also: How much RAM does your PC really need?

In a new blog post published Tuesday, Microsoft touted the gains in speed, performance, and memory management in Windows 11 achieved by the latest updates. These especially impact PCs with just 8GB of RAM, which can now run multiple apps and files faster and more efficiently than before.

To reach this goal, the company said it had three notions in mind.

The first was to make better use of the existing memory on each Windows 11 PC. The second was to protect the tasks that need to feel instant even as more memory gets used. And the third was to ensure that key apps and Windows require less memory. Yes, a computer with 16GB, 32GB, or 64GB of RAM can better handle more intensive activities. But Microsoft wanted to make sure that systems with 8GB could also keep pace.

Based on its own lab tests of PCs with 8GB of RAM, the company claims that Windows is now 20% more responsive and that multitasking is 40% faster than before the latest updates. Here’s how.

As more memory gets allocated, Windows must move inactive apps and files from RAM to the hard drive. When you need to access those apps and files again, you have to wait for Windows to move them from disk storage back to RAM. Normally, PCs with less memory have to do a lot of this disk swapping.

One way Windows eases the pain of this process is through compression. Here, the operating system shrinks less-active data into a smaller format so it can remain in memory. Though Windows has used compression for many years, Microsoft has fine-tuned the technology to determine how much to compress, when to move data from RAM to your drive, and when to fetch it back, especially on PCs with 8GB of memory.

Also: 5 apps I always install on new Windows PCs – most are free

As such, Windows can now keep up to 2GB more of your active data in memory rather than moving it to storage, Microsoft said. An inactive app, file, or browser that you leave open is less likely to have to reload from your hard drive when you return to it.

Opening the Start menu, launching File Explorer, right-clicking a folder or file, and searching for an item are all tasks that need to feel instant; otherwise, Windows itself feels sluggish. To achieve this on PCs with less RAM, Windows tries to prioritize certain actions you need to accomplish while backing off background tasks like search indexing, Microsoft said.

Here’s one example. After you update your computer and reboot, Windows has some housekeeping to do. But any setup work that occurs shouldn’t affect how long it takes to open an app or file.

Also: How to upgrade your ‘incompatible’ Windows 10 PC to Windows 11 – for free

The latest version of Windows 11 speeds up these types of tasks and interactions by up to 20% compared with the January 2026 version, according to Microsoft.

However, multitasking places the greatest strain on a PC with only 8GB of RAM. To analyze this, Microsoft said it conducted two tests on the same PC with 8GB of memory. One test measured the current version of Windows 11, while the other gauged the January 2026 flavor. Here, the testers opened 20 tabs in Microsoft Edge, kicked off a 4K video, and launched large files in Word, PowerPoint, and Excel, one after another. The current version of Windows is up to 40% faster than its predecessor, the company said.

To reduce the need for RAM among Windows and certain key apps, Microsoft said that it has improved how memory is managed and when it’s used.

As one example, memory is allocated to Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and Outlook more efficiently, resulting in a 360 MB savings in RAM. This maneuver also extends to third-party apps such as WhatsApp, which has reduced its memory requirements.

Also: 11 Windows apps I replace on every new PC (and the ones I keep)

On PCs with 8GB of memory, the Widgets app loads only when you open it and frees up about 200 MB of RAM when you close it. In Microsoft Edge, inactive tabs now go to sleep after 15 minutes, down from two hours previously, reducing overall memory allocation.

Across Windows, Microsoft 365, and Edge, those improvements reduced the growth in required memory by up to 900 MB, Microsoft said.

How does Microsoft test these scenarios to see whether the latest Windows updates and fixes are helping PCs with less memory?

“We test those fixes across a broader collection of over 20,000 PCs in our labs, including current 8 GB models, using automated workloads based on activities such as browsing, working in Microsoft 365 apps, joining video calls, and downloading files in the background and even using high-speed cameras to measure the time from an action, such as opening Start or launching an app, to the moment the result appears on screen,” the company explained.

Also: Why your RAM options cost 4X more now than last year

The ability to use Windows without much RAM on your PC is critical these days in light of the “RAMageddon” crisis. With AI companies scooping up massive amounts of memory and flash storage chips, remaining supply is limited, and the prices have surged. The more memory you add to a new or existing PC, the more you’re going to pay. That’s always been true, but now more than ever.

Of course, memory is only one part of the picture. Your PC’s processor and other hardware also play an important role. Here, Microsoft found that a 2026 Dell XPS 13 with 8GB of RAM showed 94% faster multi-core CPU performance than a 2021 8 GB model. But the same 2026 8GB PC performed on par with a 2021 16 GB system. This shows that memory does matter for multitasking, but that the processor also impacts performance.

Whether your Windows 11 PC has 8GB of RAM, less, or more, how can you take advantage of the latest enhancements? For that, you’ll want to make sure that you’ve updated to the newest version of Windows. That would be Windows 11 26H2, build 26300.9818 or later, according to Microsoft. But that includes the latest optional preview build released in late October. If you don’t want to install that one, you’ll be fine with build 26300.9711 for now.

Also: The best laptops: Expert tested and reviewed

To check, head to Settings, select System, and then click About. The section for Windows Info shows the current version and build. If you need to update, stay in Settings and go to Windows Update. Assuming your PC qualifies, you should find the latest Windows 11 26H2 build ready to install.

Beyond updating Windows, you also want to keep your apps current. If you use Microsoft 365, open any app in the suite, click the File menu, select Account, click Update Options, then select Update Now.

With most other apps, you have to update them manually or individually. To ease the process, consider a good software updater program. These will automatically scan most of your installed applications to identify which need updating, then download and install the updates for you.

#3171. Bread as a Sponge for Oil Is the Best Kitchen Hack I Learned All Year

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Oily pans, stews and sauces are no match for the bread sponge trick.

If you want to degrease a pan or the top layer of an oily sauce without ruining a sponge, a single slice of bread could be your new favorite cleaning sidekick.

While we have vastly improved how we dispose of most things, excess cooking grease still presents a problem. Down the sink? Not advisable. Neither is the dishwasher—even the garbage bin can become a gnarly affair.

Getting the bulk of the grease out of a pan after cooking a batch of bacon or burgers is a good first step, but that greasy pan will either take down a sponge or half a roll of paper towels. What if a humble slice of past-its-prime sandwich bread was the all-natural solution for greasy pans you’ve been looking for?

It’s cheap and easy, and you can toss the used-up bread into a compost bin or countertop food waste processor without disrupting its yuck-free operation.

So, is it ever OK to pour excess grease or used cooking oil down the sink? Even if you run the hot water tap at the same time? Short answer: no. Long answer? Here’s an expert for the “no.” “When grease cools, it solidifies, coating the interior of the pipe,” says Jacylyn Basilone, chief operating officer of Brooks Plumbing. Even if you’re running hot water, the grease will eventually cool further down the line and cause future problems. “Over time, the solidified grease in the pipes can catch debris, thus making a partial clog grow larger and larger,” she says, reducing the pipe’s circumference little by little if you do this repeatedly.

Unlike a clogged shower drain, which you can usually clear easily, “a normal sewer machine or ‘snake’ can’t alleviate this type of stoppage,” says Basilone. “While grease solidifies, it can’t be captured by the claw head. Grease removal is best remediated with a hydrojetter, which tends to be more expensive than the traditional drain-cleaning services.”

Bread is the real answer, and I can’t believe I haven’t been doing this all along. (*Hangs head in shame, fully guilty of relying on the obviously very sketchy hot water method.*)

Bread has always been a superb grease-mopping tool; we usually think of it in a culinary context rather than for waste removal. Just as you’d drag a crusty baguette or hunk of ciabatta across the drippings on your plate, bread is an excellent sponge for all manner of oil, whether or not it is appealing to consume. Using bread to soak up excess oil essentially turns liquid food waste into a solid, making disposal much easier.

If it’s not obvious, this is also a great way to use bread that might otherwise go to waste: the ends of the loaf you can’t bring yourself to eat, or bread that’s gone stale or is starting to show the first mold spores. If you’re going to discard the bread anyway, at least put it to good use.

The bread trick comes in handy in almost endless ways. If there’s a pool of oil, it’s the mop for the job. I initially tried it after cooking bacon. A single, small slice of bread was enough to absorb what was easily four to six ounces of liquid grease left in the pan. I dragged the slice around the pan like a mop, but even after letting it sit a few extra moments, it kept working and eventually soaked up all the liquid grease. (If you’re feeling indulgent and used a fresh bread slice for this purpose, the temptation to make pretty epic croutons here is quite strong — another upside.)

If your air fryer has space between the drawer and the basket, you can place the bread there to soak up grease while cooking. Even for oily, slow-cooked proteins like pork shoulder, you can press the bread onto the meat to soak up grease before serving.

Once the bread has absorbed the oil and needs discarding, responsible food-waste methods are much easier to manage. Depending on how much oil the bread has absorbed, you can safely put the soaked bread in the compost bin or countertop composter without risking a major oil spill and a mess to clean up later. Oil can slow decomposition, so composting large amounts isn’t recommended. Small amounts, such as a few tablespoons at a time, are safe.

Even if you have no other option but to throw it away — and if that is the case, please consider getting a small composting appliance — at the very least, you’re not involving an easily recyclable glass container.

For more home tips, learn this neat trick for reusing frying oil and learn the 10 worst things to pour down your drain.

#3169. I tried Sonos’ latest app features – these 2 small upgrades fix big annoyances

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Home & Office > Home Entertainment > Speakers

New Sonos software and firmware updates are rolling out. Here's what you can expect.

Sonos’ promise to release its AI-upgraded voice assistant is nearing its “Fall 2026” deadline, and before fans can use the highly anticipated update, the company continues to make small improvements to its app and player features.

Also: Sonos Ace Ultra vs. Sonos Ace: Who should upgrade

This time, Sonos added System Health, a new in-app page to access a more comprehensive view of your system(s), though it’s only available on iOS for now. However, a new blog post states that iOS and Android users can expect volume presets, more interaction with the app miniplayer, and spoken voice prompts for the Ace Ultra headphones.

I poked around in the app and tried some of the latest features. Here’s what to expect.

If your system consists of multiple speakers, a mix of modern and legacy speakers, or multiple systems, you’re bound to experience a hiccup and be unsure which speaker is causing the issue.

It usually takes me some time to Google my issue and scroll through the Sonos Community forum, Reddit, or the official Sonos help documents to find suggestions and troubleshoot it. Sonos’ new System Health feature provides an overview of your systems, showing your network status and name, as well as the number of speakers and rooms in each system.

Also: I used Sonos’s new home theater feature – it’s a competition killer

According to Sonos’ blog post, System Health can detect a Double Network Address issue, which usually occurs when you introduce a new router to your home or plug a mesh system into your ISP-provided router. The result is two home networks, and your Sonos speakers will split their connection between them, flagging “System not found” errors, missing speakers, or connection dropouts.

System Health is in the Settings tab, under the Help Center menu.

Once you tap into your system, you can see all of its speakers, with unconnected speakers bearing a red “Not connected” badge, and wireless speakers showing a black “Powered off” badge when they’re off.

Then, you can see a speaker’s connection information, including status, Wi-Fi signal strength, signal/noise ratio, frequency, IP address, and more. You can also find its volume output, Trueplay setup status, line-in connection, voice control status, serial number, hardware model and version, and which Sonos platform it operates on.

System Health can also show you your account details, Sonos ID, Controller ID, and your current app build version. System Health comes after Sonos updated the System Updates tab, which now displays an overview of your app, system, and headphone update status. This page also links to the Sonos release notes.

Sonos’ blog post states that this feature is new and still open to change, especially if the Sonos community has a particularly overwhelming response to it. The blog post also disclaims that this feature is a first look, not a deep dive.

However, after a brief first use, I see it as a great way to quickly access all the details you need about your systems and speakers, especially if you’re doing some rewiring, moving a speaker to a new room, or general troubleshooting.

System Health is rolling out to iOS users first. I updated my Sonos app in the App Store and was able to access it, but Sonos’ blog post states that this update is a phased rollout.

Updates to the Sonos app and its player are a long time coming. After receiving several new ways to control your speakers’ volume (I think we’re up to three), Sonos is realizing that granular volume control is a high priority for many Sonos users, including me.

The in-app volume dial is cool, and the interactive volume scrubber is a nice touch, but there’s nothing more jarring than wanting to play some tunes on my kitchen counter speaker, only for it to blast at 80% from when my husband was watching football the night before.

Sonos’ latest big update to volume this time around is Presets, a way to start playback in a specific room at a set volume. I haven’t found this feature in my app’s update yet, but I think it’s because my hardware needs an update. Presets will be available on iOS and Android.

Fortunately, I did use another update to the Sonos miniplayer: swipe to skip. What a teeny, tiny but useful feature. It works just like the miniplayer in Apple Music and Spotify; when the app is open, you can swipe left to skip to the next song.

One major caveat: swiping right to replay a track doesn’t work — at least not yet. Swiping both ways seems like a given to me, so it feels odd that you can’t. Still, being able to swipe the miniplayer to the next track is better than always having the main player open to toggle tracks. This feature is also coming to iOS and Android.

Sonos’ miniplayer is getting so much better; you can swipe to the next track and easily control volume from it, even when you have the Ace or Ace Ultra connected (I tried). The in-app volume dial also works with Sonos headphones.

Also: Sonos Play vs. Sonos Move 2: Why I’d go with the $200 cheaper Bluetooth speaker

Speaking of the Ace Ultra, a firmware update is available. A new Vocal Guidance feature can announce the battery percentage when you power on the headphones, when the audio mode changes from ANC to Transparency, and which device your headphones are connected to via Bluetooth.

It feels like this update is the final stretch before Sonos 27voice arrives, as the release notes suggest. It appears Sonos is laying the groundwork for speakers to support the AI-powered voice assistant in Early Access. Once it’s here, I’ll test it as soon as I can.

#3168. Scientists Build Biocomputer That Runs on Bacteria to Solve Hard Problems

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The study relied on the bacterium E. coli and V. natriegens to run the calculations.

Move over, microchips. The next generation of supercomputing might just run on living bacteria. For 20 years, an international team of scientists has been developing a biocomputer that uses bacteria to process information. Scientists from McGill University in Montreal announced their findings on Nov. 3 and published a paper detailing the results earlier this year in Nature.

Researchers from Canada, Europe, the United Kingdom and Australia contributed to this work, which combines biology with computer science and engineering. The researchers say the resulting biocomputer could be used to solve problems that give standard computers a hard time.

“Electronic (sequential) computers are not meant, or designed, to solve decision trees,” Dan Nicolau, a McGill bioengineering professor and senior author for the research paper, told CNET via email.

Nicolau noted that if electronic computers are to solve these types of problems, the computers will need a lot of RAM.

The study relied on the bacterium Escherichia coli and Vibrio natriegens to run the calculations. The researchers used E. coli because it moves through fluid in a predictable, measurable way and V. natriegens because it reproduces very quickly.

By using live bacteria rather than digital processing, the team says the biocomputer can solve big, complex problems at a small fraction of the memory and resources that regular computers require.

The researchers tested the biocomputer with a seemingly simple math problem called the Subset Sum Problem, which famously becomes exponentially harder as the number of inputs increases.

When the Subset Sum Problem inputs grow too large, the problem is known to give traditional computers issues, such as taking centuries, or even millions of years, to solve the problem.

The researchers translated the problem into a graph that branches off into each possible combination of inputs. Next, the team created a tiny physical structure that mirrored the Subset Sum Problem graph.

Inside the structure, they built a network of tunnels to mirror the graph branches. Each fork in the tunnels represents a decision point, and every possible route through the tunnels represents a different solution to the problem.

The researchers unleashed bacteria, which rapidly reproduce, inside the tunnels. The fast-growing bacteria moved through the tunnels, exploring many routes to the solution simultaneously.

Compared to digital processing, the bacteria are slow. But rather than tackling a problem sequentially, as traditional computers do, the bacteria can examine many solutions at once. And if you need more computing power, bacterial reproduction within the tunnels creates additional processing units to help solve the problem.

The team used automated image analysis to follow the bacteria through the correct tunnels. In this way, the researchers were able to tell which paths through the network satisfied the problem’s constraints.

The researchers were also able to adjust temperatures to prevent bacteria overcrowding while traveling through the network.

Enterprising fans have figured out how to run Doom, the groundbreaking 1993 first-person shooter video game, on everything from E. coli to a thermostat. Nicolau says Doom could probably run on the new system, with an important caveat concerning the biocomputer’s size.

“(The biocomputer) must be huge!” Nicolau said. Because bacteria make slow processors, you would need a massive biocomputer to host enough bacteria to run a video game.

But because no RAM is needed, Nicolau said biocomputing could help to solve the global RAM shortage, and even broaden our understanding of what a computer could be.

“A computer is a device which accepts (input) numbers and gets out (output) numbers. Full stop,” he said. “All other uses of the word computer (are) from our point of view, well, poetical.”

On slide 16, this outlines the drilling inventory in our legacy Haynesville area at the end of the third quarter. We have 770 gross non-operated locations with a 12% working interest, or 96 net locations. 442 of our 899 gross operated locations, or nearly 50%, have laterals exceeding 10,000 feet, and the average lateral length in our inventory stands at 10,212 feet. Our gross operated inventory is evenly split between the Haynesville and the Bossier. Also included in the legacy Haynesville inventory is 108 gross horseshoe locations with 50% Haynesville and 50% in the Bossier.

We currently have four rigs, they are running on our legacy Haynesville area, which provides us with a long runway of future drilling locations. Slide 17, this outlines our estimated drilling inventory in the Western Haynesville. We have 3,255 gross operated locations and 2,507 net locations in the Western Haynesville, which equates to an average working interest of 77%. Our total net locations are estimated since much of the Western Haynesville acreage has not been unitized. Roughly 40% of our 3,255 gross operated locations, or 1,317 locations, have laterals exceeding 10,000 feet. 61% of our gross operated locations have laterals exceeding 8,500 feet. The average lateral in our Western Haynesville inventory is 8,884 feet.

Our Western Haynesville drilling inventory is more weighted to the Bossier formation, with nearly two-thirds of the inventory in the Bossier, and one-third of our inventory is in the Haynesville. We currently have five rigs running on our Western Haynesville acreage today. Slide 18 is an overview of our horseshoe well drilling program, which allows for extended reach and reentry opportunities for higher return drilling locations. The improved drilling economics of the horseshoe wells unlocks previously stranded acreage by converting two sectional laterals into a single two-mile lateral. Since starting the horseshoe program, we have turned 17 horseshoe wells to sales with an average IP of 29 million cubic feet a day and an average lateral length of 10,223 feet.

The two most recent horseshoe wells have an average lateral length of 13,518 feet. As mentioned on the previous slide, we have 108 remaining horseshoe locations as of the end of the third quarter. In addition to the drilling of horseshoe wells, we have identified a number of enhancements to further improve returns, including the rotary steerable technology, redevelopment opportunities, the longer laterals, up to 15,000-20,000 foot, and drill-through applications. Slide 19 outlines our average lateral length drilled based on the wells that we drilled to total depth. The average lateral lengths are shown separately for our legacy Haynesville area and our Western Haynesville areas.

In the third quarter, we drilled 16 wells to total depth in the legacy Haynesville area with an average lateral length of 11,905 feet. The individual laterals range from 6,050 feet up to a max of 15,923 feet. The longest lateral drill to date in the legacy Haynesville area still stands at 17,409 feet. In the third quarter, we also drilled five wells to total depth in the Western Haynesville, with an average lateral length of 8,587 feet. The individual laterals range from 6,936 feet up to a max of 10,920 feet. Our longest lateral drill to date in the Western Haynesville is 14,783 feet. To date, we have drilled 54 wells to total depth in the Western Haynesville.

23 of these 54 wells have laterals exceeding 10,000 feet. Slide 20 summarizes the 38 wells that we have turned to sales in our legacy Haynesville area so far in 2026. The average lateral length was 11,530 feet, and the individual laterals ranged on the low end from 8,497 feet up to a high of 15,772 feet. The average IP for the 38 wells is 28 million cubic feet per day, and included in these 38 wells is 14 horseshoe wells. Slide 21 outlines the 17 wells that we have turned to sales on our Western Haynesville acreage so far in 2026.

These 17 wells had an average lateral length of 10,153 feet and an average initial production rate of 31 million cubic feet per day. Since our last call, we have turned six additional wells to sales with IP rates ranging from 26 to 40 million cubic feet per day and an average IP of 33 million cubic feet per day. We have a total of 47 wells currently producing on our Western Haynesville acreage. Slide 22 highlights our drilling efficiency in the legacy Haynesville area. This is for our benchmark long lateral wells that have laterals over 8,500 feet long.

In the third quarter, we drilled 14 of our benchmark long lateral wells to total depth in the legacy Haynesville and averaged 22 days to total depth. Correspondingly, we averaged 1,156 feet drilled per day on our legacy Haynesville acreage, and this represents a 14% increase versus the second quarter of 2026. Five of the wells we drilled in the third quarter were horseshoe wells. Slide 23, this highlights our drilling progress in the Western Haynesville. During the third quarter, we drilled five wells to total depth. This gives us a total of 52 wells drilled to total depth through the end of the third quarter.

We averaged 56 drilling days for the five wells drilled to total depth during the quarter. This is a decrease of three days compared to the second quarter. The drilling speed of 461 feet per day during the third quarter was 2% lower than the second quarter. The main reason the drilling speed decreased from the second to third quarter was the Dollie Jones. That was our first big hole lateral we drilled during the second quarter, and this well drilled 25% faster than our other wells. If we'd taken the Dollie Jones, it would have been excluded. Our drilling speeds would have improved in the third quarter.

Slide 24 details our D&C costs through the third quarter for our benchmark long lateral wells in the Legacy Haynesville area. These costs reflect all of the wells with laterals over 8,500 foot long. The drilling costs are based on the quarter in which the wells were reached TD, and the completion costs are based during the quarter on the wells that were turned to sales. During the third quarter, we drilled 14 of our benchmark long lateral wells to total depth, including five horseshoe wells. Our third quarter drilling costs averaged $634 a foot. This is an 11% decrease compared to the second quarter.

Our improved drilling performance in the third quarter can be attributed to having much stronger lateral drilling performance compared to the second quarter, which outweighed the impacts of the slightly higher service costs we did experience during the quarter. The rotary steerable drilling technology being deployed in our Legacy Haynesville area, especially in our horseshoe wells, has continued to deliver superior results. It is driving our drilling efficiencies higher. During the third quarter, we also turned 15 of our benchmark long lateral wells to sales on our Legacy Haynesville acreage, of which five were horseshoe wells. The third quarter completion costs came in at $715 a foot. This is a 5% increase compared to the second quarter.

The higher completion costs in the third quarter is partially the result of completing three single well pads during the third quarter, compared to nine during the second quarter. We also experienced the higher service costs during the third quarter. On slide 25 is a summary of our D&C costs through the third quarter for all wells drilled in the Western Haynesville. During the third quarter, we drilled five wells to total depth in the Western Haynesville. Average lateral length was 8,587 feet. The third quarter drilling cost averaged $1,934 a foot. This represents an 11% increase compared to the second quarter.

The biggest factor in our higher drilling costs for the third quarter was the shorter average lateral length of 8,587 feet for the wells in this quarter. To a lesser extent, the higher service costs we experienced also contributed to the higher drilling costs for the quarter. During the third quarter, we drilled our second big hole lateral. This time we drilled it to a more challenging lateral target in the Haynesville, but again, our results met our expectations. During the third quarter, we also turned six wells to sales in our Western Haynesville acreage that had an average lateral length of 9,829 feet. The third quarter completion cost averaged $1,959 a foot.

This is a 22% increase compared to the second quarter, and we had several drivers affecting the higher completion costs during the quarter. The primary drivers have been the transition to pumping the larger fracs. This led to we had a 12% higher proppant loading in the third quarter compared to the second quarter. Couple that with the higher service costs that we had. We also tubed up all but one of our third quarter wells, as opposed to only tubing up one of our wells in the second quarter.

Back to the drilling side, we have been very pleased with the results of our first three big hole lateral wells, and we are planning more of these wells for the future. The bigger hole in the lateral creates the lower downhole temperatures, and we are seeing longer, more reliable runs from our downhole drilling assemblies, and it has also provided us with much better steering ability so that we can keep our laterals on target. One last item I want to update from our last call, we should be deploying our first 10,000 PSI rig in the Western Haynesville towards the end of this month, which we fully anticipate will lead to faster drill times.

We are planning to upgrade two more of our rigs to 10K capability in the second quarter of next year. I will now turn the call back over to Jay.

Jay Allison: Dan, great job. Roland, great job. If you will go over to slide 26, we will summarize our outlook for 2026. Again, our primary goal continues to be advancing our Western Haynesville that will position Comstock to benefit from the longer term growth in natural gas demand. We have five operated drilling rigs in Western Haynesville to continue to delineate the new play. We expect to drill 19 wells and turn 20 wells to sales in 2026, and we expect drilling efficiencies and changes to our completion design to continue to drive up productivity and drive down D&C costs.

We have four operated rigs drilling in Legacy Haynesville to support production growth in 2026 and 2027, and expect to drill 52 wells and turn 45 wells to sales in 2026. The Jones drilling venture allows us to generate free cash flow in the fourth quarter while supporting the ongoing delineation and development of the Western Haynesville. The SOCAR transaction will allow us to retire half of our debt outstanding, providing us a strong balance sheet as we enter 2027. Comstock has captured the massive Western Haynesville footprint and been successfully drilling wells there since 2021. At the same time, we own Pinnacle Gas Services, our midstream, to ensure takeaway.

We believe natural gas will be undersupplied by 2029, with the demand growth of LNG going from about 20 BCF a day now to 35 BCF a day by 2032, plus the additional 12 BCF needed to provide power for turbines for data centers. Where our Haynesville Bossier leases are located is the sweet spot for demand. Our goal is to protect our natural gas assets, protect our midstream company, PGS, prudently develop our Western Haynesville footprint and add to it monthly, protect our balance sheet, and have the best partner in the world on our side. With the addition of NextEra, Sixth Street, and SOCAR, I believe we have the winning team.

When Jerry Jones and his family touched Comstock in 2018, we became who we are today. That support 100% allowed us to purchase Covey Park in 2019, close the numerous acquisitions around the Western Haynesville, acquire PGS, and lease thousands of acres in our Western Haynesville at a time of very low natural gas prices. The Jones relationship also helped secure SOCAR as a forever partner that provides us LNG marketing opportunities in Europe. On September 1st, 2026, the Jones DrillCo, $450 million, allows us to generate free cash flow in the fourth quarter while supporting the continued development and delineation of our 547,000 net acres in our Western Haynesville, as well as provide volumes to Pinnacle.

Jerry asked me to make the following comment. His commitment to Comstock is because of his unwavering faith in management, an exemplary natural gas asset base that we control, and the tremendous value of U.S. gas in the future. That is why the Jones family have invested over $1 billion in Comstock equity. With that, I want to thank you for your time. Slide 28 provides guidance for the rest of 2026, which Ron can discuss with you directly if you have questions. For the rest of the call, we will take questions from analysts who follow the company. I will turn it back over to you.

Operator: Okay, thank you. At this time, we will conduct the question-and-answer session. As a reminder, to ask a question, you will need to press star 11 on your telephone and wait for your name to be announced. To withdraw your question, please press star 11 again. We ask that everyone limit to just one question and one follow-up question. Please stand by while we compile the roster. Our first question comes from the line of John Annis with Texas Capital. Go ahead, your line is open.

John Annis: Hey, good morning all, and thanks for taking my questions. For my first one, the Dollie Jones well delivered a 40 million a day IP using the big hole design, and I think you are now drilling your fourth well with that design. What have you learned about the repeatability of results on drilling and well performance, and then ultimately, what portion of the Western Haynesville inventory could ultimately be developed this way?

Dan Harrison: That is a really good question. We are drilling our fourth well at the moment with the big hole design. We have not seen anything to date that tells us that we have any concerns with that design. We really need to drill more wells to just hone in on where the breakover is between drilling a slim hole versus a big hole design. Right now, I would probably just say it is somewhere between 10,000 and 11,000 foot lateral length.

Our goal is, of course, we had the shorter average lateral lengths that we reported for the quarter, and that is just due to where we are trying to hold acreage, and the acreage layout and geology and some other things. But in the future, we will definitely be getting the laterals longer in the years ahead. I would say probably the majority of all our future wells, maybe not within the next year or so, but further out, I would say the majority of the wells will be drilled with the big hole design. We just need some more data to just hone in on really just kind of where that crossover mark is.

But we have been super pleased with it. You asked about the Dollie Jones. That was the first one. That thing really drilled incredibly fast. That was drilled to the Bossier. Our second big hole that I kind of mentioned on one of the slides was drilled to the Haynesville. The Haynesville, just on average out here, is a little bit harder digging than it is in the Bossier. The results from the second well were about right on par with what we expected. But I think maybe one of the things to drive home is the intangible benefit of drilling the big hole.

We can steer and keep the laterals on target much more easy than we can than when we are drilling with the slim hole. When staying on target, this directly correlates to the performance of these wells. You want to keep that lateral right there in the best rock where you want it. Not only can we drill long, but even when we are drilling long, we can still keep that thing on target way out there at the end, which the slim holes, they will start walking, and we have a lot more difficulty keeping them on target when the wells get long. Then that just leads to other issues that add drilling days. Happy with the big holes.

John Annis: Got it. I appreciate all that color. Maybe staying on completion design. Last quarter, you noted the 2Q wells were the first full batch completed with 5,000 to 6,000 pounds of proppant per foot, and said their early pressures look encouraging. With another quarter of production history, are you seeing a measurable improvement in expected EURs, and is that uplift, in your view, sufficient to justify the 12% or so higher proppant loading?

Dan Harrison: Definitely. Absolutely. We actually transitioned our standard frac design when we started out, and really for a lot of early wells, was 4,000 pounds per foot. We did have one big job we pumped back early on, one of the Robertson County wells, but other than that, they were all 4,000 pounds per foot. We transitioned to the bigger fracs really starting in December of 2025 when we started popping them. Every well in 2026 has either been 5,000 or 6,000 pounds per foot. When you run the math on the economics, I mean, you only need maybe an incremental like 0.2 BCF per 1,000 to justify adding another 2,000 pounds per foot.

When you look at the well performance we have today, which it's early on some of these wells, but they do look really good. When you take that early data and combine it with the modeling and stuff that the reservoir group has done, we easily should surpass that 0.2 BCF per 1,000 incremental. That's definitely the direction we're going.

John Annis: Got it. I appreciate the time. I'll turn it back.

Operator: Thank you. One moment. Our next call comes from the line of Carlos Escalante with Wolfe Research. Your line is open.

Carlos Escalante: Howdy, Jay and Roland and team. How are you guys doing today? Thank you for taking our call. I do not think that when you gave preliminary outlook of when you thought the HBP program would be done, that you contemplated five rigs in the basin, or at least as quick as you did. I wonder if you can remind us or reframe for us, when do you think you would hit your threshold, and how do you foresee that transition from HBP-driven wells move over to value-driven or return-driven operations?

Should we see or should we expect perhaps a quicker inflection on D&C per foot when that does happen anytime sooner? Thank you.

Roland Burns: I will let Dan answer most of it, but I would just say that what the fifth rig is going to allow us to do is to put some more development wells into the program and not have to 100% keep all the projects on HBP acreage. I think we are still on the same kind of timeframe, because we are very comfortable with that timeframe to HBP the acreage. But with the additional rigs, we can now drill some more wells on the same pad, also drill in areas where we have already really spent a lot of money to figure out the area really well.

I think the ability to drill some development wells will definitely start to see a positive impact on the overall program as far as cost. That is kind of the direction. We will probably use the additional drilling rig there now that we have support of other partners, such as the Jones Partnership and SOCAR, to add infill development wells along the way in the program and meet our HBP goals with the overall drilling program.

Jay Allison: I think we will have a dual program, which we needed. We are to the point after, I think we will have drilled 60 wells at the end of this year in the Western Haynesville. I think our timeframe, even though we add acreage every month, our timeframe to hold all of it with the four-plus rigs is still the same. But now we have a dual goal. We can come in, and the millions of dollars that we have spent for gathering and takeaway and the pads, we can now drill additional wells on those pads, and I think you will see material cost savings.

Now that we have drilled around a bunch of these wells, we understand where we should keep the lateral. You add all the new drilling tools that we have, I think you will see the costs come down. I think you'll see the productivity go up, particularly with the choke management that we're using now. We'll blossom on some of the production rates we will be giving you in the future.

Dan Harrison: I think Jay and Roland gave you a pretty good answer. I do not really have a lot to add to that. We are blending in some infill development wells a little bit in 2027, which allow. Those wells we can set up with the longer laterals and in the areas where we already have proven offset well performance to kind of help balance out that HBP program.

Carlos Escalante: Sure. No, thank you to the three of you. That sounds like a solid answer, I think. On productivity, just going a step further perhaps on the prior question. If I look at your, particularly one of the Craig Smart, and I am sure I am butchering that name, Craig Smart wells, your normalized initial production rate as a very quick and dirty metric, looks to have jumped and actually posted one of the highest numbers in the two years you have been doing a lot of the drilling.

Just wondering, that is obviously just one piece of the puzzle, initial production, but what steps are you taking or what of the completion design tweaks you have done give you confidence that you can flatten the decline rate, or said another way, can lead to maximization of your EUR and really keep that production up the same way that you perhaps did with some of the earlier wells alongside that Circle M trend line?

Dan Harrison: Yeah. You got the names right, Crutchmore. I think everybody struggles with that a little bit. The answer, without making it real complicated, is the larger fracs. Definitely believe in the larger fracs like we talked about earlier. It just takes a minimal incremental EUR, which we should easily surpass, and the conservative drawdown strategy. You are contacting a lot more rock, you are creating a lot more, stimulating a lot more reservoir volume, and with the conservative drawdown, you keep that open. That is going to lead to the bigger EURs.

The early data that we have got on the wells that we have fracked in the last year with the larger fracs are showing that we are heading in that direction. We do need longer-term production to prove that out, but it is all pointing to where we expect it to go.

Jay Allison: I think the good thing on your question is, if you go probably 90 miles north to south, that is kind of a guess number, but the rock that we have found, I mean, it is consistent quality resource rock. All we are doing now is we have extended it to the north and south, starting with the Circle M, going to Elijah 1, even extended it to the north. Now we are going a little bit west. It is not the inventory, the 2,500 locations, it is not the rock. It is now really, with Dan's program, that is, we are getting to the point where we can have some repeatability.

That is another reason we are going to go in and drill some of these infill wells. Then why? Because of the demand for natural gas for the future.

Operator: One moment. The next question comes from the line of Paul Diamond with Citi. Go ahead, your line is open.

Paul Diamond: Thank you. Good morning, all. Thanks for taking the call. Just real quick on the SOCAR deal. Roland Burns: Thanks, Paul. As they lock that down, they will be able to come up with specific opportunities for us to look at. Paul Diamond: Got it. Appreciate the clarity. Talking a bit more about the rig upgrades you guys referenced, going at 10,000 PSI, potentially go 20,000, one on the way, two more being considered. Can you talk about how tangibly or quantitatively that actually translates into higher drill speeds? I guess, where does the clip-off go? How much faster do we see?

Dan Harrison: Good question. I guess we really don't know exactly what this is going to turn out to look like, but we do have the first one. Actually, we got a rig move probably coming up in a couple of weeks, and that's when the first 10,000, the first pad we drill with the 10K rig will be spudding hopefully here in a couple of weeks. I think if you just basically mathematically write, the higher pump pressures, the higher flow rates you can pump, get better efficiency out of the motors, you get more horsepower to the bit. Basically, those just conventional thinking, that's going to transfer into higher ROPs.

Some of the motors we run in the laterals, specifically like on slim holes, sometimes we don't get quite the GPMs or flow rate to the motors to have them operating at their peak efficiency. The 10K rig being able to pump faster will let us achieve those things. Very comfortable. I know there's some other operators that have already taken some 10K rigs and that are adding more 10K rigs. I think we're going to see that even industry-wide. I think you'll see this pick up a little bit more also as everybody gets comfortable with the higher performance.

Operator: One moment. Our next question comes from the line of Jacob Roberts with TPH Research. Your line is now open.

Jacob Roberts: Morning. Guys, I wanted to start on the Western Haynesville, and when we look at the 2025 and 2026 vintages and the performance we're seeing out of those against, let's call it a $35 million-$40 million cost for a 10,000-foot lateral, can you speak to where you see the full cycle breakeven gas price today, and then ultimately where you would like to see that head over the coming years? Dan Harrison: I think with the costs that we have today with where we're at, I think we're in that ballpark, just straight up breakeven. We don't see a whole lot of an increase, and maybe hopefully it retreats a little bit next year.
