But these two sales are just the latest examples of our strategy in action. We acquire high-quality businesses at attractive values, making them stronger through operational improvements and recycling capital when the time is right to redeploy into new opportunities. We've been doing just that. We closed new investments in World Freight Company and Gregg Distributors and reached an agreement to acquire Reliance Worldwide Corporation, a global leader in plumbing products with category-defining brands, resilient demand, and significant opportunities for operational improvement.

Together, these three investments represent more than $500 million of capital from BBUC. These investments are great examples of the opportunities we're seeing in today's market. They are high-quality businesses with strong competitive positions and durable cash flows. What really excites us is the opportunity to make them even better. Around the world, companies are rethinking how they operate in response to changing supply chains, cost pressures, and advances in technology. These shifts are creating significant opportunities to improve productivity, reduce costs, and make businesses more competitive. We've spent decades making businesses better, and we believe that experience gives us a distinct advantage.

Over the past two years, we've committed more than $1.2 billion to acquire seven market-leading industrial and services businesses. We see significant opportunities in manufacturing efficiency, procurement, commercial execution, and technology to grow earnings and cash flow at these businesses. We're still in the early stages of executing our value creation plans, so much of the opportunity is still ahead of us. Remember, we have a long track record of turning these operational improvements into real cash for our shareholders. Since creating BBUC, we've sold about 30 businesses, generating roughly $9 billion in proceeds and a 19% realized IRR. In aggregate, these monetizations were done at about a 12% premium to our NAV.

Looking ahead, we have a strong pipeline of new investments, a lot of upside in what we already own, and significant capital coming back to us from monetizations. This puts us in an excellent position to continue compounding value for our shareholders. One of the best examples of our approach in action is Clarios. Since acquiring the business, we've significantly grown its earnings, strengthened its operations, and positioned it for the next phase of growth. Today, Clarios is our largest investment, and honestly, we believe the best is yet to come. I'm very pleased to have Mark Wallace, Clarios' CEO, joining us today to share more about the business, the progress we're making, and the opportunities ahead.

Mark Wallace: Thank you, Anuj, and good morning, everyone. It's great to be back with you. I'd like to spend a few minutes providing an update on Clarios, including the strength of our core business and the opportunities we are pursuing that will accelerate our growth and expand our addressable markets, from supercapacitors that help stabilize power demand in artificial intelligence data centers to connected services that help commercial fleets reduce downtime while creating new recurring revenue streams. I'll also touch on how our recent portfolio actions support our long-term strategy. Let me start with our performance. We finished fiscal 2026 with our fourth consecutive year of record financial results.

That performance underscores the strength and earnings power of our core business and provides a strong foundation for long-term growth. At the center of the foundation is our highly resilient business model. Clarios is a global leader in low-voltage energy storage, approximately four times the size of our nearest competitor. We power roughly one in three vehicles on the road, and we sell more than 150 million batteries annually. Approximately 80% of our sales are in the stable aftermarket, where battery replacement is essential and recurring. This scale is supported by a well-established circular model that recovers and reuses critical minerals across the battery life cycle. That aftermarket exposure provides significant stability while also creating meaningful long-term growth potential.

One of the most important drivers is the continued shift towards higher-value advanced batteries, which we expect to be a multi-decade tailwind. Advanced batteries now represent 35% of our units sold, up from just 10% in fiscal 2015. More than 70% of the batteries we sell into the original equipment channel today are advanced batteries. While the aftermarket penetration remains significantly lower, over time, we expect the aftermarket to naturally follow as those vehicles move through the replacement cycle. Because advanced batteries generate greater revenue and profit per unit than conventional batteries, that mix shift creates an attractive long-term growth opportunity. At the same time, the role of the low-voltage power in vehicles is becoming more important.

Vehicles are becoming more electrified, connected, software-defined, and automated. That evolution requires more sophisticated low-voltage power systems to support electronics, critical vehicle functions, and safety redundancy. Importantly, that trend is largely powertrain-agnostic. Internal combustion, hybrid, and fully electric vehicles all require reliable low-voltage power. With more than 620 xEV platform wins to date, we have established a strong position as these architectures continue to evolve. For Clarios, that creates an opportunity to provide greater value to our customers and increase our dollar content per vehicle. This is the strategy behind the Clarios Power Management System, or CPMS.

By bringing together advanced batteries, supercapacitors, electronics, software, and monitoring capabilities, we can address a broader portion of the vehicle's low-voltage architecture and solve more of our customers' power management needs. More broadly, our $6 billion U.S. investment plan supports advanced battery production, critical mineral processing and recovery, next-generation technology, and state-of-the-art manufacturing. These investments strengthen our core while building the capabilities needed to support future growth. Alongside these investments, we remain intensely focused on driving operational efficiency across the business. We're utilizing AI and machine learning, advanced automation, and robotics to improve productivity, optimize our supply chain, and enhance our customer service. Continuous operational improvement is an important lever to support margin expansion and long-term value creation.

Beyond driving growth and efficiency in our automotive business, we also see opportunities to extend power management technology into new attractive markets. A great example is supercapacitors. Our acquisition of Maxwell Technologies added a complementary fast-response power technology to our portfolio. Within automotive, supercapacitors support peak power requirements, stabilization, and redundancy. Beyond automotive, we see applications in data centers, grid infrastructure, industrial applications, and renewable energy. Data centers are particularly interesting. AI workloads are creating increasingly volatile power demands that constrain existing infrastructures. Supercapacitors can respond almost instantly, helping smooth power spikes and bridge short-duration gaps between primary and backup power. We see an attractive opportunity as AI computing drives demand for fast, reliable power.

We are pursuing a similar opportunity through our connected services. By combining battery data, analytics, and our deep expertise, we can help fleet customers identify potential battery issues before they result in vehicle downtime. Today, our connected services solutions support approximately 20 commercial fleets across North America. These deployments validate the need for actionable battery intelligence that can improve uptime and maintenance planning. Over time, connected services can create reoccurring revenue opportunities, deepen customer relationships, and generate valuable insight to inform future innovation. As we pursue these opportunities, we remain focused on allocating capital to strengthen our competitive position and create shareholder value. Our recent portfolio actions are good examples.

Our planned acquisition of Ecobat U.S. operations includes three critical mineral recovery and processing facilities that together process more than 40 million batteries annually. Bringing these capabilities in-house advances our vertical integration, reduces reliance on third-party suppliers, and strengthens access to critical minerals, reinforcing both our closed-loop model and the security of domestic battery supply chains. It also allows us to benefit from greater vertical integration, creating an opportunity to improve margins over time. At the same time, we monetized our non-controlling economic interest in an equity stake in a large battery distributor while preserving our long-standing commercial relationship.

Taken together, these actions reflect a disciplined approach to managing the portfolio, investing in strategic assets and capabilities while maintaining financial flexibility for future growth and long-term shareholder value creation. As we look ahead, I am excited about where Clarios is positioned. We have a resilient cash generative core business. We are strengthening our automotive leadership as vehicle architecture has become more complex, while extending our capabilities into attractive new markets and recurring revenue opportunities. Together, we believe these growth platforms expand the markets we can address by approximately $32 billion today to an estimated $52 billion by 2040, supported in part by the growing demand for advanced power management solutions in data centers.

This strategy gives us multiple avenues to grow while continuing to drive operational efficiency, deploy capital, and with a discipline and create long-term value. Thank you, and I will turn it over now to Jaspreet.

Jaspreet Dehl: Thanks, Mark, and good morning, everyone. We generated third quarter Adjusted EBITDA of $594 million compared to $575 million in the prior period. Adjusted EFO for the quarter was $337 million compared to $284 million in the prior period. Current period Adjusted EFO includes $44 million of net gains, primarily related to the partial sale of La Trobe Financial. Turning to segment performance. Our industrial segment generated third quarter Adjusted EBITDA of $348 million compared to $316 million last year. On a same-store basis, Adjusted EBITDA increased approximately 8% over the prior period.

At Clarios, strong commercial execution, the continued favorable shift towards higher-margin advanced batteries, and higher U.S. production tax credits supported earnings, offsetting some softness in volumes and inflation-related cost pressures. BRK Ambiental delivered double-digit growth in Adjusted EBITDA, benefiting from contractual tariff increases and higher volumes. Performance at DexKo was broadly in line with last year, despite continued weakness in North American trailer markets. Improved margin within the business benefited from the team's continued effort to align its cost base with current demand, advance its commercial initiatives to offset inflation and tariff pressures, as well as accelerate automation. Moving to our business services segment, which generated third quarter Adjusted EBITDA of $204 million compared to $188 million last year.

On a same-store basis, Adjusted EBITDA increased by approximately 3% over the prior period. Sagen continued to benefit from resilient demand among first-time home buyers, even as broader housing activity in Canada remains slow. Losses and claims were higher during the quarter, reflecting increased claim severity and reserve strengthening, consistent with our expectation for normalization. The business is very well capitalized with a minimum capital adequacy ratio of 176% and continues to generate significant cash flow, which allowed it to pay us a $90 million distribution in the quarter. CDK delivered double-digit Adjusted EBITDA growth over the prior year, supported by cost-saving initiatives as well as continued cross-sell and upsell activity.

The business appointed a new CEO in August as the team continues to focus on initiatives to strengthen commercial execution and accelerate customer adoption of its modernized workforce. Finally, our infrastructure services segment generated third quarter Adjusted EBITDA of $76 million compared to $104 million last year. Prior results also included contributions from Altera's FPSO operations, which were sold earlier this year. At Modulaire, we were also impacted by softer demand and competitive pricing pressure alongside operational challenges in the U.K. A new CEO joined in September and is focused on strengthening operational execution, improving customer retention, and driving better commercial performance across the business, with the U.K. as the immediate priority.

At Scientific Games, weakened industry volumes and higher costs associated with new contract implementations weighed on results. This included higher-than-anticipated costs to deliver select international contracts. The business continues to execute on delivering a record number of implementations. These impacts were partially offset by performance improvement at BrandSafway. The business is benefiting from strong growth in white space markets, including semiconductors, power, and data centers, as well as higher fleet utilization and commercial initiatives. Turning to our balance sheet and capital allocation priorities. We ended the quarter with approximately $2.7 billion of pro forma liquidity at the corporate level. Our strong financial position provides significant flexibility to fund new investments and continue to buy back our shares.

Since launching our share repurchase program early last year, we bought back more than $335 million of shares. We continue to view repurchases as an attractive use of capital at current trading prices and will remain disciplined as we pursue new investment opportunities. As always, our priority is to deploy capital where we believe it will generate the greatest long-term value per share. With that, I will turn the call back to the operator for questions.

Operator: Thank you. As a reminder, to ask a question, please press star one on your telephone and wait for your name to be announced. To withdraw your question, please press star one again. One moment, please. Our first question comes from the line of Gary Ho with Desjardins Capital Markets.

Gary Ho: Hi, good morning. Maybe the first question is for Mark here. Thanks for joining the call. Very timely. I believe you mentioned a little bit of this in your prepared remarks, but I did see that Clarios agreed to redeem its Interstate stake for roughly $1 billion, and then also signed the supply agreement at the same time. Just wondering, why was now the right time to monetize the stake? And also maybe just tie that into your investment in Ecobat as well, kind of moving upstream in the recycling process. Just wondering if those two are kind of linked together?

Mark Wallace: Good morning, Gary. First and foremost, they are not linked together. I think just timing-wise, they end up hitting at the same time. Number one, our relationship with Interstate Batteries has been longstanding. However, I think it is important to note that we had a non-controlling stake in Interstate. So really for us, there was not a lot of value creation from the asset from that perspective. To be quite honest, we were able to monetize it at a significant multiple, as you can imagine, with that. So we were quite thankful we were able to negotiate with the family and get the multiple we received from the asset.

Plus, more importantly, we also secured a long-term seven-year agreement with Interstate Batteries because we have been their longstanding partner. From a supply chain perspective, we want to maintain that. When it relates to Ecobat, as we mentioned in our $6 billion investment plan in the United States, part of that was our critical minerals recovery. That was a great way for us to be able to, you know, basically add critical mineral recovery at a much faster pace than we would have done if we had done a greenfield, as an example.

We are quite pleased with both of these transactions, one in the amount of proceeds we received from Interstate, and more importantly, that we are able, hopefully, once it gets through the Justice Department and antitrust, we will have the Ecobat assets, which will be definitely accretive to our core business.

Gary Ho: Okay, great. Thanks for that. While I have you, maybe just a quick update on the 45X tax refund as it relates to the 2024 tax year. Just any update on that? I think in your last call, you mentioned interest is accruing and you are having regular contact with the IRS. Just any update in the last few months?

Mark Wallace: Yeah, Gary, nothing has changed. We continue our regular updates with the IRS. Yes, you are right, they are still accruing interest penalties as we go forward, but at this stage, we see no reason that would prevent us from being paid the 2024 refund.

Gary Ho: Okay, great. If I can just sneak one more in, maybe for Anuj or Jaspreet. We know it is early days, just following the midterm results in the U.S. Do you have any early read on which portfolio companies could benefit or could be affected by the outcome there?

Anuj Ranjan: No, I think, Gary, I'd say, Anuj here, look, the businesses we own and the kinds of things that we buy and have continued to invest in, these are all businesses that are purposefully resilient, can stand various different cycles. We've gone through a relatively inflationary period and with a lot of uncertainty many times before in these companies, and they've been just fine. It kind of comes back to our strategy of essential products and services, critical components and value chains, and things that customers need where we can make operational improvements. None of that has changed in our thesis for new investments or with our existing portfolio. So, nothing today.

It's, again, very early, but I'd say, so far what we're really focused on is the fundamental operations of our businesses, which are all going generally quite well.

Gary Ho: Okay, great. Those are my questions. Thank you.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Bart Dziarski with RBC Capital Markets.

Bart Dziarski: Great. Thanks for taking the questions. Good morning, everyone. I just wanted to see if we can get an update on the BPE-managed Evergreen Fund. The fair value last quarter was $490 million. What was the fair value this quarter? Just maybe talk about the momentum you're seeing there. Thanks.

Anuj Ranjan: Yeah, Jaspreet can talk about the fair value, and I will tell you a little bit about how we are doing on fundraising.

Jaspreet Dehl: Hi, Bart. It is Jaspreet. So I would say, the fair value has not changed materially quarter-over-quarter, so it is pretty consistent. We have rendered in the assets that we sold. The fair value is about $690 million, and we have gotten back close to $200 million on that. We are continuing to speak with the fund. As they are raising subscriptions, they have the ability to allocate their capital, so they have been raising capital and allocating some of the capital to pay us back.

Anuj Ranjan: Yeah, in terms of fundraising and the activity, I would say the interesting thing about the wealth channel is often, you get onboarded on the platforms, and then you start to work that platform's channel directly with the RIAs or the brokers or the end customers, and then you see the results of inflows trickle in after. That whole process is usually about a year, to be honest, before you see the cash come in. And I would just say that we continue to be at it. We are seeing quite a bit of momentum.

Our story around industrials and essential services is really resonating in this kind of an environment, and we are seeing that, you know, sort of pick up in the wealth channels as well. So, while we kind of, through what we can see in terms of leading indicators, I feel very good about the continued fundraising momentum through 2027.

Bart Dziarski: Okay, great. That is helpful. Then on the buyback, so Jaspreet talked about the pacing there and just your priority for the buyback. I am curious, where does buyback rank in the pecking order of capital deployment, and what should we expect in terms of the pacing of buybacks from here? Thanks.

Anuj Ranjan: Look, we always take a balanced approach, as you know, and both obviously deleveraging, returning capital to shareholders, and making new investments and acquisitions. We have done quite a bit of buyback in recent times because of, obviously, the stock price was a very attractive opportunity. I would say we just continue to have that balanced approach. Going forward, we do see opportunities to put capital to work, and we continue to. You have seen us make these modest-sized investments. In addition, we are doing a lot of monetizations and recycling that capital. We did a lot of deleveraging, and today, buybacks and new investments are probably going to continue to be of interest.

Jaspreet Dehl: Yeah, the only thing I'd add is that our balance sheet is as strong as it's ever been. Pro forma for the monetizations in each reference, we've got the liquidity of $2.7 billion, so it gives us a lot of flexibility.

Bart Dziarski: Great. That's it for me. Thanks for taking the questions.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Bill Katz with TD Cowen.

Bill Katz: Great. Thank you very much for taking the question this morning. I just want to start off with, it's great to see all the activity in the portfolio, both buying and selling. If we were to use the third quarter as a base level for the Adjusted EBITDA, how do we think about maybe the pro forma impact of maybe what's foregone from sale versus what might be able to come on in terms of redeployment? Thank you.

Jaspreet Dehl: I just want to make sure I got your question. Are you looking for just an understanding of where, if we look at the current quarter EBITDA and we run rate that, what does that look like?

Bill Katz: No, let me rephrase. I think you put up $594 million of Adjusted EBITDA in the quarter.

Bill Katz: I am just trying to understand, you have sold some things subsequent to quarter end, and I think you have been buying things. I am just trying to get to a, well, maybe I will rephrase. How do I think about the incremental accretion or dilution relative to the recent monetizations? Then maybe with DeployCo, how do you think about incremental synergies to maybe make up for anything that may have been sold off? Thank you.

Jaspreet Dehl: Right. Okay. Maybe if I just kind of think about that on an annual basis, it is a bit easier, and then we can get into quarter. Our annual kind of run rate EBITDA, round numbers right now, is about $2.5 billion. I think about that number, Multiplex is probably our largest sale. We have been generating circa $60 million of EBITDA from Multiplex. Then I would say, the lost contribution from La Trobe and some of the other monetizations that we have done over the last 12 months, I would say, estimated about $20 million-$25 million. Again, if we said round numbers, circa $100 million from asset sales. That gets us to about $2.4 billion.

If we think about the acquisitions that we have already made and you run rate those, plus some of the things in the pipeline, that will close end of year, early next year, I would say maybe quite not $100 million, because a lot of the acquisitions that we have been making have been smaller size and scale. But I would say we would probably get close back close to that $2.5 billion run rate number. I do not know if that gives you a bit of a high-level overview, but happy to take it offline and give you a bit more detail.

Bill Katz: Super helpful. Just as a follow-up, a little bit more of a nit question, so I apologize for the narrowness of it. On your P&L, it looked like you had a pretty high level of other income, and then the tax rate looked a little bit on the low side. I was wondering if you could just provide some guidance on how we should think about both those line items going forward?

Jaspreet Dehl: Sure. So, in other income and expenses, we generally have a lot of our non-cash movements, derivatives, items like that. So, there is some movements there. There is also LTIP accruals, just around payments, share-based payments and compensation on eventual monetizations. So, it is again, just movements and those types of things. Nothing very specific that I would call out there. On taxes, we had some tax recoveries, and actually call out Clarios. We had a deferred tax recovery at Clarios this quarter, which drove the overall tax cost lower.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Scott Fletcher with CIBC.

Scott Fletcher: Hi, good morning. Thinking about the strength of the balance sheet that you mentioned, Jaspreet, and the size of the recent deals you mentioned as being smaller. Given that strength, is there an appetite to maybe increase the size of the deals or the participation in the deals going forward? Or are you comfortable with this smaller, spreading it out across the smaller deals here?

Jaspreet Dehl: Yeah. Look, we tend to be very opportunistic in terms of the investments that we make. In the pipeline today, and some of the recent acquisitions that we've done, that mid to slightly larger style industrial businesses is where we've been very focused. Our proportionate share of investments is typically about a third when we invest alongside the funds. So, for now, we foresee making similar size investments. But as you said, we've got a lot of pro forma liquidity, and we've got a lot of flexibility. So, if we see something that's really compelling, we could do something larger. But for now, the plan is to continue to invest alongside the fund.

Based on the current pipeline, the size of investments that you've been seeing, that's probably reasonable.

Scott Fletcher: Okay, thanks. That's helpful. Then maybe one for Mark on the Clarios side of things. Just, could you share your priorities or plans for capital allocation? Now that you've sold, monetized an asset, done some M&A, is there more of a focus on investing in the build-out, or is there other opportunities for maybe M&A along in your pipeline? Thanks.

Mark Wallace: Yeah. Scott, nothing's changed in our strategy. So first and foremost is a continued investment in the underlying business itself and strengthening the balance sheet. As you can imagine, I talked about some of the new growth areas for the company. So, we're always active in the inorganic markets as well. So, we continue to be quite inquisitive of things that could be accretive to the business longer term. So, those would be priorities. Then lastly, as you can imagine, with our free cash flow generation ongoing, we definitely can support more shareholder-friendly activities in the future.

Scott Fletcher: Okay, great. That is helpful. Thank you.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Devin Dodge with BMO Capital Markets.

Devin Dodge: Yeah, thanks. Good morning, everybody. I am going to start with a question for Mark. Mark, you highlighted a few new offerings to augment the core low-voltage auto battery business. Some of these are not overly material today, but just wondering if you could frame how much revenue comes through these other products now, and if we dream the dream, what the potential contributions could be over the next, call it, three to five years?

Mark Wallace: Yeah. In the case in the automotive technology business that I kind of referenced, which is a combination of energy storage devices, supercapacitors, embedded software and electronics, that is kind of what I call our advanced auto technology business. Most of that is going to be launching starting in 2028. But the ramp-up will happen around, full ramp-up will happen around 2030. So, when you look at it more from a revenue perspective, we have over $2 billion of backlog just in that space itself. That is all contractual. We have two factories that are being retrofitted as we speak, and those will start, like I said, production in 2028.

When it comes to the, let us call it the non-automotive space, especially data centers, with the acquisition of Maxwell, there is quite a high demand for our supercapacitor systems for data center utilization. We're going to be bringing on two new factories over the next 18 months just to support what I call the near-term demand that we're seeing in data centers. Those two businesses combined, we're expecting our addressable market to grow by 50%. We definitely see those having a more larger impact in our earnings profile and our revenue growth closer to the end of this decade.

Devin Dodge: Okay. That's interesting. Thanks for that. Okay. I'm not sure who wants to take this, but it's another one on Clarios. We've seen financial leverage, I think it's down to the low fours if you back out the credits, and you should decline further once more credits are received. It just seems like you're likely nearing another decision for how to monetize this business. I was just wondering if you could talk about your exit options that you're considering. You've also owned this business for nearly eight years, and I'm not sure if there is a need to return capital to Brookfield's private fund investors plays into the exit options being considered.

Anuj Ranjan: Yeah, I'll take that. I think, look, Clarios is an amazing business. It's highly, highly cash generative. In the future, when we look forward, the potential, the power of that cash flow for BBU is incredible. I'd say just starting with, we're very, very pleased. I'm really excited about what Mark and the team have done and what's actually, frankly, what's ahead, as in my earlier comments, is probably better than what we've seen in the past.

That being said, obviously, we're always open to opportunities to crystallize value, and there's a lot of ways that we can look to crystallize value, which could include, of course, selling the business, but it could also include ways to capture some sort of value at the parent with maybe partial sales or other kinds of opportunities without necessarily needing to sell the entire business. All of these various, we want to retain optionality. The nice thing is when you got this highly cash-generative of a business, that will pay a very stable and growing dividend over a long time, we have all kinds of alternatives at our disposal.

It frankly will come down to in coming time as to what is the best value that we can achieve compared to the cash yield that we're getting. But again, with that sort of a cash yield, we're not in any hurry.

Devin Dodge: Okay, makes sense. Thanks for that, Anuj. Okay, and just one last one. I was going to ask about Nielsen. It is a business we do not talk very much about. Just wanted to know if you could give an update, a high-level update, how the business is performing, and just any color on why Brookfield elected not to participate in the recent acquisition there, and what that pro forma ownership will look like?

Jaspreet Dehl: Yeah, I can answer maybe the last part and then hand it over to Adrian to maybe just talk about what we are seeing in the business. I think you are referencing the DoubleVerify transaction that Nielsen recently announced. That transaction is primarily debt-funded and with a little bit of equity. As you know, we have got a pref investment in Nielsen, so convertible pref. The, you know, we are quite excited about the transaction, and we think it will be very accretive to the business and continue to kind of set it up for growth, and it will add value to our kind of converted share of the business.

The business was able to do that without requiring additional equity from us, and it really does not kind of impact our overall return profile. That is kind of the approach that we took on it.

Adrian Letts: Just to comment on the performance of the business, we are getting through all the large renewals now, and we are seeing upticks in the value of those renewals as we start to include other products and services, particularly around streaming. The Gracenote business is improving. If you look into the new products and services that we are launching, we are starting to see strong momentum on that. Look, overall, look, we remain very optimistic in terms of the opportunity of the business.

I think to Jaspreet's point, the DoubleVerify acquisition really adds to the portfolio of products and services that we can offer to our customers on either side of the marketplace, and it is a business that is performing well.

Devin Dodge: Okay, good color. I appreciate it. I will turn it over.

Operator: Thank you. As a reminder, to ask a question, please press star 11 on your telephone. Our next question comes from the line of Jaeme Gloyn with National Bank.

Jaeme Gloyn: Yeah, thanks. Good morning. Just a few questions on some of the company performance. First, Sagen, just wanted to get a sense as to the breakdown of what's driving the reserve build this quarter. Is it entirely macro-driven, or is there something you're seeing with either loss curves or just the underlying performance?

Jaspreet Dehl: Yeah, it's Jaspreet. I'll take that. I'd say the overall, what you're seeing in the losses is really a normalization towards the long-term, long range. I think we've said this before, but the long-term loss expectations are in that 15%-25% range, and we're seeing a normalization. Since we bought the business kind of late 2019, going through COVID and the home price appreciation, we've seen abnormally low loss ratios over a large period of time that we've held this business. Our expectation has always been that losses will increase and head more in that 15%-25% range. That's what we're seeing now.

In the quarter in particular, and kind of this year, we've seen continued downward pressure on home prices in Canada. I'd say, as you'd expect, the Ontario, GTA, those markets where we saw a substantial increase in home prices, that's where we've seen the largest correction, and I'd say the largest pressure. The loss ratios that we're seeing come through, part of it is the actual kind of experience, and then part of it is just shoring up reserves as we look forward, and we're looking at economic uncertainty. Rates went up, so just making sure that we've got that resilience in our reserves, given kind of the broader macro.

Jaeme Gloyn: Yeah. Okay, understood. Mostly severity from house price decline. The next one would be CDK, showing in growth and Adjusted EBITDA. Anything to draw out from that quarter's performance? The debt markets are obviously one thing, but the operating performance, the cash flow of the business continues to be positive and to grow on a year-over-year basis. Maybe just sort of talk through some of the initiatives that are still rolling through there at CDK?

Jaspreet Dehl: Yeah. Maybe I'll just make an opening comment and then hand it over to Adrian to talk about operating performance. I'd say the business had a good quarter this year. We have annual price increases, there's cross-sell, and the overall performance has been better. Churn in the business is still elevated, and we are kind of managing through that. What I would say is, you know, while the business is on the right path, and I'll let Adrian talk to everything that we're doing in the business, one quarter, we shouldn't extrapolate that as the trend. We are kind of proactively working on debt. The business just does generate a positive free cash flow.

It continues to invest in its modernization efforts, so the cash flow profile of the business is still good. But we are in active dialogue and looking at the debt maturity.

Adrian Letts: Just to build on operational performance, Jaspreet commented on this quarter's Adjusted EBITDA. Look, continued cross-selling and upselling initiatives, coupled with the appointment of a new CEO who brings deep operational experience in building and scaling large-scale technology and new products, the business is continuing to focus on executing its technology modernization program. That will also underpin CDK's product capabilities. It also improves customer support, improved retention, which gives us a really strong basis to drive cross-selling. It's important to remember, look, CDK's platform is deeply embedded into customer workflows.

It's one of the largest, it remains the largest dealer management software provider in North America, and has a really strong market position, and draws on 40 years of proprietary data, which we think, as you go through the ongoing modernization efforts, the business is really well-positioned to leverage AI as an opportunity to deliver much more value to customers.

Jaeme Gloyn: Okay. Then, last one, maybe similar to an earlier question. Elections in Brazil, a couple of Brazilian assets, obviously the market's maybe not as well received, but anything to draw out from an impact or effect that might affect those businesses on a go-forward basis?

Jaspreet Dehl: Yeah. Look, I'd say our two largest assets in Brazil, BRK Ambiental, our wastewater business, and Unidas, which is our fleet management and car rental business. Both of those businesses, operating performance has been very good. I think we called out that BRK Ambiental had double-digit EBITDA growth. We continue to optimize the operating costs in that business. We've recently bid on and acquired a new concession, so we're in the process of rolling that out. So business and operating performance has been excellent. But for both businesses, as with any business, extended periods of very high interest rates aren't really constructive.

So, we have seen high rates in Brazil for a long period of time, which has curtailed capital market activity. The rates have been coming down. I think the punchline from the elections is that the expectation is still that rates will come down, maybe a little bit of moderation on how quickly they come down. So I'd say our focus continues to be on operating these businesses well, compounding value, and being ready to monetize them when we get the appropriate window.

Operator: Thank you. I am showing no further questions. With that, I will hand the call back over to CEO Anuj Ranjan for any closing remarks.

Anuj Ranjan: Thank you all for being here this quarter. I look forward to speaking with you again next quarter.

Operator: Ladies and gentlemen, thank you for participating. This does conclude today's program. You may now disconnect.

Netflix is adding a new Discover feature, which recommends tailored streaming selections. Here's how it works.

AI tools are all over the internet, in the workplace, in your apps — and now there’s one coming on Netflix. The streaming giant just announced a new AI feature for the TV app called AI Discover, which will help users find titles that match their moods and interests. It’s initially being rolled out to a small group of users in the US whose language is set to English. To find out if you have access, check your Netflix navigation bar for the word “Discover” with a red gem icon next to it and a “New” label.

Also: Roku is taking away a fan-favorite screensaver

The AI Discover tab will be centered around themes. You’ll be able to pick from a range of themes depending on what you feel like watching, or how long you want to watch. You’ll also see selections that match what you’ve been watching lately and what’s popular.

You can refresh the list of suggestions or dive deeper with more complex search prompts. If you’d like to start over, you can pick the “Something different” option. To support AI Discover, Netflix is also adding a new button next to Play and My List that’ll let you tune your recommendations. You can press this button to keep a recommendation or to request that you don’t be recommended a title again.

Most streaming apps already rely quite heavily on machine learning and AI algorithms to offer user recommendations, even if they’re not marketed as AI features. Though most rely on traditional AI algorithms, like Prime Video’s “Recommended for you” tab, they personalize title recommendations based on your viewing history, likes and dislikes, and rental behavior.

Other platforms offer generative AI and features more similar to Netflix’s AI Discover. For example, YouTube features Gemini-powered searches that let you ask complex questions or use open-ended prompts to get results you want.

Also: The best early Black Friday TV deals are all at Best Buy

Some smart TV interfaces — including including Roku, Fire TV, Google TV, and, coming soon, Apple TV — have also adopted generative AI in their operating systems to let you use voice search with more naturally worded requests, and the system generates cross-platform results.

While I am itching to test this feature to see just how accurate it can be, Netflix hasn’t made it widely available yet. The company will gradually grant users access over the coming weeks, so stay tuned.

#3150. A New Water Heater Technology Kills Bacteria Right in the Tank

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

I asked the inventor about his design and when consumers might see the tech in their homes.

One challenge of current water heater designs is staying hot enough to kill harmful bacteria like Legionella pneumophila, which can cause Legionnaires’ disease. A new water heater design, developed and patented by researchers at the National Institute of Standards and Technology, aims to raise tank temperatures to 160 degrees Fahrenheit, which spells instant doom for Legionella bacteria.

Legionella bacteria love warm water, so while they struggle to survive in a water heater tank set to 120 F, they’re more than comfortable elsewhere in a home’s hot water pipes. It’s technically possible to achieve sufficient temperatures with existing water heaters, but those temperatures are also likely to scald human skin whenever you turn on the faucet.

The biggest innovation of this new design is how it finds a new use for heat exchangers, the same technology behind air conditioners, heat pumps, furnaces and refrigerators. I wanted to know more, so I reached out to David Yashar, a NIST mechanical engineer behind the new design.

As Yashar and his team researched ways to kill Legionella bacteria, they needed to figure out how to make tank temperatures around 160 F safe and practical for humans. They ultimately landed on the concept of using cold water entering the water heater to cool the hot water leaving the tank with an unmixed heat exchanger that contains the water inlet and outlet.

The principle behind unmixed heat exchangers—where the fluids don’t mix—is that incoming cold water gets a heating boost from the hot-water outlet while cooling the water to safe levels for people. As a result, the tank can maintain the high temperatures required to prevent pathogen growth behind illnesses like Legionnaires’ disease, which has a fatality rate of around 10%, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Beyond the safety benefits, the process recaptures some waste heat and can improve heating efficiency for the cold water, since it enters the tank warmer.

I’ve covered various heating, ventilation and air conditioning tech over the years, so I immediately recognized similarities between the new design’s unmixed heat exchanger and those used in HVAC and refrigerators. For example, air conditioners use a heat exchanger for the refrigeration cycle (also called the Carnot cycle) to pull heat from air inside your home (evaporator coil) and push it outside (condenser coil) without pulling in outside air. Additionally, heat pumps may use a heat exchanger for defrosting ice buildup when in heating mode.

When I asked about the similarities, Yashar noted that it wasn’t a coincidence that his patent took inspiration from HVAC and refrigeration tech. Yashar said, “My background is in HVAC&R, and it is very common to use unmixed heat exchangers like this to manipulate the bounds of the Carnot cycle to achieve some specific condition. I came up with the idea when I first learned about Legionella and the existing mitigation strategies.” He goes on to explain that using an unmixed heat exchanger “across the inlet and outlet was a very simple, effective, and inexpensive way to push the water temperature up to that condition and back down.”

It’s fitting that Yashar discovered better ways for heat exchangers not only to kill pathogens, but also to improve energy efficiency. Finding new applications for existing technology is certainly an underrated aspect of invention.

As exciting as this tech is, a patent doesn’t necessarily mean it will hit the market immediately. Yashar notes that while his research “proved the concept using a 60-gallon tank,” it depends on when manufacturers license the technology and get their engineers working on designing consumer products suitable for homes. This process could happen quickly or take several years.

It may be years before we see consumer heaters that use the promising new technology.

Because Yashar’s concept essentially modified an existing water heater, I asked if it would be possible to retrofit products in people’s homes. He notes that NIST’s project started with the intention of modifying the tank’s hardware and controls. “The steps we took might not be simple tasks for an existing application,” said Yashar. “It really depends on a lot of things, so it is best if people learn how this works and understand how to achieve it within their existing application.”

He brings up one important consideration: Retrofit tanks will need extra insulation to be worth it. It’s “absolutely necessary for a retrofit because the tank temperature will be about 40 degrees hotter than what the existing system was designed for. If this isn’t done, the standby losses would be very large.” Without appropriate insulation, any efficiency gained by the heat exchanger would be lost to heat loss in standby mode.

So, while a retrofit might be possible, it seems more likely to engineer a product from the ground up based on this design, especially if consumers want to keep utility costs manageable.

For more tips, see the best temperature to set your thermostat this winter and learn how to find air leaks in your home for more efficient heating.

#3148. Safari finally gets 3 popular browser features – and I can’t wait to try them

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

New developer beta release notes point to deeper Siri AI integration and more Safari customization.

Developer betas for MacOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and iOS 27.3 are here, with a few major upgrades to the Safari browser. Vertical tabs, adaptive dark mode, and deeper Siri AI integration are on the way to the public, but are first in beta for testing.

Also: Your Apple Watch has 2 new controversial listening features – but you have to opt in

Siri AI is expected to be further woven into Music, Messages, Photos, Calendar, and Safari. Adaptive dark mode will allow for any website to be viewed in dark mode, even if the site doesn’t support it. Finally, vertical tabs are pretty straightforward, enabling vertical navigation and drag-and-drop tab reorganization.

Here’s what you can expect when the software goes public in mid-December.

Also: 3 handy iPhone features that make my life easier – even doing laundry

Siri AI gains more access to your Apple devices, allowing more cross-app functionality and the ability to execute complex, multi-step tasks within your apps.

According to 9to5Mac, you can ask Siri AI to create a playlist in Music and save it to your library, request messages to be scheduled for a later send, organize and label photos, and create a detailed calendar invite — all with your voice.

The same reporting also states that Siri AI features will appear in Maps, Weather, Shortcuts, and Notes, signaling that an AI-supercharged Siri will live in every crevice of your Apple devices.

Also: iOS 27 will organize your open Safari tabs now

I’m not one to complete tasks like the ones mentioned above on my iPhone — I’m far more likely to do them on my MacBook Air, since I associate the laptop with productivity. Every blue moon I’ll rearrange my entire Apple Music catalog, every month I fill out my calendar, and sometimes I’ll go through Photos and try to organize it. I can see myself automating certain steps in these tasks, and I’m excited to try it.

A WebKit blog post details that adaptive dark mode is coming to Safari, how it will work, and what users can expect. According to the post, 40% of web page loads are from dark mode users, but only 10% of web pages natively support it.

I’m particularly excited about this feature, as I set my Apple devices to automatically enable dark mode at 7 p.m. to encourage a more relaxing evening scrolling vibe, especially while reading. I read a lot on my MacBook, and in a dark room, a bright page can feel too bright, but dimming my laptop’s display doesn’t quite do the trick.

Also: Your AirPods got better in iOS 27 – three new ways I’m using them

The WebKit blog post states that adaptive dark mode uses “a color matrix to invert the luminosity of colors while preserving hue” and distinguishes between when a page’s color is purely decorative and when it carries substantial meaning, to ensure the user experience remains consistent between light and dark modes.

Vertical browser tabs aren’t a new concept, but they’ll soon be new to Safari. I see the value in vertical tabs: a list view is easier to scan, web page titles aren’t smushed when several tabs are open, and they’re particularly useful when you’re working on a widescreen monitor.

Many people who spend hours using their Mac or MacBook may find this upcoming feature useful. I do believe that Safari is the superior browser for personal use, given its integration with your Apple devices, especially with features like Handoff.

Also: 7 AI-free iOS 27 features that make old iPhones exciting again

However, I do have one major gripe with vertical tabs: they’re usually locked to the left panel, and I prefer the right. If Safari allows this customization, I’ll seriously consider switching from horizontal tabs.

#3147. I Took the iPhone 18 Pro Max to Japan and Its New Camera System Brought Out My Creative Side

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The iPhone 18 Pro got fun new camera features and they made my bucketlist travel destination more memorable.

Apple gave its pro iPhones a crucial camera and battery boost this year. As a frequent traveler, these upgrades had me stoked for the iPhone 18 Pro Max, so I took it with me to Japan. Going vintage watch hunting through the streets of Tokyo to 6 a.m. hikes in Kyoto’s Fushimi Inari and the Shinto shrines, I used the new phone as my main camera. It made me rethink my shots, pushed me to experiment more with my perspective and surprised me in the most unexpected ways.

The variable aperture, manual camera controls and new Photographic Styles make the iPhone 18 Pro the most fun camera system from Apple, even if they are just minor upgrades from the 16 Pro and 17 Pro. The starburst effect in f4, grain in Photographic Styles and adjustable shutter speeds add drama, depth and more personality to even the most mundane shots.

From my time landing in Osaka to landing back in Delhi, the iPhone 18 Pro Max had me experimenting for two weeks. Here’s what I shot and how the new upgrades made an impact on my first trip to Japan.

The iPhone 18 Pro has manual controls baked into the Camera app. I can adjust the focus, choose the lens aperture from four stops, pick a shutter speed and select the white balance without needing to install a third-party app. The variable aperture is the main attraction here, letting me experiment with lighting as I visited various shrines.

You can go from f/1.48 to f/4 on iPhone 18 Pro’s main camera to adjust the amount of light hitting the sensor. Apple has programmed the f/4 (its narrowest) setting to give you a starburst effect with bright light sources, which showed up as light blobs on older iPhones. I used f/4 to get starbursts from the reflections of sunlight hitting a shrine:

Not every photo needs this effect, but starbursts add a unique style that you won’t find on any other phone. I was busy framing my shots to get the most reflections and the cameras didn’t disappoint.

Combine this with adjustable shutter speeds (takes a bit getting used to) and it leads to endless new possibilities. On the night I landed in Osaka, I went out for a stroll near my hotel, and took about 250 shots at a red light. I only got a few decent light trails, but it forced me to get more creative with my photography

After a few days I finally got the shot of a moving car stabilized with a blurred background. The trick? Finding the right shutter speed (1/15 in this case) through trial and error and moving my iPhone at the same speed as the car. At night, I stuck to 1/2s for moving vehicles with handheld stabilization. I’m happy with the results.

From light trails at night to a speeding car in daylight, the iPhone 18 Pro Max cameras create an effect that was previously only possible through third-party apps. This is different from simply taking a live photo and tapping Long Exposure in edits. You can track a subject to focus and the rest of the movement creates visual effects like the ones in my photos.

Apple’s manual controls are all about getting creative with your frames. You can then personalize these with the new film look and grain in Photographic Styles. These are like simulations that you’d find on the Fujifilm X100 series or Ricoh GR cameras.

For example, I edited this cyclist shot in the Photos app. I used the Dramatic + Film Style because I liked the blue tint in the sky and background, while keeping the skin tone intact. It gave my shot a moody look without editing the colors on my subject, like a regular filter would.

For these two nature shots, I brought all three aspects: adjustable shutter speed, f4 aperture and new Photographic Styles into a single frame. I love the grain, film and glow effects on the iPhone 18 Pro this year. They make the iPhone cameras exciting again.

However, there are a few things I’d like to change about this software.

The grain and film look are nice additions but I’d have loved to adjust the intensity of grain, much like my Vivo X300 Ultra. The current look is good for photos shot in bright light, but anything dim starts looking too artificial. The grain is too aggressive for most situations.

As much as I appreciate the new manual controls, I’m not fond of their placement in the Camera app. I missed a slow shutter shot of the Shinkansen because I was busy finding the manual control. These bullet trains are just too fast!

The new manual controls can be added to the top of the viewfinder or accessed through the six-dot settings menu at the bottom-right corner. In both positions, they aren’t made for one-handed use. It’d also be nice if I could adjust the position of certain toggles in the six-dot menu on the viewfinder. I need the aperture and shutter speed on the rightmost side, but I can’t edit it. The two icons aren’t instantly recognizable up on top. I believe that if I could change their positions in the bottom menu, I’d recognize them faster and remember their positions for a more reliable shooting experience.

Then comes the Camera Control. It doesn’t support any of the new manual controls. So, you can’t adjust the shutter speed or choose an aperture. If I have an extra button dedicated to the camera, I’d ideally like to use it for manual controls. It’d allow faster access to the new features.

In my opinion, Apple should also let us assign two separate Photographic Styles on the front and back cameras. On my trip, I had set a Fuji-like look for street photography, which seemed great for my surroundings but not for my selfies. You can always edit these photos in post, but if I’m out with new friends and sharing these photos with them, it’d be easier if I could set two different Photographic Styles for the front and back cameras.

During my trip, I didn’t have to top up my iPhone 18 Pro Max more than once a day. I left it on charge overnight as my mornings were reserved for breakfast and figuring out the train connectivity through Google Maps. (Seriously, I don’t know how I’d travel without this app.)

Japan is a unique mix of next-gen technology and decades-old systems. While it has a Suica card for public transport, I couldn’t add it to my Apple Wallet. Most stations don’t accept Visa contactless payments. I had to run to the nearest 7/11 to get cash and purchase train tickets. Some markets are also cash-only, so my iPhone was constantly running Maps, Music and Camera for a healthy 6 hours a day.

It lasted me through long photography sessions and constant navigation without any issues. In my experience, this is a huge upgrade over my iPhone 17 Pro Max, which required two charging instances if I was pushing it with Camera and Maps usage. The new model also doesn’t get as warm as its predecessor. I noticed the heat dissipates quicker when using the iPhone 18 Pro Max without a case. I’ve tried three cases so far and each one traps heat, making it warm to touch. If you can, going caseless is a good idea on the new pro iPhones.

The added battery life is a fantastic addition to this year’s model, and will be appreciated by anyone who travels regularly. This is in line with CNET’s tests, where the iPhone 18 Pro Max emerged as the longest-lasting battery life of any iPhone Apple has ever made. I just wish it was lighter. At 248 grams, it is one of the heaviest phones on the market and if you put a case on it, the iPhone 18 Pro Max becomes bulky and hard to use with one hand. I hope Apple finds a way to give us an even better battery life in a lighter form next year.

On the front, you also get a smaller Dynamic Island, which can expand to show up to three live activities (up from two) simultaneously. However, some apps aren’t yet fine-tuned to accommodate the change. On one occasion, when I ordered food through Uber, while running Spotify and Maps navigation, the Live Activity cut the “2” in 27-minute ETA for the order. So I had the next direction, music and an incorrect ETA as glanceable info on top of my screen.

Japan was one of my bucket-list locations and I’m glad I took the iPhone 18 Pro Max with me. This is the most fun I’ve had with an Apple camera system in a long time. From the shrines in Kyoto to the riverside walk along the Sumida River in Tokyo, these cameras invited me to get more experimental. The film-like Photographic Styles, new manual controls and variable aperture helped me get more creative with my perspectives.

It took me more than 250 shots at a crossing in Osaka before I figured out which shutter speed was ideal for what occasion. Similarly, I experimented with my frames to find the best angles for the starburst effect in f/4. Then came the film simulations in Photographic Styles to stylize my shots within the Photos app. All of these new iPhone camera features give me a more analog feel, and I’m here for it.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max, thankfully, has the battery life to support my curiosity and slow learning pace. Through my trips last year, I had to carry a power bank with me, but the iPhone 18 Pro Max changed that. I’m more confident it will last through the day. While none of those camera features would appeal to casual users, the battery life enhancements and improved heat dissipation are tangible upgrades that would benefit everyone.

#3146. Want an AI job? Deployment engineers are earning executive-level pay – up to $1.45M a year

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

AI has ushered in new jobs, and some of them are paying handsomely, according to a new study.

AI engineers are making well over six figures in salary — and plenty more in bonuses and equity, according to data from a new report by executive search firm Christian & Timbers.

Enterprises now pay “elite” AI deployment engineers between $586,000 and $1.45 million annually in total compensation, with senior leaders in the field earning up to $2.25 million, according to the report. This figure approaches the median compensation of executive officers of public companies, the authors note.

Also: ‘So perfect, they are literally identical’ – Your AI-polished resumes are recruiters’ new top stressor

Christian & Timbers is an AI executive search and leadership advisory firm, recruiting CEOs, board members, technology executives, and AI engineers for enterprises. The new report draws on more than 550 interviews with engineers, deployment leaders, and executives conducted from January through June 2026, along with closed and current open offers. The compensation bands are Christian & Timbers’ estimates and represent ranges rather than statistical averages.

“Enterprise CEOs are under pressure to deliver returns for their AI investments. The most important decision is how to build the team that delivers on that goal,” said Jeff Christian, founder and CEO of Christian & Timbers, in a press release.

Also: What workers are really using AI for in 2026 – and what they aren’t

The report noted that the staggering salary range includes base salary, bonus, and annualized equity. Christian & Timbers said it defines an “elite” forward deployment engineer (FDE) as “a senior AI-native deployment builder, typically with 7 to 15 years of experience, including at least two years building and deploying agentic automated workflows that deliver measurable ROI with a documented enterprise impact of $10M or more,” who has also led a team of other forward deployment engineers.

Also: 50% of companies generate value from AI now – here’s how

The large salary ranges reflect increasing enterprise investments in AI talent and employee development. Microsoft, AWS, and OpenAI have announced more than $7.5 billion in corporate and partner investment in AI deployment over the past six months, Christian & Timbers noted in the release.

Also: Nearly 70% of workers use AI regularly now – but many get no time to upskill

There’s an increasing need to fill roles such as Senior Principal AI Engineer, AI Solutions Engineer, and Head of Deployment — but there is a limited pool of qualified candidates. The firm estimates that only 2,000 of the most senior deployment leaders exist in the US market, according to a previous Christian & Timbers study, which does not meet demand — so companies are competing for the same small group of professionals, hence the increasing salaries.

While the report underscores lucrative yields for certain engineering roles, the firm said that public job titles make comparisons more challenging.

“Christian & Timbers’ elite category spans several titles, while advertised FDE roles cover a broader range of experience and responsibilities. Experienced deployment engineers may be recruited directly or promoted into the work under titles such as staff software engineer or principal AI engineer,” the study said.

Plus, equity and bonus make up 52% to 66% of senior engineer pay, and most job postings don’t include that value in the salary, the report noted.

But what we do when we build a forecast, we wanna make sure we get in front of our partners. Everybody on this call and all the investors in law, and make sure that when we say we are going to hit a number, we are going to hit a number. So keep that in mind. Now with regards to our product offering, we do not see any I will say it this way, any changes between new aircraft, old aircraft, old engine, new engine for the parts that we are making today. They carry Ford from legacy right through to the future. We are not, as you know, making engines. We are not making wings.

The things that actually move the needle when it comes to fuel efficiency and those things. We are making switches and push buttons and you know, latching mechanisms. Right? And what the opportunity set is, is a little bit of improvement. Showing up on time with a body product, and you get to stay on that platform, and a new gen. So that is how we think about the products that we offer to our customers. So hopefully, in there somewhere, Sheila, I answered your question.

Sheila Kahyaoglu: that is it. Thank you, Dirkson. Maybe can I ask another 1? I guess on 2-part on M&A, what is holding you back the most, I guess? Is it just. I know you stick to your knitting when comes to M&A, the margin profile, the valuation. So what is holding you back? And as you think about the past year, you had LMB in December, Harper in January. #3144. Motorola’s $1,600 Signature 27 Is Throwing Every Ultra-Level Phone Feature Together

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Motorola's new Signature 27 has one of the fastest wired charging speeds we've seen for a US phone.

After teasing it during Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Summit in September, Motorola’s $1,600 Signature 27 phone will be unveiled on Thursday, and it clearly wants to make a big impression for that high starting price.

Even with the ongoing RAM shortage leading to higher prices for most phones, it would be understandable to think a $1,600 candybar-style phone sounds extravagant. It is. But it’s actually priced competitively against the 512GB model of the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra (also now $1,600 following its own fall price increase).

The Signature 27’s biggest feature could be its 200-megapixel periscope telephoto camera, which is capable of a 3x optical zoom and what Motorola calls a 100x Super Zoom Pro. That camera is joined by a 50-megapixel wide camera, a 50-megapixel ultrawide camera and a 50-megapixel front camera. An Event-Based Vision action sensor will also be included to assist with photographing fast-moving subjects.

But particularly eye-opening to me — as someone who’s constantly tracking how quickly phones can recharge — is that the Signature 27 will have 90-watt wired charging. For context, the Galaxy S26 Ultra and the iPhone 18 Pro Max charge at 60-watt speeds, with both phones being among the fastest we’ve tested. The Signature includes a 7,000-mAh silicon carbon battery, which is a newer battery technology that’s able to pack more capacity into less space.

The phone will have a 6.8-inch 1.5K-resolution display that runs at a 120Hz refresh rate, but has an absurdly high 12,000-nit peak brightness. By comparison, many phones we’ve tested lately have included 2,000- and 3,000-nit brightness levels that make it easy to see the screen in sunny environments.

Powering it will be Qualcomm’s new Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 processor, which Qualcomm says will be particularly helpful for gaming at high-graphics settings, recording video at 8K resolution as well as 4K at 60 frames per second and for on-device AI tasks. The phone’s audio system is created with a partnership with Bang and Olufsen, which we’ll have to hear but should help tune the phone well for music and movies.

The Signature also gets several Android 17 features that debuted on Google’s Pixel 11 series, including Rambler for voice transcription that uses AI to remove “umm”s from the text as well as understanding commands. There will also be a Create My Widget feature for having Gemini create personalized homescreen widgets, and the ability to use American Sign Language for texting. Motorola’s own Qira AI assistant will also be available on the Signature 27, which Motorola says will work across Lenovo devices.

Like the Razr Fold, the Signature 27 will get seven years of software and security updates — which brings Motorola firmly in line with what Google and Samsung provide to their flagship Pixel and Galaxy phones. The Signature will come in two Pantone colors: the dark coal smoke and the green capulet olive. I am interested in feeling both phones because the coal smoke model is described as having a “tactical weave finish” akin to materials used for cars while the olive is said to have a textile-inspired finish that may be closer to the vegan leather backings we’ve seen on the Razr line.

The Signature 27 may be expensive, but I do see where there may be an audience. With the recent retreat of OnePlus from the US phone market, fans of that brand may be looking for a new gamer-friendly phone alternative with both a high-end processor and fast phone charging. The Signature 27 is also arriving after years of growth for Motorola’s Razr line of foldable phones, which itself has included a number of luxury-minded variants such as Razr phones that include Swarovski crystals.

The Signature 27 will release first in the US, going on preorder on Nov. 19 before going on open sale Nov. 26. Both the coal smoke and capulet olive models will come with 512GB of storage and 12GB of memory.

#3143. Researchers asked people to use AI chatbots for election info – results were mixed

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Chatbots can skew election-related information and act as an intervening layer in a voter's search.

Most search tools now put a layer of AI between you and the information you’re looking for, especially Google.

Also: Tired of AI Overviews? I found 9 Google Search alternatives

In a new study, Yale researchers found that a third of users asked a chatbot to help them pick a candidate. Grok often recommended candidates on its own without any information from users, while ChatGPT recommended candidates most often overall, and twice as much as Claude.

The researchers asked nearly 2,500 people in 35 states with Senate races to query ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, or Gemini about the election. Participants in the study, which ran for a few weeks in October leading up to the Nov. 3 midterm elections, were adults who already use chatbots weekly.

Most users asked chatbots for basic facts about the election, including who was on the ballot. But 36% asked a chatbot to help them pick a candidate to vote for, often by describing their priorities and asking the chatbot to assess which candidates aligned with them.

The former query has slightly less room for error, because the internet has a ton of data on the basic facts of an election, such as who is running where. Chatbots interpreting candidate positions, on the other hand, is a bit more dicey, and relies significantly on the sources a chatbot uses (a statement from a candidate’s own website, for example, is more reliable than a social media clip of an opponent characterizing them in a certain way).

Also: How to keep your chatbot conversations as private as possible

In one example, a user asked ChatGPT to give them the “pros and cons” of each candidate in Virginia, an inherently subjective question.

When it came to recommending candidates, chatbots varied widely.

“When users asked who to vote for but had not yet said anything about themselves, only Grok regularly recommended a candidate, in 14% of chats,” the researchers wrote. “Once users shared their views, ChatGPT recommended a candidate in 79% of chats and Claude in 40%, with Grok and Gemini in between.”

Pew Research found that 42% of US adults surveyed use chatbots to search for information. That’s a broad umbrella that can include election information — but Pew also found that only 8% of US adults reported using chatbots to find election-related information in this year’s election.

What those users are looking for matters, though. Pew found that of that group, 76% were inquiring about where candidates stand on certain issues, and 71% were fact-checking information they’d heard about candidates or issues.

Also: OpenAI will merge ChatGPT’s chat and work tabs

Given that chatbots are still not reliable summarizers, the nature of these questions poses a misinformation risk if users don’t also check a chatbot’s linked sources. An overwhelming majority of users don’t, at least when it comes to Google’s AI Overviews. At least one study found AI platforms gave users “outdated or inaccurate” information that could mislead voters in some cases by missing a deadline or failing to mention a step about voting logistics.

This election cycle was particularly plagued by AI-generated deepfakes and misinformation as tools have become much more sophisticated since the 2024 election. OpenAI and Anthropic reportedly set up election “war rooms” to monitor misuse and information accuracy, according to exclusive reporting by Politico and Semafor.

While an August study from the Brennan Center for Justice found that chatbots did push back surprisingly well against certain falsehoods related to election disinformation campaigns, it also found that AI models easily generated “misleading election-related images and video” when asked.

“Many of their safeguards for preventing this were ineffective, inconsistently applied, or functionally absent,” noted the study, which tested ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, Meta AI, Runway, and Flux.2.

Also: 50 AI agents tried to build a thriving Minecraft civilization – it didn’t end well

Apart from these factors, however, there is a broader theme in AI use that is equally consequential for civic engagement: cognitive offloading. The political media landscape can already be dense and hard to parse for a voter trying to stay informed. Layering a chatbot — which has opaque training data sets, filters, and other settings determined at the discretion of AI labs — on top of that information search process can further muddy the waters while appearing like a convenient and neutral summarizing tool.

While some studies test how AI chatbots respond to election questions by using standardized questions, this approach let users themselves engage with chatbots as they normally would. While the Yale researchers’ queries and standardized study queries show a lot of similarities, the distinction is valuable for evaluations.

“This is a small step toward evaluations that measure AI’s political influence on the questions users actually ask,” the researchers noted.

Outside of users self-reporting what they asked a chatbot, only AI labs have records of what users are really asking about elections. In October, Anthropic analyzed 250,000 conversations with Claude and determined people “rarely ask Claude whom or what to vote for,” finding that “0.51% of all conversations are specifically about elections or voting,” though it expected election-related queries to increase closer to Nov. 3.

Also: 6 AI agent workflows I use to hand off everyday tasks

“More often, we observed people asking Claude questions that could help them reach their own conclusions, like where candidates stand on a particular issue. Requests that violated our election integrity policies were even less common, appearing in about 0.002% of conversations,” Anthropic’s report said.

The Yale researchers said the next step for a study like theirs is determining how accurate and unbiased models are in their responses, as well as what models learn about users, and whether their recommendations actually match users’ needs.

“In multi-turn chats, users often answered the chatbot’s questions, and those answers led to its recommendations. The questions a model asks shape what users tell it and what it recommends,” the researchers explained.
