#3114. Don't let inflation bite — how to hedge with TIPS, commodities and infrastructure funds

The Consumer Price Index hit 3.7% in September – the latest sign that inflation remains a problem that isn't going away.

It's a tough situation for investors looking for protection, but there are some good ways to hedge.

Long-term Treasury Inflation-Protected securities (TIPS) yield 2.9%, near multi-decade highs. Beyond TIPS, analysts suggest commodities, infrastructure, and other assets that can hedge against rising prices.

While inflation is down sharply from its 9.1% peak in 2022, it's still well above the Federal Reserve's 2% target. Headline CPI's 3.7% rate in September topped estimates for 3.6%. Core CPI, excluding food and energy, reached 2.6%, also higher than expected. Rising energy prices drove much of the increase. But the Personal Consumption Expenditures index, the Fed's preferred gauge, also remains elevated at a core 3% rate.

Americans' inflation concerns are also rising. The New York Fed's Survey of Consumer Expectations showed the one-year inflation outlook in September climbed to 3.9%, its highest level since May 2023.

Despite their name, TIPS haven't provided much inflation protection this year. The iShares TIPS Bond ETF, which tracks the ICE U.S. Treasury Inflation Linked Bond Index, has a total return of -1.16% year-to-date.

Like most other bonds, TIPS have been hit hard by rising rates. The 10-year Treasury note is up sharply this year and spiked Wednesday to 5.29%, near the highest levels since 2002. Bond prices and yields move inversely, and as rates climbed many TIPS funds suffered.

But higher yields have made TIPS more attractive. The 10-year TIPS' 2.9% yield is up from roughly 1.9% early in the year.

"Given where rates are, it's getting interesting," says Jason Draho, head of asset allocation Americas at UBS Global Wealth Management.

TIPS pay a fixed coupon, or interest rate, but as inflation moves higher, the principal value of the bond increases. The adjustments reflect changes in inflation, based on the non-seasonally adjusted CPI for All Urban Consumers, with a three-month lag.

The upshot is that TIPS investors earn interest on a higher principal value over time. That's the essence of the protection compared to traditional Treasuries.

TIPS' poor performance this year isn't because of a surge in inflation expectations. Almost all the increase has been due to rising real yields — the nominal yield minus expected inflation. Real yields are up because of factors like robust economic growth and a U.S. fiscal deficit around 6% of gross domestic product (requiring far more government borrowing).

If nominal rates were rising just due to inflation, then TIPS total return — a mix of yield and price — would be fine, said R.J. Gallo, chief investment officer of global fixed income at Federated Hermes. But that isn't the case.

"TIPS have produced losses in total return because their income accruals have been insufficient to offset the price decline produced by the rising underlying real yields," Gallo explained.

TIPS maturing in 10 years or more are highly sensitive to duration risk, Draho notes. "You're making a big call on rates not rising any further if you buy TIPS, especially longer maturities of 10-year plus," he said.

The bull case is that inflation comes down quicker than expected. That's not the market's expectation, based on short-term Treasury yields, notes Draho. But if inflation does ease next year, which he expects, the yield curve would adjust lower.

One way to manage duration risk is to own individual TIPS rather than a fund that has to maintain duration consistent with a benchmark index. Investors could create a TIPS bond ladder with varying maturities, pegged to their income needs over the next decade, for instance.

If you hold a TIPS to maturity you may experience price volatility, but you'll get the original principal or inflation-adjusted price, whichever is greater, when the bond matures.

Short-term TIPS provide more protection against rate increases and they look attractive, said PIMCO portfolio manager Greg Sharenow.

"While as a firm, our view is that inflation will ultimately come down, that view keeps on being pushed out as real world events unfold," he said. "We've seen over and over again the last five to seven years — where we're now in our third supply shock — that you end up actually underpricing versus realized inflation," he added.

Funds focusing on short-term TIPS include Vanguard Short-Term Inflation-Protected Securities ETF, iShares 0-5 Year TIPS Bond ETF and PIMCO 1-5 Year US TIPS Index ETF.

TIPS, of course, aren't the only way to go. Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, suggests a multi-pronged strategy, including equities, commodities, and alternative assets.

"I'd start layering in more income, keep interest-rate exposure moderate, and then what a lot of people are doing is use things like alternatives to to create more balance in a portfolio," he said. "That makes a lot of sense to me."

Broad inflation-protection funds include State Street Multi-Asset Real Return ETF, Fidelity Strategic Real Return Fund and PIMCO Inflation Response Multi-Asset Fund.

The PIMCO fund's holdings include TIPS, commodities, gold and real estate investment trusts.

"The idea is to have a number of different exposures so that we can have a more balanced return and not try to be so specific in getting the exact right asset class at any one moment," said Sharenow, a manager on the fund.

He adds that he sees "significant value" in TIPS, which have the heaviest weighting in the portfolio. Commodities are the next largest holding. They have price "pass-throughs," which is how much companies can shift costs to customers through price increases. That is beneficial to investors, he noted.

Separately, the fund holds about 10% each in gold and REITs.

Draho recommends commodities, based partly on long-term asset-allocation studies that include the 1970s when inflation was far higher. "Over a long period they can help reduce risk and improve diversification," he said. "Their benefits have been most pronounced when inflation was overshooting expectations."

Rather than picking individual commodities, he suggests owning a basket that's consistently rebalanced. Gold and oil, for instance, perform well in different economic and monetary policy scenarios, and it can be tricky to get the timing right.

Commodity ETFs to consider include the Invesco Optimum Yield Diversified Commodity Strategy ETF (PDBC) and the iShares S&P GSCI Commodity-Indexed Trust (GSG).

Another asset class Draho suggests is infrastructure — operators of roads, ports, bridges, and other hard assets. Companies in the space tend to be toll takers, collecting long-term revenue under contracts that include inflation riders or built-in price adjustments.

Investors can get exposure to infrastructure through ETFs such as the iShares Global Infrastructure ETF (IGF) and ProShares DJ Brookfield Global Infrastructure ETF (TOLZ).

Draho isn't sounding alarms on inflation but says it makes sense to add protection against another move higher.

"The risk now is there will be supply side shocks that could push up inflation again," he said.

— CNBC's Daren Fonda contributed reporting.

#3113. Meet *sshole, the vulnerability that lets hackers SSH into Linux devices

Certain configurations of Linux are affected. Other distros may be as well.

Devices running some configurations of Alpine Linux, and possibly other distributions, are affected by a decade-old vulnerability that allows attackers to log into devices with no password.

The vulnerability exists in the interaction between OpenSSH, the code library implementing SSH connections, and musl, a lightweight alternative to the libc library that, unlike most other Linux distributions, is used in Alpine. Further, OpenSSH using musl (pronounced muscle) must not use PAM (pluggable authentication modules), a framework that handles user authentication and account-access checks. Alpine is a lightweight, widely used Linux distribution. Other platforms may be affected if they use the same configurations.

There are two other conditions necessary for successful exploitation. First, a system must have at least one user account that’s accessible using a password that is hashed using the SHA256 or SHA512 functions. Second, the target system account must be configured to be passwordless, by way of specifying a “*” in the password field in /etc/shadow, the Linux file where password hashes are stored. Passwordless accounts are commonly used for accounts that use certificate-based authentication. This setting is common for certain types of accounts.

When all the conditions are met, the consequences are high.

“An attacker who can reach your SSH port can log in without knowing any password,” Alpine maintainers said Thursday. “It takes one connection, works every time, and needs no retries.”

When logging into a passwordless account, the attacker can gain access by inputting more than 256 characters in the password field.

Security firm Checkpoint said that the use of the SHA256 or SHA512 functions “matters because sshd borrows that account’s salt. Without it, the attack fails.”  Company researchers said their testing also showed that the account must be active, not just hold a hash. Checkpoint further reported that root accounts are safe under the default PermitRootLogin prohibit password setting, though reachable accounts with doas or sudo rights can still become root.

Despite the prerequisites, *sshole—the vulnerability name given by the person who discovered it—likely threatens large numbers of systems. The Docker Hub base image for Alpine has more than 1 billion downloads. Alpine has long been popular in routers, smart TVs, industrial controllers, and other types of embedded devices, many of which can’t be easily updated, if at all. More recently, Alpine has been adopted for use in desktops and servers. Alpine is also used in many container images.

According to security firm Detectify, Shodan lists around 22 million systems with SSH open on port 22. Only a fraction meet the conditions necessary for exploitation, but given the ease and speed of testing each one, locating vulnerable devices won’t require much effort or time.

It’s not entirely clear where the vulnerability resides. OpenSSH, which issued an update Thursday, said: “We consider the root cause of this bug to be outside sshd, but it is exploitable via sshd and can be avoided there.” Musl developer Rich Felker, meanwhile, wrote: “It is my position that this is not a bug in musl just an erroneous use by the caller.” Felker went on to say that musl developers have wanted to make changes to the mechanism “for a while now” and planned to do so in an upcoming release. Alpine has also issued an update.

It’s not yet known what other packages may be vulnerable. The person who discovered *sshole said OpenWRT is affected, but by default, that OS uses the Dropbear package, not OpenSSH, for SSH connections (though maintainers provide instructions for installing the latter). The discoverer also names the packages buildroot and yocto as being affected, but that isn’t yet confirmed.

Despite the uncertainty, anyone using a Linux system that uses both musl and OpenSSH should take time to immediately investigate if they’re affected. A good starting point is here. Both Alpine and OpenSSH patches should be installed on all affected systems. There is no known CVE designation for the vulnerability.

Magnolia generated $224 million of adjusted free cash flow in the third quarter with adjusted operating income or pretax margins of 43% and annualized return on capital employed of approximately 20%. Third quarter total production company production volumes grew by 17% year-over-year to 107 thousand barrels of oil equivalent per day and in line with our earlier guidance.

Oil production grew by 24% and averaged 49.1 thousand barrels per day. Total Giddings production volumes increased by 23% year-over-year to 97 thousand barrels of oil equivalent per day with Giddings oil production climbing 39% to 37.1 thousand barrels per day. Giddings production accounted for approximately 83% of Magnolia's total volumes and will make up a higher proportion of our overall company production in the fourth quarter as a result of full quarter contribution from wildfire. Production in our Karnes area was roughly 20 thousand barrels of oil equivalent per day during the third quarter, a level which we expect to sustain for an extended period while generating a significant amount of free cash flow.

As I have often said, Magnolia's goals and objectives are to be the most efficient operator of our best in class oil and gas assets, to generate the highest returns on those assets while employing the least amount of for drilling and completing our wells. Overall, our strong momentum has carried into the fourth quarter, the first period with a full contribution of the wildfire assets. Supported by these strong operational and financial results, Magnolia returned approximately $103 million of its free cash flow to shareholders during the quarter, through a combination of our base dividend and ongoing share repurchase program where we bought back 2.3 million shares.

We also reduced our net debt by $100 million to approximately $1.9 billion from the time we closed the WAF acquisition to the end of the third quarter. Finally, Magnolia's Board has increased our share repurchase authorization by an incremental 15 million shares, bringing the remaining authorization to 22.6 million shares nearly 8.5% of current shares outstanding. This is indicative of the confidence of our ability to repurchase shares at a minimum of 1% per quarter level either opportunistically or when warranted. Turning to Slide 4, we highlight some key milestones achieved since we announced the Wildfire acquisition.

First, we divested some non core assets in the Western Eagle Ford during the third quarter for a sales price of $47.5 million while also receiving consideration of 6.02 thousand net acres in our contiguous block of acreage, primarily in Gonzales County in our Karnes area. This divestiture not only improves the focus of our portfolio, it also increases our working interest in our operated track in this acreage block to approximately 98% with an average NRI of 80%.

Second, we have already made strong progress on reducing debt ending the third quarter with approximately $1.9 billion of net debt and achieving our goal of less than 1x net debt to forecasted EBITDAX by the end of 26, more than a year sooner originally planned when announcing the wildfire acquisition. At current product prices, we expect to fully repay the outstanding debt on a revolving credit facility in early 27. Next, we proactively and opportunistically added some oil hedges using costless collars with a floor price between $70 and $75 provide greater assurance around our ability to reduce debt should oil prices experience a sharp decline while maintaining exposure to the current higher prices.

Finally, continue to make good progress in capturing synergies from the acquisition, which is proceeding a bit faster than we anticipated and expect to realize at least 1-third of the more than $100 million of estimated annual run rate synergies by year-end 2026. Looking at Slide 5, the integration of wildfire continues to progress very smoothly and we are meeting all our planned milestones. As I mentioned, synergy capture is moving ahead of schedule, but we now expect to realize that at least 3-fourths of the projected annual run rate synergies by mid-27.

Part of the speed of the integration and synergy capture could be ascribed to this significant overlap of the wildfire acreage to our existing Giddings, in addition to our strong existing knowledge of field operations and the subsurface. Nearly all the D and C and subsurface efforts have now been transitioned with the full operations team expected to be in place next month. We are currently running 4 rigs and 2 completion crews and have recently substituted some equipment to capture further operational and capital efficiencies and are in the early stages of implementing Magnolia's playbook of operating practices and procedures.

D and C synergies that have been identified amount to at least a million dollars per well and include procurement benefits, faster drilling times, transitioning to multi well pads, lower cost of sand resulting from our ownership of the sand mine, which cuts our sand costs by roughly 1-third, and completions optimization to name a few. These are incorporated in our current estimated 2027 capital budget of $900 million to $950 million. Over time, we anticipate additional synergies through completion design improvements and the drilling of longer laterals.

Recent Austin Chalk well results on Wildfire's operated acreage are encouraging And Are Supportive Of Our Geologic Model That Led To Magnolia's own strong Austin Chalk development plan over the last several years. These results have increased our confidence in the acreage and suggest greater inventory potential than our earlier baseline acquisition analysis. TL;DR: Mortgage rates eased again today, giving buyers modest relief from rates above 7%.

Mortgage rates are continuing to cool off as we head into November.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage dropped to 6.93% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 14 basis points lower than yesterday and 17 basis points lower than a week ago. (See our chart below for more specifics.) A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.

A significant drop is eye-catching, but bear in mind that you should consider mortgage interest rates' overall direction, not just what's going on today. Since September, mortgage rates have been hovering around 7%. That’s a full percentage point higher than they were at the beginning of 2026.

This week’s employment data could potentially push mortgage rates one way or the other — more on that below the graph.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

This week, the Nerds will be watching the October jobs report, which comes out on Friday, Nov. 6. If it shows that employment remained steady (or even improved), that will build a stronger case for the Federal Reserve to raise overnight borrowing rates again at their next meeting on Dec. 8-9.

While the Fed doesn’t directly set mortgage rates, it does set the federal funds rate, which is the fee that banks must pay to borrow from one another (which is how they fund mortgages). Lenders raise mortgage rates any time they think that the federal funds rate is about to go up.

Central bankers hiked the federal funds rate in September, so a relatively steady jobs report would suggest the labor market could withstand higher rates.

The Fed has a dual mandate to control inflation while supporting maximum employment, and raising the federal funds rate is their main tool for bringing inflation down. If they can work to lower inflation without hurting employment too badly, central bankers may feel more confident to act.

The September Personal Consumption Expenditures price index (PCE), the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, was released last Thursday. The data shows inflation was 3.6% year-over-year in September, up from 3.4% in August.

September’s federal funds rate hike came in the middle of the month, so October’s inflation data will really capture its effect on inflation. The October PCE report will come out on Nov. 25.

» Learn more: How the Fed affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.43% or higher — but there aren't too many people for whom that's true.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

» Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit.

#3110. T-Mobile owner on Elon Musk launching a wireless carrier: ‘Welcome to the party’

Starlink Mobile could cost SpaceX at least $200 billion, Deutsche Telekom CEO Tim Höttges says.

Starlink Mobile could cost SpaceX at least $200 billion, Deutsche Telekom CEO Tim Höttges says.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The head of T-Mobile’s parent company is casting doubt on SpaceX’s plans to make Starlink Mobile a “major” carrier in the US. During an earnings call on Thursday, Deutsche Telekom CEO Tim Höttges says he takes the Elon Musk-owned company “super serious,” but that it will cost at least $200 billion to pull off:

He [Musk] has now bought 76 megahertz of spectrum. By the way, we have 400. So if you now say he can buy the spectrum prospectively, do your math. These are kind of triple-digit billions which are needed to gain the spectrum position. If he has the money, go for it. Then he has to build a network. I can tell you, we have 85,000 towers. No, he can rent towers, no question. But this is another $20 to $30 billion which are required.

Put antennas on it. You can buy antennas… and you can get [them] maybe even in a cheaper way, or you construct it in a new way, but you need money for that. So therefore, my assessment is that SpaceX at least — if they want to play in that industry — needs at least minimum $200 billion. But even beyond that, to play in an industry which we have, let’s say, professionalized over the last 20 years — okay, welcome to the party.

Last month, SpaceX laid out its plans for Starlink Mobile to compete against T-Mobile, AT&T, and Verizon by using a combination of direct-to-cell satellites and a terrestrial network. One recent report suggests that SpaceX could tap into 80,000 cell towers throughout the US, while another indicates that Musk was in talks to acquire Boost Mobile. This week, Qualcomm announced that SpaceX will use its cellular infrastructure technology to support Starlink Mobile’s network buildout.

At the same time, Höttges is aware of the potential threat Starlink Mobile could pose to the mobile industry by creating a “new” type of service.

“He [Musk] has chipsets, he has data centers, he has AI, he has satellites… He will go as well for maybe integrating social media or at least agent models into his service. So he is creating a new way of communication services,” Höttges says. “That is why I’m saying I take that super serious because I was witnessing what happened to the car industry. They were ignoring it for too long, and we have to face the situation. But it’s not a free lunch. And you see that with Tesla as well in the car industry.”

#3109. Gulfport Energy (GPOR) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Liquids output jumped 67% as a continuous Appalachia program takes shape.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Gulfport Energy Corporation (GPOR -2.53%) reported a transition toward continuous operational programs in Appalachia to improve capital efficiency and lower development costs. Management stated the company reached a production inflection point in the third quarter, driven by the completion of liquids-rich pads in the Utica shale. The company indicated it is reallocating capital from the SCOOP asset in Oklahoma to Appalachia while assessing alternative drilling horizons in the Anadarko Basin. Furthermore, Gulfport expanded its shareholder return framework through an increased share repurchase authorization and secured long-term supply agreements to capture premium pricing from growing regional power demand.

Operator: Greetings. Welcome to the Gulfport Energy Corporation Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. A question-and-answer session will follow the formal presentation. And please note, this conference is being recorded. I will now turn the conference over to Jessica Antle, Vice President of Investor Relations. Jessica, you may begin.

Jessica R. Antle: Thank you, and good morning. Welcome to Gulfport Energy Corporation's Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. I am Jessica, Vice President of Investor Relations. And with me on today's call are Nick Dell'Osso and Matthew H. Rucker. Nick will give a brief overview of our results and then we will open up the teleconference for Q&A. I would like to remind everybody that during this conference call, the participants may make certain forward-looking statements. Actual results and future events could differ materially from those that are indicated in these forward-looking statements due to a variety of factors. Information concerning these factors can be found in the company's filings with the SEC. In addition, we may reference non GAAP measures.

Please refer to our most recent earnings release and investor presentation for important disclosure regarding such measures, including reconciliations to the most comparable GAAP financial measures. An updated Gulfport presentation was posted yesterday evening to our website in conjunction with the earnings announcement. Please review at your leisure. At this time, I would like to turn the call over to Nick.

Domenic J. Dell'Osso Jr.: Good morning and thank you for joining our third quarter earnings call. Starting off, I would like to congratulate our team on our very strong third quarter results. Production, capital and operating costs all landed right in line with guidance. As you are aware, we forecasted total and importantly, liquids production to be up meaningfully from second quarter and we delivered on that planned ramp. In fact, liquids production represented 13% of total production in the quarter on the strength of our recent wet gas Utica TILs. That higher value mix, strong realized liquids pricing and our disciplined cost structure translated into strong EBITDA and adjusted free cash flow, both up meaningfully from the second quarter.

Similarly, the fourth quarter is off to a good start and we remain on track to execute within our original guidance ranges. Last quarter, I said our number 1 priority was delivering better and more consistent results for shareholders. And a clean, predictable quarter is evidence of that focus. We are pleased with the predictability of our business and remain focused on the next phase of business improvements to generate higher returns for shareholders. Our strategy will be built around 3 key value drivers. Improving our capital and operating efficiency, positioning our gas to respond effectively to growing in basin demand and growing our acreage position in areas with high return potential to Gulfport shareholders.

An important first step in maturing this strategy is our plan to move to continuous operations in Appalachia. We have included a slide in our presentation this morning to highlight the value of moving to a continuous 2-rig program in Appalachia and the expected improvement to our D&C cost per foot and the near term development of our highest return long lateral wet gas pads. Connected to this decision is the contracting of an electric frac fleet beginning in mid-2027, allowing us to reduce diesel exposure and total completion spend. All combined, we have line of sight to reduce our D&C cost per foot by more than 20% between now and 2028.

The reduced white space in our development plan lower costs and higher liquids content all point to improved returns on capital and a free cash flow inflection. In 2028. Just as important, a lower cost structure reduces the reinvestment rate required to hold the business flat. And that in turn raises free cash flow per share in every year that follows. Not just the next 1. Related to growing in basin demand, we are very pleased to have used our firm transport to access premium markets in the Upper Midwest to sign another supply agreement at attractive pricing beginning in Q4 2028, that supports growing demand in the region.

We are maintaining floating exposure to a basis location that has historically been a premium pricing point while locking in a higher spread to that location than we have received in the past. We like the structure of retaining strategic exposure to a dynamic we believe has further upside, while establishing ourselves as an important source of supply with an attractive spread. Combined with our 10-year agreement, delivering into Ohio beginning in mid-2027, this incremental contract secures advantageous pricing for about 10% of our forecasted Appalachia production over the life of the agreements. Contracted at a premium to what we have historically received for those same molecules all using firm transport we already hold.

We think this is strong evidence of the demand pull nature of Appalachia gas markets and how marketers and customers are looking to secure available supply. Of our peers recently described acreage along the Ohio River as beachfront real estate to this growing demand. If that is the beach, we have our toes in the water at Gulfport. Our core position sits in the heart of Ohio. Where new gas fired generation and data center load are just starting to show up. We have about 30% to 40% of our production sold in basin to benefit as it grows.

Third, from an acreage growth perspective, we closed $83 million of Ohio State land acquisitions this quarter, and are finishing out our $140 million 2026 discretionary program, $50 million to $55 million of remaining spend before year end. This will continue to add valuable life to our portfolio of attractive drilling opportunities and support our ability to run a more effective development program. This program will continue into 2027, and we expect to focus on areas that have great rock at attractive upfront bonus and royalty structures leading to opportunities for greater returns. Looking at our SCOOP asset in Oklahoma, we are seeing some really compelling development by our peer companies targeting different horizons.

We believe it is prudent to reduce our activity in the SCOOP during 2027 and reassess our development plan in consideration of these opportunities beyond our historical primary target. We will work through the year to reset our longer term development program to better capture the upside we believe exists in this acreage. While the reduction in SCOOP capital helps to fund the shift to capital in Appalachia. We will provide 2027 financial guidance concurrent with our Q4 earnings, as we typically do, but want to give investors a few things to consider today as laid out in our slide deck.

As we move to a more efficient continuous 2-rig program in Appalachia, realize the savings from the e fleet and incorporate recent high quality acreage in the wet gas window with long lateral units. Our wells drilled per year and liquids content will increase and cost per lateral foot will decrease. This in turn positions us to better serve our growing demand base in Appalachia and realize higher value per unit and further creates advantages in returns on expected acquired acreage. We believe this strategy will generate attractive returns for shareholders in a more sustainable fashion over the coming periods. We are not adding activity to grow volumes for their own sake.

We are doing it because every dollar we invest will generate more cash. A more efficient base of operations means more efficient cash flow generation, and our flexibility to allocate that cash to the highest return opportunities increases with a reduction in the reinvestment rate and allows us to clearly evaluate the merits of buybacks, balance sheet, acreage and drill bit. Every dollar competes on the same basis. What it adds to cash flow and value per share, For 2026, we expect adjusted free cash flow to grow more than 15% over 2025 at $3 gas. That discipline remains true in 2027.

Even with low projected gas prices and the repositioning of our capital, we expect free cash flow to remain strong. Still a double digit free cash flow yield at $3 gas. And we expect to be active across the full suite of investment opportunities. To that end, we announced today a 33% increase in our share repurchase authorization, to $2 billion, having repurchased approximately 1.2 billion of our stock since the program began. And we will do all of this while maintaining a strong balance sheet. To sum up, we are lowering our cost structure and our maintenance capital, increasing cash flow per share and allocating every dollar to what is most accretive per dollar invested.

Third quarter execution was on track. Continuous operations make that execution more efficient. 2027 is the investment that drives higher returns and free cash flow inflection from 2028 and beyond. Excited about where Gulfport is headed, and I look forward to updating you on our full 2027 plan in February. Operator, we will now open the call for questions.

Operator: Thank you. We will now be conducting a question-and-answer session. Thank you. Our first question is from Bert Donis from William Blair. You may ask your question.

Bert Donis: Thanks team. I really appreciate Slide 6. It gives us all a pretty good idea of what you are maybe thinking about next year. I could not help but notice the second rig is maybe targeting a smaller pad size on average. Is that by design so that you could you know, quickly adjust it up or down, or is that a little bit too cute? And maybe, you know, does that fit perfectly with that frac crew, or would you need to adjust the frac crew if you move that around?

Matthew H. Rucker: Yeah, Bert. This is Matthew. Appreciate the question. This is an illustrative slide for 2027. We still got a lot of work to do to shore up the budget, which we will come out with here in a few months. But, by and large, we drill a mix of anywhere between, you know, 3 to 5-well pads. And that is in this program. I think any shuffling around will fit very nicely with 1 continuous frac fleet as we do have a little bit of white space in there with some wiggle room as we shift things around. So I would not read too much into that and or. And specifically around a rig drilling smaller type pad. That.

That will be a blend between both rigs, somewhere between 3 and 5 wells per pad.

Bert Donis: Perfect. And then on Slide 8, you put another help helpful graph where you show the economics between your wet gas and your dry gas. And you noted that your turn in line schedule right now is liquids rich weighted at least in the near term, but it looks like it would take is a, you know, $0.20 move in gas or a $0.20, you know, maybe a dollar move in liquids or something like that to flip the economics the other way. Is that something that we would look at as a 2028 event where you would change it, or do you have flexibility to maybe impact second half 2027 plans based on the strip?

Domenic J. Dell'Osso Jr.: We are pretty flexible. We can move things around a bit. Our highest-return opportunities right now as a company are clearly in the wet gas area of long laterals. So we are going to focus there. Initially, and I think that will hold up through a fair amount of price sensitivity. So we have a lot of flexibility. But I have said before, I think it is really hard to think about timing your allocation of capital around the cycles of commodity prices that the cycles of commodity prices move a lot faster than your cycles of capital.

So to the extent that, you know, $0.25 on gas or $1 or $2 on oil, swings 1 pad to the next, you are really trying to go with your highest return at a mid cycle price. And, you know, just execute in a really well-planned fashion. Well said.

Operator: Thank you. Next question comes from Jacob Phillip Roberts of TPH Research. You may proceed with your question.

Jacob Roberts: Good morning. Nick, I wanted to ask on the SCOOP asset. I think you guys are keeping your ear to the ground there in 2027 and kind of backing a little bit, obviously. But just wondering what you are seeing from your peers in terms of zone delineation and resource development. and what you are seeing, what you are hearing? And then what do you think this means for your asset and inventory over time?

Domenic J. Dell'Osso Jr.: Yeah. Great question. I will start, and I think Matthew has some stuff to add here. We are seeing a lot of capital form around the area. there is been some transactions recently with some pretty well informed capital showing up in and around our position. Those producers are targeting other zones, a little shallower than the Woodford and some really quite productive. And so we are pretty interested in what we are seeing from everybody and recognize that this acreage may have more value than we have historically thought about. So we are gonna really try to assess that.

Matthew H. Rucker: Yeah. And Jake, just to add to that, I think some of the activity we are paying a lot of attention to is around the inventory we have talked about historically that we have not really been drilling and so you think about the Springer specifically the Sycamore and then the deeper dry part of the Woodford that we have inventory located there that we have not drilled historically. We have been in the condensate window of the Woodford. We are going to take the time to assess, look into the data that we have that we participate in on a nonoperative basis. Learn from that, and then assess how we want to develop this moving forward.

Domenic J. Dell'Osso Jr.: You know, I think I talked about this on the last call, but I would reiterate that gas in Central Oklahoma does have some pretty good value as you think about the power market dynamics as it can access markets via existing pipes You do not need incremental infrastructure to get that gas to pretty attractive markets. And given the interest in developing data centers and new power options, Oklahoma is a really good market for that. So you know, we will see where that goes. But it is interesting optionality to have gas resource in this part of the country right now.

Jacob Roberts: You kind of covered my second follow-up, so I will pivot a bit there on the good ZIP code commentary. We generally agree. I guess this might be a tougher 1 and a bit longer term, but when we think about the illustrative 2027 and the elimination of white space, with the 2 rig cadence, I think your slides note 13 years of inventory at that pace. In a 29 scenario when we hope to see much higher demand regionally than there is today, Would you feel comfortable going back to a 2.5 rig program where there is that white space?

Or are we going to be thinking about the longer term growth dynamics of this play as trying to be as efficient as possible and waiting to add those rigs until you can kind of fill it up and maintain that 15+ year type of inventory.

Domenic J. Dell'Osso Jr.: Well, you are kind of laying out a few different theories there that are a bit hard to react to, in a vacuum. But I would say that you know, you we always think about allocating capital based on a mid cycle price. And so if our mid cycle price view were to change dramatically, then your threshold for capital efficiency as to how you think about where you are willing to invest might move. I do not actually really expect that to happen. In 2028 or 2029. I think more of what you see is this continued rising of the floor of gas.

There will be moments where gas spikes up high, and those are going to be great times for our company and for our industry. But there is a lot of gas. And there is a lot of opportunities to bring gas to market. And so I am not I am not thinking that we are underwriting a $5 or $6 gas strip anytime soon. I do think it will grind higher. Over the next few years from. You know, we are kind of $3.50 people. I think it will grind higher from there, and that can certainly ease up how you think about you know, the hurdle rate from a well cost perspective.

But I am really not focused on that right now. And instead, I think we, as a team, are focused on continuing to drive that cost per foot down. That opens up the ability to invest more consistently at any point in the cycle It opens up the ability to generate more cash from every dollar you spend. Which gives you more financial flexibility in how you think about every decision from returning capital to shareholders, to reducing debt, to adding valuable assets to the portfolio. So that is really what our focus is right now. And we will stay you know, pretty tight on that.

Operator: Thank you. Next question is from Tim Rezvan of KeyBanc Capital Markets. You may proceed with your question.

Tim Rezvan: Hi. Nick, I want to ask about the Marcellus Gulfport has done a pretty good job delineating the inventory in Eastern Ohio, and you have talked about 100 locations. Returns seem a bit lower, but it is still pretty an intriguing kind of liquids lever. It seems likely there would be more opportunity to drive efficiencies here given your newer in the drilling program. So can you talk about how activity may trend going forward as, like, a percentage of your TIL count? Or is it sort of TBD until you get that next 2-well pad online?

Matthew H. Rucker: Yeah, Timothy. Appreciate the question. I think you can kind of see that a little bit on Slide 6. In the shaded bars. We give an indication of what percentage that mix looks to be for us, and I think that is the right percentage right now. that is going to include really the core Marcellus that we have talked about where we have the M3 midstream and processing agreements. For 2027, it does include the turn in lines of the 2 delineation wells to the north. And so as we have talked about before, that is really a good test for us to the liquids mix in that northern acreage block that we have.

And the long term productivity of the gas so we can go to market, on negotiations for a gathering and processing agreement where that acreage is undedicated. So we will follow a similar playbook as the core Marcellus that is going to take some time to develop. And so as we have those conversations, I would not expect the percentage of Marcel's development to go up significantly from what we have been doing. Until we get that in place. And then by that time, call it 2029 and beyond, we will have more drillable inventory ready to go. And that certainly. That mix could change depending on market conditions. From an efficiency standpoint, I think you are spot on.

We have drilled 2 now 4-well pads in the core area. We have seen those drilling times go down on every single pad that we have done, and we have seen our dollar per foot decrease dramatically from the first 2 wells that we did in the state of Ohio. I expect that to continue as we develop 2 more full development pads next year. And that is part of the math here on the dollar per foot that you see in our efficiency improvements next year and beyond. Okay. Good context. I appreciate that.

Tim Rezvan: And as a follow-up, Nick, in your prepared comments, you mentioned continuing discretionary leasing in 2027. I am not trying to pin you down to a number because I know you will not give 1. But is the opportunity set, do you feel like that $100 million level is that out there? Could you transact in that? Or could you transact more? Just trying to understand what the opportunity set is I know that the board has to decide on what that budget is. But what does that opportunity set look like, I guess, what I am trying to ask Thanks.

Domenic J. Dell'Osso Jr.: Good question, Timothy. And you are right that it is a little early for us to give you a specific number here because we are going to work through our budgeting process as we typically would. But, there is plenty of opportunity out there. We are excited about a lot of things we are seeing. Our team is super active. They keep in close contact with a number of different, you know, directly with landowners and with other brokers and really trying to assess the opportunities. And they exist across a number of different, I would call them, subparts of the play. And we will be active.

So I am pretty optimistic about this company's ability to continue to add great acreage to this portfolio at really attractive prices. And I think our governor will be we think about capital allocation, the competition for capital allocation from the balance sheet, from the value of our stock, from all of those things. So I think the governor will be what do we choose to do as opposed to are there enough opportunities.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question is from Gabe Daoud from Truist Securities. You may proceed with your question.

Gabe Daoud: Nick, you alluded to this in just your prior answer, but was curious how the buyback fits into the capital allocation framework in 2017. I know there is a lot of calls on capital as you run a continuous 2-rig program as you highlighted, but curious maybe where the buyback sits?

Domenic J. Dell'Osso Jr.: I mean, again, it is competitive. Right? We will have excess free cash flow in the year. And the way I think about that excess free cash flow is we will be looking hard at exactly how we implement this decision to go to 2 rigs, And the timing of that, we will be looking hard at reducing debt or strengthening our balance sheet. We will be looking hard at buybacks, and we will be looking hard at adding really valuable acreage. And all those things have tension against each other. And depending on market conditions and anticipated return of anything you are looking at, you have the opportunity to you know, make a call.

I think you know, I like that. I like the ability to have a number of options for where to allocate our capital in ways that generate the highest rate of return. that is what we are paid to do as management teams and I think we have a full suite of options in front of us, and we increased the authorization so that it was clear that option remained relevant and on the table. And it will continue to compete against everything else that we do.

Gabe Daoud: Okay. That makes sense. Appreciate that. And then just as a follow-up, going back to Slide 6, you gave us a D&C per foot, and with an e-fleet locked in. I would imagine you contracted the second rig for a longer period of time But just curious, like what type of inflationary pressures, if any, are kind of embedded in those D&C per foot numbers?

Matthew H. Rucker: Yeah. Good question. We have baked all that in for 2027 based on our service contracts. I think on a stand alone basis, we would have expected to see around 5% inflation for 2027. And our typical cadence of development. what is really attractive about this development plan is we have been able to, offset all of those inflationary costs with our efficiency gains that we planned both from what we are going to feel like we see on the drilling side and the frac side on being a little bit better at what we do.

But, the ability to go sign up and lock in an e-fleet, which is significant dollar savings, on an annualized basis versus us utilizing our dual fuel fleets that we have used historically. So all of that to us is really an offset and then the. You know, any increase in capital you would see next year would be all activity based, Gabe. Right. All right. Awesome. Thanks, Matthew.

Operator: Our next question is from Carlos Escalante of Wolfe Research.

Carlos Escalante: Hey, good morning, Nick and Matthew and team. That part of the question is actually a perfect segue to what we want to ask. So going back to Slide 6 on DNC rollout, but there is some clear savings that we can see on the middle chart. But I am trying to understand, parse through what is the breakdown of those savings how much does it come from the continuous operations versus the electric frac fleet starting in mid-2027. And then when you think about decision triggers into early 2027, are there any conditions under which you would stay at a lower cadence versus what you anticipate today?

Domenic J. Dell'Osso Jr.: I will answer the second 1 first. Look. We are clearly headed in this direction, and we are going to start the year with 2 rigs because that is the typical cadence that we have. And so, you know, I will never say never. there is always some market conditions that cause you to rethink your capital allocation. So that is clearly why we are not giving guidance today and why we want to get through winter, and we want to have the full setup of plan laid out in front of us and make sure that we are ready to commit to a full year of this. We want to have all of our vendors lined up.

We wanna have all of the pads ready to go, and there is just a lot of detail that you have fairly well baked in November, but not completely. So we will hold on giving a formal answer to that until we give guidance. But, you know, we are clearly looking at this hard and wanting to be moving in this direction. On the breakdown, it is really hard to separate. They are very connected. The contract for the e fleet really becomes a lot easier for us to have taken on when we know that we are going to be moving to a more active program in Appalachia. Those fleets require commitment.

That commitment, in this case, is 18 months. And so, you know, we wanted to be in a place where we felt like we had good line of sight to having this level of activity. Now that said, we can sublease that out if we need to or work with the vendor to allow others to use it at times if we have a pullback in activity. So feel really good about the way that commitment is structured. But, they are interlinked. Sure. Thank you. Appreciate that, Nick.

Carlos Escalante: And then perhaps just as a quick reminder to us on the North Marcellus and maybe how that relates to how you view the next 2 years. What is the underlying assumption of a successful appraisal where you see results you like on that well. That go into the 2028 target and goals. And whether that is that would pose upside case, or would it simply mean that you have more optionality in your capital allocation program moving forward.

Matthew H. Rucker: Yeah. Carlos, I think the latter, to your comment there, the way we are viewing that is we have got a plan for next year that is baked generally speaking, with our core Marcellus. We will delineate through, completions and turn in line the 2 northern Marcellus wells, early next year. We will evaluate the production results. We will go to market for our midstream and processing agreements, which takes some time. And then upon successful completion of that, I view it as more optionality in our development program.

Our expectation is that this area will be very similar to our core Marcellus, and so you can think about the successful delineation there being an extension of the well set that we have currently that we are developing. So just more flexibility and optionality and that would be something we would determine at a later date.

Carlos Escalante: Appreciate the color. Thank you, Nick and Matthew.

Operator: Our next question is from Peyton Doorn of UBS. You may proceed with your question.

Peyton Doorn: Hey, good morning everybody. Thank you for having me on. I thought the new gas supply agreement that you detailed was a positive. Is this something that you see Gulfport looking to expand in the future if possible? Maybe said in a different way, is there a certain upper bound longer term in terms of how much gas you would like to dedicate to these types of supply agreements?

Domenic J. Dell'Osso Jr.: it is a great question. I think about an agreement like this as essentially a hedge. We are taking gas that we have been selling at Rec Zone 3 in Chicago Citygate, and we are still gonna sell it at those locations. What we have done is we have agreed to a fixed spread for our gas to that location. So the only part of the hedge that is in place is the spread we receive to those 2 pricing points. We still float at that point and just get a spread to it. And that spread is pretty attractive relative to what we have received in the past. So it is an uplift. And we like that.

We did not have to take on any more cost to do it. Because this is with firm transport that we already had. So this is a really good trade for us. Again, these 2 contracts combined to be about 10%. So I think there is plenty more that we could do here. And we have had other inbounds from people trying to secure gas across Appalachia thinking about the role that Gulfport plays in that. We are going to continue to listen carefully. We are going to continue to study the market and understand how it is evolving and understand where our gas has the most value, understand where we believe the most upside is.

And make, you know, further hedge decisions with all of that information over time. So I do think there is more upside here. I think you know, Gulfport will be a beneficiary of this growing demand. And we talked last quarter about how some companies will do really long term agreements that maybe are not the right fit for a company like Gulfport, but an agreement like this, which is, 5 or 10 years on the long end, fits much better. And, you know, again, the pricing that we can realize here is a great premium to what we have had in the past, and we are really happy with it.

So open to doing more, but it has to be on the right economics.

Peyton Doorn: Yeah. Makes sense. And I appreciate all the detail there. And I just want to ask on the balance sheet. You know, debt crept up a bit this quarter. With free cash flow in the fourth quarter looking like it is going to be a nice jump up. I am curious if you are comfortable with where the current leverage stands or if it is kind of at a point where you might try to take it down a little into next year? Thank you.

Domenic J. Dell'Osso Jr.: It will be down at year end. It will be back more towards 1x at year end. Or right about 1x. Actually at year end. So, yeah, I think, you know, look, it is it is up this quarter. We closed on the big state lands acquisition during the quarter, and we had a lot of priorities this year. And, we are generating most of our cash in the second half of the year, so it will come back down. Still think about that 1 times as a good mid-cycle place to be. And so now that we have ticked above it here for a quarter, we would expect it to come down. Okay.

Peyton Doorn: that is helpful. Thanks for having me on.

Operator: Thank you. Our last question is from Michael Scialla of Pickering Energy Partners. You may proceed with your question.

Michael Furrow: Hi, good morning. Thanks for taking our questions. I would just like to start with a big picture question for you, Nick. So now that you have had more time in the seat and a chance to really look under the hood, where do you see the room for the most improvement? And are there certain opportunities that are clearer to you now than they were from the outside looking in?

Domenic J. Dell'Osso Jr.: Yeah. I think, you know, not to beat the dead horse here, Michael, but I would just point you to Slide 6. I mean, that is why we laid out all this detail in the deck. This is the biggest opportunity for the company, and Matthew and I are both really excited about how this positions us for the next several years of development in Ohio. We are going to be a lot more efficient. We are going to drive our cost structure lower by better vendor contracting, by better execution, by better planning.

And we think there is an opportunity to continue to add great acreage to the business because we have the efficiency that is showing up and turn that acreage into great returns for our shareholders. So we think all of this is connected, and I go back to those 3 priorities that we are gonna have, which is improve capital and operating efficiency, positioning our gas for the growing demand, and adding valuable acreage to the portfolio. And I think, you know, this move that we are making here is the real catalyst to unlock that. So that is what this is all about. And, yes, my confidence has grown as I have been here. on executing exactly this plan.

Michael Furrow: Understood. Appreciate the response, and, I agree. it is a great slide, and the benefits look pretty clear. Just as a follow-up, we could not help but notice the layering on of hedges for next year, particularly the additional swaps. Do you feel like the 2027 hedge book is in a good place at this stage? And additionally, does the hedge protection kind of change your decision to allocate capital towards buybacks or do you kind of view it as a separate decision?

Domenic J. Dell'Osso Jr.: Separate decision. Always. Hedges are. You know, they are a trade you can take on and off. But no, I am happy with our hedge position for 2027. I mean, given where the strip is, I would love to have more at the average hedge price that we have And if we were to get some cold this winter that were to pop gas prices up, to an attractive level again, then I think we would hedge more. I do not really see us hedging beyond 2027 at these levels. But we are always nimble around hedges. And if we like prices in a given period, we can add more.

So feel pretty good about the protection we have for 2027. We are continuing to monitor basis hedges, basis hedge opportunities as well as, think about 2028 and 2029. Appreciate the time. Alright. Okay. Thank you all. I appreciate everybody's time on the call this morning and all the questions. We really do have a great inflection in front of us at Gulfport. We are very excited about what is to come in 2027 and beyond I think the setup for this company is really fantastic. So look forward to seeing you all in between now and earnings as we will be out on the road a little bit, and then we will talk about 2027 on the next quarter.

#3108. Traders pile into 'bubble puts' on CoreWeave as neocloud stocks plunge

A key corner of the artificial intelligence trade is taking a beating on Wednesday and traders are betting it could get even worse.

Shares of neocloud companies – businesses that offer access to the GPUs powering artificial intelligence as a service – plunged Wednesday after debt yields for Nvidia-backed CoreWeave continued to reach new heights. (An article in The Financial Times that the company is targeting insurance companies for further debt financing apparently didn't help things either.)

Meanwhile, in a post on X, Social Capital founder Chamath Palihapitiya raised questions about a private credit bubble alongside a screengrab showing CoreWeave's bonds hitting a 15% yield. Elon Musk replied "yikes." CoreWeave stock plunged 15%. Nebius Group and Iren, popular trades connected to the data centers build-out, also fell as much as 10%.

Options volume in CoreWeave surged to more than seven times the 30-day average, Nebius almost four times, and Iren twice the normal volume. More calls traded than puts in Nebius and Iren, but in both, more calls were likely initiated by sellers than buyers, according to Cboe LiveVol data.

The most bearish action was in CoreWeave, where traders bought just shy of 200,000 puts, compared to 106,000 calls.

One standout trade happened around 10 a.m. ET when someone opened a new position of 26,000 37.5-strike puts expiring Dec. 18 that traded near the ask price, suggesting the puts were purchased, according to SpotGamma data.

"These are bubble puts," said Scott Bauer, CEO of Chicago-based Prosper Trading Academy. "These are not rip-ups that you buy thinking they'll go to zero. This is the hub, the center of the AI trade, and likely some kind of margin play for someone to hedge their exposure in highly correlated stocks or maybe even the Nasdaq."

The contracts sold for 74 cents apiece for a total of $1.9 million and need CoreWeave to erase another 42% over the next two months to pay off. Prior to this trade, there were just over 1,000 open contracts, meaning the position is a new one.

CoreWeave IPO'd in March 2025 at $40 per share.

"Maybe this is someone that was in early or in on the IPO saying this is my breakeven level," Bauer added. "Maybe they couldn't get this kind of protection in other stocks, the index, or other products."

#3107. How Modular Data Centers Will Scale AI Infrastructure

Steve Altizer, President & CEO of Compu Dynamics & Compu Dynamics Modular, pioneers high-density modular infrastructure for the AI era.

AI is forcing us to rethink how we design, build and operate data centers. In this new era, data centers will look less like buildings and more like an industrial plant, made up of modules that plug into common power, cooling and network “utilities” the way you plug an electric car into a charger.

For decades, we treated data centers like landmark buildings: You select a site, pour concrete and build a facility for a wide variety of IT customers. That model still makes sense for cloud or enterprise IT workloads running at five to 30 kilowatts a rack.

However, AI requires an entirely different infrastructure stack. AI racks can draw significantly more power: 150 to 250 kilowatts or more. When AI systems are installed in a facility designed for the cloud, you end up with a football-field-sized white space containing tiny islands of racks. It is an expensive way to support a small amount of equipment.

What I see emerging instead is an industrial platform: a site that standardizes power, liquid cooling and networks, and then accepts factory-built IT modules the way charging stations accept cars. You roll a module up, plug into the electrical bus, the liquid cooling loop and the fiber, run your workload, then swap that module for another when the next generation of GPUs is available.

We refer to this future AI design as “bring your own white space,” but it is only half a joke. Imagine a site owner providing a robust utility yard, including medium-voltage power distribution, heat-rejection systems and backbone networking, while tenants bring their own white space modules the way they bring their own IT gear into a colocation facility today.

Colocation providers already standardize power distribution systems, cooling plants and meet-me rooms. We are taking that same mindset a bit further: Standardize site infrastructure, including power, cooling and network connectivity, while tailoring data hall modules to each AI customer’s requirements for rack layouts, power distribution, liquid cooling and cabling. Factory-built white-space modules ranging from 5 MW to 20 MW can accommodate both traditional colocation and high-density AI workloads, allowing operators to adapt capacity as hardware requirements evolve without rebuilding the entire facility.​

AI is not just another workload inside a traditional data center. It is a different species of facility. While a typical cloud rack operates at roughly 10 kW, an AI rack demands 150 kW, driving a 10 to 15 times increase in density that requires an entirely new approach to power distribution. This shift forces the primary cooling medium from air to liquid, dictating completely different plant designs and controls. Furthermore, because AI requires significantly lower floor space per megawatt, traditional space planning breaks down completely.

GPUs are advancing so quickly that we do not have 10 years to “prove” a design before deployment. As Peter Gross has said, “The data center industry loves innovation as long as it is 10 years old.” AI does not give us that luxury. We are essentially bolting the wings on the plane while we are in flight.

Modular fits because modules are designed around a specific rack density and cooling strategy, so you can optimize fluid temperatures, pump energy and distribution losses in ways far harder in a traditional data hall. A modular campus can adapt over time by swapping obsolete modules for new ones instead of stranding an entire building, as we see with 20-year-old sites in top tier markets that were never designed for current densities.

Sustainability is not just about power usage effectiveness (PUE); it is about how much you build, how long it lasts and how hard it is to change. Modular allows incremental scaling to add modules as demand grows, enabling compact layouts that reduce land disruption, and making higher-temperature liquid cooling more practical, which improves overall energy efficiency.

An emerging AI trend is the willingness to consider architectures without traditional UPS systems and diesel generators. For an existing colo, ripping out that infrastructure is unthinkable. In a modular world, you can create AI-specific modules that assume a different risk posture from day one. No traditional UPS battery strings or diesel generator sets, and a power path optimized for efficiency rather than ride-through. All while still plugging into standardized site utilities.

Trying to retrofit that into an existing colo is like trying to turn a passenger jet into a cargo ship without ever landing it. Building it into a modular design from the start is far more rational.

In conversations with AI customers, two words dominate: speed and scale. If you can deliver fast and compress a traditional 18-to-24-month build cycle down to six to nine months, you are very popular at the party. If you cannot, you may not get invited. Factories have a hard throughput limit, and the capacity now being requested for AI and cloud can easily outpace the industry’s manufacturing base.

That is why I often compare modular data center assembly lines to automotive lines. Once designs are standardized, you want modules rolling out like cars off an assembly line: same chassis and interfaces, different “trim packages” for each AI customer.

Leaders evaluating modular partners should look behind the marketing and ask whether the company truly manufactures at scale, if the standard module fits their AI use case, whether the provider can deliver a turnkey solution and not just drop off a box and whether the commercial terms reflect the capital intensity of modular manufacturing with appropriate milestone or staged payments.

In AI, the mission of a data center is straightforward: Produce tokens at the lowest possible cost, with the least energy and land, as close as practical to the users who need that compute. That increasingly points toward modular data centers that are truly and purely token factories rather than architectural trophies.

Both the Citi® / AAdvantage® Platinum Select® World Elite Mastercard®  and Citi Strata Premier® Card can help you rack up AAdvantage miles. The former earns them directly; the latter transfers points to American Airlines at a 1:1 ratio. So which one is better for American Airlines flyers?

For earning rewards, the Citi Strata Premier® Card is the winner. Although it's not an American Airlines credit card, it can make it easier to accumulate AAdvantage miles on many purchases with its higher earning rates and the option to transfer ThankYou points to American.

Still, the Citi® / AAdvantage® Platinum Select® World Elite Mastercard® can help you achieve AAdvantage elite status and offers perks when flying American Airlines, including a free checked bag and preferred boarding. In 2027, the annual fee will increase, but the card will add new bonus categories and other benefits.

The Citi Strata Premier® Card is a better fit for travelers who want to earn American Airlines miles without committing all their rewards to a single airline program.

Although the Citi® / AAdvantage® Platinum Select® World Elite Mastercard® is an American Airlines credit card, the Citi Strata Premier® Card can be a faster way to accumulate AAdvantage miles on many purchases.

That's because Citi Strata Premier® Card holders can transfer ThankYou points to American Airlines AAdvantage — and several other loyalty programs — at a 1:1 ratio.

Currently, the Citi Strata Premier® Card offers more rewards than the Citi® / AAdvantage® Platinum Select® World Elite Mastercard® in every bonus category. On Jan. 24, 2027, when the benefits on the Citi® / AAdvantage® Platinum Select® World Elite Mastercard® change, that will change — but only in a couple of narrowly defined categories: select streaming services and eligible Rides and Rails purchases, which include taxis, rideshares, subways and trains. Unless those categories make up a significant portion of your spending, the Citi Strata Premier® Card will likely yield more points overall, even if your ultimate goal is American Airlines miles.

The Citi Strata Premier® Card also offers a $100 annual hotel benefit when you book a single hotel stay of $500 or more, excluding taxes and fees, through Citi Travel. Using the full benefit can more than offset the card’s annual fee, and hotel bookings through Citi Travel earn 10 ThankYou points per dollar.

Just keep in mind that booking through Citi Travel may mean giving up hotel loyalty program benefits you would receive by booking directly. Whether the $100 hotel perk offers enough value to justify booking through Citi Travel will depend on the property, the rates available and how much you value those hotel loyalty benefits.

» Learn more: Is the Citi Strata Premier® Card worth its annual fee?

One of the biggest advantages of the Citi Strata Premier® Card is the ability to earn ThankYou points, which can be transferred to several airline and hotel loyalty programs. If you want the option to transfer points to American Airlines but also see value in the card’s other airline and hotel partners, the Citi Strata Premier® Card is a better choice.

Transfer ratios will vary depending on which card you have.

Although you can transfer points from the Citi Strata Premier® Card to American Airlines, you won’t get any Loyalty Points.

The Citi® / AAdvantage® Platinum Select® World Elite Mastercard® is a strong choice if you want American Airlines benefits. Keep in mind that the card is getting revamped in 2027 with a higher annual fee and new benefits. See NerdWallet's coverage for more details.

The Citi® / AAdvantage® Platinum Select® World Elite Mastercard® comes with several benefits that can significantly offset the annual fee:

Free checked bag: Get a free first checked bag on domestic American Airlines itineraries for the primary cardholder and up to four companions traveling on the same reservation. If you check bags with American, this benefit alone could make the card worth getting.

Preferred boarding: The primary cardholder and up to four companions on the same reservation receive preferred boarding.

American Airlines Vacations discount: Save 10% on eligible American Airlines Vacations packages.

Inflight discount: 25% off inflight food and beverage purchases. This perk is being replaced on Jan. 24, 2027, with an inflight statement credit.

$125 flight discount: Spend at least $20,000 during your card membership year and renew the card to receive a $125 American Airlines flight discount. This perk is also changing in 2027; see below.

Starting Jan. 24, 2027, the card will offer:

Inflight statement credits: Receive up to $100 back in statement credits annually on inflight purchases. This replaces the old 25% off inflight food and drink purchases.

$150 flight discount: Spend at least $20,000 during your card membership year and renew the card to receive a $150 American Airlines flight discount. This replaces the $125 flight discount; the spending requirement is the same.

The inflight statement credits, in particular, will be easy to maximize and could potentially offset a meaningful portion of the card’s annual fee. Combined with the ability to earn Loyalty Points toward elite status and the card’s other perks, that can make the card more valuable for American’s flyers.

The Citi® / AAdvantage® Platinum Select® World Elite Mastercard® offers Turo credits. You receive up to $180 annually in statement credits on eligible Turo rentals, with up to $30 back per eligible rental.

On Jan. 24, 2027, the card will add several more perks:

Walmart+: Primary cardholders receive a complimentary annual Walmart+ membership, valued at $98.

Global Entry or TSA PreCheck: Receive up to a $120 application fee credit every four years.

FOX One: Get 50% off an annual FOX One subscription.

Travel protections: Get trip delay protection, trip cancellation and interruption protection, worldwide car rental insurance and lost baggage protection.

It’s unusual to see a Global Entry or TSA PreCheck credit on a card with an annual fee under $200. When that perk kicks in, the card could become a good option for travelers who prioritize AAdvantage miles but also want a credit card that fully reimburses the application fee for Global Entry or TSA PreCheck.

» Learn more: American Airlines credit card benefits guide

Cardholders receive 1 Loyalty Point for every eligible AAdvantage mile earned from purchases. That means everyday spending can move you closer to AAdvantage elite status, in addition to earning miles you can redeem for flights. American’s entry-level elite status requires 40,000 Loyalty Points, so putting significant spending on the card can help you reach that threshold.

If you want to earn rewards on everyday spending and have the flexibility to move those points to American Airlines — and you don’t need the airline-specific benefits — the Citi Strata Premier® Card is the best choice.

That said, the Citi® / AAdvantage® Platinum Select® World Elite Mastercard® makes more sense for frequent American Airlines flyers who can take advantage of benefits such as a free checked bag and preferred boarding, or for travelers who want to earn Loyalty Points toward American Airlines elite status through credit card spending.
