#3105. Aemetis (AMTX) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Federal model update lifts dairy RNG credits and returns Aemetis to profit.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Aemetis, Inc. (AMTX +38.40%) reported a return to profitability driven by the recognition of federal production tax credits and operational growth across its fuel segments. Management stated that the update to the federal carbon intensity model significantly increased the value of credits generated by dairy renewable natural gas production. The company is advancing infrastructure projects intended to reduce fossil fuel consumption at its ethanol facility while expanding feedstock production for the renewable diesel market. Additionally, the company is pursuing international growth through biodiesel exports and a potential public offering of its subsidiary in India.

Operator: Hello, and welcome to the Aemetis Third Quarter 26 Earnings Conference Call. Joining us on today's call are Eric A. McAfee, the chairman and chief executive officer, Todd A. Waltz, chief financial officer and Andy Foster, president of Aemetis Advanced Fuels.

Todd A. Waltz: I will now turn the call over to Todd A. Waltz. Thank you, and welcome, everyone. Before we begin, I would like to remind you that during the call, we will be making forward-looking statements within the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 2000. These statements involve risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from those expressed or implied. Please refer to our earnings release and SEC filings for a discussion of these risks. We will also refer to adjusted EBITDA, a non-GAAP measure, A reconciliation to the most recently comparable GAAP measure is included in our earnings release.

Before reviewing in detail, I want to highlight that the company posted net income of $5.2 million or $0.07 per basic share in the third quarter and adjusted EBITDA of $24.8 million For the third quarter of 26, revenues grew 49% to $88.2 million compared with $59.2 million in the third quarter of 25. With growth in both the California ethanol and dairy renewable natural gas operating segments, from both operations and 45Z clean fuel production tax credits. Section 45Z production tax credit revenue was 24.7 million in the quarter, comprised of $20.1 million from dairy renewable net-- Net-- dairy renewable natural gas and $4.6 million from California ethanol.

45Z revenue included an $11 million cumulative true up for the first and second quarter of 26 from the regulatory updates to the 45Z GREET model. Biodiesel sales in the third quarter were $7.3 million rebounding from $2.5 million in the second quarter as delivery to 3 India oil marketing companies resumed under a $17 million allocation to our India subsidiary. Operating income was $20.9 million in the third quarter, an improvement of $29.4 million compared to the third quarter of 2025 which had an operating loss of $8.5 million Net income was $5.2 million, equal to $0.07 per basic share. An improvement of $29 million compared to a $23.7 million loss in the third quarter of 25.

Adjusted EBITDA was $24.8 million in the third quarter, an increase of $29.8 million compared to the negative $5 million in the third quarter of 25. For the first 9 months of 26, adjusted EBITDA was $33.2 million compared with negative $21.5 million during the same period of 2025. Cash at quarter end was $3.4 million In September, we received $22.4 million from the sale of section 45C production tax credits. In August, Aemetis Biogas amended its series a preferred unit agreement to extend the redemption date to December 31, 2026 and to reduce the interest rate on the credit agreement that would apply if the units are not redeemed to the greater prime plus 5% or 12%.

Capital investments supporting our energy efficiency projects and investments in biogas production were $20.2 million in the third quarter, and $35.3 million for the first 9 months of 2026. With that overview, I will turn the call over to Eric A. McAfee.

Eric A. McAfee: Thanks, Todd. Let's highlight 3 key takeaways from the third quarter. First, Q3 continues the financial inflection points we noted during the Q2 earnings call with the posting of net income of $5.2 million and adjusted EBITDA of $24.8 million during the third quarter. We continue to grow with consolidated revenue up 49% year-over-year, and improvement in operating income of $29.4 million and increased adjusted EBITDA by $29.8 million compared to the third quarter of 25. Second, we now generate higher revenues due to the California Air Resources Board approval about a year ago, of 7 new low carbon fuel standard pathways for our renewable natural gas business.

At an average carbon intensity score of negative 380 compared with the negative 150 default carbon intensity score for these digesters, which was shown in Q2 25 revenue. The approval of 7 diget-- Biogas digesters has been providing additional revenue with a higher LCFS value each quarter since Q3 25. And additional biogas digester pathways are nearing approval These LCFS pathway approvals substantially expand the LCFS credit generation per MMBtu of RNG produced. And will continue to drive meaningful revenue increases as we scale production. And third, our capital projects are advancing with $20.2 million of investment during the quarter. Review these projects and how we continue to create value as federal and state laws are being implemented.

In our dairy renewable natural gas business, every MMBtu of dairy RNG generates 4 revenue streams, natural gas molecule, a California low carbon fuel standard credit that is sold to oil companies, a federal d 3 RIN that is also sold to oil companies, and a section 45Z production tax credit. The LCFS credit and the 45Z tax credit are calculated using the carbon intensity of our biofuel. So credits are generated in proportion to how far below the standard a biofuel is scored. An LCFS pathway at negative 380 generates substantially more credit per MMBtu than the negative 150 default score.

We have 7 approved California LCFS pathways, averaging negative 380 carbon intensity, with 6 more pathways nearing approval by CARB. For the 45Z production tax credit, the Department of Energy issued its updated 45Z CF GREET model on September 8th of this year, Which decreased the carbon intensity scores used to calculate 45Z credits for dairy RNG credits we sold in July were valued at $15.20 per MMBtu. The credits we sold in September generated from ethanol and RNG production during 2026. Represent a tax credit value of approximately $62 per MMBtu for dairy RNG, and $0.33 per gallon of ethanol. For 2026, before sales debt discounts and transaction costs.

We received $22.4 million from the September 45Z tax credit sale and our third quarter results included an approximately $11 million cumulative true up for RNG dispensed in the first half of the year. As dairy renewable natural gas volume grows, all 4 revenue streams grow. But the approval of LCFS pathways in California is expected to create significant increases in revenues from the renewable natural gas production. We operate 14 biogas digesters today, taking waste from 17 dairies and transporting biogas through a 36 mile pipeline to our RNG production facility that is connected to the utility gas pipeline. We have more than 50 dairies that have signed participation agreements. 2 new methane capture digesters were completed last month.

And we have received 13 additional cleanup and compression units that will be located at the next 13 digesters to come online. Regarding our California ethanol business, we have 2 projects that are slated to significantly improve our financial performance. In addition to further improvements in 45Z values, and expected increases in LCFS credit prices. Our mechanical vapor recompression system installation is an energy efficiency project that is expected to add approximately $32 million in annual cash flow from 3 positive impacts on our operations. We will reduce about 80% of the natural gas needed for our operations, and the 45Z credit and the LCFS credit generated by every gallon of ethanol. The MVR project is making excellent progress.

Key equipment arrived this summer, and we have completed major steps in construction of the system. Including placement of the 6 3.5 thousand-horsepower turbofans. #3104. AI Is The Accommodation Nobody Has To Approve

Dave Goyal | CEO, Think AI | Author | Speaker | Harvard AI Certified | 30+ yrs in Data & AI | Inc5000 Honoree.

​When I roll into a conference on my electric scooter, I see it on people’s faces: sympathy, then distance. When I reach out, some people pull back. When the room starts to mingle, I often get left out.

My first thought used to be, “I shouldn’t have this problem.” My second thought is the one that built my career: “Let me shine through with my knowledge and connect with a few people.”

Founders are expected to move city to city, state to state, country to country. Physical limits hit hardest right when you want to grow fastest.

Mindset is the bigger fight. You spend years trying to show you are not different.

Then there is money. Entrepreneurs with disabilities average about $61,000 a year in revenue, less than half the $135,000 of other entrepreneurs, according to a 2025 fact sheet from AEO based on NORC data.

Yet we choose this path more often. In 2025, 9.1% of employed people with a disability were self-employed, compared with 5.9% of everyone else, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.

The ones who make it have serious grit. But grit is tied to mindset, and it runs low. What keeps mine going is a life mission. Find your one superpower and a mission for life. Without them, it is very hard to survive, let alone grow.

An employee with a disability asks HR for an accommodation and waits for a yes. A founder has no HR. AI is the accommodation you can give yourself.

This summer I drove 3,200 miles: Los Angeles to Seattle to Yellowstone, back through Las Vegas and home. My car’s supervised self-driving system let me drive without my braces, using only my left leg. An AI assistant connected to a mapping service planned every day: miles between stops, where to eat and which hotels had the access I need. Not every hotel does, so I packed a folding shower chair.

Founders like me are already leaning in. Twenty-two percent of entrepreneurs with disabilities use generative AI, compared with 10% of other entrepreneurs, per the same AEO fact sheet.

Franklin D. Roosevelt had polio, like me, and founded the March of Dimes. Richard Branson and Ingvar Kamprad built Virgin and IKEA with dyslexia. Stevie Wonder, blind since infancy, has owned a Los Angeles radio station since 1979. Tony Robbins grew up poor and turned it into a lifelong mission to feed families.

Music was my own calmer. Learning to sing, write songs and play guitar built my confidence and songwriting taught me to write.

I have started nine companies, and five failed. AI helped me learn the full process of building a business, end to end, check it against what those nine taught me and turn it into a repeatable system. AI can keep the notes, so you do not have to carry it all in your head.

Preparing my first podcast episode took 24 to 30 hours: guest research, follow-ups, questions and how to bring my own thinking into the conversation. Today an automated process does that work, and I plan an entire episode, including recording, in two to three hours.

Start by tracking which tasks drain your energy for a week. Hand off the worst ones first.

I earned an MBA in international business with a finance major and studied toward the CFA, yet dyslexia meant I swapped numbers and never fully trusted them.

Now my AI works from a read-only copy of my accounting data. Nothing goes back without my approval, and client names are stored apart from the amounts, so the AI never sees who paid what. It sorts every transaction and catches my slips. It also catches the email where I meant one name and typed another. I finally trust my numbers.

I run an agentic operating system: an AI C-suite that holds daily stand-ups and works through a now, next, later task list with time for reflection. Several AI models share one knowledge base, so when something drops, it gets picked back up quickly.

Every agent has hard stops. Never delete anything. Never touch the financial system. Never send anything to clients or anyone outside the business. It all runs on a separate computer, cut off from the internet, that takes input only through a firewall.

My belief system: Practice active and reflective listening, offer solutions on the spot and never judge. Give without expecting money or work in return. If you give someone one thing in value, you get 10 times back in the long run. Just do not give because you hope for it.

To founders with disabilities: Find your superpower and get out in public. Do not worry about how you look, how you speak or what you do. Be open about your story, build in your niche and, once you succeed, give back. I have helped build tools that have reached a few thousand children with learning differences, most of them ages 6 to 13.

To technology leaders: Build communities and systems that teach people with disabilities to start and run businesses, and help them grow.

AI will not fix access to capital, health insurance costs or other people’s bias. But it can give back the energy, the hours and the confidence those barriers take.

Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

#3103. ScanSource (SCSC) Q1 2027 Earnings Call Transcript

Margin pressure and Brazil credit issues tempered a strong quarter.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

ScanSource, Inc. (SCSC -20.90%) reported a 30.1% increase in net sales for the first quarter, alongside margin pressure resulting from the sales mix. Management stated that broad-based hardware demand in North America led to the revenue growth, while profitability was impacted by a shift toward larger, lower-margin contracts and specific bad debt reserves in Brazil. The company completed the acquisition of MicroAge during the quarter to expand its footprint in cloud, cybersecurity, and artificial intelligence solutions. CFO Jones attributed the margin dynamics to timing and specific reserves, expressing confidence in the underlying earning power of the business.

Mortgage rates jumped after stronger-than-expected jobs data raised expectations for a Fed rate hike next month.

Mortgage rates are higher today on the heels of strong labor market data released yesterday.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage jumped to 7.07% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 14 basis points higher than yesterday but 25 basis points lower than a week ago. (See our chart below for more specifics.) A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.

Mortgage rates are always on the move, so if you're tracking rates day-to-day, you're going to see a lot of volatility.

As for today’s jump: Job openings hit a four-month high of 7.5 million in September, according to the Labor Department’s Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey released yesterday. Hiring picked up, too, while layoffs declined. Friday’s jobs report, showing October data, could potentially push mortgage rates one way or the other.

To understand the link between jobs data and mortgage rates, keep reading below the graph.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

This week, the Nerds will be watching the October jobs report, which comes out on Friday, Nov. 6. If it shows that employment remained steady (or even improved), that will build a stronger case for the Federal Reserve to raise overnight borrowing rates again at their next meeting on Dec. 8-9.

While the Fed doesn’t directly set mortgage rates, it does set the federal funds rate, which is the fee that banks must pay to borrow from one another (which is how they fund mortgages). Lenders raise mortgage rates any time they think that the federal funds rate is about to go up.

Central bankers hiked the federal funds rate in September, so a relatively steady jobs report would suggest the labor market could withstand higher rates.

The Fed has a dual mandate to control inflation while supporting maximum employment, and raising the federal funds rate is their main tool for bringing inflation down. If they can work to lower inflation without hurting employment too badly, central bankers may feel more confident to act.

The September Personal Consumption Expenditures price index (PCE), the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, was released last Thursday. The data shows inflation was 3.6% year-over-year in September, up from 3.4% in August.

September’s federal funds rate hike came in the middle of the month, so October’s inflation data will really capture its effect on inflation. The October PCE report will come out on Nov. 25.

#3101. The Evaluation Framework: The Most Underbuilt Part Of An AI System

Hiren is CTO & co-founder of Simform, an AI-native digital engineering services company.

When a production AI system starts to lose quality, spotting the decline is only part of the problem. The harder question is whether the team can explain what changed and judge, with enough confidence, whether the next fix will actually improve the system.

I was brought in to assess a production AI system that had begun to regress after months of stable performance. The production metrics showed the deterioration, but the team could not pinpoint when the behavior had shifted or tell whether the proposed fix would recover the quality they had lost.

My first question was whether we could take the same representative interactions and compare how the last-known-good version and the proposed fix handled them. We could not. The system was being monitored in production, but the measurement infrastructure needed to compare behavior across versions had never been built.

In that situation, engineering could make another change, but it could not show with confidence that the change improved the behavior that mattered. For the business, that meant additional engineering effort without consistent evidence of a better customer outcome, less manual intervention or a lower cost of completing the work.

What the team needed was a repeatable way to judge every proposed change against the same production-relevant expectations before it was released. Evaluation had to become part of the release process rather than a periodic quality check.

A production evaluation framework has three parts: a maintained set of representative examples, a defined way to judge how the system performs on them and clear thresholds for deciding whether a change is ready to release. Together, they answer a practical question: What evidence is enough to say that the next version is better?

It may begin with historical or curated examples, but it should incorporate real production interactions, known failure patterns and situations the team did not anticipate before launch. When a meaningful production failure occurs, that case should become part of the evaluation set so future versions have to prove they do not recreate it. This is especially important for low-frequency failures that carry a disproportionate cost, such as an incorrect action, unnecessary escalation or work that has to be corrected manually.

Some behaviors can be tested automatically, such as whether the system used the correct policy, extracted the expected information or passed the right inputs to another system. Others depend on context and require human review against defined criteria. The scoring method needs to stay consistent enough that changes in performance reflect the system, rather than changes in how it was assessed.

Teams should decide in advance which regressions are serious enough to block a change. A decline in a critical behavior may matter more than an improvement in the overall score, especially when that behavior affects customer experience, manual effort or the cost of completing the work.

Evaluation and observability thus serve different purposes in the release process. Observability helps engineers understand what is happening in the live system and investigate failures as they occur. Evaluation tells them whether the version they are about to release performs better on the behaviors that matter. The two should work together: production failures feed the evaluation set, and that evaluation set informs the next release decision.

The trade-off for CTOs is between investing engineering time in validation before it becomes urgent and prioritizing product work with a more visible near-term payoff. When the system is performing well, the value of stronger evaluation can be difficult to demonstrate compared with the next feature, integration or model improvement.

But deferring evaluation does not remove the work; it pushes it into future releases. Engineers may then have to reconstruct test inputs, inspect outputs manually and rebuild confidence around each significant change. What appeared to save time earlier becomes recurring validation work, slowing delivery when the team is already trying to move quickly.

The cost also shows up in the economics of the system. A change may reduce inference spend while increasing retries, escalations, human review or reopened work elsewhere in the workflow. For outcome-based applications, I care more about the fully loaded cost per resolved outcome than the cost of any one technical component. A cheaper configuration is only an improvement if the organization is also completing the work successfully at a lower overall cost. Evaluation should therefore reflect the outcome the system exists to produce, not only the quality of its output.

An evaluation framework should sit directly in the change process rather than be reviewed occasionally. Before release, the candidate version should run against the maintained evaluation set and be compared with the current version against agreed thresholds. After release, new production failures should feed back into that set, with clear ownership for keeping it current.

And before that work is cut from scope, I would ask one question: If we change this system next month, what evidence will tell us that the change helped?​

Net income slipped, but full-year guidance held as data center demand climbed.

MDU Resources Group, Inc. (MDU -6.51%) reported a decrease in quarterly net income to $14 million while reaffirming its full-year earnings guidance. Management noted that the company reached a positive final investment decision for the Bakken East Pipeline, a multibillion-dollar project designed to transport natural gas across North Dakota. The utility operations saw growth in sales volumes, particularly within the electric segment serving data center loads. The company stated it is following a disciplined capital allocation strategy, which included the decision to exit a renewable natural gas project in Oregon due to shifting regulatory requirements and rising costs.

This decision reflects the customer commitments we have secured our confidence in the strategic importance of the project, and our belief in the long term economic opportunities it creates for MDU resources North Dakota, and the broader region.

We have narrowed our estimated capital investment range to between $2.8 and $3.1 billion and finalize the project design, which will include segments of 42-inch, 36-inch, and 30-inch diameter pipe. As we have discussed previously, our approach to serving data centers and other large load customers is grounded in protecting existing customers while ensuring growth creates value for the communities we serve. We continue to follow the principle of cost causation, Customers that create costs are responsible for those costs through contracts, approved tariffs, and regulatory mechanisms.

This approach allows existing customers to benefit from broader utilization of our system, while supporting economic development opportunities within our service territory. And results in a reduction to customer bills. As an example, since 2023, we have returned $45.4 million to our North Dakota customers with this approach. We currently have over 1 gigawatt of data center loads signed, under ESAs, with approximately 280 megawatts currently online and additional volumes expected to ramp online over the next few years. As I did mention, during the quarter, we did make the decision to discontinue development of the Knot Landfill renewable natural gas project in Oregon.

Due to continued increased development costs and changes enacted by rulemaking that have shifted the timing and reduced the volume of our need for the renewable natural gas. In the state. #3098. Data Sovereignty Isn't About Where Your Data Lives—It's About Who's In Control

Emma McGrattan is the Chief Technology Officer at Actian.

In June 2025, a French Senate committee asked a Microsoft executive if he could guarantee that data stored on Microsoft Azure in France would never be handed to U.S. authorities without explicit consent. He said he couldn’t. His answer confirmed that controlling where your data is stored is only part of data sovereignty. You also need to control who can access it, under whose authority and for what purpose.

I’ve spent much of my career helping organizations navigate changes in enterprise data architecture, from the days when they ran nearly everything themselves to today’s increasingly complex cloud and AI ecosystems. More recently, my work on data and AI sovereignty has brought a recurring concern into focus: Organizations often have far less control over their technology than they think. Splitting my time between Dublin and New York, I see the same challenge playing out on both sides of the Atlantic, even as the regulatory and political pressures differ.

​Many technology executives I speak with still reach for a map when I ask about their data sovereignty. But location alone doesn’t equal sovereignty.

So, how do you know whether your organization genuinely controls its data or simply complies with the rules governing where it resides? I’ll explore why traditional approaches to sovereignty are falling short, how AI is raising the stakes and what technology leaders should be thinking about as they build more resilient businesses.​​

Twenty years ago, most business-critical applications ran inside environments that organizations largely owned and controlled. Today, enterprise data flows continuously across cloud platforms, SaaS applications, integration services, partner ecosystems, AI models and autonomous agents. Every new integration introduces another dependency that sits outside the organization’s control.

In this environment, knowing where your data is stored tells you surprisingly little. A company may be able to demonstrate full compliance with every residency requirement. Yet, it still depends on cloud infrastructure, foundation models, identity providers, APIs and software platforms that it has little ability to influence.​

As we’ve seen, data residency in France alone can’t prevent U.S. authorities from demanding access to it. So, France is replacing Microsoft with a local provider as a step toward controlling the country’s own health data.​​

Over the past few years, external forces have continually reshaped technology ecosystems. Governments introduce technology restrictions with little warning. Cloud providers change licensing models and commercial terms. AI platforms release new capabilities and retire others at remarkable speed. Constant change is now the normal operating environment.​

That’s why I believe data sovereignty is an architectural property rather than a compliance initiative. Compliance proves that today’s requirements have been met. The architecture determines what an organization controls, what it depends on and how quickly it can respond when circumstances change.

​To build a resilient sovereignty strategy, review the following:

• Technology Landscape: Map every system, platform and integration that touches critical data. Know what the organization controls, depends on and breaks if external services change or become unavailable.

• External Dependencies: Clarify the organization’s reliance on cloud providers, AI services, software vendors and other infrastructure.

• Critical Data: Identify business-critical systems, sensitive information flows and external services involved in decision making to prevent misallocating resources by risk area.

• Alternative Options: Identify alternatives for each critical service or technology. The range of options impacts the degree of resilience.

Successful organizations don’t apply the same level of control to every system. Identity systems, customer data and intellectual property require organizational ownership. Analytics and metrics on non-sensitive data may stay in the cloud. Decide what matters and build accordingly.​​

A 2026 BARC survey showed that a total of 89% of respondents consider data sovereignty either “very important” or “rather important,” but just 10% have budget for it. This tells me sovereignty is on the executive agenda, but the lack of dedicated funding means that they haven’t yet operationalized it.​​​

​AI is one reason why sovereignty has become urgent. In the BARC survey, increased use of data and AI in core business processes was the top-ranked driver of sovereignty initiatives, cited by 62% of respondents. The reason stems from the way AI reasons across data from multiple sources, infers new relationships and makes recommendations that previously required human judgment.​​

As organizations introduce autonomous agents into production, sovereignty extends far beyond where information is stored. It now includes where models execute, what information agents are permitted to access, which external tools they invoke, how their decisions are governed and whether those decisions can be reconstructed months later when someone asks why.

It’s hard to establish trust in the data used by AI. When an AI agent acts, organizations must know which data informed it and be able to explain the decision and how governance policies were applied. Without transparency, organizations can’t deploy AI responsibly at scale.

Organizations that invested in governance before generative AI became fashionable are further along in their AI journey. They know which data can be trusted, who owns it and how those governance policies are enforced. Instead of slowing innovation, their architectures allow new AI technologies to be adopted with confidence because they already have the guardrails in place.​​

The biggest misconception about data sovereignty is that it requires organizations to isolate themselves from the rest of the technology ecosystem. Complete independence has never been the objective. Modern enterprises will always depend on external technologies, partners and cloud providers. What matters most is maintaining meaningful control over critical capabilities and being able to pivot quickly if the need arises.

When data sovereignty comes up in your next board meeting, resist the urge to reach for the map. Instead, ask yourself: If one of our most important technology providers changed its commercial terms, exited a key market or simply disappeared tomorrow, how much of our business would continue to operate as it does today?

I suspect the answer will reveal far more about your organization’s sovereignty than any map of your data ever could.

#3097. 1 Unstoppable Cryptocurrency That Could Join Bitcoin in the $1 Trillion Club

If Solana can replace Ethereum as the top Layer-1 blockchain network, then it has a potential path to a $1 trillion valuation.

Bitcoin remains the only cryptocurrency that has ever hit a $1 trillion market cap. Today, Bitcoin has a market cap of $1.6 trillion, roughly on par with Tesla's or Meta Platforms'.

While a number of cryptocurrencies have been talked about as potential entrants to the $1 trillion club, the one I have my eye on right now is Solana (SOL -7.18%). Here's why.

Right now, Solana has a market cap of $54 billion. For the sake of argument, let's call this $50 billion. So, for Solana to become a $1 trillion digital asset, it would need to increase in value by roughly 20x. Given Solana's current price of $90, that works out to a future price of approximately $1,800.

That's obviously a stretch goal, but it's within the realm of possibility. As a smart contract platform with a highly diversified blockchain ecosystem, Solana has several pathways to a trillion-dollar market cap.

If you assume Solana hits $1 trillion in market cap, you should also expect it to eventually supplant Ethereum (ETH -8.93%) as the top Layer-1 blockchain network. That's how Solana gets to a $300 billion valuation, which is the current value of Ethereum.

From there, Solana needs to continue eating Ethereum's lunch in key areas such as decentralized finance (DeFi), and it needs to keep winning over users and developers with its faster speeds and lower costs.

Beyond that point, Solana will need to more than triple in value, rising from a $300 billion valuation to $1 trillion. This will likely require a wholesale revamp of how investors, users, and developers view Solana. It will need to transform from a blockchain primarily used for trading and speculation in digital assets into one that is part of the global financial infrastructure.

In short, Solana will need to grow up and realize its full potential. It will need banks and financial institutions to use the Solana blockchain to move money and settle transactions. And it will need to remain at the forefront of important fintech trends, including stablecoins and real-world asset tokenization.

The good news is that Solana could go much higher than $1,800 (the price needed to reach a $1 trillion market cap). Back in October 2023, investment firm VanEck outlined an ultra-bull-case scenario, in which Solana eventually hit a price of $3,211. That assumed major market share gains in DeFi, huge growth in institutional adoption, and expansion into new blockchain niches.

Just be aware: Investing in Solana is not for the faint of heart. While Solana has had some truly eye-popping years, such as 2023 when it soared in value by 924%, it has also seen some truly horrendous years.

An investment in Solana will not go straight up, and there will be plenty of volatility along the way. But sometime within the next decade, investors could be talking about Solana as the next trillion-dollar cryptocurrency after Bitcoin.

Dominic Basulto has positions in Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Solana. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Bitcoin, Ethereum, Meta Platforms, Solana, and Tesla. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

If your pet is young and healthy, the cost of coverage may not seem worth it. But that math can change fast.

Senior Writer & Licensed Insurance Specialist

It feels natural to protect your pet’s health with insurance in the same way you protect your loved ones with health insurance. After all, fur babies are part of the family.

But if you’ve shopped for pet insurance recently, you might have cringed at the cost. Should you really pay hundreds of dollars every year for something you might not use? For some pet parents, the answer is yes, even if their pet is young and healthy. And that’s partly because of how pet insurance handles pre-existing conditions.

A pre-existing condition is any illness or injury that shows symptoms before your pet insurance policy takes effect. Pet insurers usually won’t cover these conditions.

Dr. Rebecca Greenstein, chief veterinarian at Kleinburg Veterinary Hospital and veterinary expert for rover.com, says she’s seeing an increase in claim denials based on pre-existing conditions. “The whole point of insurance is you want broad spectrum coverage for a variety of things,” she says. “By the time they're excluding major organ systems and anything related to that, you may be paying monthly for coverage that doesn't actually help you when you need to go make a claim.”

If you’re considering pet insurance, it’s best to buy a policy before your pet needs it.

Your pet’s pre-existing conditions will determine which treatments and procedures insurers cover down the road.

Say your dog has a history of allergies. If you buy a policy after your four-footed friend has shown symptoms, pet insurers typically won’t pay for allergy shots or other treatments. The exclusion might also apply to related problems like itchiness or ear infections, says Dr. Michael Goldstein, medical director at Billerica Veterinary Hospital and Thrive Pet Healthcare.

He offers the example of a dog who goes to the vet for a hotspot one year and an ear infection the next. If you got pet insurance for your dog between those visits, the insurer might deny your claim because both issues could be caused by underlying allergies.

The best way around this type of scenario is to buy coverage when your pet is young, before any symptoms develop.

» MORE: The best pet insurance for pre-existing conditions

It’s tricky to figure out if pet insurance will actually save you money in the long run. The most common type of plan covers accidents and illness. It costs an average of $836 for dogs and $435 for cats each year, according to the North American Pet Health Insurance Association (NAPHIA). You could pay these premiums for years before an emergency surgery or chronic illness makes its way to your financial doorstep.

It’s impossible to know for sure whether your pet will stay healthy or run up sky-high vet bills. But you can assess the potential value of pet insurance by looking at common chronic conditions that pets develop with age and how much it costs to treat them.

For instance, “cats generally, as younger animals, don't have a lot of problems,” Goldstein says. “But as they get older, there are definitely common issues. Older cats in particular get chronic kidney disease.”

In cats over age 10, the Cornell Feline Health Center estimates that as many as 40% have chronic kidney disease. The annual cost to treat this condition can top $1,200.

Another example is atopic dermatitis from skin allergies, a common ailment affecting as many as 15% of dogs, according to the Cornell Richard P. Riney Canine Health Center. A single vet visit to address these itchy, persistent symptoms can cost $250 or more. And while that’s a fraction of what you might pay for pet insurance, costs of chronic conditions can add up over your pet’s lifetime.

Vet bills can also balloon quickly if chronic conditions require surgery. One example of this is hip dysplasia, a genetic disorder that can cause arthritis and pain in large-breed dogs. Depending on the procedure, you could pay up to $10,000 for hip surgery.

Many pet insurance plans cover treatments for hip dysplasia, including surgical costs, as long as it's not a pre-existing condition. However, some policies have waiting periods of six to 12 months for orthopedic issues like hip dysplasia. If symptoms develop during that waiting period, the condition will be considered pre-existing. That’s another argument for buying your pet’s coverage earlier rather than later.

Most importantly, having insurance means you can choose the best treatment for your pet no matter the cost. “It's really tragic when it's a life and death decision that is needed and it’s based on someone's financial constraints,” Greenstein says. “What is best and what's affordable often are not on the same side of the spectrum.”

One option to keep pet insurance affordable is to buy an accident-only plan. This type of coverage is usually much cheaper, costing about $190 annually for dogs and $112 for cats, according to NAPHIA. These plans cover injuries resulting from accidents, which include not just wounds and broken bones but also objects or toxins your pet might swallow.

However, an accident-only plan won’t help with some of the most common vet expenses. Illnesses, not injuries, are behind most claims submitted to pet insurer Lemonade, the company said in an email. In the past year, more than 60% of Lemonade's pet insurance claims stemmed from illnesses. That’s twice as many as the next-largest claim category, which was preventive care. A similar trend can be found in data from Nationwide, where chronic diseases make up a clear majority of pet insurance claims submitted to the company in 2025.

If you opt for an accident-only plan or no coverage at all, it’s still smart to set aside some savings for those inevitable pet emergencies and illnesses. This pool of funds can keep you from having to make difficult decisions about your pet’s care based solely on the cost of treatment.

#3095. CoreWeave credit default swaps hit distress levels as investors sour on AI debt

CoreWeave's credit stress continued to spiral on Thursday amid a broader sell-off in AI-related names.

CoreWeave — a so-called neocloud company — has taken on more than $51 billion of debt and obligations to finance its AI infrastructure build-out. It's now facing a rebellion from stock and bond investors as concerns mount about AI overspending and debt levels.

Yields on CoreWeave debt have continued to climb, with the yield to maturity on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 reaching 15.78%. Bond yields move inversely to prices. Meanwhile, the spread on its five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, at one point soared above 1,140 basis points. It last stood at nearly 1,038 bps — a 16% week-over-week jump and 164% higher than a year ago.

Credit concerns are spreading into AI equities too. CoreWeave's stock dropped during trading Thursday before recovering and closing 5.94% higher. The moved followed Wednesday's 15.5% nosedive.

Other neocloud stocks were under similar pressure. Nebius also sank before climbing higher to close 1.29% and and Iren ultimately ended the day down less than 1%.

Anxiety about AI overspending is also spreading. For instance, shares of Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices sold off following a big sell-off in South Korean chip stocks. Micron closed up 1.87%, while AMD fell 1.5%.

While AI debt worries have been rising steadily, investors have suddenly grown skittish about the underlying finances of companies borrowing heavily to buy chips, build data centers, and rent out computing power.

Coreweave's credit default swaps are one place to see that stress.

Credit default swaps are contracts where buyers pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. The spread widening in CoreWeave's CDS means investors view the debt as riskier.

The market is "basically saying 'no mas' to AI debt without operating cash flow support," the Evercore ISI trading desk said.

A spread level of 1,000 basis points or above is generally a sign of credit distress, said Gavan Nolan, executive director of fixed income pricing at S&P Global Market Intelligence.

No one is questioning whether demand for CoreWeave's services is real, since the company has contracts with all the big hyperscalers, Nolan said. The question is whether the cash flows will ultimately arrive.

"It's obviously heavily negative free cash flow at the moment, and it needs that cash flow to arrive really to justify all the capex that it's spending," Nolan said.

CEO Mike Intrator dismissed the market moves on Wednesday, according to a memo obtained by CNBC.

"When you are building a new type of technology company there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally," he wrote. "We are confident in our backlog which more than supports all of our debt obligations."

The backlog is over $100 billion, with around two-thirds of it with investment-grade counterparts including Microsoft, Meta, IBM and Caterpillar, Deutsche Bank said in a note Thursday. The firm reiterated its buy-rating on the stock Wednesday, calling the dislocation a buying opportunity.

"The problem is this kind of concern can prove to be a self-fulfilling prophecy, and risks triggering broader issues in other AI-related names," said Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research.

Domino effects may already be happening. Oracle's five-year CDS spread also spiked this week. It was last at 282 basis points, a roughly 10% increase in one week.

"A downgrade from its BBB rating would risk pressuring IG-only investors into forced sales," Reid said.
