Because of these risks and uncertainties, investors should not place undue reliance on forward-looking statements. Forward looking statements made in this conference call are made as of today. And the company undertakes no obligations to update or revise any forward-looking statements except as required by law. The third quarter financial supplement and financial news release, as well as the related financial statements are available on the SEC's website. With that, I will turn the call over to our Chief Executive Officer, Casey Hoyt.

Casey Hoyt: Thank you, Trae. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us. Before getting into the results, I want to thank our roughly 1.5 thousand employees. Their daily work with patients and referral partners is what makes our growth possible. I appreciate the care they provide and the work they put into serving more patients as Viemed continues to grow. The third quarter was another strong quarter for Viemed. With record revenue of $80.7 million representing 12.2% growth over last year. Just as importantly, that growth translated into stronger earnings. Net income attributable to Viemed increased 32% year over year and approximately 68% from the second quarter. We are continuing to grow the business at a double digit pace.

Demonstrating the earnings potential of the platform we have built. For the first time since the Lehan acquisition, both the current and prior year quarters include a full 3 months of Lehan's operations. That gives us a much clearer picture of our growth with a 12.2% increase reflecting expansion across our existing businesses rather than the incremental revenue contribution of an acquisition. Sleep therapy was a particular source of strength this quarter. And we are also seeing encouraging results from bringing maternal health services into our established Viemed markets. The success those initial maternal health markets gives us confidence to broaden the rollout.

We are now on track to enter 2 additional states per quarter beginning in the fourth quarter, establishing a regular pace of expansion. The markets we have already entered are still early in their development. We see years of opportunity to build volume within each state as we develop referral relationships and reach more patients. Each launch adds to that opportunity and so growth can continue within our existing markets as we expand into new ones. Breast pumps and related supplies are a practical example of how we can do more with the capabilities already in the company. Lehan brought a specialized experience in this business.

Viemed's existing payer relationships and reimbursement capabilities give us a way to extend it into markets we already know. The early results have given us the confidence to take that next step. As we open those markets, we will be paying close attention to fulfillment and reimbursement. We want the additional volume to become a productive part of the business with reliable service for mothers who depend on us. The 2-state cadence gives our teams a clear operating plan for the next stage. Our growing sleep patient population shows how we are expanding Viemed's reach and serving more people.

During the quarter, we served 43.9 thousand therapy patients, over 6 thousand more than the second quarter and 37.5% above a year ago. PAP setups also increased both sequentially and year over year. Growth is coming through in patients receiving therapy as well as the activity bringing patients into care. Resupply grew alongside that activity. We served 40.9 thousand resupply patients. Up approximately 22% from a year ago and 10.5% from the second quarter. Our expanding PAP patient population creates further opportunity to grow resupply and increasing participation in the program is a priority.

We are simplifying order processing to support that growth and make it easier for patients to receive supplies on time with the service that keeps them engaged over the course of their therapy. In ventilation, we have a longer revenue trend to assess under the revised CMS coverage rules issued in 2025. Ventilator rental revenue has increased in each quarter this year, from $35.4 million to $36.4 million and now $37 million For the first 9 months, was approximately 8% above the same period last year. The comparison is particularly meaningful because much of the 2025 period preceded the new CMS coverage rules.

Growing ventilation revenue against that comparison supports our confidence our ability to expand the business under the new framework. More broadly, we view the legislative and rule making environment as generally favorable to establish providers that invested in clinical care and compliance. Audit activity has increased across the DME industry including for providers with strong compliance programs. Our own teams are spending more time and resources responding to those reviews We are encouraged that CMS is examining its audit contractor model and specifically asked how to reduce unnecessary provider burden and protect patient access. We see an opportunity for more targeted consistent oversight and we intend to bring our experience to that discussion.

So providers can devote more of their resources to caring for patients. Our responsibility is to help patients receive the care they need. We support appropriate oversight and we will advocate for coverage policies and review processes that preserve timely access to medically necessary care. Our clinical teams see the needs of these patients every day and we intend to make sure those needs remain part of the policy discussions. The third quarter showed that we can grow the business under the new coverage framework and convert more revenue into earnings. We are serving more patients and the opportunities ahead in sleep and maternal health give us the confidence that we can enter into the final quarter of the year.

Todd will now discuss the financial results and operating priorities supporting our next stage of growth.

William Todd Zehnder: All right. Thank you, Casey, and good morning, everyone. All figures are in U.S. dollars, and our full results have been filed with the SEC. And I will refer to information included in the quarterly financial supplement which is also available on our Investor Relations website. Net income attributable to Viemed was $4.6 million or $0.11 per diluted share compared with $3.5 million or $0.09 per diluted share a year ago. And $2.8 million or $0.07 per diluted share in the second quarter of this year. Net income increased 32% year over year approximately 68% from the second quarter. Adjusted EBITDA was $17.1 million an increase of approximately 6% from the prior year quarter and 24% sequentially.

Adjusted EBITDA margin was 21.1% compared with 17.6% in the second quarter and 22.4% a year ago. The sequential margin expansion was approximately 350 basis points. Revenue continued to grow this quarter and SG&A declined from the second quarter. Both contributed to the sequential increase in profitability with several compensation and benefit adjustments also affecting the results. Revenue increased 3.3% from the second quarter with growth across rentals, equipment and supply sales and services. Other equipment rentals grew approximately 13.1% year-over-year and equipment and supply sales grew approximately 23.7% supported by sleep and women's health. Ventilator rental revenue was $37.5 million up 7.4% from a year ago supported by higher average patient count.

Gross profit was $46.2 million or 57.3% of revenue, compared with 57.5% a year ago and 57.7% in the second quarter. Revenue from sales and services represented 32% of revenue compared with 30.1% a year ago. The year over year shift forward shift towards equipment and supply sales affects gross margin because these offerings generally carry lower margins than equipment rentals while also requiring less capital investment. As we discussed last quarter, we added a new distribution partner that together with our existing suppliers gives us supplier capacity well beyond our current needs across all product lines to support future growth.

We are still implementing the related cost savings and expect them to improve gross margin by approximately 50 basis points once fully in place. SG&A was $35.5 million or 44% of revenue, compared with 47.5% in the second quarter and 44.4% a year ago. SG&A declined approximately $1.6 million sequentially. Year over year revenue grew faster than SG&A even as we added resources to support the larger business. Lower compensation related accruals and benefit expense contributed to the sequential decline. Phantom stock expense also came down substantially as expected following the large mark to market adjustment in the second quarter associated with the increase in our share price. Benefit rebates also reduced expense during the quarter.

Regular payroll and software spending increased as we added to serve a growing patient population. That additional capacity is supporting higher volumes, including a 12% sequential increase in the PAP resupply orders. At the same time billing expense declined approximately 12% as revenue grew. Reflecting the workflow changes and implementation timing. Our focus is on getting more volume through with the people and systems that we have in place. Compliance is another area where our personnel and systems can provide a competitive advantage as oversight increases across the industry. Enforcement and claims audit activity have picked up and our teams are devoting more resources to those reviews.

The documentation and follow-up work adds administrative and professional costs, and in some cases can extend payment timelines. Our success rate under these audits remains very strong. Those outcomes support our confidence in the care we provide and the documentation supporting it. Our teams are focused on submitting complete responses moving reviews towards resolution. The increase in accounts receivable had several drivers this quarter. Audit related payment timing was 1 contributor alongside other billing and collection factors including delays associated with system migrations. We believe the related revenue remains fully realizable. These delays have extended the timing of cash collections and temporarily tied up more cash and working capital.

Collections in October were extremely strong so we are confident that this will work itself out during the fourth quarter. Operating cash flow was $11.5 million After net CapEx of $7.5 million, free cash flow was $4 million Net CapEx represented approximately 9.2% of revenue. For the first 9 months of 2026, operating cash flow was $35.5 million and free cash flow was $15.2 million compared with $33.5 million and $17.3 million respectively a year ago. Lower equipment sales proceeds also affected the year to date cash flow comparison. As the prior year period benefited from the ventilator return program.

On a trailing 12-month basis, free cash flow was approximately $26.1 million The business continues to generate cash after funding equipment needs although the current quarter's collection timing reduced cash conversion. We continue to reduce debt and return capital during the quarter. We made an additional $2 million term loan repayment in October. Further reducing our outstanding debt. Our first use of capital is supporting the growth within Viemed.

Including the maternal health expansion and the needs of the larger sleep business. We retain the flexibility to consider acquisitions that fit our operations and return requirements and to repurchase shares when the value is attractive. The balance sheet allows us to evaluate those choices without committing to a fixed allocation among them.

Turning to our outlook, we are raising the lower end of our full year revenue guidance and now expect revenue of $316 million to $320 million compared with our previous range of $314 million to $320 million We are narrowing our adjusted EBITDA guidance to $64 million to $66 million compared with our previous range of $64 million to $68 million With 9 months complete, the narrower range reflects our results through September and our updated expectations for the fourth quarter. #3086. Brian Sullivan: Why the 'real' price of oil is likely $30-$40 higher than where it is now

Oil, in reality, is $125 per barrel or higher.

That's the real cost of a barrel of oil because buying the physical commodity is a very different story from a number on traders' screens.

Oil futures are just that: paper contracts indicating a price today, tomorrow, next month or further out.  If you want to buy the physical commodity, it may be a totally different story — and price.

As I've reported, prices for oil delivery have skyrocketed. Last week, a VLCC (aka a "supertanker" in non-shipper parlance) was chartered from the U.S. Gulf Coast to China for $76 million. Another very large crude carrier went for $77 million from the U.S. to South Korea. That's 10 times more than the price of the same trip less than one year ago.

Assuming these ships hold about 2 million barrels of oil, that charter price means each barrel on the ship costs about $38 over the price of the oil itself.

I'm certainly not saying to avoid looking at oil futures prices, but you need to know that the price on the CNBC screen or CNBC.com isn't always the full price being paid. These days, any company that needs oil shipped by sea, rail or truck will pay a hefty premium over the price of the oil itself. So, while the volume of oil moving through Hormuz is closing in on pre-war levels, costs are not. And there's no sign that they're going anywhere but up.

You know what else is up? The stocks of the shipowners. Look at their moves this month and this year.

On a more serious note, I want to express my condolences for the awful attacks on the airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The cowardly strike on civilians—some of whom were religious pilgrims—took the lives of at least 14 people and injured more than 300.

The airport was attacked at least three times as travelers and energy industry professionals from around the world were flying into Riyadh for the World Petroleum Council conference. I was scheduled to fly in on Saturday, but the trip was canceled because of the strikes. The WPC went on as planned — here's one panel that took place Tuesday — and I look forward to seeing all my global energy friends again soon.

Thanks for reading—and watching. Be safe in these crazy and often scary times.

The supercap oil and gas stock to watch right now is Shell (SHEL). Shell is not a shell of its former self. It's back to being what energy investors wanted: a major player in global energy, focused on what it does best. Shareholders are being rewarded.

Shell hit a new high this week. While analysts remain bullish, the stock is getting close to its target price.

Shell may be underappreciated for its huge liquefied natural gas business. RBC analyst Biraj Borkhataria writes: "Without a sustained resumption in Qatari volumes and with European storage levels below seasonal lows heading into winter, European gas prices continued on an upward trajectory in 3Q26. With HH broadly unchanged throughout the summer, export margins have increased to the widest levels seen since 2022, on our estimates nearly double the level in 2Q26 (~$13/mmbtu vs. $7/mmbtu)."

Borkhataria expects Shell and other companies with huge U.S. LNG positions — TotalEnergies (TTE) and BP (BP) — to benefit from wider margins on exports to Europe.

Speaking of RBC and energy, the firm lists ConocoPhillips as one of its top 30 global stock ideas. The company is covered by analyst Scott Hanold, who believes it has a "returns-focused value proposition, a strong balance sheet, and peer-leading distributions." He loves its "global and diverse" asset base and management's clear "investment propositions." Hanold has a $152 target on COP. That's more than 20% upside.

In oil and gas, refiners and big energy stocks are generating cash for investors, and Morgan Stanley is optimistic more is coming.

The firm says the diesel shortage is now spilling over into gasoline, potentially marking another leg of the "golden age" for refiners. Morgan Stanley has been revising its earnings estimates higher for companies including ExxonMobil (XOM), Valero (VLO), Phillips 66 (PSX) and PBF (PBF).

Fun Fact →  While nearly every other company calls Texas home, refiner PBF is headquartered in a suburban office park just off a highway in New Jersey.

Two big calls to quickly highlight in power production.

First, Truist says you have to buy First Solar (FSLR). The analyst upgrades it to Buy with a $270 target. Tariffs should help the Phoenix-based company, giving it pricing power for at least four more years. The Section 232 tariffs—which are too complicated to detail here—should help First Solar raise solar module prices and boost earnings. We agree, having written about the company and stock back in July.

Another call on the Power Insider radar: TD Cowen is starting coverage of TeraWulf (WULF) with a Buy rating and a $21 target. That indicates about 50% upside for the stock, but it's actually one of the Street's lower price targets. TeraWulf and other AI power companies have seen their stocks hit hard following months of big gains, but Cowen analyst Michael Elias says the valuation is now attractive and a likely lease in the second half of 2027 at a Kentucky location could be a catalyst.

In the wake of the terror attacks on Saudi Arabia, we spoke with RBC Capital Markets' Helima Croft about the attacks, energy and more.

The entire energy world is watching Europe's natural gas storage levels. The question is whether the continent will have enough gas to make it safely through the winter. Power Insider wrote about the topic in the last issue.

The fact that JPMorgan highlights expected weather patterns should tell you how much temperature matters when it comes to gas storage. The early forecast calls for October and November to be average or slightly warmer than the 10-year average. The red line represents the 10-year average.

Europe has been largely "saved" by mild temperatures over the past few years. Natural gas storage levels are lower this year than in years past, so the thermometer will matter a lot when it comes to how well countries can, ahem, weather the winter. Random, but interesting.

Second, national security sustained defense funding is driving warhead modernization and pit production. Activities that require nuclear containers, criticality alarm systems, remote handling, and bespoke engineered solutions.

And third, commercial nuclear energy, where growing power demand and renewed interest in nuclear generation are supporting investment in extending the life of existing facilities and developing next generation technologies. Collectively, these demand areas support our expectation for consistent mid single digit growth over the next 5 years. Turning to slide 10, our long-term strategy is built around a straightforward but powerful approach to compounding value. We start with high quality businesses operating in attractive markets, where recurring demand a commitment to innovation, strong competitive positions, provide a foundation for consistent organic growth. We then leverage the CADRE operating model to continuously improve performance and drive greater value across our businesses.

Importantly, the combination of organic growth and operational improvements supports attractive margins and strong cash flow generation. This provides us with the financial flexibility to reinvest in our existing businesses pursue strategic acquisitions, and consistently return capital to shareholders. As we expand our platform, we look to repeat this process across a larger more diversified portfolio creating a substantial, sustainable cycle of growth reinvestment, and long-term value creation. While the true value of our strategy is realized over time, our third quarter performance provides further evidence of the benefits of our disciplined approach to growth, operational improvement, and reinvestment.

Turning to slide 12, we delivered financial results that exceeded our expectations with net sales of approximately $203 million and adjusted EBITDA of $41 million both ahead of our guidance. Net income increased 46% year over year and adjusted EBITDA margin expanded 110 basis points to 20.2%. Following our acquisitions of TIER Tactical, and Alien Gear earlier this year, both businesses continue to perform in line with expectations and contributed to our strong third quarter results. Alongside our continued focus on operational, we are encouraged by some of the initial use cases we have completed to date.

So you know, they continue to differentiate their products against others.

Mark Smith: Good morning. This is Eegan on for Tomohiko. Perfect. And then I just wanted to ask on acquisitions. You did a small bolt on here. Are you guys still looking for 1 more this calendar year? And then any insights you can give us on kind of what you are seeing out there in the pipeline?

Blaine Browers: Good morning. This is Eegan on for Tomohiko. So, we are-- I mean, we are always active. You know, here we are in, you know, early November, so the year's not far away. So we will kinda see what the rest of the year holds for as far as M&A for the remainder of this year. But, yeah, the funnel continues to be robust. Lots of opportunities. TL;DR: Rates fell today, but not by enough to change your mortgage math.

Mortgage rates fell today, possibly helped by post-midterm election clarity and a drop in oil prices.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage ticked down to 7.01% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is six basis points lower than yesterday and 17 basis points lower than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

Here are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for context:

As for what’s next: Tomorrow’s jobs report, showing October data, could potentially nudge mortgage rates in either direction. To understand the link between jobs data and mortgage rates, keep reading below the video.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

Tomorrow, the Nerds will be watching the release of the October jobs report. If it shows that employment remained steady (or even improved), that will build a stronger case for the Federal Reserve to raise overnight borrowing rates again at their next meeting on Dec. 8-9.

While the Fed doesn’t directly set mortgage rates, it does set the federal funds rate, which is the fee that banks must pay to borrow from one another (which is how they fund mortgages). Lenders raise mortgage rates any time they think that the federal funds rate is about to go up.

Central bankers hiked the federal funds rate in September, so a relatively steady jobs report would suggest the labor market could withstand higher rates.

The Fed has a dual mandate to control inflation while supporting maximum employment, and raising the federal funds rate is their main tool for bringing inflation down. If they can work to lower inflation without hurting employment too badly, central bankers may feel more confident to act.

The September Personal Consumption Expenditures price index (PCE), the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, was released last Thursday. The data shows inflation was 3.6% year-over-year in September, up from 3.4% in August.

September’s federal funds rate hike came in the middle of the month, so October’s inflation data will really capture its effect on inflation. The October PCE report will come out on Nov. 25.

» Learn more: How the Fed affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.51% or higher — but there aren't too many people for whom that's true.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

» Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit.

#3083. Stock Market Today, Nov. 5: Amazon Shares Slide as Technology Selloff Erases Early Gains

On Nov. 5, 2026, Amazon shares reversed an early rally as rising yields and tech selling took over the session.

Amazon.com (AMZN -2.19%), a global e-commerce, cloud computing, and logistics platform, closed at $260.21, down 2.19%. Thursday's move reflected early election-related gains that faded as technology selling and higher yields took over. Investors are watching the company's AWS cloud computing division's profitability and AI infrastructure spending next.

Trading volume reached 83.5 million shares, coming in about 117% above its three-month average of 38.5 million shares. Amazon.com IPO'd in 1997 and has grown 265,645% since going public.

The S&P 500 (^GSPC -4.36%) closed at 7,354, down 4.36%, while the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC -5.52%) closed at 24,315, down 5.52%. Among e-commerce, digital advertising, and retail logistics peers, Walmart closed at $127.72, down 1.12%, while Costco Wholesale closed at $1,065.59, up 1.83%.

On Thursday, Nov. 5, Amazon shares gained during early trading after the company announced a partnership with Uber that provides its Prime members with free restaurant-delivery benefits through Uber Eats. However, that didn't last, as a broad sell-off of tech stocks took place today in the wake of U.S. midterm election results.

The Democratic Party gained control of Congress, raising worries that incoming Democratic leadership could demand tighter AI regulations and put a hold on data center construction projects key to the artificial intelligence (AI) boom. This could result in a major impact to Amazon's AWS business just as the company is spending substantial sums to expand its AI infrastructure.

At the same time, Wall Street is concerned about the e-commerce giant's AI costs. Last week, Amazon's third-quarter earnings report missed revenue estimates while the company's capital expenditures continued to rise, resulting in negative Q3 free cash flow (FCF) of $42.4 billion compared to positive FCF of $14.8 billion in the previous year.

In a macroeconomic environment of rising interest rates, which makes borrowing to fund an AI buildout more expensive, and persistent inflation likely to impact consumer spending and Amazon's sales, the company is facing a challenging time right now. But over the long run, its AI investments could position it for success. Management forecasted AWS revenue to grow by 40% year over year in 2027 and 2028 as well, thanks to strong demand for its AI offerings.

Robert Izquierdo has positions in Amazon, Uber Technologies, and Walmart. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Amazon, Costco Wholesale, and Walmart. The Motley Fool recommends Uber Technologies. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3082. Genesis Energy (GEL) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Deepwater shortfalls and Shenandoah updates shaped the quarter's results.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Genesis Energy, L.P. (GEL -5.81%) reported third-quarter results and addressed operational delays in the Gulf of Mexico. Management stated that results were impacted by lower-than-expected volumes from certain deepwater production facilities and a planned turnaround at Salamanca moved into the third quarter. The company continued its capital allocation strategy by reducing high-cost preferred units and maintaining no borrowings on its senior secured credit facility. Management indicated that while some production has shifted to later periods, the long-term outlook for offshore infrastructure remains supported by active drilling on dedicated leases.

Operator: Greetings. Welcome to the Genesis Energy, L.P. Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. A question-and-answer session will follow the formal presentation. If anyone should require operator assistance during the conference, please press star zero on your telephone keypad. Please note, this conference is being recorded. I will now turn the conference over to Dwayne Morley. Thank you. You may begin.

Dwayne Morley: Good morning, and welcome to the 2026 third quarter conference call for Genesis Energy. Genesis Energy has three business segments. The offshore pipeline transportation segment is engaged in providing the critical infrastructure to move oil produced from the long-lived, world-class reservoirs in the deepwater Gulf of Mexico to onshore refining centers. The marine transportation segment is engaged in the maritime transportation of primarily refined petroleum products. The onshore transportation and services segment is engaged in the transportation, handling, blending, storage, and supply of energy products, including crude oil and refined products, primarily around refining centers, as well as the processing of sour gas streams to remove sulfur at refining operations.

Genesis' operations are primarily located in the Gulf Coast states and the Gulf of Mexico. During this call, management may be making forward-looking statements within the meaning of the Securities Act of 1933 and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. The law provides safe harbor protection to encourage companies to provide forward-looking information. Genesis intends to avail itself of those safe harbor provisions and directs you to its most recently filed and future filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. We also encourage you to visit our website at genesisenergy.com, where a copy of the press release we issued this morning is located. The press release also presents a reconciliation of non-GAAP financial measures to the comparable GAAP financial measures.

At this time, I would like to introduce Grant Sims, CEO of Genesis Energy L.P. Mr. Sims is joined by Kristen Jesulaitis, Chief Financial Officer and Chief Legal Officer, Ryan Sims, President and Chief Commercial Officer, and Louie Nicol, Chief Accounting Officer. With that, I will now turn the call over to Grant.

Grant Sims: Good morning, everyone, and thanks for joining us today. As noted in our earnings release this morning, our third quarter results came in modestly ahead of where we thought we would be internally. In broad terms, the third quarter played out consistent with what we described in August, with the back half of the year being shaped by two things largely outside of our control: hurricane season and the timing of producer activity in the deepwater Gulf of Mexico. The weather cooperated in the third quarter, as we had no weather-related disruptions during what is typically the most active part of hurricane season.

Unfortunately, the benefit we would have otherwise expected to see was partially offset by lower-than-anticipated volumes from certain production facilities which flow exclusively through our pipelines. While volumes from a couple of these deepwater facilities are expected to be lower than originally anticipated in the fourth quarter, and in all likelihood, last through the early part of 2027, it is important to remember we have visibility to at least four new high-impact wells that are scheduled to be completed and turned to production over the coming quarters.

Ultimately, none of these temporary impacts change the amount of oil in the ground, the acreage that is dedicated to our pipelines, or the fact that none of this incremental production requires any additional capital from Genesis. It simply becomes a discussion around timing and when, not if, we will move the volumes through our offshore infrastructure. In the Gulf, things can slide to the right, but rarely is there a total geophysical bust. If there is, lost volumes are virtually certain to be replaced by new discoveries that are developed in the same geographic neighborhood.

Elsewhere, our onshore transportation and services segments once again performed ahead of our expectations, and our marine transportation segment was generally in line with our expectations, despite our final blue water dry docking of the year unexpectedly extending into the third quarter. Both of these businesses are being supported by the same set of macro fundamentals: strong Gulf Coast refinery runs, shifting crude and product flows into and around the Gulf Coast, and in marine, a Jones Act market that is, if anything, getting [audio distortion] level of activity around our irreplaceable midstream infrastructure in the Gulf of America, as well as the macro fundamentals driving our other businesses. With that, let me turn quickly to the balance sheet.

Following the significant financing activities we completed in the first half of the year, there is very little new to report this quarter. We ended the quarter with no borrowings outstanding under our $900 million senior secured credit facility, approximately $41.5 million of unrestricted cash on hand, no debt maturities until 2029, and a bank-calculated leverage ratio of approximately 5.03x. In February, we issued $750 million of 6.75% senior unsecured notes due 2034 and used the proceeds to take out, in full, the higher-cost 7.75% notes due 2028, which pushed our nearest senior note maturity out to 2029. We also upsized and extended our revolving senior secured credit facility with our extremely supportive bank group.

Additionally, as a reminder, we entered this year with approximately $529 million of our Series A cumulative preferred outstanding, paying a current cash rate of 11.24%, clearly the most expensive current pay paper anywhere in our capital structure. In nine months, we have retired roughly 40% of it, taking the remaining face amount down to approximately $311 million. I would point out, had we paid down debt rather than retiring this very expensive security, our bank-calculated leverage ratio would have been closer to 4.7x. We think running a little higher leverage ratio in the near term to get rid of such high-cost security is in the best interest of everyone else in the capital structure.

We will continue to focus on right-sizing and optimizing our capital structure, and we expect to be able to drive future cash savings over the next several years from three places. We will focus on reducing debt in absolute terms, opportunistically refinancing our higher coupon senior unsecured notes with lower coupons and extended maturities as they become callable at more attractive premiums beginning in the first half of 2027, and redeeming the remaining approximately $311 million of the 11.24% Series A cumulative preferred still outstanding, all as we work towards our ultimate long-term leverage target of around 4x.

Consistent with the all-of-the-above approach to capital allocation that we have discussed, both prior to and since turning cash flow positive, our board of directors declared a quarterly distribution of $0.20 per common unit. That is unchanged from last quarter, but represents an increase of approximately 21% as compared to the third quarter of last year. We would otherwise expect to thoughtfully and prudently grow distributions to our common unit holders over time, all while preserving our financial flexibility to pursue attractive organic and inorganic opportunities as they may emerge in the future. With that, I will go into a little more detail on each of our business segments. Let me start with the offshore.

As I mentioned earlier, our offshore pipeline transportation segment operated without any weather-related downtime during the quarter. The offset was lower-than-anticipated volumes. Specifically, that included unplanned curtailments at a couple of our legacy connected fields, the continuing challenges from two of the initial wells at Shenandoah, and a planned turnaround at Salamanca that the operator moved forward from the fourth quarter into the third quarter. As we said last quarter, we do not believe any of these items have long-term negative implications for the ultimate recovery reserves already discovered and being developed.

In the operator's view, and we would concur, these impacts are transitory and simply result in timing differences for when those reserves are produced and when those barrels enter our pipeline for transportation to shore. In this pricing environment, the producers are clearly incented to figure it out. They do, however, tend to play the long game, accepting lower current production in order to maximize total ultimate recoveries from these world-class hydrocarbon reservoirs. Things can indeed shift to the right, but that's precisely why we have minimum volume commitments, or MVCs, in most of our new contracts. We are protected to the downside, even if it takes longer than expected for them to execute.

Owing to certain things, about which we are not in position to go into a lot of detail, Shenandoah operated at or slightly below the MVC level in the third quarter and is expected to do so until several new wells come on. A rig is on location drilling a second well at the Monument field, and both wells will be tied back to Shenandoah at the producer's expense.

It is now projected that production from the first well has slipped into early next year, but we would expect additional throughput from these two Monument wells to be in the range of 20-25 KBD, or thousand barrels a day of oil, reaching that level sometime in the first quarter of 2027. Excuse me. The rig will then return to Shenandoah and drill a fifth producing well, with initial production from it expected to be ±20 KBD. A subsea pumping system is scheduled to be installed in 2028, improving well performance and, most importantly, maximizing the ultimate reserves to be recovered from Shenandoah.

Beyond 2028, there are at least four, and possibly as many as eight additional locations at Shenandoah proper, possibly another location at Monument, two, maybe three locations at the Shenandoah South field, and as we understand it, there are already four additional exploratory prospects that have been identified within a 30 mi radius of the Shenandoah production facility. Suffice it to say, regardless of near-term challenges, we expect significant volumes to flow across the Shenandoah production facility and exclusively into our 100% owned SYNC pipeline and onto shore through our 64% owned CHOPS pipeline for decades and decades to come without requiring any additional capital from us.

At Salamanca, there are currently two rigs on location drilling wells to be completed and tied into the Salamanca facility, the production from which will flow through our 100% owned SEKCO lateral and onto shore through our 64% owned Poseidon pipeline. We expect both of these wells at Salamanca to come online early in 2027, which should move total production closer to the facility's design capacity of 60 KBD-70 KBD.

Harbour Energy, doing business in the U.S. as Louisiana Land Oil and Gas, has added a second rig to their Gulf of America program, and this activity at Salamanca, as well as expected additional activity there and at Buckskin, which also is transported exclusively through our facilities, is consistent with their stated goal of doubling their production out of the Gulf by the end of 2028. Elsewhere across our connected fields, the expansion of BP's Atlantis facility, which I mentioned last quarter, came online in July.

A new development well at one of our legacy connected hubs is expected to be turned to production during the fourth quarter, and multiple well intervention and remediation projects are scheduled before year-end that, if successful, could add meaningfully to the volumes moving across our infrastructure. Stepping back from the individual fields for a moment and focusing rather on the macro, there are 16 deepwater drilling units currently active in the Gulf of America, and nine of them are working on leases contractually dedicated to flow through our existing pipelines, even though we move just a third of the current production out of the Gulf.

Our pipelines are in the sweet spot for future activity, especially the rapidly developing Deep Wilcox or high-pressure, high-temperature geologic play, and yet we believe there is a lot of runway left in the more mature Miocene play in the central Gulf. There is no doubt the deepwater Gulf is a world-class basin. Our infrastructure is in the right place at the right time and is already paid for. Producer interest remains robust. Interestingly, every single one of the new nine-square-mile blocks leased by the federal government in the central Gulf in its most recent sale sits within tieback range or within a 30 mi radius of an existing production facility connected exclusively to our existing pipelines.

The resource underneath and around our dedicated acreage, both discovered and yet to be found, is vast. The pace at which it gets developed will be set by our producer customers, not by us. But whenever those barrels are produced, they will move to shore through our pipelines under existing or new life-of-lease dedications and without the need for any growth capital from us. This is exactly what has supported our offshore business for the last three decades, and we will continue to support it for decades and decades to come.

Turning to marine, our marine transportation segment performed in line with our expectations during the quarter, despite the dry docking of one of our larger offshore units that began in the second quarter and extended further into the third quarter than originally planned. There are no dry dockings for offshore vessels expected for the rest of this year, so the fleet is back at full capacity in the fourth quarter. We're experiencing, in essence, 100% utilization of available capacity, and negotiated spot rates for all classes of vessels are extremely robust, which we believe will ultimately allow term contracts to follow higher.

Demand continues to be supported by strong Gulf Coast refinery runs, and in particular, we are beginning to see the impact of increased volumes of Venezuelan crude being run at Gulf Coast refineries and the derivative effect that heavy crude is having on demand to move intermediate refined products from one location to another along the Gulf Coast and connected inland waterways. Our fleet of inland heater barges is specifically designed to transport exactly these heavy intermediate refined products, and we are well-positioned to benefit as that demand continues to develop. On the supply side, nothing has changed.

There is essentially no net new construction of comp tonnage, and we see very little on the horizon that could significantly affect this tight supply and demand balance for marine tonnage. Our onshore transportation services segment once again performed ahead of our expectations. We continue to see strong volumes through our Texas City terminal and associated pipeline systems, as well as through Raceland and South Louisiana, supported by increasing volumes offshore moving onshore. In addition, certain of the opportunistic marketing opportunities that arose last quarter continued into the third quarter.

We believe that we could possibly benefit from such opportunities in 2027 and perhaps beyond, as some of the dislocations caused by the Iranian situation, the required reinjection of barrels previously withdrawn from the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve, as well as the resumption of significant crude imports from Venezuela, take years to fully return to historic norms. We are not building a business plan around it, nor are we budgeting for it in future periods, but we will capture such opportunities as they present themselves. Our legacy sulfur services business performed slightly below our expectations as operational issues at our largest host refinery reduced the supply of sour gas available for our sodium hydrosulfide, or NaHS, production.

Much of that seems to be behind us, and we are currently seeing higher operating rates as well as additional sulfur removal requirements as our two largest host refineries start running more sour crudes. We also remain in active dialogue with multiple parties to diversify our host refinery locations and restore our supply flexibility to historical levels. Looking ahead, we believe the market opportunity for NaHS will increase in future periods. In a post-COVID world, we lost market share in South America to low-cost flake NaHS coming out of China.

More and more of our historical copper mining customers are starting to realize the apparent short-term cost savings simply are not worth the operational headaches they have encountered from their trials of the inferior Chinese flake product. Taken together, we are hopeful we will be able to recapture a meaningful portion of the NaHS segment margin that we have lost in prior years, but that we know is there, given our historical level of activity and financial performance from this market-leading business. As we look towards the remainder of the year, we will likely be near or even possibly below the low end of our original guidance for adjusted EBITDA for the year.

Having said that, I would reiterate that coming in at or below the low end of 2026 guidance has little to do with the underlying fundamentals and the ultimate cash flow generating capabilities of our businesses, especially in our largest segment. In any event, we will remain disciplined and focused on what we can control. Stepping back and keeping everything important in focus, 2026 has indeed turned out to be a transformational year for Genesis, just as we anticipated.

Our businesses, while not without third-party operational challenges relative to our and our producer customers' expectations at the beginning of the year, have performed well enough to allow us to make meaningful progress on right-sizing our balance sheet and reducing the ongoing cash cost to run our business. This has been a very solid year under almost any objective metric, and we are proud to have delivered it. The operational side has simply taken a little longer than we and our producer customers had reasonably expected. We believe in the long-term value of our franchises, and we intend to execute the next phase of right-sizing our balance sheet and go after those additional cash savings available to us.

Rather than focusing on what could have been this year, our attention is squarely on executing that plan, and we believe it represents a compelling setup to continue creating value for everyone in the capital structure. Finally, I would like to say that the management team and the board of directors remain steadfast in our commitment to building long-term value for all our stakeholders, regardless of where you are in the capital structure. We believe the decisions we are making reflect this commitment and our confidence in Genesis moving forward. I would once again like to recognize our entire workforce for their individual efforts and unwavering commitment to safe, reliable, and responsible operations.

I am extremely proud to be associated with each and every one of you. With that, I will turn it back to the moderator for any questions.

Operator: Thank you. We will now be conducting a question-and-answer session. If you would like to ask a question, please press star one on your telephone keypad. A confirmation tone will indicate your line is in the question queue. You may press star two if you would like to remove your question from the queue. For participants using speaker equipment, it may be necessary to pick up your handset before pressing the star keys. One moment while we poll for questions. Your first question comes from Wade Suki with Capital One. Please proceed with your question.

Wade Suki: Good morning, everyone. Appreciate you all taking my question. Just quickly, Grant, Kristen, maybe you might be able to elaborate a little bit on some of these disruptions maybe spilling into next year. I guess, I know you have not put out 2027 guidance yet, but to the extent maybe you could sort of bracket what you think the impact might have been relative to your prior expectations on, let us call it, just segment profit or something, that would be very helpful.

Grant Sims: Well, again, we have not rolled out 2027 yet at this point, but I would say that consistent with our prepared remarks, we think that we will be at the minimum volume commitment level at Shenandoah for the rest of this year and until the two Monument wells come on, one of which is because of using the rig to do some work on one of the Shenandoah wells. The first Monument well has been pushed back into the first quarter, but as I said, we anticipate both of those coming on within the first quarter, but slid a little bit to the right.

Additionally, we had anticipated another well from Salamanca to be on by the end of the year, but we think both of them that are currently drilling are going to be first-quarter events. That's kind of what we meant by slipping in a little bit, sliding to the right in the first quarter. But again, everything seems to be on track at this point, and we're pretty excited about what 2027 looks like.

Wade Suki: Understood. Thank you. Appreciate that. I guess not to dwell on it, but I'm just kind of curious. Take a step back. We've seen some reservoir issues, it seems, maybe some well issues, mechanical issues, some infrastructure issues, obviously all out of your control. But I'm just wondering, not speaking to any specific operator, but I'm just curious what your thoughts are here. I mean, it's hard to imagine these operators are getting up the learning curve, but if there's something deeper going on here in the background, pun not intended, that you could sort of kind of share with us, I'd be very interested. Thank you.

Grant Sims: No, I don't think it's any specific operator. These are complicated, especially kind of the frontier play of the high-pressure, high-temperature Deep Wilcox play. This is a new frontier. People are figuring it out. I know that other deepwater operators that are there on an unnamed basis or on the early stages of development have run into some issues, and primarily around completions, design in a new high-pressure world. So, it's taken, and those other operators actually go through other competitive infrastructure. So, it's not an unusual circumstance. I think that we're dealing with very competent operators. They'll figure it out, as I said, and I don't think any of it has to do with the reserves in place.

It has to do with figuring out how to get them out as efficiently as possible, and they're all smart people, and they'll figure it out.

Wade Suki: Understood. Makes sense. Thank you so much. Appreciate it.

Operator: As a reminder, if you would like to ask a question, please press star one on your telephone keypad. A confirmation will indicate your line is in the question queue. You may press star two if you would like to remove your question from the queue. Your next question comes from Elvira Scotto with RBC Capital Markets. Please proceed with your question.

Elvira Scotto: Hey, thanks. Good morning. I understand that the long-term outlook remains intact, robust growth for decades to come. Just looking at 2026, and really just for modeling purposes, you talk about being near or possibly even below the low end of the original guidance. What could drive the results higher or lower than the low end? What are some of the milestones we should be watching? Grant Sims: Yeah. As we see it today, I think that we would be ±570 for the year, but we will keep an eye on that. It is a little bit at or below, I guess, original expectations. Again, we think 2027 is set up to be better than that, hopefully, based upon the known additional wells.

But we will see as we, when we talk again after the fourth quarter, we will have a better idea on how to discuss 2027.

Elvira Scotto: Great. Thank you. On the marine segment, the margin was up year-over-year. Utilization is effectively, I think you said 100%. You noted that the spot rates are robust and term contracts should follow higher. Can you provide any quantitative framing around that gap between the current negotiated spot rates where legacy term contracts are rolling off? What percent of your fleet reprices to spot or new term over the next 12 months?

Grant Sims: Yeah. I would say that certainly in the latter part of the quarter and continuing on into the early part of fourth quarter, we are seeing rates firm well over 10% on a spot basis, and in some cases even higher than that. We have on our inland fleet, I think we have basically only 10% of our inland fleet is contracted beyond December 31st. We think that a large portion of that is going to get recontracted at higher rates. So that's a good situation to be in. Probably half of our offshore fleet is also going to be repriced, we think, into a substantially higher market.

As we've mentioned before, there is robust demand for the American Phoenix, which comes off of long-term contract in the third quarter of 2027. We would fully expect after she finishes a 45-day dry dock for her to potentially reprice into a 15%+ to 20% higher value than what she's currently working for.

Elvira Scotto: Okay. Excuse me. That's great. I guess just really a long-term question, because it does sound like there's a lot of growth potential over the next several years. I think you mentioned there's nine of the 16 active deepwater Gulf rigs are working on leases dedicated to your systems, and two new rigs are expected to enter service over the next several years. Is there any incremental color on timing of those couple new rigs? Can you size the potential throughput uplift if and when all of those nine currently active rigs complete their current wells and those wells reach peak production? I'm just trying to understand, what is the real potential upside here?

Understanding that it could take a while.

Grant Sims: Yeah. I think there is one rig coming in, expected to come into the Gulf, I believe in 2029 and another in 2030. So, not going to have any near-term implications on that. As a general proposition, rigs that are deepwater drilling units, which are drilling today, can take 120± days to drill and complete a well. Most of these wells would be anticipated to have IPs in the 10,000-15,000 barrel a day range, and ultimate recoveries to ±25 million-30 million barrels per wellbore. So, you can do a little bit of arithmetic around that. Now, obviously, you do have some amount of decline from legacy fields and wells that have been previously drilled.

But it is certainly the level of activity, and our view is more than adequate to offset the decline. We are hopeful to see a net increase in total production, and we will give you a better idea of what 2027 looks like, as I said, when we have a discussion around the fourth quarter.

Elvira Scotto: Great. Thank you very much.

Grant Sims: Again, thanks everyone for listening in this morning, and we look forward to visiting with you in future periods. Thanks again. Bye-bye.

#3080. What Does a ‘Blue Wave’ Mean for Mortgage Rates?

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

Democrats won big in the midterms, but mortgage rates have bigger forces to reckon with.

Mortgage rates fell again this week, extending a gradual slide that began well before Election Day.

The average rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage fell 13 basis points to 7.05% APR in the week ending Nov. 5, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.) We calculate our weekly average using daily APRs recorded over the past five business days.

Homebuyers’ budgets are feeling the pinch from high mortgage rates, steep home prices and a shortage of listings. On the campaign trail, candidates from both parties promised to make homeownership more affordable. But solving that problem is like untangling 20 years’ worth of Christmas lights from your attic. Yank on one strand, and three more tighten.

“Jumpstarting the housing market relies on a calmer geopolitical environment and bond market in the short run and more housing supply plus a more dynamic labor market in the long run,” Jake Krimmel, senior economist for Realtor.com, said in an email.

A shift in political power won’t erase those challenges overnight. Here's what's driving mortgage rates right now — and where a Democratic Congress might have some pull.

How that affects mortgage rates: The relief of one less uncertainty is giving rates some breathing room.

Election results have cleared up one big unknown for investors. With Democrats controlling Congress and Republicans holding the White House, markets are bracing for the reality that any major spending bills could face roadblocks.

Political gridlock isn't always popular, but weirdly, investors sometimes welcome it. When a divided government limits new spending, the government may need to borrow less than expected — which could turn down the heat on mortgage rates.

But there’s a catch. That same gridlock could make it harder to pass laws to help bring down housing costs.

How that affects mortgage rates: Heavy borrowing from the government and tech companies adds upward pressure to the bond market, where mortgage rates take their cues.

When the government spends more than it collects in taxes, it borrows the difference by selling Treasury bonds. When there's lots of debt for sale, investors may demand higher returns, called yields. Mortgage rates tend to follow the yield on the 10-year Treasury note.

The new Congress still faces a mountain of government debt. What they choose to do about it can ripple through the economy to affect your monthly mortgage payment.

“Sound fiscal policy, rather than deficit-financed spending and standoffs over budgets and the debt limit, can help keep rates in check,” Andy Winkler, managing director for housing and infrastructure policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center, said in an email.

Meanwhile, Big Tech companies are borrowing a boatload of money to build AI data centers. To get the cash, they issue corporate bonds, giving investors another place to put their money. More bonds flooding the market can push Treasury yields higher, taking mortgage rates along for the ride.

But how long can the AI building boom last? Voters across party lines pushed back against data centers in the midterms. Even if lawmakers pump the brakes on new construction, a slowdown in tech spending doesn't guarantee cheaper mortgages.

How that affects mortgage rates: Wartime disruptions to global oil supplies can fuel inflation, pushing borrowing costs higher.

The unpopular war in Iran likely added to the voter frustration that helped fuel Democrats' midterm victories. Higher energy costs can hit household budgets in multiple ways: at the pump, through pricier goods that need to be shipped, and through higher interest rates on loans (including mortgages) as inflation heats up.

“A resolution would likely improve oil supply, helping to ease price pressures and potentially providing relief for mortgage rates,” Krimmel said.

A Democratic Congress could push for a different approach to ending the war, but it can't make Iran agree to a deal.

Meanwhile, stubborn inflation from the Iran war has raised the prospect of another Federal Reserve rate hike at its Dec. 8-9 meeting. Futures traders now put the odds of a quarter-point increase at more than 80%, according to CME FedWatch. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates directly, but investors anticipate its decisions — so mortgage rates often move before the Fed does.

If buying a home makes sense for your budget now, there's little reason to wait just because Congress changed hands. Buyers can sometimes score lower prices in winter, when sellers are more willing to negotiate. But with today’s mortgage rates hovering above 7%, higher borrowing costs can eat into those savings, so it’s important to compare mortgage lenders to get the best rate.

For longer-term hope, look to the bipartisan 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which became law this summer. This legislation shows lawmakers can, in fact, work together to make meaningful progress on housing affordability.

“Even with divided government, lawmakers and the administration can build on that common ground to further boost housing production, preserve existing affordable homes, and help families struggling with high housing and utility costs,” Winkler said.

But new homes take time to build, and your house hunt doesn't have to follow Congress's calendar. Your homebuying budget and local market conditions matter more than the next political headline.
