#3079. CION Investment (CION) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

CION cuts debt to $897 million and sets up a new joint venture for loan sales.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

CION Investment Corporation (CION -6.38%) completed its balance sheet deleveraging strategy during the third quarter by reducing total principal debt to $897 million. Management reported the repayment of public Israeli bonds and the early termination of a senior secured credit facility, which brought the net debt-to-equity ratio to the low end of its targeted range. To support this deleveraging, the company limited investment activity to follow-on commitments and formed a new joint venture, Senior Loan Fund Partners, to which it sold $180 million in first-lien loans. Management stated that these actions, while impacting near-term earnings and resulting in a 17% reduction in the 2027 base distribution, were intended to strengthen the balance sheet for future share repurchases.

Operator: Good morning. And welcome to Cion Investment Corporation's Third Quarter 26 Earnings Conference Call. Earnings press release was distributed earlier this morning before market opened. Copy of the release, along with a supplemental earnings presentation, is available on the company's website at www.cionbdc.com. In the Investor Relations Resources section and should be reviewed in conjunction with the company's Form 10 Q filed with the SEC. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded for replay purposes. Please note that today's conference call may contain forward-looking statements, which are not guaranteed of future performance or results and involve a number of risks and uncertainties.

Actual results may differ materially from those in the forward-looking statements as a result of a number of factors, including those described in the company's filings with the SEC. Joining me on today's call will be Michael A. Reisner, Cion Investment Corporation's Co Chief Executive Officer Gregg A. Bresner, President and Chief Investment Officer. And Keith S. Franz, Chief Financial Officer. With that, I would like to turn the call over to Michael A. Reisner. Please go ahead, Michael.

Michael A. Reisner: Thank you, and good morning, everyone. Last quarter, we told you management had a plan to strengthen Cion's balance sheet. This quarter, we executed on it. Repaid $114.8 million of public Israeli bonds in full at maturity. Which avoided any contractual make whole fees prior to that date. After expiration of the make whole period, we also fully repaid the $200 million outstanding under our JPMorgan secured facility. And completed its early termination. Further, we completed a new non recourse off balance sheet joint venture Senior Loan Fund Partners with a large institutional partner. As a result, we ended the quarter at 1.3 times net debt to equity.

Down from 1.52x last quarter and lower than the approximately 1.35x target we previously provided. The execution of this deleveraging plan impacted our near term earnings during the quarter. We reported net investment income of $0.25 per share, compared to $0.29 last quarter. Partially impacted by 1 time non recurring items. Our net asset value ended the quarter at $13.20 per share, down 2.7% from $13.57 last quarter mostly from unrealized mark to market price decreases on certain investments. And distributions in excess of NII. Gregg will walk you through the specific names with transactions this quarter.

Our near term earnings decline was largely the result of strategic decisions we made rather than an overall decline in the credit quality of the portfolio. To retain cash for deleveraging, we made no new platform investments this quarter. Our only investments were follow ons to our existing portfolio companies. New platform investments often provide enhanced economics through incremental origination and structuring fees In this quarter, there were none. In addition, our earnings were impacted by our debt repayment activity. Most specifically the early repayment and termination of our JPMorgan facility ahead of its scheduled maturity. That alone reduced NII by approximately $0.03 per share, due to the accelerated amortization of the facility's remaining debt issuance costs.

We were also impacted by non recurring costs associated with forming the new joint venture, the reduction of a deferred fee on a legacy tranche of a portfolio company as a result of a new prim-and-tuck tranche that we led for the company. The elimination of accrued income on our term loan investment in Thrill 1, Following the company's post bankruptcy reorganization, in which we received a new investment tranche. Together, all these items reduced NII by roughly $0.15 per share. We announced the completion of our deleveraging in our September 29 press release, but I think it bears repeating.

In a single quarter, we reduced our balance sheet debt from $1.17 billion to $897 million The joint venture was also another validator of certain of our loan marks. Last quarter we sold more than $54 million of our assets at approximately 99% of par. This quarter, a large independent institutional partner comprehensively diligence 20 of our first-lien loans and purchase them through the joint venture at $180 million or 99.8% of par. As Greg will discuss, our total sales and repayments this quarter came in at a blended value above 99.6% of par. Further confirmation of certain of our fair value marks. Firstly, investments dipped to about 72% of the portfolio.

Largely because our portfolio is smaller after deleveraging and after selling certain loans to the JV. Where we hold now an equity interest. We expect that percentage to rise as we seek to continue to monetize equity positions such as Longview Power which alone currently represents more than 6% of our total investment portfolio. The media is still focused on private credit defaults and macroeconomic risk. Fitch's U. S. Private credit default rate recently reached 6.3%. Against that backdrop, we are very pleased with how our portfolio is performing. We placed no new names on nonaccrual status this quarter and 97.8% of our portfolio is risk rated 3 or better. Gregg will take you through some of these details.

We previously announced declared base distributions of $0.10 per share for each of October, November and December which is unchanged at $0.30 for the fourth quarter. For 2027, we expect to set base distributions at $0.25 per share per quarter. And here are the reasons. First, we have reduced our debt on our balance sheet which makes Cion a stronger company but also leaves us with a smaller earning portfolio. Second, until we have completed share repurchases, we will be selective about growing our investment portfolio through new platform deals. Resulting in a reduction in the fees they tend to generate for us.

We would rather pay a distribution we are confident we can cover from core earnings than stretch to keep a level that depends on robust transaction activity. We continue to expect the publicly announced sale of Longview Power to a strategic acquirer to close in the fourth quarter of 26. Or the first quarter of 27. Subject to regulatory approval. We expect significant gains on the sale which we believe will provide us with enhanced liquidity and our first priority will be to seek the resumption of share repurchases. We did not repurchase shares in the third quarter and I want to explain why. First, we were conserving cash to complete our deleveraging strategy.

Second, we were in possession of material non public information about David's bridal and Pearl. Which prevented us from signing a new repurchase plan. Gregg will walk you through the proposed David's Bridal and Pearl transactions So I will focus on why it matters to Scion shareholders. David's Bridal is our largest exposure. If the transactions are completed, our consolidated investment will be divided into 2 separately governed companies a meaningful percentage of that investment will be publicly traded. That would provide our investors with visible market values for the publicly traded portion of those investments and we believe will give us a path to monetize and reduce our exposure over time.

These transactions are currently under a non binding letter of intent There is no assurance that definitive agreement will be signed or that the transactions will close on the terms or timeline publicly disclosed or at all. However, we are cautiously optimistic. Last quarter, we said the market seems worried about 4 things. Our marks, our ability to delever, the dividend and software exposure. Since then, third parties have priced certain of our loans at or near par once again. We have delevered below our target. We have given you our 2027 base distribution expectations in advance, based on our reasonable estimate of core earnings and software is still around 2% of our portfolio.

With the Longview sale expected to close in the coming months, we intend to seek resumption of repurchases of our stock at what we believe is a significant discount to its value. With that, I will now turn the call over to Gregg,

Gregg A. Bresner: Thank you, Michael, and good morning, everyone. As Michael discussed, during the quarter, we focused on completing our deleveraging plan as we seek to position the company to recommence share repurchases. We also exclusively focus our Q3 funded investment activity on supporting our existing portfolio companies, and we received approximately $45 million in full repayments from borrowers during the quarter. We limited our Q3 investment activities to our existing portfolio companies for corporate investments working capital, and other strategic transactions. The weighted average yield for our new direct first lien investments for the quarter based on our investment cost was the equivalent of SOFR +6.1%.

As we discussed in previous quarters, the majority of our PIK income is strategically derived from either highly structured first lien investments, or our PIK income is incremental to our cash coupon. Together, these categories represented approximately 81% of our total PIK investment income in Q3, down from approximately 85% in Q2. Over 99% of our PIK investments are in first lien assets. As a result, we believe this PIK income does not compare to restructured PIK income from a deterioration in borrower credit. Turning now to our Q3 investment and portfolio activity. Our Q3 funded investment activity was solely for our existing portfolio companies as we made no new platform investments during the quarter.

We funded add on investments in existing portfolio companies, including Anthem, ARC, Avison Young, Berlitz, David's Bridal, Innovative, STATinMED, and Trademark Global. During Q3, we completed approximately $78 million in investment commitments across 11 existing portfolio companies of which $72 million was funded. We also funded a total of $11 million of previously unfunded commitments. We had sales and repayments totaling $256 million for the quarter at a blended value of over 99.6% of par which included our new first lien senior loan joint venture with an institutional investor. Where we sold $180 million of such loans at a price over 99.8% of par.

We additionally received full repayment of our first lien positions in Giving Home Health, Lux Credit and RumbleOn. As a result of all these activities, our net funded investments decreased by approximately $173 million during the quarter. In his commentary, Michael mentioned the announced sale transaction of Longview Power to a strategic acquirer.

Longview was 1 of our earliest investments within our opportunistic special situation strategy where we identify and acquire lightly syndicated first lien loan tranches in what we believe are quality companies at significant discounts to par due to technical or balance sheet related issues and then may have an active role in the processes that drive the restructuring or recapitalization of these investments to position the companies for future success. Our investment in Longview began with a discounted first lien term loan purchase in September 2018 followed by a series of strategic add on investments. Additional examples of our special situation strategy included our investments in Yachmat, Carestream Health, ESP Associates, McNeil, Pride, Heritage Power, and Dayton Superior.

We have a number of special situation investments remaining in the portfolio that have yet to be realized, and we are actively working to achieve our monetization success for these investments. As Michael mentioned, our NAV movement during the quarter was driven primarily by unrealized mark to market price decreases on certain of our investments. Marks were still somewhat affected by the macro sentiments regarding the potential crack in private credit most specifically the software concentrations within the private capital sector and the potential impact of AI on those investments.

As a reminder, Cion has not been a significant software investor historically, and has only 2% of its portfolio in the software sector with no ARR based loans as of Q3. Our increase in unrealized values during Q3 was primarily driven by our equity investments. Our largest increases for the quarter were equity positions in Carestream Health, David's Bridal, Juice Plus, and Palmetto Solar. Our largest unrealized decliners for the quarter were our investments in Berlitz, K&N and Avison Young. The decline in the carrying value of our Longview Power equity investment was driven by the company's payment of a cash dividend during the quarter.

As we have mentioned on previous quarterly calls, we expect to see significant quarter to quarter volatility in the value of David's bridal equity due to the larger overall relative size of our investment as well as the highly seasonal nature of the company's operations and working capital profile. As we mentioned last quarter, David's is in the process of separating Pearl, David's AI powered wedding planning, media commerce, and vendor marketplace platform from David's traditional retail brick and mortar operations in order to enhance future prospects for both companies. Post quarter on October 22, David's bridal publicly announced that it executed a letter of intent for a proposed business combination between Pearl and K&N Growth Acquisition Corp.

II, a publicly traded special purpose acquisition corporation. Proposed business combination would establish Pearl as a standalone public company and is expected to accelerate growth and innovation through its proprietary AI technology, scalable pure play online business model, and continue synergistic relationship with David's Bridal established physical retail business. The executed letter of intent values Pearl at a pro forma enterprise value of $350 million and contemplates a $75 million PIPE investment transaction. The parties are working towards the completion of definitive agreements. The targeted closing date for the proposed transaction is during the first half of 27, subject to the completion of definitive agreements and the satisfaction of closing conditions.

Last quarter, we discussed the bankruptcy of Thrill 1, During Q3, Thrill 1 exited bankruptcy with a plan of reorganization whereby our legacy term loan investment was exchanged into a new investment tranche. While this transaction was contemplated and valued in Q2, the exchange resulted in a realized loss on the legacy term loan investment with the unrealized value of the new reorganized investment tranche in Q3. From a portfolio credit perspective, our non accruals amounted to 1.63% and 4.85% of the total investment portfolio at fair value and amortized cost, respectively. At the end of Q3 which increased from 1.44% and 4.41%, respectively, at the end of Q2.

There were no new names added or removed from nonaccrual status in Q3, and the changes in percentages were driven by the decrease in total portfolio value primarily due to the execution of our deleveraging plan. On an absolute basis, non accruals continue to be in line with historical experience and we are pleased with the continued credit performance of our portfolio, particularly in the current macro environment. Overall, our portfolio remains defensive in nature with approximately 72% in first-lien investments. As Michael discussed, we expect the percentage of first lien in the portfolio to increase over the next few quarters as we seek to monetize equity investments such as Longview Power.

Approximately 98% of our portfolio remains risk rated 3 or better. Our risk rated 3 investments are investments where we expect full repayment but are either spending more engagement time and or have seen increased risk since the initial asset purchase increased from approximately 14.1% in Q2 to 17.5% in Q3 the majority of which was driven by the decrease in total portfolio value primarily due to our deleveraging plan. I will now turn the call over to Keith.

Keith S. Franz: Okay. Okay. Thank you, Gregg, and good morning, everyone. During the third quarter, net investment income was $12.3 million or $0.25 per share compared to $14.2 million or $0.29 per share reported in the second quarter. Total investment income was $48.3 million during the third quarter, as compared to $49.8 million reported during the second quarter. A decrease of $1.5 million or about 3%.

The decrease in total investment income was driven primarily by lower interest income earned on our investments due to a reduction in the size of our portfolio as a result of our deleveraging activities during the quarter lower transaction fees earned due to lower quarterly investment activity and the reduction of our legacy transaction fee on an investment. This decrease was partially offset by an increase in dividends received from 1 of our equity investments and an increase in prepayment fees received during the quarter. On the expense side, total operating expenses were $30 million compared to $35.6 million reported in the second quarter.

The increase in operating expenses was primarily due to higher G&A expenses due to non recurring legal fees incurred in connection with the restructuring of an investment and costs associated with forming our new strategic joint venture. This increase was partially offset by a decrease in advisory fees when compared to the prior quarter. Interest expense was impacted during the quarter by the write-off of $1.5 million in unamortized debt issuance costs in connection with the repayment of our JPMorgan credit facility partially offset by lower interest expense due to the decrease in the average debt balance outstanding during the quarter.

At September 30, we had total assets of approximately $1.6 billion and total equity or net assets of $650 million with total debt outstanding of $897 million and 49.2 million shares outstanding. Our portfolio at fair value ended the quarter at $1.47 billion down from $1.65 billion in the second quarter. And the weighted average yield on our debt and other income producing investments at amortized cost was 10.6%. Which is consistent with the second quarter. At September 30, our NAV was $13.20 per share as compared to $13.57 per share at the end of June.

The decrease of $0.37 per share or 2.7% was primarily due to unrealized mark to market price decreases and under earning our distribution during the quarter. We ended the third quarter with what we believe is a strong and flexible balance sheet with about $1.4 billion in unencumbered assets a strong debt service capacity with an interest coverage ratio of about 1.6x. We had over $50 million in cash and short term investments and $25 million available under our credit facility. In terms of our debt capital, at September 30, we continue to have a healthy and diversified debt mix about 90% in unsecured and 10% in senior secured bank debt.

Our well diversified debt structure is focused on unsecured debt in order to maximize our balance sheet flexibility and at the same time creates a strong buffer for our financial covenants. At the end of the quarter, our net debt to equity ratio decreased to 1.3x from 1.52x at the end of June. And the weighted average cost of our debt capital was about 7.6%. Which is slightly up when compared to the second quarter. The decrease in our net leverage ratio was a direct result of our deleveraging plan to better position our balance sheet.

#3078. From Pilots To Payoff: The Top IT Priorities Every Executive Should Accomplish Before Year-End

Scott Francis is Technology Evangelist at PFU America, Inc. and Ricoh Document Scanners.

​As the end of 2026 draws near, the central question for business leaders has shifted from asking whether their organization is adopting and deploying AI fast enough to assessing whether AI is performing as expected. With IT budget planning for 2027 well underway, organizations should use the waning months of this year as a reality check that will serve to separate organizations positioned to scale in 2027 from those still catching up.​

There’s no question that the demand for AI is skyrocketing. What is unclear is whether organizations are meeting the projected return on investment thus far. Gartner predicts AI spend will reach $2.59 trillion globally this year, a substantial 47% increase over 2025.​​

With the end of the year quickly approaching, there is an opportunity to take stock and refocus on overcoming challenges to achieving ROI and readjust where necessary. Rather than taking a scattershot approach to AI deployments, organizations should take a measured, strategic approach on where to apply AI; for example, using one workflow, establishing KPIs and then tracking those quarter-over-quarter before expanding to more departments or enterprise-wide.​

As the saying goes, “life moves fast.” And we’ve seen from technological advancements over the last few years that AI moves just as fast. Many companies are already in the planning phase of employing agentic AI, according to McKinsey’s report, with 40% of companies surveyed already scaling agents, up from 27% in 2025.

Despite the positive uptick in deployments, organizations should prioritize getting current AI deployments right, determining what’s hindering ROI and preparing for the next phase of digital transformation.

AI systems are only as trustworthy as the data foundation, which is a major reason why prioritizing data quality is imperative. Flawed data takes on a new meaning in the AI era because it has the potential to undermine the models built on it.

The “2026 State of Data Integrity and AI Readiness” survey of data and analytics leaders puts a spotlight on data quality challenges: 43% of respondents cite data readiness as the most significant barrier to AI alignment with business objectives. Creating proactive strategies to fix bad data, including data errors, redundancy and more, is still one of the most inexpensive approaches to protecting against downstream damage. This imperative step provides organizations with the confidence that their AI deployments will meet performance expectations and transform data into the dependable foundation that reliable, high-performing AI requires.

Before expanding AI deployments and introducing agents, executives should audit whether the underlying systems can actually support agentic workflows, including clean data pipelines, defined APIs and integration between the systems agents need to touch.

Preparing teams well before AI is rolled out across the organization is critical. Skipping this step can breed employee resentment and pushback and result in lowering morale.

Workplace tension is already a challenge, and for good reason. A WRITER study found that “92% of the C-suite are actively cultivating ‘AI elite’ employees, while 60% plan layoffs for non-adopters.” Business leaders should not view AI as a replacement for skilled personnel; it should be used to surface insights and recommendations, while consequential decisions, especially those affecting employees or customers, remain in human hands.

Training, communication and genuine feedback loops are what separate adoption from chaos, making change management well worth the investment. Reskilling and preserving the human element build trust and catch the blind spots LLMs can’t.

IT leaders should be aware that AI is not immune from volatility, and a backup plan is mandatory. One well-publicized example of AI disruption is Anthropic’s suspension of global access to Claude Fable 5 and Mythos 5 following a U.S. government export control directive. Access was later restored under a modified compliance structure; however, business leaders should take this incident seriously and acknowledge that government-initiated suspension or access restriction can occur without advance notice. Business leaders can address regulatory instability by identifying which models and vendors they rely on and identifying fallback options before a suspension forces an unplanned migration.

There is also a growing regulatory divide between jurisdictions. The U.S. export rule’s workforce application means enterprises with frontier AI API integrations and global engineering teams may be exposed to compliance risk regardless of where their servers are located. Gartner projects more than a third of enterprises will run localized AI platforms by 2027, up from just 5% in 2025. For multinational firms, this means agentic AI strategy can no longer be a single global architecture; it will need to incorporate jurisdiction-based contingency planning.

​The gap between AI pilots and AI payoff won’t close on its own. The executives who make real progress before year-end will be the ones connecting these three priorities to long-term success to achieve business goals and ROI goals. I believe it’s imperative for business leaders to focus on the fundamentals this year before expanding AI projects and incorporating agents, treating their data quality, teams, economics and risk as interconnected.​

#3077. The Austin Powers steamroller: How to trade CoreWeave's slow moving crisis

In Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery, a Virtuocon guard famously stands in front of a commandeered steamroller, screaming "No!!" three times before being run over. The joke, of course, is that the hazard moved so slowly he had ample time to step out of the way.

For months, equity traders holding CoreWeave (CRWV) have played that guard. Despite credit markets flashing warnings, equity holders essentially just stood there. Now, after a shocking 27.5% drop from last Friday's close to this Thursday morning's 52-week lows, followed by a whiplash 17% rebound, equity investors, if not squashed like Dr. Evil's henchman, are dazed and confused. Shares are down another 5% today.

With earnings just a few weeks away, massive leverage, a heavily split sell-side, and 15.4% short interest, the stock remains primed for explosive volatility.

The hazard approaching CRWV equity wasn't hidden. The AI cloud infrastructure platform essentially didn't exist five years ago and has accumulated $51.6 billion in debt (~$46 billion net of cash) against a backdrop of zero historical profitability. That was well known, but the CEO's comments that the company aspired to be investment grade so it could borrow "unlimited sums", even as investors already anticipated nearly another $60 billion in debt in the next 18months, spooked folks. (Trick or Treat!) Especially since the debt issued only in June had already fallen 20% since.

From an options trader's point of view, it was hard to reconcile deteriorating credit and rising leverage with falling options premia; as recently as last week, they were in the 6th percentile, 1.5 standard deviations below the one-year mean. At 72%, options weren't cheap in absolute terms, but given everything going on, they should have been higher. The stock also looked somewhat complacent, with the equity chopping around historical support levels dating back to May 2025. The credit side was on tilt:

Because CRWV is levered by more than 2:1, a 10% move in enterprise value translates to a nearly 22% swing in equity value.

Despite the dire credit picture, equity sentiment remains fiercely divided, driving this week's 17% bounce from the lows. For example, HSBC maintains a Sell rating with a $39 price target, essentially calling for the stock to be cut in half. Conversely, banks like BNP and Cantor Fitzgerald (my former employer) suggest these fears are overblown and the stock should more than double from here.

It's not just bankers defending the company either. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang downplayed systemic concerns, and ARK Investment stepped in to buy 192,000 shares. BofA argues that CRWV's ability to bring active power online at scale, combined with higher pricing from Nvidia's upcoming Vera Rubin deployments, will drive faster-than-expected revenue growth. They described execution risk as a bigger concern than financing; I'm not sure those who bought the 2032 8 1/2s at par would agree.

With CRWV's credit heavily distressed but its equity heavily defended by high-profile dip-buyers, going outright long or short into earnings carries excessive directional risk. A November/January Call Diagonal, currently trading for just under $6 per spread. Almost 9% of the current stock price. Normally, that's a lot, but given this stock has fallen 27.5% and then gained 17% in the past 5 sessions, it isn't.

The right card for you may depend on where you travel, how often, and your level of elite status with Bonvoy.

Two of the popular credit cards in the Marriott Bonvoy portfolio deliver various benefits to their users. The right one for you may depend on your typical travel patterns and history, such as if you already have a high level of elite status with Marriott or you travel only to certain regions.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card and the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card both come with valuable perks, but there are quite a few considerations that are worth a thorough review. Many travelers prefer not to have two cards from the same loyalty program, and these two cards are actually quite different from each other (including being issued by different banks).

Let’s take a look at these two Marriott co-branded cards to see if one may serve your needs over the other.

Here's how the cards stack up on the basics.

Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card

While the “winning” card for some may not apply to everyone, we wanted to analyze the card that provides exceptional benefits for travelers looking for a Marriott card in exchange for the cost of the annual fee. Those new to Marriott will find this to be a solid entry-level card, but it also works for Marriott Bonvoy fans looking for some extra perks without a huge outlay of money for an annual fee. These are the benefits that handed this card the win.

The annual fee on the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card is notably less at $95 compared with $250 on the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card. While the earning rates when using the card to pay for Marriott stays are nearly the same, and both have bonus categories where you can earn multiples of points based on everyday spending, the lower-annual-fee card offers a lot of points earning for its low annual fee.

On top of the lower annual fee, it comes with an automatic annual free night award, Silver Elite status and a fast path to achieve Gold if you use the card often. Add to that an annual $100 in airline credits and DoorDash DashPass membership, and you have more than covered the annual fee without considering the other perks.

The Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card card’s $250 annual fee is higher, and its annual free night award requires spending $15,000 in eligible purchases. But the card comes with automatic Gold Elite status and more bonus points earned.

There are other cards (like American Express Platinum Card®) that also include free Gold Elite status with Marriott that can provide decent value for their annual fee (enrollment required). From a pure cash maximization perspective, the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card wins because it provides more bang for your buck.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card is the only one of the two cards to include an annual free night award, and it has a lower annual fee. It can be used at properties up to 35,000 points a night. This can render great value and is more than worth the $95 annual fee. Hands down, it is the winner in this category.

If you spend more than $15,000 on the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card in a calendar year, you can unlock a free night certificate valid at up to 50,000 points. This is even more valuable than the included certificate that comes with the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card, but it also requires you to spend more on this card to get it.

It is important to consider the opportunity cost of not putting certain types of spend on other cards where you could be earning greater multiples of points for the same type of spending. Would losing those points be worth the value of a one-night-free certificate? Since Marriott relies on dynamic pricing, which means that points rates for a redemption night can fluctuate regularly, in many cases the value may not reach the level of the missed points opportunity.

While both cards offer decent travel protection benefits, only the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card comes with a flight credit. You can earn up to $100 in statement credits when making purchases directly with airlines by spending $250 on the card before the end of 2026 for a $50 statement credit and another $50 credit by spending $50 before June 30, 2027. That gives another point to the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card Boundless card.

» Learn more: Should I be loyal to a single airline?

If you don’t already have a Marriott co-branded credit card and you want to diversify what’s in your wallet, this could be a great option for big spenders. And if you are looking for one of the fastest paths to high Marriott elite status, this card can help you get there.

Both the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card and Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card cards offer bonus points on spending, but the more expensive annual fee Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card card offers more points on more spending opportunities, including the below:

18.5X points on Marriott Bonvoy property spending (1.5X more than the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card card).

4X points at global restaurants, including U.S. takeout and delivery plus U.S. Supermarkets on up to $15,000 in combined purchases, then 2X points (that’s 1X more than what Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card offers and available on $9,000 more in spending).

1,000 bonus points when staying at a Marriott Bonvoy property.

Depending on how much you spend in these categories, you have the ability to earn more points with this card than the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card, including when you are not traveling. And then when you are, you earn 1,000 Marriott bonus points for each paid, eligible stay booked directly with Marriott. This gives it an edge, even though the annual fee is higher.

» Learn more: Hilton versus Marriott — Which one is right for you?

When you get the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card, you’ll receive 15 elite night credits deposited into your Marriott account. This is on top of the instant Gold Elite status you earn with the card, which normally requires staying 25 nights. To reach the next tier, Platinum, you only need an additional 10 nights to reach its 50-night minimum.

This means not only do you start out at a higher elite tier with Marriott just for having this card, but also you can progress more quickly to Platinum. For frequent travelers, the best value of this card is the opportunity to reach the next status tier faster. And if you wanted to keep going, you would only need 35 more nights to get to Titanium, which is rich with on-property perks like lounge access, welcome gifts and room upgrades.

Earning these nights within a calendar year is not difficult for Marriott loyalists, especially if you hit the jackpot during a promotion that offers double elite nights.

The status perks don’t stop there. Once you hit Marriott’s Titanium status, you can then link your account with United Airlines to earn United’s Premier Silver elite status for more benefits when you fly United, including greater baggage allowance and free extra-legroom economy seats at check-in.

» Learn more: Marriott elite status: what you need to know

Both of these cards provide Marriott Bonvoy points earning and elite status, and they both offer a great way to expedite points earning or receive travel and purchase protections when using the card. But the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card packs a greater punch in its benefits for a lower annual fee. It becomes a great additional card to others you may have (like the American Express Platinum Card®, which has its own impressive travel perk lineup).

If you are a Marriott frequent guest, the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card offers higher-tier Gold status and a faster path to even better tiers for perks. But, it costs more each year and does not offer a free annual night.

Deciding which perks are more important for you, as well as looking at what benefits come from other cards in your wallet, will help you make an informed decision on which of the two best suits your needs.

For rates and fees of the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card, please visit American Express' rates and fees page.

#3072. Your Monitoring Stack Isn’t The Problem. The Detection-To-Ownership Gap Is

Judit Sharon is the founder and CEO of OnPage Corporation, an advanced, secure critical communication and collaboration platform provider.

​At 2:07 a.m., a monitoring platform detects that a customer-facing application is failing. It creates a ticket, sends an email and posts to an operations channel. At 2:19 a.m., no engineer has taken ownership of the incident.

The monitoring system did its job. The response process did not.

Detection-to-ownership time is the elapsed time between detecting a critical incident and a qualified responder acknowledging and accepting responsibility for it. Unlike mean time to detect (MTTD), detection-to-ownership time measures the human-response gap after monitoring has already identified the problem.

For CIOs, IT operations leaders and site reliability teams, those 12 minutes represent a distinct failure: The organization knew something was wrong, but no one was responsible for acting on it.

Alert delivery does not guarantee incident ownership because delivery confirms that a notification reached a destination, not that a qualified responder saw it, accepted responsibility or began acting on it.

An alert may reach a shared inbox nobody is watching. A Slack or Microsoft Teams notification can disappear into routine conversation. Email-to-text gateways provide another notification path, but they may still fail to get attention. An answering service can also delay ownership while it determines urgency and locates the on-call responder.

The mistake is assuming that, because a notification went out, the right responder has taken charge. To see where the handoff breaks down, distinguish five states:

• Detected: A system identified the problem.

• Delivered: The alert reached its intended destination.

• Read: The responder has seen the critical alert.

• Owned: A qualified responder has acknowledged the incident and accepted responsibility for the next action.

• Resolved: The issue was addressed, with the alert status synced back to the originating system where supported.

Delivery is not ownership. For a critical incident, “someone received it” is not enough; the team needs to know who read the alert and took ownership, when and what happened next.

An event should trigger an immediate page when it has meaningful business or customer impact, requires timely human intervention and the responder can act on it.

IT and digital operations teams need telemetry, warnings and diagnostic information, but not every event warrants immediate interruption. When routine conditions and genuine failures arrive with the same urgency, responders discount the signal and alert noise becomes alert fatigue.

Set stricter paging criteria. A customer-facing outage, a failed payment workflow or a major security event may require immediate response. A transient warning that clears without intervention may belong in a dashboard or ticket queue.

The distinction should depend on business impact, service criticality and whether the responder can take useful action. A page-worthy alert should clearly state what service is affected, what failed and where the responder should go next. It should also stand out, override silent mode when required and persist until someone responds.

On-call schedules and escalation policies reduce response time by automatically routing critical alerts to the person currently responsible and escalating when that responder does not acknowledge the incident within a defined period.

Static contact lists and manual routing can slow response when people change roles, take leave or rotate through on-call shifts. Schedule-based routing directs the alert to whoever is currently responsible. Round-robin routing can distribute incidents across several qualified responders while preserving individual ownership.

To keep critical pages meaningful, teams can use deduplication, suppression or brief delays for conditions likely to clear on their own. A workflow might begin with SMS, email or a phone call, followed by a persistent mobile page if no one responds. More urgent incidents may warrant immediate paging and automatic escalation.

Consider a database supporting a customer-facing application that becomes unavailable. Monitoring detects the failure and pages the assigned on-call engineer. If that engineer does not read the incident within the defined interval, the alert escalates to the next responder. The notification path continues until someone qualified assumes responsibility.

Automation does not make the technical decisions needed to resolve the incident. Engineers still diagnose and resolve the problem. Automation removes avoidable delay in getting the right person involved.

Slack and Microsoft Teams help coordinate incidents. A channel notification alone, however, does not establish who must respond.

Posting to a channel tells a group something happened. Paging assigns responsibility to a specific responder and creates an escalation path if that person doesn’t respond.

Integrations into on-call management and alerting workflows can reduce context switching by allowing teams to initiate a paging workflow from the Slack or Teams conversation where an incident is already being discussed.

Whether these practices work should be visible in the data. Detection-to-ownership time starts when the system identifies the incident and ends when a qualified person accepts responsibility. Teams can break that interval into delivery time, acknowledgment time and confirmed ownership.

Those measures reveal different problems. Fast delivery but slow acknowledgment may point to alert noise, alert fatigue or ineffective notification methods. Quick acknowledgment without clear ownership suggests unclear responsibilities. Frequent escalation may expose gaps in staffing or on-call coverage.

Testing matters, too. Test the workflow during shift changes, after hours and when the primary responder is unavailable. Test what happens when the first page goes unanswered.

Monitoring tells you what happened. An effective incident alert management process determines who needs to act, whether they received the alert, whether they responded and who owns the incident now.

If the organization already knows a critical service is failing but still cannot say who owns the response, faster monitoring will not close that gap.​

#3070. NorthWestern Energy (NWE) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Colstrip losses and mild weather pressured margins this quarter.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

NorthWestern Energy Group, Inc. (NWE +0.02%) focused the third quarter on finalizing its merger with Black Hills Corporation while managing the financial integration of expanded ownership in the Colstrip generation facility. Management affirmed its standalone 2026 earnings guidance but cautioned that results are trending toward the lower end of the range due to unfavorable market power prices and mild weather patterns in the Pacific Northwest. The company is advancing a multiyear capital plan centered on regional transmission development and new natural gas generation in South Dakota to meet updated resource adequacy requirements. Strategic efforts also include the development of a large new load tariff in Montana to facilitate the integration of energy-intensive data center customers into the regulated rate base.

#3068. 2027 Tax Brackets and Federal Income Tax Rates

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

Each year, the IRS adjusts tax brackets to keep pace with inflation. The 2027 tax brackets were announced on Nov. 5, 2026.

The IRS has released updated tax brackets for 2027, which apply to the taxes we file in 2028. You may notice that the seven tax rates generally stay the same year-to-year — so why do tax brackets get adjusted?

Well, due to inflation, our money might not stretch as far as it did the previous year. To combat that, the IRS adjusts tax brackets so taxpayers can keep a little bit more of their money in a lower tax bracket compared with the previous year.

For example, a single filer could make up to $50,400 in 2026 and pay a top tax rate of 12%. But in 2027, they could make up to $52,025 and still only pay a top tax rate of 12% thanks to these inflation adjustments.

Not sure how to read the tax bracket tables below?

Find your total taxable income in the "tax bracket" column. The corresponding tax rate is the highest rate you'll pay — it doesn’t apply to all your income; it applies only to the portion that falls within that bracket. The income in the lower brackets is taxed at those lower rates.

For example, let's say you’re a single filer and you expect to earn $150,000 this year. The top rate you’d pay on a portion of your income is 24%. The rest would be taxed at 10%, 12% and 22%.

Here's a rundown of changes to some well-known tax provisions for the 2027 tax year.

Each year, the IRS updates common tax provisions, such as income tax brackets and the standard deduction, to ensure the tax code is keeping pace with the rising cost of living.

These tweaks — formally known as inflation adjustments — help prevent “bracket creep,” where taxpayers who received a cost-of-living raise can pay more in taxes even though their purchasing power remains unchanged.

Inflation adjustments for the 2027 tax year were set at 3.2% — larger than the previous two years as inflation heated up. This could mean lower tax bills for some people when they file in 2028.

In the U.S., there are seven marginal rates — 10%, 12%, 22%, 24%, 32%, 35% and 37% — which will remain unchanged for 2027.

Contrary to a popular myth, it’s uncommon for people to pay a single flat federal tax rate on their taxable income. Instead, portions of a person’s income can be taxed at different rates depending on which tax brackets they fall into. For example, some of a person’s income could be taxed at 10%, another chunk at 12%, and so on.

For 2027, the IRS is adjusting those tax brackets — the windows of income that dictate where a tax rate ends and begins — for each filing status. The adjustments mean that some people may be able to keep some of their income in lower tax brackets, and those who received a cost-of-living raise may avoid getting a portion of their income pushed into a higher bracket.

Married filers, for example, can make up to $104,050 to remain with a top tax rate of 12%, compared with $100,800 in 2026. This increase could allow some couples to shelter an additional $3,250 from a higher tax rate in 2027.

2026 vs. 2027 tax brackets: Single filers

2026 vs. 2027 tax brackets: Heads of household

2026 vs. 2027 tax brackets: Married filing separately

» MORE: See the full 2027 tax brackets for each filing status

The IRS lets most filers lower their taxable income by taking the standard deduction or itemizing their returns. The standard deduction, a flat amount based on filing status and age, is popular, as it requires less work to claim and is often more beneficial for those who might not have deductible expenses.

For 2027, the standard deduction will be $16,600 for single filers and those married filing separately, a $500 increase from 2026. Joint filers will be eligible to take $33,200 and heads of household can take $24,925, a $1,000 and $775 increase over 2026, respectively.

» Need help deciding whether to itemize or take the standard deduction? Learn about the differences

Also included in the IRS' 32-page inflation release are various updates to several tax provisions beyond the federal tax brackets. Plus, a brand-new tax credit will go into effect in 2027.

Starting in 2027, taxpayers who contribute to a health flexible spending account (FSA) can contribute up to $3,500 and, if their plan permits, carry over up to $700 into the next tax year.

For those with health savings accounts, the 2027 limit for contributions will rise to $4,500 for self-only coverage and $9,000 for family coverage.

The annual exclusion for gifts, which limits how much taxpayers can give an individual without filing a gift tax return on certain gifts, will be $20,000 per person in 2027, an increase of $1,000 compared with 2026.

The lifetime estate tax exclusion establishes a threshold for the taxation of estates upon a person's death. In 2027, estates valued at or below $15.48 million will not be subject to estate tax, up from $15 million in 2026.

The Education Freedom Tax Credit will launch on Jan. 1. According to the IRS, it aims to support private contributions for K-12 scholarships. Taxpayers who donate to a "scholarship granting organization" in one of the 30 participating states can receive a nonrefundable tax credit of up to $1,700 ($3,400 for couples filing jointly).

#3062. ArcelorMittal (MT) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Tariff quotas and Ukraine charges shaped a quarter of sharp EBITDA gains.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

ArcelorMittal S.A. (MT -3.31%) focused on the structural improvement of its earnings capacity through the implementation of enhanced European trade measures and strategic growth investments in key markets. Management reported that the new tariff rate quota framework has successfully reduced import penetration, allowing the company to restart all its European blast furnaces and strengthen its domestic order book. The company is navigating temporary headwinds from elevated energy costs in Europe and weather-related disruptions in its mining operations while maintaining its 2026 capital expenditure guidance. ArcelorMittal stated that its strategic projects in India, Brazil, and Liberia are progressing to support higher earnings and cash generation as they reach full capacity in 2027.

Daniel Fairclough: Good afternoon, everyone. This is Daniel Fairclough from the ArcelorMittal Investor Relations team. Thank you for joining this call to discuss ArcelorMittal's performance and progress in the third quarter of 2026. Leading today's call will be our CFO, Mr. Genuino Christino. Before we begin, I would like to mention a few housekeeping items. As usual, we will not be going through the results presentation, which was published this morning on our website. However, I do want to draw your attention to the disclaimers on slide 24 of that presentation. Following some opening remarks from Genuino, we will move directly to the Q&A session.

If you'd like to ask a question, then please do press star one on your keypad to join the queue. With that, I will hand the call over to Genuino.

Genuino Christino: Thanks, Daniel. Welcome, everyone, and thanks for joining today's call. As usual, I will keep my remarks brief. Let me begin with safety, which remains our highest priority. We are now approaching the end of the second year of our safety transformation. Through disciplined execution of our safety roadmaps, we are seeing more consistent performance across the group. This is encouraging, and we remain firmly focused on our ambition of achieving zero fatalities and zero serious injuries as quickly as possible. Turning now to the business, I would like to focus on three key points. First, our results continue to demonstrate the structural improvements in margins. Third quarter EBITDA was $2 billion, up 34% year-on-year.

EBITDA per ton increased to $155, which is $44 higher than a year ago and well above historical averages. This demonstrates that our portfolio optimization and strategic execution are delivering results, and I believe there is significantly more to come. Importantly, these results do not yet reflect the full benefit of the new European trade framework, which is restoring sustainability to the European steel industry. Given the length of our order book, the increases in steel prices flow through to earnings with a lag. In addition, around 25% of our European flat product volumes remain under annual contracts that have yet to reset. This brings me to my second point.

As imports normalize, customers are increasingly looking to domestic supply, and we are responding. The TRQ framework provides the opportunity for recently idled capacity to restart, restoring employment and providing direct benefits to the local and regional economy. During the quarter, imports of flat steel products were approximately 50% lower than a year ago. As expected, our European flat product shipments were higher in the third quarter against the second quarter, which is counter to the normal seasonal pattern. As inventories normalize, we expect more of this reduction in imports to translate into higher domestic shipments. Our order book continues to strengthen, and we expect shipments growth to accelerate in the fourth quarter and show a double-digit year-on-year improvement.

This momentum is expected to continue to build into 2027. As customers shift back towards domestic steel supply, we will see higher, more sustainable capacity utilization. With Dąbrowa, Asturias, and Fos back in operation, all of our European blast furnaces are now running, and we are well-placed to serve our customers reliably and efficiently. Higher utilization should support a return to healthy and sustainable levels of profitability and returns on capital across the industry. My third and final point is that ArcelorMittal is exceptionally well-positioned to deliver higher earnings, stronger returns on capital, and continued value creation for shareholders. An increasingly regionalized steel market provides a stronger foundation for sustainable profitability throughout the cycle.

I have already talked about the significantly improved outlook for our business in Europe. Our business in India continues to perform well. We are ramping up our higher added value capacity, and the year to September represented a new shipment record. In North America, we are seeing positive momentum across our franchise. Better import protections are a common theme, and lean inventories alongside growing demand from data centers, energy, infrastructure investment creates a positive outlook for 2027. Against this improved backdrop, ArcelorMittal is well-positioned to succeed. Our scale, our leadership positions in key markets, and our strong track record of product and process innovation will continue to set us apart from the competition.

We are proud of the entrepreneurial culture, which promotes accountability and a relentless focus on continuous improvement. A more supportive industry structure gives us an even greater opportunity to convert these advantages into higher earnings and stronger returns. Over the past four years, we have invested consistently in high-return strategic growth projects that are increasing our earnings capacity. Importantly, many of these projects have not yet reached their full potential, providing a further source of earnings growth as we move into 2027 and beyond. The value created through these investments is further enhanced by our buyback program. This has been a powerful driver of shareholder value.

Given the positive outlook for free cash flow this year and beyond, I expect this to continue. With that, Daniel, I believe we can start the Q&A.

Daniel Fairclough: Great. Thank you, Genuino. We have quite a long list of questions to get through, but we will start with a question from Alain at Morgan Stanley. Hi, Alain. Please go ahead.

Speaker 2: Hi. Thank you for taking my question. Hi. Two questions from my side. I will start with the first one, which is the usual one, if you do not mind discussing the profit bridge into Q4, and specifically around Europe, where we are seeing many moving parts, including shipment growth, spot prices moving higher, but also elevated or sticky energy costs. Perhaps the same question applies to the other divisions as well, so if you do not mind starting with the bridge. Thank you.

Daniel Fairclough: Yeah, sure. Thank you, Genuino. Thanks, Alain. Looking at the major components, the building blocks, the major themes into the fourth quarter, I think it is clear from Genuino's comments and the release that we expect higher volumes in the fourth quarter. That is a common theme, but in particular, we would expect that from Europe, where we have guided to flat volumes being accelerating in the fourth quarter and increasing year-on-year at a double-digit rate. Second component would be generally higher steel prices across the segments. Brazil, perhaps a slight exception to that, just given mix effects, so that is probably going to be a little bit more stable quarter-to-quarter. The third bucket or theme would be higher costs.

You talk about that in your question, the way you posed it, but I think everybody can appreciate the evolving cost dynamics, particularly in Europe, as energy prices have continued to evolve through the quarter. We will have to see how energy prices continue over the next six weeks or so. It is difficult to be specific there on the guidance, but that will clearly be a theme. The last component would be mining. We have guided to a stronger quarter to end the year from our mining segment, given the continued progress at Liberia and our expectation that should be operating at capacity in the fourth quarter. It should be a good quarter from a shipment standpoint.

Then, it is difficult to be specific on the iron ore and freight factors, but I am sure you can accommodate that in your expectations as they become apparent. Then I think just my final comment would be on free cash flow. If you look at our release, if you look at the presentation, we are expecting a good free cash flow performance in the fourth quarter, and that will be in substantial part driven by an expected seasonal release of working capital.

Speaker 2: Thank you, Daniel. Thank you. My second question is, if we stay with Europe into 2027, you talked about the annual contract resets. Do you mind reminding us how many tons will be up for repricing on 1st of January and how quickly this will feed through your ASP? In Europe as well, in your presentation, you talk quite extensively about the benefits of the TRQ framework, which hasn't fully yet fed through your profit and margins. What do you expect to see as we head into early 2027 that will drive the margin upside for your European division? Thank you.

Genuino Christino: Okay. Thank you, Alain. Let me take your second question. First of all, I think it's important to say that TRQ, Q3, of course, was the first quarter in which we could see the benefits of the new framework. We are, of course, very happy with what we have seen. As we were guiding at the time of quarter two, we see higher shipments and flat despite the seasonality, and despite the fact that we were going through a destock during the quarter. It's really working as initially designed, which should then allow us to bring back the capacity that I also talked about at the beginning in my opening remarks.

We will really see the full benefits of the new framework, of course, in 2027, Alain. Also what it does, and we believe it should really be extremely helpful, it allows the industry now to pass on higher costs, right? We are seeing now, we were in a positive trend in terms of recovering our margins. Of course, we were hit by higher energy costs. We are in the process of recovering that. When I look at the pricing guidelines that we have already for January, I'm sure you have seen it's already significantly higher than what you see at the moment coming from index. That's all very positive. We're going to be working through the destocking.

Our expectation is that destocking should largely end in Q4. When I look at the business and the moving parts, I think we can be very optimistic for 2027.

Daniel Fairclough: Thanks, Genuino. Then just coming to your question on contracts, Alain. I think in our release in the presentation, you can see, and you already know it, that 25%, or approximately 25% of our flat volumes in Europe are annual contract. That is predominantly with the automotive customers, and the significant majority of those contracts follow the calendar year. So, a significant majority of that 25% of our flat volumes is set to reprice as we start 2027, which is another significant component of your positive bridge, I think, into the first quarter and for 2027 as a whole.

Speaker 2: Thank you. Thank you very much.

Daniel Fairclough: Great. Thanks, Alain. We will move now to take a question from Reinhardt at Bank of America. Hi, Reinhardt.

Reinhardt: Afternoon, Genuino and Daniel. Thank you very much for the time. Just want to ask about the European furnace restart so far. Can you give us an update on where exactly they are in their ramp-up process and when you think they are going to hit steady state production? I guess related to that, it would be good to get your thoughts on when you think there will be enough demand in Europe for you to actually start bringing some slabs in, perhaps.

Genuino Christino: Yeah, Reinhardt. Sure. First of all, we are bringing capacity as we see demand, right? I think that's number one, I would say. We are not bringing capacity unless, of course, we can see that in our order books. That's why we feel confident to bring back the capacity, because we are seeing order books strengthening. In terms of the ramp-ups, as you know, I mean, it's not easy to bring back capacity, especially when the furnaces have been idle for some time, which was clearly the case here. Poland, we are now up and running since the end of September. We have basically completed the ramp-up. The furnace is running well.

Fos, we are still going through the ramp-up phase. Not yet where we want it to be, but progressing there. In Spain, we are up and running. Two out of three furnaces are running well, and Fos is still in the process of ramp-up.

Reinhardt: Got it. That's clear. A comment on slabs, if you can?

Genuino Christino: Sorry, what was your question on the slabs, Reinhardt?

Reinhardt: When you expect demand to be sufficient in Europe for it to make sense for you to bring in slabs into the continent?

Genuino Christino: Well, I mean, look, I mean, this is something that, of course, remains a possibility for us. Our focus right now, Reinhardt, is to ramp up our capacity domestically, right? So that we can utilize our existing furnaces and tools that we have here. But of course, we have that flexibility. We know already what is the potential for higher volumes next year, just because of the TRQ and low imports that we expect to materialize. We're going to see the full benefits in 2027, right? But of course, we believe that we will have the capacity domestically to take care of that. But as a group, we have optionality, we have flexibility.

Reinhardt: That's very clear. Thank you. Maybe just one more question on developments into Q4. So, I mean, you've previously called out that some of this new capacity does have higher carbon costs associated with it. So, as you're building volumes into the fourth quarter, how should we think about improved fixed cost absorption and EBITDA per ton from that volume increase?

Genuino Christino: Yeah. Our message is the same, Reinhardt. Yes, as we bring back capacity, there will be more CO2 costs. But fixed costs, we shouldn't be really adding much in terms of fixed costs. So, profitability of this volume should be at least as par with the existing business, if not a little bit better.

Reinhardt: Very clear. Thank you very much, Genuino and Daniel.

Daniel Fairclough: Great. Thanks, Reinhardt. We'll move now to take a question from Tristan at BNP Paribas. Hi, Tristan. How are you?

Tristan: Yes. Hi. Thank you for taking my questions. I have two. First one is on Europe. One of your peer said that the shutdown of Ilva would be a game changer for the market. Do you share that view? Do you see a scenario where Southern European prices would trade at a premium to Northern prices? Does that mean ultimately that it could be upside risk to the market share gains you initially contemplated? That would be my first question.

Genuino Christino: Yeah, Tristan. Look, I mean, we all know in which levels ADI was running at, right? We all know. It was not running at very high levels. As a company, we feel we are in a good position here to service that market. As you know, we started Fos, the second furnace in Fos in the south, and we started also our furnace in Spain. It places us in a very good position to supply the market in south. Where prices finally settle in south, I mean, historically, as we know, south has always traded prices were always at a discount to north because of the more exposed to imports, which, as we know now, is being corrected by TRQ.

We'll see where prices finally settle. I wouldn't expect that to trade at a significant premium, but it will depend on trade and other aspects. But again, I think for us, it's a good opportunity to service that market from our facilities in the south.

Daniel Fairclough: Yeah. To round up that comment, I think as we look out there, I wouldn't say Ilva is going to have a significant impact. Just reinforcing Genuino's comment that they've been operating at very, very low levels. So the fact, if they drop down a little bit further, I don't think it's really going to change that supply-demand balance notably. So I wouldn't expect any significant or material impact on the market.

Tristan: All right. That's very clear. My second question is on North America. Could you discuss a little bit the strike impact in Canada and also what happened in Mexico? Is there anything structural at play, given it's been a couple quarters with some hiccups? How much of those, I mean, if you could quantify those one-offs and how much you expect to get back into Q4, that'd be great. Thank you.

Genuino Christino: Sure, Tristan. We had two events in North America. One was the strike in our longs division in Canada. That has been addressed. The facilities have been running since beginning of the quarter, so there shouldn't be any further impact from the strike. Back to normal levels. In Mexico, we had reliability issues with our DRI facility, which has also been resolved, addressed. I would expect us to be running at a normal capacity in quarter four, Tristan.

Tristan: And the negative impact, could you quantify it?

Genuino Christino: We are talking about in Q3, I mean, the losses, I would say in the range of 150kt.

Daniel Fairclough: Great. Thanks, Tristan. We'll move now to take a question from Ephrem at Citi. Hi, Ephrem. Please go ahead.

Ephrem: Thanks, Daniel. Two questions. I'll just take them in turn. First, I'm just trying to gauge how conservative your guidance for double-digit year-on-year growth in flat products, volume shipments in Europe is for Q4. Very rough math. I mean, you did about 6.5 million tons in total last year in Europe. 70% assume that is flat. A 10% implies somewhere around a 450,000 tons increase year on year for Q4 2026. If imports are coming down by 2.5 million-3 million tons per quarter, and you maintain your market share of about 30%, I mean, you should be expecting about 700,000 to 800,000 or 900,000 tons increase.

It's almost a 20% increase in shipments, unless volumes have gone down or you're losing market share. Would that be a right math, or please point me where I'm wrong on terms of the amount of volume increase in flats you could expect?

Genuino Christino: Well, I think you've got all the moving parts right. I think the only one that I would also point to you, as we discussed before as well, is we are still going through what we believe is the destock in Europe, which, as I said, should normalize now during the quarter in Q4, which then should, of course, help us as we start 2027. I think that's the only missing piece that I would point to you. Daniel, anything else here you want to highlight?

Daniel Fairclough: No, Genuino. Yeah, it's a good question, Ephrem, and thanks for putting it forward, because as Genuino says, you're picking up the moving parts there. Because inventories are really providing a cushion over the second half period as we transition into this new mechanism. We saw the reduction in imports in Q3. We're going to see, or we expect to see that similar reduction in imports in Q4. But because inventories are being consumed through that period, it's not fully translating yet into our shipments, into our volumes.

But as soon as those inventories are consumed, as soon as they're at normal levels, and as Genuino said in an earlier response, we expect that by the end of the year, then all of that will be translating into our shipments and our production. We're ready for that. We're primed for that. We're going to see progress and evidence of it in Q4, but that then, that momentum is going to continue. It's going to provide a good foundation for the bridge into Q1 and 2027 as a whole as well.

Ephrem: Thank you. Sorry, my second question is on India and Hazira. Obviously, now you're saying ramp up in, or start in 2027, which was obviously flagged a little bit earlier. But should we kind of realistically expect any shipments from the incremental, any new capacity in 2027, or is it really a 2028 story in terms of more volumes? Could you kind of give us a sense as to where we are in the completion of construction process and ramp-up process in terms of the incremental 6 million capacity there?

Genuino Christino: Yeah, sure. I can maybe comment on that. As you know, we have already commissioned the downstream, so the new cold mill, automotive lines for the finishing. We are testing now the new coke oven batteries. We are making good progress with now with the upstream, the furnaces. We do expect to see already in 2027 higher volumes coming from the project. Our expectation is that in the first half of 2027, we will start to see already some action there. We will, of course, provide you guys with some more guidance on that as part of our Q4 results. But we should definitely see already some improvements in 2027, especially in the second half.

Daniel Fairclough: Thanks, Ephrem. We are going to move now to take a question from Timna at Wells Fargo. Hi, Timna.

Timna: Yeah. Hey, good afternoon. I wanted to switch gears to the Americas, if I could, and beginning with Brazil. The investments you are making there are pretty notable. How do you get comfortable with the outlook there given smaller trade protections, the recent election, and at least one of your other competitors there was sounding a bit more cautious than you are? If you could elaborate on the Brazil strategy, please.

Genuino Christino: Daniel, to be honest, I could not hear well the question. Have you heard it?

Daniel Fairclough: Yes, I have. Perhaps I can start, Genuino, and I am sure you will complement. But it was basically, Timna was asking around the outlook for Brazil given the election results, what our plans are for investments there.
