#3060. Open-Source Dependencies: 19 Trust Signals Worth Checking

Open-source libraries power much of today’s software, allowing developers to build on existing code rather than start from scratch. But every dependency a team adds also brings potential risks tied to its maintainers, the software it relies on, and how security issues are handled. Popularity and download counts can create a false sense of safety, and even a widely used package may be neglected or slow to receive security fixes.

Knowing what to look for before adding or retaining a dependency can mean the difference between a solid foundation and an inherited liability. Here, members of Forbes Technology Council share the trust signals teams should evaluate when choosing open-source dependencies or reviewing those already in use.

Check the transitive dependency footprint. A tiny package that pulls in dozens of libraries, install scripts or native binaries expands your attack surface far beyond the code you chose. Trust is not only about the package itself; it is about the chain of code and maintainers you inherit with it. Prefer the smallest dependency graph that solves the problem. - Alexandro Picolini, COMM

I’d evaluate how safely the project development is going. A reliable dependency should have planned releases, proper migration procedures and no surprises with breaking changes. While security is very important, stability is equally vital. When every update is an engineering challenge, the dependency will silently turn into tech debt despite its popularity. - Ajay Pandey

Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

One critical trust signal is verifiable software provenance. Teams should know who maintains a dependency, how releases are built and signed, and whether artifacts can be traced to trusted source code. Popularity and download counts are not security guarantees. Provenance verification, combined with continuous vulnerability monitoring, strengthens software supply chain resilience. - Sai Krishna Manohar Cheemakurthi, U.S. Bank

First, run it through OpenSSF Scorecard. It’s a useful, free and automated check of practices that covers branch protection, code review, pinned dependencies and signed releases. A low score isn’t automatically disqualifying, but it can tell you what risk you’re inheriting and give every team the same repeatable bar instead of a gut feel based on GitHub stars. It’s one tool you can use to evaluate and get consistent results for open-source software. - Dan Sorensen, Nexus Security Advisors

Check when the maintainer last responded to a reported vulnerability, not when they last pushed code. Commit frequency tells you the project is alive. Response behavior tells you whether someone is actually watching the door. A repository with 10,000 stars and an 18-month-old unresolved security issue is not a dependency—it is a liability with good documentation. - Mukul Arora, Persistent Systems Limited

Examine who gets to become a maintainer. Attackers have learned it is easier to earn a tired maintainer’s trust over months than to find a flaw in the code. Check whether new maintainers are vetted by more than one person and whether handoffs happen in public. A project’s process for trusting people matters as much as its code. - Flavius Plesu, OutThink

One trust signal I’ve observed is how maintainers respond to reported security issues. It’s critical to look for clear updates and evidence that they fix problems rather than relying on download counts. A popular dependency can still leave your team waiting for a fix. - Mark Vena, SmartTech Research

The most useful trust signal is the patch track record. With AI now finding vulnerabilities in open source faster than ever, the question is no longer whether a flaw will be found but how quickly it can be fixed once it is found. Teams should look at the dependency’s current vulnerability history and update cadence and determine whether maintainers respond rapidly to security issues. A modern software project that is popular but patches slowly should be avoided in the AI era. - Anuj Goel, Cyware

Check who is actually maintaining it. A popular library with millions of downloads can still rest on one unpaid volunteer who hasn’t merged a fix in a year. Look at recent commit activity, how quickly security issues get patched, and how many active maintainers there are. Download counts measure popularity, not durability, and you’re inheriting the support risk. - Steven Singer, Arbill

Open source runs on shared ingenuity. Give that ingenuity a security check: look for a current assessment of the exact package version you’ll deploy, inspecting its contents for malware, tampering and suspicious behavior alongside known vulnerabilities. Check each update and reassess existing dependencies as threats emerge. Trust the community, and give it the backup it deserves. - Mario Vuksan, ReversingLabs

Look at support and usage. Open source is great in terms of lesser cost and general support, but with general support, there is more risk. An open-source project can have security flaws or problematic issues that are not easily spotted by even the most advanced professionals. Look for something that serves one purpose and has been proven before by use in other high-profile projects or companies. Then go for it—with contingencies in place. - WaiJe Coler, InfoTracer

A useful signal is whether another party can rebuild the published release from the tagged source and get the same artifact. Signed provenance says who claims to have built it; reproducibility lets an independent team check that claim without trusting the maintainer’s pipeline. Before adoption, try this on one release and see whether the project documents the toolchain, inputs and steps needed to repeat the build. This makes artifact integrity independently testable. - Jagadish Gokavarapu, Wissen Infotech

A trustworthy project actively updates its own upstream dependencies, maintains clear semantic versioning, and demonstrates steady commit velocity. If a library has millions of downloads but hasn’t shipped a patch or addressed security pull requests in six months, its technical debt becomes yours the moment you import it. - Japjeev Kohli, Transurban

Look for active community adoption and scrutiny. Widely used, actively maintained packages benefit from more people reviewing, testing and finding problems. I would also avoid automatically adopting a new release on day one. Give the community time to validate it before bringing it into a critical environment. - Alex Spokoiny, Check Point Software

Ask who chose it. More dependencies now arrive because a model suggested them, not because an engineer compared options. At Google, adding a dependency meant someone had to argue for it and own it afterward. That argument is the trust signal. If nobody on the team can say why this package is better than the alternatives, you have not evaluated a dependency. You have accepted a recommendation. - Prashant Jalan, Guickly

I’d look at whether the project has an active, healthy maintainer community. Not all open-source projects are resilient. A dependency can be technically excellent yet still introduce risk if it’s maintained by only one or two individuals, receives infrequent updates, or lacks clear governance. Healthy open-source projects tend to show consistent releases, responsive issue management, transparent security practices and a diverse contributor base. - Ciaran Cosgrave, Nearform

Read the license on the model weights, not only on the code. Teams now pull open-weight AI models into products the way they pull in libraries, and some of those licenses ban commercial use, cap the number of users, or restrict whole categories of use. The code around a model can carry an MIT license, while the weights you ship come with different terms. - Jerry Tang, Atlas Cloud

One key trust signal is whether an open-source dependency creates accurate and consistent results. Libraries used in calculations, data conversion or scientific computing can cause errors that affect major decisions. Test key functions against trusted reference results and check for rounding errors or erratic outputs. A package may meet security standards but still produce wrong results. Trust must include functional accuracy, not just security and maintenance. - Salice Thomas, Wipro Limited

Essentially, I look for good governance signals. How large and spread out is the group of top maintainers—the more coherent, the better—and what’s their relationship with the project? How fast do they fix issues, especially security issues? Are security tests embedded in the build and release pipelines? Are there external security validations like OpenSSF? Regarding general health, how many stars and how many forks? What’s the recent commit and release cadence? - Julien Vantyghem, Quintess AI

#3057. Tokens Built The Digital AI Business. Physical AI Needs A Different Unit

Brandon Barbello is co-founder and COO of Archetype AI, with over 10 years of product leadership across Fortune 500 and startups.

​Almost every industrial AI deployment I’ve seen lately eventually reaches the same meeting. The pilot worked, the operations team wants to expand to more machines and finance asks what the numbers look like at 300 assets instead of three.

Increasingly, that question comes with another: Will you charge us by the token?​

Enterprises have spent the past few years learning a new vocabulary around AI economics: tokens, inference, context windows, consumption-based pricing and discovering how hard those costs are to predict. Accenture recently reported that one in three organizations exhausts its AI token budget before year’s end.​

For digital AI, token economics are justifiable. Jensen Huang has said he’d be “deeply alarmed” if a $500,000 engineer didn’t consume at least $250,000 of tokens a year, because the spend buys output. For knowledge work, he’s right.​

But a compressor is not a $500,000 engineer. It produces signal every second it runs, regardless of whether anyone asks it a question. It makes more sense to analyze that signal locally, on hardware the customer already owns, than to ship every second of it to the cloud.​

We have an opportunity to build business models that reflect those differences instead of importing LLM economics into the physical world.​

Most LLM interactions are episodic: A person asks a question or gives an agent a task, and the model produces an output.

In the physical world, cameras, vibration monitors, pressure gauges and other sensors generate data continuously, and applications are inherently always-on. Meter by the token, and the bill grows with every hour the equipment runs.

The underlying data is different, too. Language models are trained on text and images. They don’t understand what a bearing sounds like at 4,000 RPM. That takes a model built to interpret physical signals directly.​

Industrial data is also often too proprietary to leave the facility. Streaming that data to the cloud puts the company’s core IP at risk. This affects how physical AI gets deployed, scaled and priced.​

The practical answer is to run intelligence where the data originates. Smaller, general-purpose models can increasingly run on customers’ own hardware, keeping sensitive information on-site and letting decisions happen where the data is produced.

One municipal customer of Archetype AI, for example, uses cameras across hundreds of intersections to improve pedestrian safety. Based on internal analysis, each intersection produces roughly 43 gigabytes of camera data daily. Moving that data to the cloud would cost an estimated $850,000 to $1 million annually before any AI processing. Distilling a larger model into a smaller one let physical AI run on hardware the customer already owns, using its existing cameras.​​

Running at the edge, the system can determine if a pedestrian is still in the crosswalk without sending data to a remote data center and waiting for a response. That round trip could take longer than the window to act.

Training, fine-tuning and fleet-level analysis can continue to happen in the cloud, while time-sensitive decisions happen closer to the edge. Use the cloud where scale is valuable and the edge where speed, cost and responsiveness matter most.​

When AI runs primarily as a metered cloud service, consumption-based pricing makes sense: Someone has to pay for the compute.

But once physical AI runs on the customer’s infrastructure, compute is already paid for, so pricing doesn’t have to correspond to every unit of inference. It can follow from the unit where the customer actually receives value.​ Industrial businesses already think this way, and it’s how they buy software.

This points to a different model: licensing per asset, machine, facility or application, rather than charging when the system processes data. That brings predictability. Finance teams can count machines more easily than forecast tokens; a company expanding from 10 machines to 1,000 knows the cost before deployment.​​

The operational value becomes clearer at scale. In one Archetype AI customer deployment, analysis of data from more than 40 sensors across 63 wind turbines identified nine previously unknown failure modes, revealing critical problems before they cause downtime.​

The trade-off is that per-asset licensing can be less economical for equipment that needs only occasional analysis. Companies should consider how often the system will be used and the operational value it delivers.​

Inference is getting cheaper. Gartner predicts inference on a one-trillion-parameter model will cost providers over 90% less by 2030 than in 2025. Elsewhere, however, Gartner expects inference spend per agentic workflow to climb more than fivefold through 2028, since agentic systems use five to 30 times more tokens per task than chatbots.

In other words, falling unit costs don’t guarantee savings. Every new sensor adds volume, regardless of operational value.

NVIDIA researchers argue that smaller LLMs are already powerful and economical enough for many agentic tasks. Physical AI takes that further, with models built from the start to understand physical signals and run where signals originate.​

Physical AI is still in early days. We shouldn’t assume what worked for digital AI is right for physical. Pricing per asset means vendors grow as customers expand, and customers expand as the system proves its value.

Before expanding a pilot, businesses can bring operations, IT and finance together to compare the total cost at three assets, 30 and 300, including licensing, hardware, integration and ongoing support. Weigh those costs against measurable outcomes such as reduced downtime or maintenance hours, and agree on what would justify expansion.

When finance understands what 300 assets will cost and operations can demonstrate the value, the conversation can move from how usage will be billed to whether—and how quickly—to scale.​​​

#3055. This Janus Henderson fund manager owns CoreWeave debt — here's why he's sticking with it

CoreWeave can overcome the market's skepticism about its debt.

That isn't the consensus view — some Coreweave debt remains deeply distressed with yields above 15%. But Coreweave should power through this tough stretch, according to John Lloyd, global head of multi-sector and corporate credit at Janus Henderson.

"It's a little bit of overreacting," Lloyd tells CNBC, referring to the sell-off in Coreweave bonds, which have tanked along with its equity.

Lloyd owns Coreweave 9.75% bonds due in 2031 in the firm's Multi-Sector Income Fund. The yield to maturity on the debt is now 15.97%, a more than 70% jump since its issuance in April. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

"Bond prices are lower, spreads are wider, yields are wider, and I don't see a huge fundamental change in the ecosystem right now that would warrant that, other than their higher cost of financing, which I think they can get creative with," Lloyd added.

CoreWeave has taken on a massive amount of debt to fund its data center buildout. The company has roughly $51.6 billion in total debt, including about $35 billion in notes, bonds and loans.

The market is getting nervous about how CoreWeave will be able to keep financing its data centers, and at what cost. Its stock has tumbled 20% over the past week, while the spread on its five-year credit default swaps is nearly 1,081 basis points — lower than earlier in the session but up 13% week over week. Spreads of 1,000 basis points and above are generally a sign of credit distress.

CoreWeave shares moved roughly 2% higher on Tuesday, after tumbling over the past several days and hitting a 52-week low earlier in the session. Its bond yields and spreads remain highly elevated.

Lloyd believes the selloff is a bump in the road for the neocloud company.

The market has been spooked by the jump in Treasury rates, which pushes up funding costs for companies, he explained. The focus largely turned to companies like CoreWeave that have refinance risk when rates move higher, he said.

CoreWeave leverage is high with a debt-to-equity ratio of 702%, up from 290% a year ago. Moreover, CoreWeave will spend an estimated $36.4 billion on capital expenditures this year against Ebitda of $7.5 billion, according to consensus estimates.

Revenue and Ebitda will ramp up next year, hitting $26.5 billion and $16.7 billion respectively, analysts estimate. But capex will hit $47.9 billion, indicating the company may need to finance its data center buildout with more equity issuance and/or debt.

Lloyd isn't necessarily worried about CoreWeave's ability to finance its capital expenditures, despite the fact that its capex outweighs its free-cash flow.

"Next year … they're going to be generating operating free-cash flow that'll support some of that capex need," he said.

The company can also turn to other methods of funding, like more GPU financing, which will allow it to borrow against its graphics processing units or rental contracts, he noted. In addition, CoreWeave could ask its biggest customers — including Microsoft, Meta Platforms and OpenAI — to increase their prepayments, he added.

"They can probably get creative enough where they don't even need to come to the high-yield market," Lloyd said.

The company also doesn't have any near-term maturities, which means it isn't facing a refinancing risk anytime soon, he added.

Meanwhile the supply/demand dynamic should remain tight across the AI compute landscape. Overall adoption rates within the ecosystem are running above consensus demand curves, he said. Add to that a bottleneck in supply, with chips and memory power sold out, and it's a nice set up for CoreWeave.

"All data point to the business model functioning very, very well," Lloyd said. "CoreWeave is one of the best-in-class at getting data centers up and actually running them," he added, noting that CoreWeave's financials have been improving throughout the year.

Another turning point could come if Anthropic goes forth with an IPO, expected in November, followed by OpenAI. Successful IPOs for the frontier labs could soothe market nerves and help support the neocloud operators.

"You just need more of those data points where people become more comfortable with the AI demand side," Lloyd said.

CoreWeave still needs to convince markets it can handle higher market rates and get through the financing bottlenecks.

Lloyd sees the company making it, albeit with some bumps along the way. The bonds should recover, he says, "just not in that straight line."

#3049. GEO Group (GEO) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Adelanto sale proceeds funded a major debt cut and a bigger buyback program.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

The GEO Group, Inc. (GEO -8.57%) reported record-breaking quarterly financial performance, achieving its highest-ever levels of quarterly revenue and Adjusted EBITDA. Management stated that the results were driven by the activation of new facility contracts signed in 2025 and an expanded scope of services for federal agencies. The company completed the $950 million sale of the Adelanto complex to the federal government while retaining a multiyear contract to provide support services at the site. This divestiture enabled the redemption of $650 million in senior secured notes, significantly reducing corporate debt and lowering net leverage to approximately 1.0 times Adjusted EBITDA. Management also increased its share repurchase authorization to $1.25 billion, signaling a shift in capital allocation toward shareholder returns as the company transitions toward a support services-focused business model.

Operator: Good day, and welcome to the GEO Group Third Quarter 26 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in a listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. To ask a question, you may press star then 1 on a touch tone phone. To withdraw your question, please press star then 2. Zoley, Chairman, Chief Executive Officer and Founder and Shayn March, senior vice president and chief financial officer. This afternoon, we will discuss our third quarter results as well as our outlook. We will conclude the call with a question-and-answer session. This conference call is also being webcast live on our Investor website at investors.geogroup.com. Today, we will discuss non GAAP basis information. A reconciliation from non GAAP basis information to GAAP basis results is included in the press release and the supplemental disclosure we issued this morning.

Additionally, much of the information we will discuss today including the answers we give in response to your questions, may include forward looking statements. George C. Zoley: Thank you, Pablo, and good afternoon, everyone, and thank you for joining us. Our diversified business units have continued to deliver strong financial and operational performance through 2026. And our third quarter 2026 results marked a record breaking quarter for GEO. Compared to the same period in 2026, our third quarter 2020 revenues increased 12% to approximately $761.1 million. While our third quarter 2026 net income attributable to GEO operations was approximately $49.2 million. Compared to the same period in 2025 our third quarter 2026 adjusted EBITDA increased 21% to approximately $145.3 million. And our adjusted net income increased 48% to approximately $51.8 million.

These results represent the highest level of quarterly revenues and adjusted EBITDA ever reported in our company's history. Even better than expected performance in 2026 has been driven by the significant revenue growth from the new contracts that we entered into throughout 2025. They included the activation of 4 facilities to house ICE detainees totaling 6 thousand beds. Valued at approximately $280 million in annual revenues. So far in 2026, we have had an even more successful year for the new expanded services entering into new contracts for the activation of 4 additional facilities to house ICE detainees totaling approximately 4.8 thousand beds.

These contracts, along with the expanded scope of services at existing facilities created an overall value of approximately $500 million in incremental annual revenues. First, we entered into a 5 year support services contract with ICE for the activation of a federal immigration processing center at the 1.19 thousand-bed Bighorn facility in Hudson, Colorado while also entering into a lease agreement with the facility owner. The Bighorn support services contract is expected to generate approximately $85 million in annual revenues in the first full year of operations. Starting in the first quarter of 2027.

We then entered into a 5 year support services contract with ICE for the activation of a federal immigration processing center in the geo owned 1.32 thousand-bed Rivers facility in Winton North Carolina. The Rivers support services contract is expected to generate approximately $80 million in annual revenues in the first full year of operations, also starting in the first quarter of 2027. More recently, we announced earlier this week the city of Big Spring in Texas has entered into a 10 year intergovernmental service agreement with ICE for the activation of a federal immigration processing center at the 2.33 thousand-bed Big Spring complex comprised of 1.4 thousand-bed flight line facility and the 925-bed Cedar Hills facility.

GEO will provide support services at the Big Spring complex which is expected to generate approximately $200 million in annual revenues for GEO in the first full year of operations. Starting in the second quarter of 2027. Under all 3 of these contracts, ICE will reimburse GEO for the capital expenditures needed to reactivate these 4 facilities as well as providing funding for start up expenses during the activation period. Following the activation of these 4 facilities, our total ICE beds under contract will increase to approximately 33 thousand beds at 29 facilities. The current census across our active ICE facilities is approximately 24 thousand representing approximately 1/3 of the current national ICE population of approximately 73 thousand.

Over the past 2 quarters, we have also entered into new or modified contracts for the continued provision of support services at existing ICE processing centers. First, during the third quarter, we entered into a contract modification to increase staffing levels at the 1.94 thousand-bed Adelanto ICE processing center to support the increase in the scope of services at the facility adding $60 million in incremental annual revenues. More recently, last week, we announced that we have entered into a new 10 year management contract with expanded support services at incremental annual revenue value of $50 million at the GEO owned 1.64 thousand-bed Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, Washington.

The new 10-year contract is expected to generate approximately $140 million in total annual revenues for GEO and continue through 10/27/2036, making it the first contract we have entered into ICE with a full base term of 10 years. This new contract was awarded under ongoing procurement that involves 3 other geo owned facilities, the Aurora facility, the Moshannon Valley facility, and Broward ICE Processing Center. Which are also expected to receive new 10-year contract awards. ICE enforcement initiatives nationwide are supported by significant funding that has already been approved by the United States Congress. ICE was allocated $45 billion for the detention under the 1 big beautiful bill which is available through 9/30/2029.

We believe that less than $10 billion of $45 billion has been spent so far. Under the Secure America Act, ICE also received $38.5 billion in baseline appropriations funding as well as an additional $30 billion for other priorities under the 1 Big Beautiful bill all of which is also available through 9/30/2029. As ICE continues to pursue these enforcement initiatives, we expect GEO to continue to be part of the solution as a 40-year partner to the agency. Following our recent contract announcements, we now have approximately 2.9 thousand idle beds that remain available at 4 company owned facilities, which are well suited for the needs of the federal government.

At full capacity, these 2.9 thousand idle beds could generate approximately $170 million in combined incremental revenues. Additionally, we have expansion capacity of several thousands of beds at existing geo managed ICE facilities. Our third quarter 2026 results also reflect a significant expansion in our secure transportation services on behalf of ICE, and the US Marshals Service. As a result of new or amended contracts we entered into in 2025. The support services that we provide under ICE Air transportation subcontract have continued To Steadily Grow Driven By The Increase In The Number Of Removable Flights.

Additionally, Our New Bighorn Rivers and Big Spring contracts with ICE are expected to generate approximately $28 million in combined additional annual transportation services revenues once normalized in 2027. Importantly, during the third quarter of 2 thousand 26, our ISAP contract continued to experience a steady technology shift to more intensive and higher price monitoring devices such as ankle monitors. ISAP is the only ICE program currently in place to provide electronic monitoring and case management services for individuals on the non-detained docket.

The program relies on several forms of monitoring including GPS ankle bracelets, or wrist worn devices that provide real time tracking as well as the SmartLink phone app, which relies on facial recognition voice ID, and GPS to confirm a person's location during the predetermined check-in. The current overall ISAP count is approximately 190 thousand participants up from 184 thousand participants 3 months ago. The number is 58 thousand currently, from 17 thousand early in 2025. We also continue to experience a steady increase in the number of ISAP participants assigned to case management services, which involves staff interaction and monitoring for approximately 121 thousand individuals currently.

As a result of these trends, revenue and net operating income for our electronic monitoring and supervision services increased during the third quarter of 2026 compared to the same period a year ago, reversing a multiyear trend of revenue and net operating income declines. Additionally, during the third quarter of 2 thousand 26, we generated revenues of approximately $3 million from our skip tracing contract. Moving to our outlook, we have increased our net income and adjusted EBITDA guidance for 2026 to reflect the strength of our results in the first 3 quarters of the year. Our fourth quarter 2020 revenue and adjusted EBITDA guidance exceeds our third quarter 2 thousand and 26 results.

Positioning GEO to set another record breaking quarter. Looking forward to 2027, there are several sources of future upside compared to our 2026 guidance. They include the expected activation of 4 new ICE facilities at Bighorn, Rivers, and the Big Spring Complex. Comprised of 2 facilities. Additional growth in our additional secure services segment from the reactivation of additional idle facilities and or higher overall populations across our active facilities. The expected transition of our previously announced managed only contracts for the 1.88 thousand-bed Graceville facility and the 985-bed Bay facility in the state of Florida, which are expected to occur on 07/01/2027.

Additional volume increases and/or accelerated technology service mix in our ISAP contract, additional growth in our secured transportation services business, and additional revenue from higher utilization of our skip tracing contracts. Before I turn the call over to our CFO, Shayn March for a more detailed review of our third quarter results and guidance I would like to provide you with an update regarding the plan by ICE and DHS to purchase existing privately owned turnkey ICE processing centers. As we announced last month, we completed the sales of our 1.28 thousand-bed Adelanto West ICE processing center 660-bed Adelanto East, 704-bed Desert View Annex to DHS.

For an aggregate gross sales price of $950 million and net proceeds after taxes and transaction fees and expenses of approximately $705 million. We expect to continue providing support services at the Adelanto complex under our existing contract with ICE, which has a full effective term through 12/19/2034. We used proceeds from the sales of the Adelanto complex for the redemption of our $650 million 2029 senior secured notes and we also entered into an amended and restated credit agreement extending the maturity of our $550 million revolving credit facility to July 2031. And also increasing our restricted pay payment capacity, including share repurchases.

Following the redemption of the 2029 senior secured notes, our total outstanding corporate debt consists of our 2031 senior unsecured notes totaling $625 million. As we previously announced, our Board of Directors has increased our share repurchase authorization, which is effective through 12/31/2029 by $750 million to $1.25 billion. Based on our current leverage and so long as we remain below specified leverage levels, GEO is permitted to make unlimited restricted payments, including share repurchases under both the amended credit facility agreement and the senior unsecured note indenture.

Given the intrinsic value of our assets including 48 thousand owned beds, our strong financial performance in providing diversified secured support services and our expected future growth we believe that our stock continues to be significantly undervalued and offers a very attractive investment opportunity. Therefore, in addition to further debt reduction and other general corporate purposes, we intend to allocate a substantial portion of future facility sales proceeds and recurring free cash flow toward our expanded share repurchase authorization, which may include structured share repurchases on an accelerated basis. Following the recently completed asset sales, ICE now uses approximately 34 existing detention sites nationwide that are owned and operated by private contractors.

CoreCivic now owns and operates approximately 12 ICE detention facilities. While GEO owns and operates 20 ICE detention facilities. In addition to the facility sales we completed last month, we remain engaged in active processes for the sale of multiple other company owned facilities to ICE subject to mutual agreement on price and GEO's continued management of those facilities under long term support services contract. We believe we have 2 types of assets, the building and the businesses of providing support services. We are pursuing additional potential sales of the buildings but we want to retain the business of providing support services.

We continue to consider ourselves primarily a support services operator and will place particular importance on our ability to continue our support services at any additional facilities sold to ICE. Specifically, we believe that our current active negotiations could result in additional sales before the end of 2026 for up to 4 additional facilities. We believe that the future sales are likely to have similar valuations to the transactions that have already been completed by ICE. With standard adjustments with respect to geography, facility size, and age. And it is possible that the number of facilities targeted for acquisition by ICE could continue to grow in the future.

At this time, there is no definitive agreement in place and no precise timeline for the closing of any additional transactions. And GEO can provide no assurance that any additional transactions will in fact occur. While the exact timing of government actions is always difficult to estimate, we remain focused on pursuing new growth opportunities and allocating capital to enhance long term value for our shareholders. At this time, I will turn the call over to Shayn to review our quarterly results and increase guidance.

Shayn March: Thank you, George. Good afternoon, everyone. Our adjusted EBITDA for the third quarter of 2026 increased to approximately $145 million up from approximately $120.1 million in the prior year's third quarter reflecting a 21% increase. Driving this historical quarterly performance, our owned and leased secured services revenues increased by approximately $46 million or 13% compared to prior year's third quarter.

This increase was driven by the activation of 3 company owned facilities under new contracts with ICE, which was partly offset by revenue lost from the sale of the Lawton Oklahoma facility. Quarterly revenues for our managed only contracts increased by approximately $31 million or 19% from the prior year's third quarter. This increase was primarily driven by the joint venture agreement for the management of the North Florida detention facility, as well as certain transportation revenue increases that are reported in this segment. Quarterly revenues for our owned and leased reentry services increased by approximately $3.5 million partly offset by a $3 million decline in nonresidential services revenues compared to the prior year's third quarter.

Finally, third quarter 26 revenues for our electronic monitoring and supervision services increased by approximately 1.6% compared to the third quarter of 25, reversing a multiyear trend of quarterly revenue declines for this important segment and demonstrating the strength of the continued favorable technology and case management mix shift in our ISAP contract, which more than offset some price reductions previously reported. Turning to expenses. Approximately 9.1% of the prior year's third quarter revenue the result of additional business development expenses. Our effective tax rate for the third quarter of 2026 was approximately 27%. Moving to our outlook. We have updated our guidance for the fourth quarter and the full year 2026. We have also increased fourth quarter 2026 adjusted net income guidance to a range of $46 million to $51 million or a range of $0.35 to $0.39 per diluted share on a quarterly revenue of $777 million to $827 million We have increased our fourth quarter 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance to a range of $149 million to $154 million If this guidance is achieved, the fourth quarter of 2026 would set another record breaking quarter for GEO. While also positioning our company for a strong 2027 outlook.

For the full year 2026, we have increased GAAP net income guidance to a range of $726.3 million to $730.5 million which includes the gain on sale of the Adelanto, California, ICE complex in the fourth quarter of 2026. We have also increased full year 2027 adjusted net income guidance to a range of $185 million to $190 million a range of $1.40 to $1.44 per diluted share on annual revenues of $2.975 billion to $3.025 billion and based on an effective tax rate of approximately 28% inclusive of known discrete items.

This represents a 56% increase over 2025 adjusted net income at the midpoint of $187.5 million We have increased our full year 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance to a range of $568 million to $573 million representing a 23% increase at the midpoint of $570.5 million We expect total unreimbursed capital expenditures for the full year 2026 to be between $140 million and $150 million and expect normal unreimbursed CapEx to decline to approximately $100 million in 2027. Moving to our balance sheet.

Following the sale of the Adelanto complex in October, we completed the redemption of our $650 million senior secured notes and executed an amendment to our $550 million revolving credit facility extending its maturity and increasing our restricted payments capacity including share repurchases. Our total outstanding corporate debt consists of our 2031 senior unsecured notes totaling $625 million. Our available liquidity is approximately $600 million including cash on hand and revolver availability. Net of cash, our current leverage is approximately 1x adjusted EBITDA, And based on our current outlook, we have reset our capital strategy to remain at or below this net leverage level going forward.

The Wizards entered last night's game against the Atlanta Hawks having played the NBA's easiest schedule so far. Their opponents had an average scoring differential of -9.83 per game. The Hawks — a middle-of-the-pack team missing their best player — were a step up.

The Wizards weren't bad in this measuring stick kind of game, but they did get outplayed by a bit. Not every possession, but they got beat to the punch regularly throughout the contest — outshot, out-rebounded, out-competed.

Which is okay for an eighth game of the season after a three-year tank. The Wizards are trying to win this season, and against teams of similar talent level, they'll need to up their level of compete. Games like this one could help them do that — if they seize the opportunity to learn what true NBA competition requires.

The chief area in need of some attention is ending possessions when they get the other team to miss a shot. They entered the game ranked 26th in defensive rebounding percentage and gave up 19 offensive rebounds to a tiny team with two guys 6-9 or taller, one of whom (Asa Newell) hyperextended a toe and missed the second half.

The Wizards get a second crack at the Hawks Friday night in their second NBA Cup game. If Washington wants to contend for something other than the bottom of the play-in this season, they'll need to figure out a way to clean up the defensive boards — at least to some degree. It'd be great if they could force some opponent turnovers too (they're 27th in defensive turnover rate). But first things first — defense in the NBA is mostly about making the other team miss and then getting the rebound. That's where the focus should be.

Bilal Coulibaly doesn't look to be an offensive threat, which ultimately undermines his defensive value because he's a self-check. Chase Hughes and the Monumental broadcast team tried to turn it into a positive (the segment about how trying to win slots young players into their proper roles and now Coulibaly doesn't have to force anything), but…it's basically nonsense. Coulibaly doesn't have to be an alpha scorer, but he does need to be able to take an open three, attack a closeout, or drive competently a few times a game.

An example — in the first quarter, Trae Young passed to Coulibaly — defended by the much smaller and less athletic CJ McCollum — in the dunker spot. Coulibaly gave zero thought to attacking. He just passed it back out to Young. The possession stalled, Young passed it back to Coulibaly at the three-point line, and McCollum stripped him. The lack of aggression converted a clear offensive advantage into a turnover instead of a good shot.

Later in the first quarter, Coulibaly provided a counter-example — he drove right, got a paint touch, collapsed the defense, and kicked it out to Alex Sarr up top. Sarr missed the wide open three, but the point here is the excellent shot created by Coulibaly attacking. Reminder: last season, opposing defenders had trouble staying in front of Coulibaly when he decided to drive, even when they gave him space and dared him to shoot.

The Monumental broadcast never ceases to amuse. At the end of the first half, Chris Miller raved about the Wizards closing on a 9-0 run. It was indeed nice. Worth mention: they still trailed by seven.

Kyshawn George turned in a pretty good game — 25 points on 10-14 shooting along with four rebounds and seven assists. That's the good stuff. He also committed four turnovers and four fouls. I want to believe in him, but he's gotta cut out some of the negatives if he's going to help drive winning.

Anthony Davis scored 26 points on 12-19 shooting, had 10 rebounds, 3 assists, and 3 blocks. Of note: zero turnovers, zero fouls.

Below are the four factors that decide wins and losses in basketball — shooting (efg), rebounding (offensive rebounds), ball handling (turnovers), fouling (free throws made).

eFG% (effective field goal percentage, which accounts for the three-point shot)

TOV% (turnover percentage — turnovers divided by possessions)

FTM/FGA (free throws made divided by field goal attempts)

PPA is my overall production metric, which credits players for things they do that help a team win (scoring, rebounding, playmaking, defending) and dings them for things that hurt (missed shots, turnovers, bad defense, fouls).

PPA is a per possession metric designed for larger data sets. In small sample sizes, the numbers can get weird. In PPA, 100 is average, higher is better and replacement level is 45. For a single game, replacement level isn't much use, and I reiterate the caution about small samples sometimes producing weird results.

POSS is the number of possessions each player was on the floor in this game.

ORTG = offensive rating, which is points produced per individual possessions x 100. League average so far this season is listed in the Four Factors table above. Points produced is not the same as points scored. It includes the value of assists and offensive rebounds, as well as sharing credit when receiving an assist.

USG = offensive usage rate. Average is 20%. Median last season was 17.7%.

ORTG and USG are versions of stats created by former Wizards assistant coach Dean Oliver and modified by me. ORTG is an efficiency measure that accounts for the value of shooting, offensive rebounds, assists and turnovers. USG includes shooting from the floor and free throw line, offensive rebounds, assists and turnovers.

+PTS = "Plus Points" is a measure of the points gained or lost by each player based on their efficiency in this game compared to league average efficiency on the same number of possessions. A player with an offensive rating (points produced per possession x 100) of 100 who uses 20 possessions would produce 20 points. If the league average efficiency is 115, the league — on average — would produced 23.0 points in the same 20 possessions. So, the player in this hypothetical would have a +PTS score of -3.0.

Players are sorted by total production in the game.

#3040. Cathie Wood Just Sold AMD Stock and Bought This AI Chip Stock Instead

Should investors follow Cathie Wood's recent AI stock play?

Cathie Wood founded Ark Invest in 2014, and the CEO has made a name for herself as an investor to watch when it comes to growth stocks. Ark provides exchange-traded funds (ETFs) that are heavily built around innovative new technologies with explosive growth potential, and the company takes a very active approach to portfolio management. In other words, Ark's investment teams tend to buy and sell stocks frequently for the funds that they manage.

Notably, Ark offers investors a huge degree of transparency and regularly catalogs all of its trades even when it is not required to do so for regulatory purposes. Due to Wood's status as a high-profile growth investor and the high visibility of her company's trading activities, the investment firm's buying and selling moves tend to attract a significant amount of attention -- and Ark just sold Advanced Micro Devices and bought Nvidia (NVDA -9.26%).

Ark Invest CEO Cathie Wood. Image source: Getty Images.

At the end of September, Ark made a notable move for its flagship Ark Innovation ETF. It sold shares of AMD valued at roughly $111.1 million and effectively used the proceeds from the sale to buy $81 million worth of Nvidia stock. The transactions seem to send a clear message: Ark believed that Nvidia was the more attractively valued of the two artificial intelligence (AI) semiconductor stocks.

As of this writing, Nvidia is trading at roughly 22 times this year's expected earnings. Meanwhile, AMD is valued at roughly 63.5 times expected forward profits. The valuation disparity reflects expectations that AMD will be able to grow earnings significantly faster going forward.

While Nvidia continues to dominate the market for advanced graphics processing units (GPUs) used for AI computing, investors have been betting that AMD will score market share wins in the GPU space and take advantage of huge opportunities as the central processing units (CPUs) become increasingly integrated in the broader artificial intelligence compute stack. CPUs are a category that AMD currently leads Nvidia in, and growing demand for CPUs for AI inference applications could be a powerful demand catalyst for the company.

On the other hand, Nvidia is making a big play for the future of the CPU space -- and its moves in the category could help explain why Wood's company is buying the AI hardware leader's stock while also reducing its exposure to AMD. Nvidia's new Vera Rubin server platform combines the company's next-generation GPUs with its next CPU offerings, and the tech pairing could threaten AMD's growth opportunities.

Keith Noonan has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Advanced Micro Devices and Nvidia. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3036. Paul George is still elite and it’s time to talk about it

When Paul George was traded to the Boston Celtics back in July, it became a "summer of discontent." Obviously, it was because they traded George for Jaylen Brown to the rival Philadelphia 76ers, but even the most optimistic Bostonian would tell you there were so many different outcomes when it came to the potential of George's play for the Celtics.

I am happy to say through eight games this season, George is exceeding those expectations and then some, becoming a leader for this team both on and off the court.

In the Celtics win over the Milwaukee Bucks, George finished with a team high 25 points along with 5 assists, 4 steals and 3 rebounds on 8-18 shooting from the field and 5-9 shooting from three. George hit some clutch shots in the fourth quarter after Milwaukee surged back to erase a 22-point deficit, but he was once again the closer Boston needed to end up with a win.

There were questions on how the team would look without Jayson Tatum in this contest, especially after George was out against the Houston Rockets on November 2nd in a 109-93 loss, but I would argue both of these strengthened the argument for how important Paul George really is to this Celtics team.

With George out against Houston, Boston's non-Tatum lineups were abysmal, finishing with only 14 points on 4-23 (17.3%) shooting from the field and 3-14 (21.4%) from three while getting outscored by 16 points. George would have made a huge different. Before the Bucks game, he had a+26.2 net rating and 140.0 offensive rating when Tatum is off the floor, showing that he can keep Boston afloat when Jayson Tatum rests.

Not only did Paul George hit the clutch shots that were needed, he also played 35 minutes, the 2nd most he's played all season so far. George played the entire first and fourth quarters and when asked about his rotation, head coach Joe Mazzulla said, "…first half, he kind of had a good groove going, so I wanted to keep him in there. Second half I trust him for those 12 minutes straight in the 4th quarter. So managing the 3rd quarter and then putting him in to start the 4th, I knew he'd be in position to deliver for us, and so just switched the sub pattern there."

Later in the press conference, I asked Mazzulla his thoughts on how important George's impact on the identity of this team is. "Really, extremely, even beyond basketball," Mazzulla said. "Defensively, he's been elite since he stepped on the court. Offensively, it's been a fun journey with him, just growing through it and learning the system and how to play and being unpredictable and looking at different things."

Derrick White, who also had a solid game finishing with 24 points and 7 assists on 7-18 shooting, was also asked about Paul George's impact beyond basketball. "He cares about the person next to you." White said. "He's someone you can hang out with, just have a good time with him. Obviously, on the court he does a lot offensively and defensively for us. He's got a really good fantasy football team, too."

Paul George has engrained himself into the Celtics culture and its really cool to see him embrace Boston so much. We have also seen George's relationship with Jayson Tatum grow throughout the season. Wheather its publicly voicing his support for Tatum in postgame press conferences or showing emotion on the court after hitting a dagger, George has been a great partner in crime.

When asked about his approach without Tatum for the first time this season, George said, "try to be a little more aggressive, without trying to do too much or take myself out of the offense. I thought to try to let the game still come to me, but still you know, a little more aggressive, more so to make sure the ball moved, and just be in attack mode."

Paul George is averaging 21.3 points, 5.6 rebounds, 5.0 assists, and 2.6 steals on 46% shooting from the field and 41.4% from three which is a completely different stat-line than last season. Through his first 7 games with the 76ers last season, George averaged 14.4 points, 4.9 rebounds, 3.1 assists and 1.7 steals on 42.2% shooting from the field and 35% from three. Obviously, this was in a different role where George was the third or fourth option in Philadelphia, but it does show how productive he can be when healthy and in the right situation.

Maybe it is an overreaction to a 7-game sample size, but I really feel like Paul George can keep up this level of production throughout the rest of this season, barring injury. George is incredibly important to this team and it is important to keep him healthy or Boston could find themselves in a troubling situation quickly. Either way, Paul George has been elite in his role with the Celtics and I look forward to watching his redemption arc this season.

#3033. BlackRock's Rick Rieder sees 'historic' opportunity in high-quality bonds

Investors may be wary of the volatility hitting parts of the bond market right now, but they have an "historic" opportunity to grab attractive yields in high-quality credit, Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

Hypothetically, it's now possible for investors to build a diversified portfolio that yields more than 7% with less than three years of duration and an average credit quality of A-, he said. Duration is a measurement of a bond's price sensitivity to fluctuations in rates, and issues with shorter maturities tend to have lower duration.

"Not only is it historic in that these yields are where they are, but the only time these yields are ever here is when there's some problem, like an economic problem or default problem," Rieder said in an interview about his fourth-quarter outlook, released Wednesday.

That isn't the case now, where the economy remains strong, he said. "So you don't really have to worry about defaults of any significance."

While Rieder didn't specifically identify the credits in the aforementioned portfolio, the iShares Aaa - A Rated Corporate Bond ETF (QLTA) has a 30-day SEC yield of 5.68% and an effective duration of 6.48 years — higher than Rieder's low duration focus.

The iShares Flexible Income Active ETF (BINC), which is managed by Rieder, has a 5.66% 30-day SEC yield and three-year effective duration, but its portfolio extends beyond investment-grade credit.

Rieder sees the best opportunity right now in investment-grade corporate bonds — which he pointed out he hasn't said "in a really long time." Investment grade bonds are rated AAA through BBB- by S&P and Fitch, while Moody's rates them Aaa through Baa3.

That includes hyperscaler bonds, which have flooded the market with issuance this year as they ramp up their AI infrastructure. Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms and Oracle have issued a total of about $228.4 billion in bonds year to date, as of Oct. 20, according to LSEG.

"They're very low leverage. They have tremendous amounts of cash flow coming in," Rieder said of the hyperscalers in general. "You're now getting to buy these entities which are higher quality, paying you a very attractive yield to get it."

Rieder's iShares Flexible Income Active ETF has upped its allocation to investment-grade corporates to 14.3% of its portfolio. In July, that stood at 8.5%.

That said, investors need to be patient and sit tight since rates could still move higher from here, he advised.

"Your starting point is by far your best barometer of what your return is going to be," he noted. "So if you get seven and a quarter, maybe you get eight, maybe you get six, but ... if your holding period is a year or longer, you're going to get that yield."

Caution should also be exercised outside of investment-grade credit, which requires more selectivity and deep research, he warned. That includes AI names.

"There's parts of the data center supply that's not hyperscaler guaranteed or hyperscaler backed," he said. "That we've been more cautious around, and we'll continue to be."

The bond market, particularly high-yield credit, has been rocked as investor concern grows over the massive amount of debt some companies are taking out to fund their artificial intelligence build-out.

Junk-rated CoreWeave has become the poster child, seeing its stock drop, bond yields jump and credit-default spreads widen. Oracle, which is sitting in the lower end of investment grade and is seen as a bellwether on the broader AI market, has also taken some hits.

Rieder is also keeping an eye on the Federal Reserve, which is expected to raise its federal funds rate again in December to combat inflation. The market is currently pricing in a nearly 90% probability that the central bank will hike at that time, according to the CME Group FedWatch tool.

The money manager expects that to happen, although he does not agree with it. Higher rates are hurting parts of the economy, like housing, while not having much of an impact on other areas — such as tech companies' capital expenditures, which have become a big driver of growth, he said.

"They're not borrowing off the overnight funds rate," Rieder noted. "There's a lot of floating rate finance in housing, credit card, auto loan finance, and you're seeing those areas already under pressure."

Instead, the market is and will continue to price the AI supply coming into the market, he added.

Rieder sees a number of possible risks ahead, including rising levels of government debt across the globe. In the United States, the budget deficit has grown to $2 trillion for fiscal 2026.

"The more the central banks raise the rates, the cost of debt to these to already indebted governments is something we've got to be careful about over time," he said.

Bond supply coming from AI companies should also be watched.

"With the amount of supply that's coming — data center, hyperscaler — there's some crowding-out effect that's taking place," he said. "With government rates moving higher, that is something that we just got to keep an eye on."

In the meantime, Rieder would just continue to reap the rewards of high investment-grade yields "and smile a lot," he said.

#3032. Himax Blames 'Abrupt and Significant Correction' in Auto Chip Demand as Stock Crashes Nearly 30%. Is Now the Time to Buy?

Himax sees fourth-quarter revenue falling 22% to 26% after a sudden pullback in auto chips. Is the slump temporary?

Himax (HIMX -26.44%), the fabless chip designer behind display driver chips for TVs, phones and car screens, expects a steep revenue drop in the final quarter of the year, and investors are punishing the stock amid an already bruising day for the market.

On the company's earnings call Thursday, President and CEO Jordan Wu blamed "an abrupt and significant correction" in automotive display driver chip orders for the new guidance. Shares had plunged nearly 28% to $7.55 by about 2:30 p.m. ET on Thursday, a steep decline exacerbated by a broader market sell-off targeting AI-linked names.

Wu told the call that the year began soft in the first quarter. Panel makers then bought heavily in the second and third quarters to keep up with surging orders from Chinese automakers expanding overseas. "Right after China's National Day holidays in early October," he said, the company saw a "sudden and sizable decline in demand among the customers that had purchased aggressively in prior quarters."Wu also said the forecast cut partly reflects Chinese automakers' "earlier, overly aggressive export expectations, along with their growing concerns over inventory levels across distribution channels." He added that panel makers mostly serving customers outside China have held their forecasts steady, and some have nudged fourth-quarter orders higher.The damage is concentrated in automotive display drivers. Wu said automotive timing-controller sales should keep growing from quarter to quarter.That earlier buying spree already showed up in the third quarter. Automotive driver sales rose in solid double digits from the prior quarter, marking the second straight quarter of strong growth, as some panel makers accelerated purchases.

Third-quarter revenue rose 8.5% to $246.8 million from the prior quarter, and gross margin improved to 34.2% from 33.1%. Profit came to $18.6 million, or 10.7 cents per diluted ADS (American depositary share), topping the company's 8 to 10-cent guidance, which Himax attributed to lower-than-expected operating expenses.For the fourth quarter, management expects gross margin flat to slightly up and profit of 4.5 to 6.5 cents per diluted ADS. That range leaves out an expected after-tax gain of about $19 to $20 million from selling its stake in an equity-method investment, a sale Himax expects to close this quarter.

Wu said on the call that automotive chip sales rose a "decent" 16% year over year in the first nine months of 2026, and he still expects about 10% growth for the full year, even with worldwide vehicle production expected to decline. The company also expects automotive timing-controller sales to grow more than 40% this year. Non-driver sales, which include timing controllers, reached $51.0 million in the third quarter, up 11.2% from the prior quarter.The chief executive framed the slump as "abrupt, short-term order adjustments by certain customers, while our market leader position remains firmly intact."Supply is the other theme. Wu said foundries and packaging and testing providers have announced significant price increases for 2027 and that capacity is the company's top priority because automotive customers demand stricter supply assurance. He added that Himax has secured capacity commitments from key suppliers and is working with customers to share rising costs. However, higher foundry prices will remain a cost to watch, with Himax and across tech stocks that rely on outside chipmakers.

It depends on how you read October. If customers simply over-ordered and are now working through inventory, the full-year automotive growth target suggests the business is intact, and that's how management describes it. If end demand for Chinese car exports is weaker than implied by those orders, the correction could run longer than a quarter.With the stock down so steeply in Thursday trading, a lot of bad news may already be priced in, particularly since it appears investors are fearing the worst when it comes to how a newly elected government could interfere with the AI build-out. Even so, a sudden guidance cut does warrant caution. Many long-term investors would likely wait for evidence that the fourth-quarter outlook holds, and anyone interested in these semiconductor stocks might keep a position small.The next checkpoints are whether fourth-quarter profit lands in the guided 4.5 to 6.5 cent range and whether the stake sale closes as expected.

#3027. Why Ecovyst Stock Topped the Market Today

The specialty chemicals company had a beat-and-raise third quarter.

Investors considered specialty chemical manufacturer Ecovyst (ECVT +2.11%) to be a special stock on Wednesday. They traded it up after the company published its third-quarter results that morning, and it closed the day more than 2% higher. That trounced the under 0.4% gain of the bellwether S&P 500 index.

For the period, Ecovyst's sales were just under $309 million, which bettered the year-ago quarter by 51%. However, that total includes sales from Calabrian, a business the company acquired at the end of June.

Getty Images. Image source: Getty Images.

In terms of profitability, net income not under generally accepted accounting principles (non-GAAP, or adjusted) increased by 18% to over $25 million, or $0.23 per share.

With those results, Ecovyst notched a pair of beats on the consensus analyst estimates. The more convincing one was revenue, as those pundits collectively modeled for under $282 million. Their adjusted earnings per share (EPS) estimate was $0.21, meanwhile.

In its earnings release, Ecovyst attributed its organic growth largely to increased export demand, which boosted sales of both regenerated and virgin sulfuric acid.

As for the proximate future, Ecovyst quoted CEO Kurt Bitting as saying, "Given current refining economics, we anticipate high refinery utilization through year-end, and we expect demand across our portfolio to remain healthy for the rest of the year."

In line with that bullish forecast, the company raised its guidance for full-year adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) to a range of $208 million to $212 million. That's well above both the previous estimate ($195 million to $207 million) and the pre-Calabrian 2025 result of $172 million.

It isn't easy to find a thriving company in the specialty chemicals space these days, and it looks as if Ecovyst has hit the sweet spot with its in-demand products. It also seems to be integrating Calabrian smoothly and quickly. With all that, its rosy forecast is fully believable, making it a stock to watch in its sector.

#3026. Open Thread: Tracy McGrady says Kevin Garnett was more impactful than Tim Duncan

On their podcast, Cousins, 2000 NBA Slam Dunk Champion Vince Carter and and 2001 NBA Most Improved Player Tracy McGrady discuss a variety of NBA topics. The cousins (it's not just a clever name for a podcast though it is not a show hosted by Boogie Cousins, as I mistakenly originally believed) discovered their familial bond at a reunion. They played together with the Toronto Raptors a year later. Both had significant NBA careers. Tracy McGrady finished his career with the San Antonio Spurs as part of the 2013 title run.

He recently posited that though Tim Ducan is considered the greatest power forward of all time, he thinks it is a benefit of how Duncan was able to design the Spurs around him. The idea is put forth that Kevin Garnett did more than Duncan, but the titles make Duncan look the better player.

My initial reaction was to defend Duncan and dismiss McGrady as having an axe to grind or something. But after listening, I have to give him some respect. McGrady clearly states that he "look(s) at the game totally different." I cannot begin to imagine the wealth of basketball knowledge, a conversation most assuredly to float above my head and waft ad the words left his mouth.

The repost from David West puts it into perspective.

It was Tim's system. One thing I realized my year with them was that Tim built the damn thing. It was his brainchild. It was his basketball genius that made that shit the monster it was. IYKYK 🤷🏽‍♂️

It opens up the conversation. Could Tim Duncan have become the Tim Duncan of the Spurs if he had been drafted by the Boston Celtics? What about if he had left San Antonio to play in Orlando? If the environment changes, doesn't the payer change in some form or fashion?

If Kevin Garnett had been given the keys to the kingdom of Minnesota? Or been drafted first overall by Golden State (hindsight being 20/20 and all), could he have cultivated an organization than won five championships?

As a Spurs fan, I am fortunate those are just questions. Tim Duncan was drafted by the Spurs, decided to stay after considering Orlando (if Doc Rivers could go back he'd give Duncan his own private jet…hindsight being 20/20 and all), and completed a nineteen year career in San Antonio bringing more than five championships to the city. He brought a culture, and a style, and a temperament that embodies the franchise's personality.

And now we Victor Wembanyama. The most talented player of his generation, a genuine gentleman, a scholar, and a player who carries some of the great qualities that have already been associated with the Silver & Black.

Honestly, McGrady's take doesn't bother me at all. I'll take what we've got.

#3025. Hudson Pacific (HPP) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Occupancy rose a fifth straight quarter as debt fell and studios held steady.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Hudson Pacific Properties, Inc. (HPP -17.05%) reported a period of active leasing and balance sheet management as it navigated shifting demand in West Coast office and studio markets. Management reported that the company prioritized debt reduction through strategic asset dispositions and the opportunistic repurchase of senior notes while maintaining a focus on high-quality assets in technology-driven submarkets. The company stated that leasing activity was primarily concentrated in the San Francisco Bay Area, supported by the ongoing recovery in the technology and venture capital sectors. Furthermore, management indicated that the studio segment showed signs of stabilization with improved production spending in New York and potential legislative catalysts in California.

Operator: Hello, everyone. Thank you for joining us, and welcome to the Hudson Pacific Properties third quarter 26 earnings call. #3024. Dalton Knecht makes most of first Knicks chance in blowout

A 30-point shellacking paved the way for Dalton Knecht to make his Knicks debut.

With Josh Hart missing Wednesday's game due to right ankle soreness, Knecht was called up from the Westchester Knicks and recorded 10 points and seven rebounds in 16 minutes in the 135-105 win over the Bulls.

A second-quarter putback dunk and third-quarter chase-down block drew loud reactions from the MSG crowd.

New York Knicks Dalton Knecht reacts after scoring in the fourth quarter against the Chicago Bulls at Madison Square Garden on Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026. Charles Wenzelberg / New York Post

"He's a scorer. He's not just a shooter. A lot of people think he's a shooter because he's white," Brown joked. "I said it for you, I hope I don't get in trouble. He can go get it."

Knecht had been playing in the G-League since the Knicks signed him to a two-way deal last month after the Lakers released him.

The former Tennessee star fell out of favor with Los Angeles after being selected with the No. 17 pick in the 2024 NBA Draft.

After tallying 9.1 points across 19.2 minutes per game during 78 games in his rookie campaign, those numbers dripped to 4.2 points spanning 10.2 minutes per contest in his sophomore season.

He did not adjust well after losing playing time following the acquisition of Luka Doncic during the 2024-25 season, and a failed trade to the Hornets only complicated matters.

Knecht ultimately averaged 7.1 points and shot 36.8 percent from deep with the Lakers.

New York Knicks guard Dalton Knecht drives down the court as Chicago Bulls forward Matas Buzelis defends on Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026, in New York. Charles Wenzelberg / New York Post

"The team changed. The needs changed, the fit changed," Lakers coach JJ Redick said before the team moved on. "I think he got better as a player over the last two years. I think each guy has, particularly last year, each guy got plenty of opportunities with the amount of injuries we had.So, I just think coming into this year, we added a lot of wings, and he's in a tough spot right now."

In his Knicks' debut Wednesday, Knecht hit four of his six shots and connected on two of four attempts from 3-point range.
